Part 4 Empirical Questions, Conclusion Rules, and Conditional Formal Propositions ​

There are four kinds of empirical question: whether a candidate grouping brings a conditional gain, called grouping gain for short; whether a specified channel has an identifiable effect on a target transition, called channel effect for short; whether history provides conditional increments beyond the current representation, called historical increment for short; and under which tasks, dynamics, and interventions a specified representation has closure, called scale closure for short. These four kinds of question are not themselves laws governing all objects. Each formal test states two things together: the factual assertion awaiting testing, and the rules for judging the evidence. The two must not be conflated in writing: whether an effect exists is determined by the world and the conditions at issue; whether the available evidence suffices to support that assertion is determined by the research design and results.

This Part separates empirical testing, the use of results, and formal proof. Formal tests answer factual questions; conclusion rules state which limited conclusions can be drawn when the existing grounds are put together; conditional formal propositions state relations that necessarily hold under explicitly stated mathematical conditions. Recording the same result again does not add independent evidence; nor does the number of empirical questions passed, or of conclusion rules met, measure the usefulness of the entire framework.

04Note

Understanding this section

Part 4 Empirical Questions, Conclusion Rules, and Conditional Formal Propositions

This part separates three things: questions about the world, evidential support for answers, and proofs within given models.

The four empirical questions can first be distinguished in ordinary language: whether grouping objects in a particular way is more useful than an appropriate comparison; whether a specified channel has an identifiable effect on a target change; whether historical information adds to the answer beyond the specified current representation; and for which tasks, changes, and interventions the current representation remains sufficient. These are four distinct directions of testing, not facts simultaneously answered by ‘everything has structure’. [T-intro；T-G]

A single formal test must state two kinds of content. The factual assertion under test states what difference occurs for which objects, conditions, and windows; evidential rules specify which study designs and outcomes count as support. An effect's existence does not depend on researchers stating these contents, but whether support may reasonably be claimed is constrained by materials and methods. ‘Not yet tested’ must not become ‘absent in reality’, nor ‘design completed’ become ‘effect established’. [T-intro；T-roles]

Empirical questions, conclusion rules, and conditional formal propositions have different responsibilities. Formal tests carry out specific empirical testing; conclusion rules restrict permissible outputs from existing results plus necessary conditions; conditional formal propositions provide provable relations in explicit mathematical models. A formal proof may expose an invalid unconditional inference without automatically validating real-world variable mappings; the result of a test does not automatically satisfy every additional condition of the relevant conclusion rule, still less generate norms or permission to execute. [T-intro；T-roles；T-CF]

Recording the same result repeatedly does not create independent evidence. Writing ten reports from the same data, or having multiple models reprocess the same input, may add analytical perspectives but is not ten new independent observations. If these analyses produce new inferential results, retain them according to their arguments; state where the contribution comes from instead of using quantity to impersonate stronger support. [T-intro；T-material]

The introduction also separates case support from whether the framework as a whole is worth using. Even if several specific tests pass, this does not automatically establish that the framework is more accurate, easier to understand, or less costly than adequate specialist methods. That requires separately specified tasks, comparators, protections, and evaluation. Readers should ask separately ‘What evidence supports this factual claim?’, ‘How do these grounds permit its use?’, and ‘What are the premises of this formal conclusion?’, rather than accumulating passes into an overall score. [T-intro; T-eval]

The strongest objection is whether separating responsibilities fragments knowledge that was connected. Separation makes clear what the next step still needs when work is connected; it does not require researchers to do only one kind of work. A study can include model proofs, real-world measurements, and action recommendations, but each claim must still hold on its own grounds and within its own boundaries. [T-roles]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Premise: empirical truth, current evidentiary support, and logical validity within a model have different conditions.

  2. 2

    Inferential connection: putting them into a single pass flag conflates untested, unidentified, proved, and other distinct states.

  3. 3

    Conclusion: G asks about specific facts, C manages bounded use and combination, and F checks proofs within models; connecting them requires adding each one’s conditions.

  4. 4

    Evidentiary responsibility: repeated material does not add independent observations, and the number of passing tests is not the framework’s net utility.

Distinctions to keep clear

An effect exists

A fact about reality under specified conditions.

≠

Evidentiary support

A judgment about whether the available design and results are sufficient.

Formal test

A specific empirical question and its test.

≠

F proposition

A proof under explicit mathematical conditions.

More reports

May be different analyses of the same material.

≠

More independent observations

Require genuinely additional material with its dependencies explained.

Teaching construction: three responsibilities for one conclusionTeaching scenario

AssumptionsEntirely a teaching scenario illustrating argumentative roles, not an audit of an actual system.

Suppose a fictional system uses a total item count to answer ‘How many items are there altogether?’ At the formal level, one can prove that an exact sum suffices for this question; at the empirical level, the completeness and accuracy of each record still need checking; allocating staff based on the total additionally requires distribution, capacity, normative objectives, and authorization. These three tasks can connect, but none completes another’s work.

BoundaryIt cannot establish that any real records are accurate or that staffing allocations have been authorized.

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleConstructed conditional counterexample: copying one observation into three test numbers and calling them three independent replications; numbering has not changed the data source.

What it limitsLimits conflation of roles, selection after results, and substitution of numbering or states for evidence.

Teaching counterexampleConstructed conditional counterexample: proving that an aggregate representation is sufficient for one target, then declaring that actual measurements are accurate and that it is also sufficient for other targets; both the formal premises and the task scope have been expanded.

What it limitsLimits conflation of roles, selection after results, and substitution of numbering or states for evidence.

What does not follow

  • Constructed conditional counterexample: copying one observation into three test numbers and calling them three independent replications; numbering has not changed the data source.
  • Constructed conditional counterexample: proving that an aggregate representation is sufficient for one target, then declaring that actual measurements are accurate and that it is also sufficient for other targets; both the formal premises and the task scope have been expanded.
  • Failure to obtain the framework’s formal qualification does not automatically cancel existing knowledge in external domains; case support likewise does not automatically establish the framework’s superiority to alternatives.

Scope and open questions

The introduction provides textual roles and argumentative navigation; teaching constructions explain the three responsibilities without attaching unrelated empirical stories or treating navigation itself as empirical support.

  • Answers for the particular tests in this part must be obtained in the corresponding objects and studies; the introduction does not preset their results.

4.1Pre-Registration and Outcome Records for Formal Tests ​

In briefFix the question and decision rules first, then append results truthfully; failing the positive criterion does not automatically pass the null-conclusion criteria.

This section provides a standard recording procedure for confirmatory testing. Under this procedure, each formal test has two sections. The first is the pre-registration: before the results are seen, the test's target, criteria, and rules are set down. The second is the outcome record: it is appended after the test has been carried out, and what was set down earlier is kept unchanged. What has not yet been done is explicitly marked “not yet evaluated”; times, observed values, or materials must not be fabricated. The two sections together determine what outcomes count as support, what outcomes count as refutation, and where conclusions may be extrapolated.

This procedure takes a single primary criterion as its default design, to prevent choosing favorable results after they appear; it is not the only reasonable form for every study. Multiple outcomes, multiple models, joint criteria, confirmatory work following exploratory work, and sequential studies can each have valid designs, but the primary target or joint rule, the selection procedure, the stopping rule, and the applicable handling of multiple comparisons must be stated in advance. The subtypes of the four empirical questions and of the human empirical hypotheses below are all written with a single primary criterion and belong to this standard procedure. Materials outside the procedure are still evaluated according to their actual research designs; they must not be judged to have no knowledge value merely because their records take a different form. Nor are the four empirical questions claimed to exhaust all scientific questions or to be logically independent axioms.

The pre-registration must fix the following seven aspects before the results are seen.

Identity and finalization of the test. State which of the four empirical questions this test falls under and which specific test it is, so that the specific test is kept distinct from the abstract type of question. Once finalized, the pre-registration is not changed; finalization precedes access to the results, and this can be checked. Only in this way can it be shown that the rules were written before the evidence.

Candidate object. Point to the candidate object tested and its definition (§3.1), preventing a name from being treated as grounds for a grouping gain or for object facts.

Scale and target. Fix the scale profile, the time window, the identity criterion, and the variables to be explained.

Subtype and success criterion. Before evidence appears, select only one subtype, then only one success criterion from those admissible for that subtype; and state the candidate proposition, the null model, the controls, and the model classes used. The null model is a comparison model without the claimed factor.

Sampling and extrapolation. State the sampling unit and the extrapolation unit separately: where the data come from and how far the conclusion may be generalized are two different things.

Decision rules. State the evaluation metric, the positive threshold, the decision rule, and the null-conclusion rule. The decision rule governs how to determine whether the positive criterion has passed; the null-conclusion rule governs what conditions must be met before the null model can be supported; the positive criterion and the null-conclusion criterion are written separately. The primary target or aggregation rule, the rule for model selection or ensembling, the handling of multiple comparisons, the equivalence or sufficiency test, the requirements for statistical power or sensitivity, and the tolerance are all fixed in advance.

Evidence mode and failure conditions. Explain whether this test is exploratory, confirmatory, a replication, or a falsification, and what the ceiling on conclusions is for each; and state what result counts as falsification and under what circumstances the test is suspended.

As the test proceeds, the status of the pre-registration and any deviations from it also need to be stated. The pre-registration has four possible statuses: draft; finalized before evidence; completed as finalized; deviated after evidence. Each deviation is recorded item by item: what deviated, when, why, and with what impact. Where there is no deviation, this too needs to be stated explicitly as “none.”

The outcome record needs to cover two aspects.

Results. The results are obtained after the pre-registration has been finalized. Record only the results observed under the primary target and rules fixed in advance; state separately whether the positive criterion passed and whether the three null-conclusion criteria (equivalence or sufficiency, statistical power or sensitivity, and tolerance) passed; finally, assign the result to one of the four outcome statuses.

Evidence and analysis materials. Point to the external materials relied on, and to the data, code, models, or logs fixed after the cutoff; all of these need to correspond to real material. The framework's internal concept codes, names that only look like a test in format, and self-claimed conclusions cannot replace a specific test.

Under the single-primary-criterion procedure, there is only one selection rule: before results appear, one subtype and one success criterion are selected. A joint or multi-outcome design must state its overall criterion separately; several individual items that did not pass must not be reassembled after the fact into a success. The evaluation metric, the positive threshold, the null model, the decision rule, the null-conclusion rule, and the falsification conditions are all fixed in advance around the selected criterion. If the results are unfavorable, several subtypes or success criteria must not be combined so as to take whichever is favorable, nor may the target, model, metric, or threshold be changed to rescue the kind of empirical question being tested.

The decision rule also closes off the room for choice that multiple targets and models leave open. If there is more than one target variable, a single primary target or an aggregation rule must be fixed before results; if there is more than one model class, a rule for model selection or ensembling must be fixed; if there are multiple comparisons, a correction rule must be fixed. Without these rules, a test can have only one primary target and one primary model. The null-conclusion rule states separately what equivalence or sufficiency test must be passed, what statistical power or sensitivity must be reached, and within what tolerance, before the null model can be supported. After the test has been carried out, the outcome of the positive criterion must be recorded item by item: the threshold, the observed value, whether it passed, and the analysis materials relied on; whether each of the three null-conclusion criteria passed is also recorded separately. Failure to pass the positive criterion is not the same as the null model having obtained support.

The outcome of a formal test is assigned to one of four statuses. Supported: an eligible test has passed the positive criterion. Not supported or unresolved: the positive criterion has not passed, and the null-conclusion criteria were not fixed in advance or have not all passed. Null conclusion supported: equivalence or sufficiency, statistical power or sensitivity, and tolerance have all passed. Not yet evaluated: this means only that the test has not yet been carried out. These four statuses are only summaries and do not replace the specific conclusion: which criteria fixed in advance passed, which were countered by evidence, and which remain unresolved only because of insufficient precision or materials must be stated separately; clear counterevidence and an inability to judge must not be conflated as one kind of evidence. The outcome record must be linked to the evidence and analysis materials relied on, and it must be possible to find out when the results were obtained, which finalized version of the pre-registration they rest on, and what deviations occurred. Neither an abstract type of question nor a correctly formatted test number can produce support on its own.

Whether a test can be used to support a conclusion rule also depends on whether it has support eligibility. Positive support comes only from a confirmatory test or a replication test, and all of the following need to hold together: before the results were seen, the pre-registration was already in the status “finalized before evidence,” and the content and time of finalization can be checked; the status at the end of the test is “completed as finalized”; the positive criterion is recorded as passed; the outcome status has been stated; and the external evidence and analysis materials correspond to real material. A falsification test may support only a pre-registered falsification judgment or null-model judgment; it must not be used in reverse to rescue a positive empirical claim. An exploratory test, a test whose pre-registration is still a “draft,” a test with the status “deviated after evidence,” or a test with undisclosed deviations can only be used to propose candidates, record deviations, or remain unresolved; where a branch of a conclusion rule requires formal-test eligibility, they must not serve as such support. The framework's internal definitions, concept labels, and the framework's descriptions of itself do not constitute empirical support for a test.

The scale invariants shared by the four empirical questions include the subtype selected in advance, the success criterion, the decision rule, and the null-conclusion rule; these must be retained during scale transfer and must not be replaced. An appeal against a test may challenge the candidate object, subtype, success criterion, null model, primary target or aggregation, model selection or ensembling, multiple comparisons, controls, positive threshold, null-conclusion rule, data split, extrapolation unit, which version of the pre-registration the test rests on, the pre-registration status, the deviation record, and the falsification conditions. If any of these is shown to have been changed after the results appeared, support eligibility must be reduced; a version produced after the fact must not overwrite a record already finalized.

4.1Note

Understanding this section

4.1 Pre-Registration and Outcome Records for Formal Tests

Fix the question and decision rules first, then append results truthfully; failing the positive criterion does not automatically pass the null-conclusion criteria.

Pre-registration and results should be separate sections. Pre-registration fixes the question and rules before accessing the relevant results; results are appended only after execution, preserving the original version. Adding a backdated table after obtaining results, or deleting the original plan, cannot establish prior constraint. What has not yet been carried out is recorded as “not yet evaluated”; expected numbers cannot masquerade as observed values. Nor does ‘guide completed’ in this deliverable mean that any actual formal test was implemented for this question. [T-41]

The single primary criterion prevents selecting the most favorable outcome after seeing results. The standard procedure first selects a subtype and then a success criterion from its allowed list; it does not run all routes and relabel the best-looking one the ‘original primary objective’. Joint-outcome, multiple-model, sequential, or exploration-followed-by-confirmation studies can nevertheless have valid designs, provided the overall rules, selection and stopping procedures, and applicable multiple-comparison handling are declared in advance. Research outside this procedure is assessed on its own design and does not lose knowledge value because its record format differs. [T-41]

The first aspect of the pre-registration, ‘identity and finalization of the test’: state which specific test this is and which of the four empirical questions it falls under; once finalized, the pre-registration is not changed, finalization precedes access to the results, and this can be checked. An attractively formatted number is only a name; a finalized version that is not changed afterward, and evidence that it predates access to results, are needed to support the procedural fact that ‘the rules were genuinely set first’. [T-41]

The second aspect, ‘candidate object’: point to the candidate object tested and its definition (§3.1), that is, its declared boundaries, variables, relations, interfaces, time window, scale, and identity. This identifies which object is being tested and prevents a different object with the same name from passing as a replication. But the definition of a structural object only fixes a candidate; a name, documents, or complete elements do not automatically supply grouping gain. [T-41; T-D0]

The third aspect, ‘scale and targets’: the scale profile must state all nine axes individually. A genuinely inapplicable axis is recorded as “not applicable” with a reason, and insufficient material as “unknown”; unexplained axes cannot be deleted. The time window bounds the time range, the identity criterion states when the object still counts as the same, and the variables to be explained identify the outcomes in question. What changes with ‘a new team’, ‘next quarter’, or ‘less misclassification’ must be explicit; one cannot retain only better-performing periods or members after seeing results and reuse the original conclusion. [T-41; T-SP]

The fourth aspect, ‘subtype and success criterion’: the selected subtype and success criterion fix the test type and single primary criterion; the candidate proposition must be made concrete; the null model must fit it; controls specify what must be controlled; model classes list the permitted model families. The null model is not a deliberately weak opponent, nor are more controls automatically better. Both depend on the target and identification design; one cannot control away the very effect claimed and then silently change the question. [T-41; T-baseline]

The fifth aspect, ‘sampling and extrapolation’: the sampling unit states whether material is obtained by person, institution, time block, or another unit; the extrapolation unit states where conclusions may extend. Many repeated measurements of one institution are not many independent institutions; generalization to new institutions or times requires matching splits and evaluation grounds. More sample records do not automatically enlarge the domain of applicability. [T-41]

The sixth aspect, ‘decision rules’, separates the evaluation metric, positive threshold, decision rule, and null-conclusion rule. The metric says how to calculate; the threshold sets the standard; the positive rule says how all design conditions combine; the null-conclusion rule separately specifies support for the null model. Multiple targets require a predetermined single primary target or aggregation; multiple models require predetermined selection or ensembling; multiple comparisons require predetermined correction. Without these rules, this standard test permits only one primary target and one primary model. [T-41]

A null conclusion requires passing three criteria: a qualified equivalence or sufficiency test, proportionate power or sensitivity, and predetermined tolerances. It asks ‘What grounds support the null model at the specified precision, domain, and tolerance?’, not simply ‘Is it significant?’ A wide interval allowing both important positive and negative effects does not establish ineffectiveness because it contains zero. Likewise, failure of a positive test may be strong counterevidence or merely insufficient precision; this must be reported specifically rather than flattened into one outcome status. [T-41]

The seventh aspect, ‘evidence mode and failure conditions’: the evidence mode declares exploration, confirmation, replication, or falsification; the falsification conditions state which result would overturn the predetermined claim; the suspension conditions specify when the corresponding execution must stop or pause. Exploration may discover valuable candidates, and a falsification design may strongly test the original assertion; neither can be renamed prior confirmation after favorable results appear, nor can contrary material already obtained be erased. [T-41]

As the test proceeds, the status of the pre-registration and deviations from it must also be stated: the deviation record preserves each deviation’s timing, reason, and effect, stating “none” when there are no deviations; the pre-registration status distinguishes draft, finalized before evidence, completed as finalized, and deviated after evidence. Sound new knowledge may require design changes; the proper response is to preserve the old version transparently and explain the new version and the status of its conclusions, rather than pretending it was always so. Recording deviations makes interpretation more honest but does not automatically restore support eligibility obtained under the originally set rules. [T-41]

The first aspect of the outcome record, ‘results’: results must be obtained after the pre-registration has been finalized; only actual results for the predetermined primary target are recorded; the outcome of the positive criterion records thresholds, observed values, whether it passed, and analysis materials item by item; the three null-conclusion criteria are recorded separately; finally, the result is assigned to one of the four outcome statuses. The second aspect, ‘evidence and analysis materials’, connects judgments to sources that correspond to real material, and to the data, code, models, or logs fixed after the cutoff; internal concept codes, names that only look like a test in format, or self-claimed ‘passes’ cannot replace these materials. [T-41]

The four outcome statuses are not four simple truth values. “Supported” means an eligible test has passed the positive criterion; “null conclusion supported” means all three null-conclusion criteria have passed; “not supported or unresolved” accommodates lack of support or a judgment not yet reached, but explicit counterevidence, insufficient precision, and material gaps must be described separately; “not yet evaluated” only means the test has not yet been carried out. Summary statuses aid location and do not permit deletion of contrary evidence. If the null-conclusion criteria were not fixed in advance or did not all pass, failure to pass the positive criterion cannot be converted into “null conclusion supported.” [T-41]

Whether a test can further support a branch of a conclusion rule that requires formal qualification also depends on whether it has support eligibility. Positive support comes from a confirmatory or replication test: the content and time of finalization can be checked, the status before results is “finalized before evidence,” the status at the end is “completed as finalized,” the positive criterion has passed, and the actual evidence and analysis materials correspond to real material. A falsification test can support only the predetermined falsification or null-model judgment and cannot be used in reverse to rescue a positive empirical claim; exploration, drafts, deviations after results, and undisclosed deviations retain candidates or unresolved claims according to their actual status, without furnishing positive eligibility for that branch of the conclusion rule. [T-41]

This does not define the existence of knowledge by formal procedural eligibility. External research may have valid multiple-outcome, sequential, or other designs and should be assessed by its actual evidence; this question cannot retroactively fill in a fictitious formal-test record for a published paper and declare that it meets every item in the book. Use as domain evidence requires explaining its design and limits; a claim to support eligibility in this standard procedure requires separately checking every applicable condition. [T-41; T-roles]

Scale transfer must preserve the preselected subtype, success criterion, and positive/null rules. Moving to another region, level, or window cannot incidentally lower thresholds while retaining a claim that the original test holds; a genuine task change requires a separate traceable version. Appeals may challenge candidate objects, subtype, criterion, the null model, primary target or aggregation, model selection or ensembling, multiple comparisons, controls, positive/null thresholds and rules, data splits, extrapolation units, versions, pre-registration status, deviations, and falsification conditions. A verified change after results reduces the corresponding support eligibility without overwriting the original record. [T-41]

The actual historical example is the public abstract of Camerer et al.’s 2018 replication study: the authors report 21 social-science experiments with analysis plans reviewed by original authors and registered before replication, separately reporting significant same-direction results and other replication measures. This illustrates advance plans and subsequent results as two layers of material. This guide checks only the public abstract, without auditing the individual registration times, code, or complete designs, and therefore cannot award qualification for branches of the book’s conclusion rules on that basis. [R-replication]

The strongest objection is whether pre-registration prohibits discovering new phenomena. It does not. Exploration, revisions, and new candidates can be retained; the key is to let readers know which questions were specified before results and which arose afterward, then confirm them with appropriate new material. Another objection is that checklists add work; adopting this procedure for a declared use therefore requires separately examining procedural costs and errors actually reduced. A filled-out table does not establish the framework’s effectiveness. [T-41; T-eval]

The result of a grouping-gain test in a formal-test record means ‘support for grouping gain’, not approval of an object’s existence. The object's elements, grouping rules, and the null model are fixed separately: membership and relational facts rest on their existing material, and the test asks only what adopting this grouping adds for the preselected outcome.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    First determine the factual assertion to test, object, scale, targets, and generalization domain, then set down in advance the rules specifying what results count as support or refutation.

  2. 2

    Before accessing relevant results, lock the subtype/primary criterion and rules for multiple targets, multiple models, multiple comparisons, and stopping, reducing room for favorable selection afterward.

  3. 3

    After execution, append only actual results and deviations, separately recording the positive criterion and the three null-conclusion criteria; a test that has not been carried out cannot have observed results entered.

  4. 4

    Summarize with the four outcome statuses while separately preserving specific conclusions about counterevidence, insufficient precision, or missing material; failure to pass the positive criterion does not imply support for the null model.

  5. 5

    To support a branch of a conclusion rule requiring formal qualification, further check the evidence mode, finalization/completion status, whether the criteria passed, and external material that corresponds to real material; having every item complete is not empirical proof.

  6. 6

    Scale transfer and appeal preserve original rules and versions; changes after results reduce corresponding support eligibility, and new versions must not overwrite old records.

  7. 7

    Valid research outside the procedure is assessed by its own design; pre-registration guarantees neither affirmative results nor the overall utility of the framework.

Distinctions to keep clear

Abstract question type

General requirements organizing a family of questions.

≠

Specific test

Explicit object, targets, design, results, and boundaries.

Whether a fact exists

The actual state of the world under the conditions asked about.

≠

Eligibility for formal support

How this standard procedure permits use of results under its evidence and version rules.

Positive gate not passed

May reflect counterevidence, insufficient material, or insufficient precision.

≠

Support for a null conclusion

Additionally requires the three predetermined criteria of equivalence/sufficiency, sensitivity, and tolerance.

Improvement after exploration

Retains candidates and sets up a separate new version or a subsequent confirmation task.

≠

Post hoc rescue

Disguising selection after results as the rule originally set.

Sampling unit

The unit in which material is obtained.

≠

Extrapolation unit

The objects or windows to which the conclusion may extend.

Recording deviations

Discloses what changed and its effects.

≠

Restoring eligibility

A record alone does not automatically regain the original confirmatory eligibility.

Logical teaching construction: the positive criterion and the null-conclusion criteria address different questionsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsIntervals, units, thresholds, and whether the criteria pass are artificial logical inputs. Each example assumes the relevant requirements for mode, finalization, and material eligibility hold. No statistical estimation or power calculation was performed; the written intervals are not claimed to come inherently from qualified statistical procedures.

A purely rule-based demonstration: the predetermined positive criterion requires the lower endpoint of uncertainty interval I to exceed 3 units. The separate null-conclusion rule requires I to lie entirely within [−1,1], with the predetermined equivalence/sufficiency procedure and sensitivity requirement also passed as stipulated. Case A has I=[4,6] and passes the positive criterion if other eligibility conditions hold. Case B has I=[−0.4,0.4] and passes the two other null-conclusion criteria, so the null conclusion passes. Case C has I=[−2,4], satisfying neither the positive criterion nor the tolerance range; record it as “not supported or unresolved” with the specific information. If the test was never carried out at all, record “not yet evaluated” and do not invent I.

BoundaryDemonstrates conditional relations rather than universal statistical thresholds. Actual testing must choose methods proportionate to the error model, sample, and target, and separately check all three criteria.

Mathematical teaching construction: choosing after inspection differs from combining beforehandTeaching scenario

Assumptions5, 0.05, and mutual independence are mathematical assumptions; all null hypotheses are stipulated true. No actual research data are used.

In a teaching model, suppose 5 mutually independent tests each have a false-pass probability of 0.05 when their null hypotheses are true. If any passing test is selected afterward as overall success, the probability of at least one false pass is 1−(1−0.05)^5=1−0.95^5=0.2262190625, approximately 22.62%, not 5%. This demonstrates the need to define an overall rule and applicable corrections beforehand. The example does not impose independence on actual correlated indicators.

BoundaryThe value generally differs for correlated tests. This example also cannot prescribe any single correction method as the sole method for all research.

Historical study: report predetermined plans and results separatelyDocumented case

The public abstract of Camerer and colleagues' 2018 study reports replications of 21 social-science experiments, with analysis plans reviewed by the original authors and registered before replication. Under the reported criterion of a significant effect in the same direction, 13 met the requirement. The abstract also reports other replication measures. This shows why prior arrangements and later results cannot be merged into a single “registered therefore successful” marker. [R-replication]

SourceCamerer et al. (2018), Nature Human Behaviour2:637—644Public Abstract: first sentence listing 21 studies; second sentence on plan review and pre-registration; subsequent sentences on 13 significant same-direction results and complementary measures. Online 2018-08-27.Reading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsOnly the public abstract was read and cited. The subscription-only full text was not accessed, and the registration times, code, or raw data of the 21 studies were not audited. 13/21 is not a universal proportion for all social-science research, nor does it confer eligibility as a formal test or under a conclusion rule in this book.

Read the case and sources

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleAuthor-constructed conditional counterexample: measure 10 indicators, report only the best 1, and say it was always the primary target. The data may be real, but the claim of prior selection is unestablished.

What it limitsLimits conflation of roles, selection after results, and substitution of numbering or states for evidence.

Teaching counterexampleAuthor-constructed conditional counterexample: a wide result interval fails the positive criterion, so one writes “the null model is established.” Without the three null-conclusion criteria, the specific unresolved status must remain.

What it limitsLimits conflation of roles, selection after results, and substitution of numbering or states for evidence.

Teaching counterexampleAuthor-constructed conditional counterexample: one hundred daily records from the same institution are written up as one hundred independent institutions, conflating extrapolation scope and sampling unit.

What it limitsLimits conflation of roles, selection after results, and substitution of numbering or states for evidence.

Teaching counterexampleAuthor-constructed conditional counterexample: a favorable direction in falsification mode prompts a switch to confirmatory mode and support for a positive branch of a conclusion rule. Mode and original target have been changed afterward.

What it limitsLimits conflation of roles, selection after results, and substitution of numbering or states for evidence.

What does not follow

  • Exclusion in the original: multiple individually failed items cannot be assembled after the result into “joint success.” A joint design must register its overall rule beforehand.
  • Author-constructed conditional counterexample: measure 10 indicators, report only the best 1, and say it was always the primary target. The data may be real, but the claim of prior selection is unestablished.
  • Author-constructed conditional counterexample: a wide result interval fails the positive criterion, so one writes “the null model is established.” Without the three null-conclusion criteria, the specific unresolved status must remain.
  • Author-constructed conditional counterexample: one hundred daily records from the same institution are written up as one hundred independent institutions, conflating extrapolation scope and sampling unit.
  • Author-constructed conditional counterexample: a favorable direction in falsification mode prompts a switch to confirmatory mode and support for a positive branch of a conclusion rule. Mode and original target have been changed afterward.
  • Research outside this procedure may have epistemic value. This section does not claim its single-primary-criterion format is the only reasonable form for all scientific research.
  • A public abstract supports only the design and results it reports; it cannot replace auditing individual pre-registration records, raw data, and analysis materials.

Scope and open questions

This unit concerns methodological judgment. Actual sources support only the listed facts; the diagram and teaching construction each retain their own status.

  • Whether an actual formal test meets the conditions of finalization before evidence, statistical design, and materials that correspond to real material requires checking that test's original plan and results. This lesson conducted no such real study.
  • The distinction between lack of support and explicit counterevidence within the four states requires the specific design. A conceptual diagram cannot adjudicate it for the reader.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    Before the test has been carried out, may the expected mean be entered as the observed result for the primary target?

  2. 2

    If the primary criterion fails, may one directly write “null conclusion supported”?

  3. 3

    Is a strong relationship discovered in exploration worthless?

  4. 4

    Can one hundred records from the same institution directly support extrapolation to new institutions?

  5. 5

    Is a test number with a formal version enough to support a conclusion rule?

  6. 6

    Why can I=[−2,4] not support the null model under the teaching rules?

  7. 7

    What is the probability of a false pass if success is selected afterward from 5 independent null-hypothesis tests?

  8. 8

    Should an existing joint study with multiple targets be rejected because it does not use this way of recording?

Before the test has been carried out, may the expected mean be entered as the observed result for the primary target?

No. Keep it as “not yet evaluated”; simulated or assumed values must retain their separate status.

Basis: Chinese source lines 569 and 625.

If the primary criterion fails, may one directly write “null conclusion supported”?

No. The three criteria of equivalence/sufficiency, power/sensitivity, and tolerance must be fixed in advance and all passed. Otherwise retain “not supported or unresolved” and explain why.

Basis: Chinese source lines 623–625.

Is a strong relationship discovered in exploration worthless?

No. It can become a candidate for subsequent confirmation, but selection after seeing results cannot be presented as the original confirmatory test.

Basis: Chinese source lines 571 and 627.

Can one hundred records from the same institution directly support extrapolation to new institutions?

Not from the count alone. Sampling units, dependencies, and extrapolation evaluation must each be checked.

Basis: Chinese source line 607.

Is a test number with a formal version enough to support a conclusion rule?

No. Applicable conditions also include the evidence mode, finalization before evidence, completion as finalized, a passed positive criterion, and evidence and analysis materials that correspond to real material.

Basis: Chinese source line 627.

Why can I=[−2,4] not support the null model under the teaching rules?

It does not lie entirely inside the predetermined [−1,1] tolerance range. Failure of the positive-support check cannot compensate for that failure.

Basis: Teaching construction and Chinese source line 623.

What is the probability of a false pass if success is selected afterward from 5 independent null-hypothesis tests?

1−0.95^5≈22.62%; this value depends on the artificial assumptions of independence and 0.05 for each test.

Basis: This section's mathematical derivation.

Should an existing joint study with multiple targets be rejected because it does not use this way of recording?

No. Evaluate its actual joint rules, selection/stopping design, and evidence. A different format does not cancel knowledge.

Basis: Chinese source line 595.

4.2Testing Human Empirical Hypotheses ​

In briefDiscussion of humans may concern behavioral differences or persistent traces, or may only classify responsibility. This section first distinguishes proposition roles, then specifies falsifiable tests for three families of empirical questions.

Three of the six human-domain clauses (§7.1) are empirical hypotheses: “Meaning and Coordination,” “Power, Mediation, and Reflexivity,” and “Historical Trace Carriers.” They do not belong to the four universal empirical questions, but they are likewise only abstract hypotheses: they cannot become true through names, through filling in the items of the human variables, or through framework definitions. Their tests form a separate kind, which admits only these three clauses and needs to state which of them is being tested. Apart from this, the two sections of pre-registration and outcome record, the marking of missing items (§2.9), no changes after finalization, the pre-registration status, the four outcome statuses, the disclosure of deviations, the positive criterion, the null-conclusion criterion, and the requirements for evidence and analysis materials are all the same as in §4.1. The corresponding tests are called the “Meaning and Coordination” test, the “Power, Mediation, and Reflexivity” test, and the “Historical Trace Carriers” test. Empirical truth belongs to these specific tests, not to the abstract clauses.

These tests must likewise preselect, before the results are seen, only one subtype and one success criterion for that subtype. The following table is the standard classification under the single-primary-criterion procedure, not an exhaustive classification of meaning, power, or historical carriers. If the object or research design at issue falls outside what the table lists, the testable question and the research procedure must be stated separately; it must not be forced into a favorable category.

ClauseSubtype or Outcome Family of Which Exactly One Must Be PreselectedAdmissible Success CriteriaStopping Point for the Conclusion
Meaning and CoordinationChoose one of three: resource allocation outcomes, action-choice outcomes, or coordination outcomesWhichever of “effect of the meaning arrangement on resource allocation,” “effect of the meaning arrangement on action choice,” and “effect of the meaning arrangement on coordination outcomes” corresponds to the selected subtypeDetermine only a conditional orientation anchor within the specified object, scale, time window, and outcome family; do not infer a unified inner state, genuine consent, or a common will
Power, Mediation, and ReflexivityChoose one of four: evidence coverage, safety of expression, object behavior, or reflexive responseWhichever of “effect of position or mediation on evidence coverage,” “effect of position or mediation on the safety of expression,” “behavioral response to mediation or publicity,” and “reflexive response to observation or publication” corresponds to the selected subtypeDetermine only masking, amplification, behavior, or reflexive response within the specified position, mediation, disclosure conditions, channel, and outcome family; do not infer malice, responsibility, or automatic real-world action
Historical Trace CarriersFirst preselect only one of the five carrier families as the subtype: institutional or textual record; role or organizational arrangement; habit or practice; trauma record; collective memory carrier. Then identify one specific carrier belonging to that familyChoose one of three: “stays above the threshold over the pre-registered window,” “detected again across pre-registered windows,” or “persists after the event or exposure ends”Determine only candidate traces within the specified carrier, observables, and time window; obtain separate evidence under §4.5 for the carrier's later effects; only a claim of a historical increment beyond the current representation additionally requires a historical-increment test

A “Meaning and Coordination” test must not treat “any favorable result establishes the claim” as a rule across the three outcomes of resources, action, and coordination. A “Power, Mediation, and Reflexivity” test must not select favorable results after the fact among evidence coverage, safety of expression, behavior, and reflexive response. A “Historical Trace Carriers” test must not search across multiple carriers or durability criteria for a surviving result. The specific carrier it points to must be exactly one: it must not be left empty, nor may it be a list; and the family to which that carrier belongs must be the very subtype selected. If these two conditions are not met, the test is already ineligible before the results are seen. Multiple targets, multiple models, and multiple comparisons still require a single primary target or aggregation rule, a rule for model selection or ensembling, and a correction rule to be fixed in advance in the decision rule. When the positive criterion does not pass, the default is “not supported or unresolved”; only when equivalence or sufficiency, statistical power or sensitivity, and tolerance in the pre-registered null-conclusion rule have all passed is the result “null conclusion supported.” An exploratory test, a test with the status “deviated after evidence,” or a test with undisclosed deviations produces only candidates or remains unresolved; it must not make the corresponding routes of the human variables “Orientation Anchor” (§7.3.3) and “Conditional Potential Field” (§7.3.8), or the route of historical trace carriers, into empirically established conclusions.

The other three human-domain clauses do not enter these tests. “Action Uptake and Classification of Responsibility” is a rule for classifying uptake and responsibility; “Institutional Write-Back” is a classification rule; “Open-Ended Undertaking” is a normative boundary. They may constrain how the human variables are classified and where they stop, but cannot produce support for an empirical mechanism merely because a classification has been made. Even if a test of a human empirical hypothesis has the outcome “supported,” it increases only the strength of description or explanation; it does not generate value, responsibility, obligation, normative justification, authorization, or real-world action.

4.2Note

Understanding this section

4.2 Testing human empirical hypotheses

Discussion of humans may concern behavioral differences or persistent traces, or may only classify responsibility. This section first distinguishes proposition roles, then specifies falsifiable tests for three families of empirical questions.

Chinese source line 633 states, “Empirical truth belongs to these specific tests, not to the abstract clauses.” The three clauses “Meaning and Coordination,” “Power, Mediation, and Reflexivity,” and “Historical Trace Carriers” are initially families of questions, not three labels proving that the world already works that way. An evaluable empirical assertion requires a specific, falsifiable question stating object, comparison, time, outcome, and criterion. “Pre-registration” here is an agreement governing how research results qualify for support, not a legal agreement whose signing makes facts true. [T-42；T-Hroles]

Tests of human empirical hypotheses form a separate kind. When its identity is stated, such a test names not which kind of empirical question it belongs to but which clause it tests, and it admits only three: “Meaning and Coordination,” “Power, Mediation, and Reflexivity,” and “Historical Trace Carriers.” Other disciplines are the same as in §4.1: finalize the pre-registration before results and append the results section afterward; retain the finalized version, the pre-registration status, deviations, evidence and analysis materials, and the four outcome statuses. Missingness still distinguishes “unknown,” “not applicable,” “unobservable,” and “withheld for protection,” with reasons appropriate to each. Unanswered cannot mean never occurred, nor may protected information be compelled merely to fill every item. [T-42；T-41]

The single-primary-criterion procedure requires selecting one subtype and its one success criterion before reading results. This table is a classification for the standard procedure, not an exhaustive account of every way meaning, power, or history exists. A reasonable question outside the table may separately specify its testable question and research design; it should not be forced into an easier-to-pass category. Valid multi-outcome or multi-model designs are not prohibited, but must fix primary targets or aggregation, selection or ensembling, stopping, and applicable correction rules beforehand. The best result cannot afterward be called the original primary question. [T-42；T-41]

The “Meaning and Coordination” test requires preselecting one of three outcomes. Resource allocation asks how funds, time, materials, and similar resources are distributed, matching “effect of the meaning arrangement on resource allocation.” Action choice asks which action is taken, matching “effect of the meaning arrangement on action choice.” Coordination outcomes ask whether multiple people's actions coordinate, matching “effect of the meaning arrangement on coordination outcomes.” Conceptual explanation does not replace operationalization: the measurement, comparison, and required magnitude of difference still need to be stated. Improvement in any one does not establish success in all three. [T-42]

The “Meaning and Coordination” test yields a “conditional orientation anchor” within a specified object, scale, window, and outcome family. In ordinary terms: under these conditions, this candidate meaning arrangement connects with an evidenced difference in resources, action, or coordination. A further causal-mechanism claim requires a matching design and bridging evidence. Shared slogans or consistent behavior cannot establish that everyone has the same inner state, gives genuine consent, or shares a will. Group behavioral indicators and individual free expression are different measurement objects. [T-42；T-Hroles]

The “Power, Mediation, and Reflexivity” test preselects one of four types: evidence coverage, with “effect of position or mediation on evidence coverage,” asks which facts or positions become visible; expression safety, with “effect of position or mediation on the safety of expression,” asks about testable conditions for expression; object behavior, with “behavioral response to mediation or publicity,” asks how action changes under mediation or publicity; reflexive response, with “reflexive response to observation or publication,” asks how being observed or learning of publication changes the object in turn. These may be related, but a result for one does not automatically settle the other three. [T-42]

The “Power, Mediation, and Reflexivity” test must specify the particular position, mediation, publicity conditions, channel, outcome, and comparison. Labels such as “platform,” “power,” and “AI” are not intermediate mechanisms. Reduced reporting somewhere may concern coverage, expression, behavior, or other distinct questions; these distinctions cannot be skipped. The bounded conclusion extends at most to the corresponding obscuring, amplification, behavioral response, or reflexive response under those conditions. It does not directly establish malice or responsibility, still less authorize bans, punishment, or disclosure. When protected information is involved, state availability boundaries honestly. [T-42；T-Hroles]

The “Historical Trace Carriers” test first selects a carrier family: institutional or textual record, role or organizational arrangement, habit or practice, trauma record, or collective memory carrier. These are entry points for classification. Naming “trauma” does not provide a diagnosis, nor does “collective memory” mean an identical inner state in everyone. Identify a specific observable, comparable carrier and trace quantity. [T-42；T-Hroles]

The “Historical Trace Carriers” test also requires two things to agree: the family to which the indicated carrier belongs must be the very subtype selected, and the specific carrier indicated must be exactly one: it cannot be left empty, nor can it be a list. For example, the teaching record R17 identifies only the selected record; it cannot be filled with a list such as “all archives, positions, and habits.” This prevents searching many places and presenting the sole remaining difference as preselected. Pointing to only one carrier constrains the target this test states, not the actual object's internal structure. Multiple-carrier research requires a separately explicit design, not a fictitious single name concealing post-result selection. [T-42]

The “Historical Trace Carriers” test then selects only one durability criterion: “stays above the threshold over the pre-registered window” requires a threshold persistence rule over the predetermined window; “detected again across pre-registered windows” requires repeated detection across windows under predetermined rules; “persists after the event or exposure ends” concerns persistence after the event or exposure ends. These respectively constrain the window, detection, and ending time. Actual thresholds and observation methods must be stated beforehand. Criterion names do not provide statistical tests, durations, or default thresholds, nor permit selecting whichever criterion passes most easily afterward. [T-42]

The “Historical Trace Carriers” test stops at “candidate traces within the specified carrier, observables, and time window.” Distinguish three further questions: whether the trace persists under the rule; whether the current carrier affects later outcomes; and whether additional historical information improves explanation or prediction after controlling the current representation. The second requires separate evidence under §4.5; only the third requires an independent historical-increment test. The same persistent trace may have subsequent effects or merely be retained without participating in the current process. A trace cannot leap directly into a path effect. [T-42；T-G3]

Outcome assessment still has two sets of criteria. Failure of the positive criterion defaults to “not supported or unresolved”; “not significant” cannot mean “null conclusion supported.” A null conclusion additionally requires that the equivalence or sufficiency test, power or sensitivity, and tolerance in the pre-registered null-conclusion rule all pass. “Supported,” “null conclusion supported,” “not supported or unresolved,” and “not yet evaluated” distinguish positive support, support for a bounded null conclusion, lack of support or unresolved status, and no evaluation yet. Each retains specific information rather than labeling an abstract human-domain clause permanently true or false. [T-42；T-41]

An exploratory test of a human empirical hypothesis, one with the status “deviated after evidence,” or one with undisclosed departures produces only candidates or unresolved status. It cannot directly upgrade the corresponding routes of the human variables “Orientation Anchor” (§7.3.3) and “Conditional Potential Field” (§7.3.8), or the route of historical trace carriers, to empirical establishment. This limits formal support status under this standard procedure. It neither erases bounded knowledge obtainable from external studies under their own designs nor permits retroactively inventing pre-registration records for historical research. [T-42；T-interfaces]

“Action Uptake and Classification of Responsibility,” “Institutional Write-Back,” and “Open-Ended Undertaking” do not enter these tests because their roles differ, not because they “have not found data yet.” “Action Uptake and Classification of Responsibility” is a rule for classifying uptake and responsibility; ability to take up does not imply obligation. “Institutional Write-Back” is a classification rule: only actual changes to records, rules, resources, and so forth, with execution records, can be determined under the rule, but classification alone does not establish long-term learning. “Open-Ended Undertaking” supplies normative boundaries; it neither diagnoses who has love nor requisitions sacrifice. Rules can classify according to material, but successful classification is not support for an empirical mechanism. [T-42；T-Hroles]

Even if a test of a human empirical hypothesis is eligible and “supported,” it strengthens only its bounded description or explanation. Value, responsibility, obligation, justification, and authority to act have their own premises. Actual adjustments additionally require the conclusion rule “Normative Bridging” (§4.14.1), explicit normative premises, itemized authorization, and operational procedures. “A publicity condition affects expression” cannot directly become “I may disclose personal identity”; “someone truly has uptake capability” cannot become “they must continue carrying the burden.” [T-42；T-Hroles]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    First distinguish roles: of the six human-domain clauses, only “Meaning and Coordination,” “Power, Mediation, and Reflexivity,” and “Historical Trace Carriers” are empirical hypotheses these tests admit. “Action Uptake and Classification of Responsibility,” “Institutional Write-Back,” and “Open-Ended Undertaking” follow operational, classificatory, or normative limitations respectively.

  2. 2

    For a specific test of a human empirical hypothesis, specify object, scale, window, comparison, observables, and extrapolation scope. Abstract names and complete items do not generate empirical truth.

  3. 3

    Before reading results, uniquely select the subtype and matching success criterion; fix in advance the positive criterion, the null-conclusion criterion, and the overall decision rule. For the “Historical Trace Carriers” test, also check family consistency and that the indicated carrier is exactly one and not empty.

  4. 4

    Obtain evidence and analysis materials under the finalized design; disclose availability, deviations, and dependencies. Write results into the append-only section without overwriting pre-registration.

  5. 5

    Assign the four outcome statuses according to the actual criteria and evaluation phase. Failure to pass the positive criterion does not mean that the null-conclusion criteria have passed; exploration or post-result selection cannot rescue formal empirical eligibility.

  6. 6

    Restrict supported conclusions to the selected outcome family, conditions, and window. Inner states, responsibility, subsequent carrier effects, additional historical increments, and actual action each require separate proof or authorization.

Distinctions to keep clear

Three empirical hypotheses

Specify a class of questions to test.

≠

A specific test of a human empirical hypothesis

Carries bounded empirical truth only with an object, comparison, criterion, and evidence.

Single primary criterion

The default design of this standard procedure.

≠

An exhaustive classification of knowledge

The table claims no exhaustiveness; other designs must clearly state their rules.

Behavioral or coordination outcomes of “Meaning and Coordination”

Measurable differences under specified conditions.

≠

Unified inner states and genuine consent

Cannot be inferred directly from group indicators.

Traces of historical trace carriers

A specified carrier meets persistence rules within the window.

≠

Current-carrier effect/historical increment

Require, respectively, evidence of subsequent effects or an independent test of increments beyond the current representation.

Responsibility/institutional write-back classification

Distinguishes uptake responsibility or actual write-back according to rules.

≠

An established empirical mechanism

Cannot be inferred from correct classification.

Teaching construction: one carrier and three different questionsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe numbers, windows, threshold, R17, and rule are teaching assumptions. To isolate the demonstration, accurate observations, a matching family, and satisfaction of the pre-registration and other necessary conditions are assumed. This example is neither a statistical test nor an actual study of historical trace carriers.

Suppose the observable trace scores of fictional record R17 are 4 and 3 in two prespecified windows, with “detected again across pre-registered windows” selected in advance and a simplified rule requiring both windows to reach 3. Both observations therefore satisfy the rule. If the second window instead scores 2, the rule fails; it cannot be changed afterward to “once reached the threshold.” Even when satisfied, this only means that R17 passes the trace rule under these logical inputs. Whether it affects the next decision, or provides a historical increment beyond the complete current record, remains unevaluated.

BoundaryActual trace judgments also require a historical event, baseline, measurement, comparison, uncertainty, and the complete positive criterion. This comparison of two numbers must not be treated as the entire empirical method.

Teaching construction: the same behavior does not uniquely identify meaningTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe two motives and their mapping to behavior are assumed; no psychological information has been collected from anyone.

Suppose two fictional participants both choose action A. One does so because they endorse the arrangement, the other because they fear losing resources. Their shared behavioral record gives only A, A; at least these two configurations of inner states can produce the same observation, so “shared consent” cannot be uniquely recovered from it. This is a nonuniqueness counterexample, not a survey of actual people's motives.

BoundaryThis does not deny that proportionate voluntary expression, interviews, or other methods can provide further evidence; it only limits direct mind-reading from a single behavioral indicator.

Actual research: counts of late pickups after a fine do not reveal parents' inner statesDocumented case

Gneezy and Rustichini's paper, published in 2000, studied daycare centers in Haifa from January to June 1998. Of the 10 centers reported, 6 introduced a fine and 4 served as controls. The paper reports an increase in late pickups, with counts remaining elevated after the fine was removed. §III explains that the recorded unit was each late-pickup event, not each parent's inner state; §IV separately lists possible explanations concerning interpretations of the situation. This section adds the observation that behavioral outcomes, meaning mechanisms, and historical carriers are distinct questions. “Counts changed” cannot directly be rewritten as “all parents considered late pickup a purchased service.” Nor does a difference persisting after removal of a measure alone establish that a specific trace carrier and its causal effect have been identified.

SourceGneezy & Rustichini, A Fine is a Price, university-hosted public copy of the original journal articleJournal of Legal Studies 29(1), 2000:1–17; printed pp. 3–5, §II design and beginning of §III; p. 8, results; p. 10, §IV explanations (PDF pp. 4–6, 9, 11)Reading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsOnly the research report, unit of observation, and explanatory levels distinguished by the authors are checked here. The original data have not been recalculated and eligibility as a current test of a human empirical hypothesis has not been audited. The authors' explanation is not treated as every participant's confirmed psychology, nor generalized into a claim that any fine necessarily backfires. Behavioral persistence is also not directly upgraded to a historical increment.

Read the case and sources

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleAuthor-constructed conditional counterexample: a preselected “Meaning and Coordination” resource-allocation outcome lacks support; after seeing improvement in a coordination indicator, the researcher declares “meaning was effective.” This does not answer the original primary question. Record the coordination clue and design a separate study, without backfilling success.

What it limitsPrevents cherry-picking across outcomes.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari, On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation

Teaching counterexampleAuthor-constructed conditional counterexample: a “Historical Trace Carriers” test states textual record R17, but only a role arrangement later persists, so the indicated carrier is replaced with that role. Even if the role change is real, it cannot masquerade as the result for the carrier fixed in advance.

What it limitsPrevents replacement of the carrier fixed in advance.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari, On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation

Teaching counterexampleAuthor-constructed conditional counterexample: complaints increase after anonymous collection. The total alone cannot distinguish improved coverage, safer expression, more actual problems, or changed recording definitions. The word “power” cannot replace comparisons and channel evidence.

What it limitsPrevents quantities or labels from masquerading as mechanisms.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari, On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation

Teaching counterexampleConstructed conditional counterexample: a rule change has actually been implemented, satisfying the material requirements for a particular write-back classification, yet it may increase errors. Classification under “Institutional Write-Back” does not mean that learning, improvement, or justification is supported.

What it limitsPrevents improvement from being smuggled in through classification.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari, On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation

What does not follow

  • Author-constructed conditional counterexample: a preselected “Meaning and Coordination” resource-allocation outcome lacks support; after seeing improvement in a coordination indicator, the researcher declares “meaning was effective.” This does not answer the original primary question. Record the coordination clue and design a separate study, without backfilling success.
  • Author-constructed conditional counterexample: a “Historical Trace Carriers” test states textual record R17, but only a role arrangement later persists, so the indicated carrier is replaced with that role. Even if the role change is real, it cannot masquerade as the result for the carrier fixed in advance.
  • Author-constructed conditional counterexample: complaints increase after anonymous collection. The total alone cannot distinguish improved coverage, safer expression, more actual problems, or changed recording definitions. The word “power” cannot replace comparisons and channel evidence.
  • Constructed conditional counterexample: a rule change has actually been implemented, satisfying the material requirements for a particular write-back classification, yet it may increase errors. Classification under “Institutional Write-Back” does not mean that learning, improvement, or justification is supported.
  • When records are insufficiently available, retain states such as “unknown” or unavailable for protection. Do not directly classify difficult-to-observe inner experiences or trauma as nonexistent, and do not compel disclosure for testing.
  • Historical research may contribute knowledge under its original design, but this explanation does not certify its eligibility as a current test of a human empirical hypothesis. Neither external cases nor teaching constructions validate the net utility of this framework.

Scope and open questions

This section concerns evidential boundaries for human behavior and mechanisms, using an original published field study to illustrate levels of observation and explanation. Explicit teaching constructions isolate the logic of historical trace carriers and consent questions without disguising them as actual cases.

  • The objects, indicators, thresholds, comparisons, and protective arrangements of actual tests of human empirical hypotheses depend on specific studies. This lesson explains the rules for the tests; it does not invent research that has already been conducted for the reader.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    If the “Power, Mediation, and Reflexivity” test preselects expressive safety but the results show only behavioral change after disclosure, may the original test be recorded as “supported”?

  2. 2

    May the “Historical Trace Carriers” test specify its carrier as [record R17, position P2] and choose either one later?

  3. 3

    If a carrier persists after a historical event ends, has a historical increment been established?

  4. 4

    Does failure to observe a significant difference mean “null conclusion supported”?

  5. 5

    If “Institutional Write-Back” material proves that a rule was actually changed, may we automatically conclude that it improved and immediately extend its use?

  6. 6

    Does a strong external behavioral experiment have no knowledge value because it did not adopt the recording method of tests of human empirical hypotheses?

If the “Power, Mediation, and Reflexivity” test preselects expressive safety but the results show only behavioral change after disclosure, may the original test be recorded as “supported”?

No rescue is possible solely through another outcome. Preserve the result for the original criterion and treat the behavioral difference as a clue for another question; a new confirmatory study should set down its design anew.

Basis: Chinese source lines 635–643; the four outcome categories of “Power, Mediation, and Reflexivity” and the prohibition on post hoc cherry-picking.

May the “Historical Trace Carriers” test specify its carrier as [record R17, position P2] and choose either one later?

No. A standard test requires that the indicated carrier be exactly one and not empty, and that the family match exactly. A legitimate study of multiple carriers requires a separately explicit design, not a post hoc choice.

Basis: Chinese source lines 641–643.

If a carrier persists after a historical event ends, has a historical increment been established?

No. Persistent traces, subsequent effects of a current carrier, and a historical increment beyond the current representation are three different judgments. A historical-increment test requires a dedicated comparison and support for the third.

Basis: Chinese source line 641 and §4.5.

Does failure to observe a significant difference mean “null conclusion supported”?

No. Equivalence or sufficiency, power or sensitivity, and tolerance in the pre-registered null rule must all pass; otherwise the result is not supported or unresolved, as the specific circumstances warrant.

Basis: Chinese source line 643.

If “Institutional Write-Back” material proves that a rule was actually changed, may we automatically conclude that it improved and immediately extend its use?

No. Write-back classification, long-term effects, normative evaluation, and permission to extend use have different responsibilities.

Basis: Chinese source line 645; §7.1, Chinese source lines 1531 and 1578.

Does a strong external behavioral experiment have no knowledge value because it did not adopt the recording method of tests of human empirical hypotheses?

No. It still supports proportionate domain conclusions under its own design; it simply cannot claim formal support status under a standard procedure it did not actually complete.

Basis: §7.0, Chinese source line 1561; the discipline of this section's tests.
