4.3Conditional Gain from Candidate Grouping (G1) ​

In briefAfter calling several records a group, ask what additional contribution that grouping information actually makes under fair comparison and with new material. The grouping-gain question separates “naming an object” from “obtaining a task gain from a grouping.”

This kind of question is called grouping gain for short. Its proposition is as follows: in a formal test whose object, scale, time window, identity criterion, candidate grouping, and threshold have all been set down in advance, if the candidate grouping still achieves the predetermined out-of-sample gain relative to a null model of comparable complexity after controlling for the common environment, sampling or classification bias, and grouping leakage, and passes boundary-perturbation checks and review using independent time blocks or independent locations, then the grouping receives limited grouping-gain support under that scale, time window, and identity criterion.

A grouping-gain test does not test “whether this object ultimately exists in the world.” It tests whether the current candidate grouping explains predetermined out-of-sample differences better than the null model; the null model here is of comparable complexity and does not use information from the grouping. The test has two subtypes: the predictive-gain subtype permits only “out-of-sample predictive gain” as its success criterion, and the intervention-gain subtype permits only “out-of-sample intervention gain.” Neither subtypes nor criteria may be exchanged after results appear. The common environment, sampling procedure, classification bias, grouping leakage, and model complexity must all enter the controls or competing explanations.

The minimum positive support requires predetermined evaluation metrics and thresholds; an out-of-sample gain relative to the null model; robustness to boundary perturbation; review using independent time blocks or independent locations; and support eligibility for the test (§4.1). If the out-of-sample gain does not exceed the positive threshold, or is not reproduced under boundary perturbation or independent review, the default is only that grouping gain is not supported or that the result is unresolved. The null model may be supported, or this grouping-gain test refuted, only when the equivalence or sufficiency test and the requirements for statistical power, sensitivity, and tolerance in the pre-registered null-conclusion rule have all passed. If any of the object, grouping, success criterion, null model, decision rules, thresholds, data split, or leakage controls was not fixed before results, the test is suspended.

Passing a grouping-gain test allows only three things to be determined: how strong the support for grouping gain is within the specified scale, time window, and identity criterion; how robust that gain is to the boundary perturbations tested; and the grouping's applicable window. Such support is only an eligibility relative to the declared explanatory or foresight task, not an overall threshold for object existence or object facts (see §10.1). It does not permit an ultimate ontological verdict, nor does it generate a subject, target, value, responsibility, or authorization.

4.3Note

Understanding this section

4.3 Conditional Gain from Candidate Grouping (G1)

After calling several records a group, ask what additional contribution that grouping information actually makes under fair comparison and with new material. The grouping-gain question separates “naming an object” from “obtaining a task gain from a grouping.”

Chinese source line 651 limits the question to whether a candidate grouping explains prespecified out-of-sample differences, rather than “whether this object ultimately exists in the world.” The object may first have its boundaries, states, relations, interfaces, time window, scale, and identity stated through the seven elements of a structural object; a grouping-gain test then asks whether this way of grouping adds value for a particular task. Reliably recorded people, institutions, or events do not cease to exist because no grouping-gain test has been performed; conversely, a name and coherent story do not prove predictive or intervention gain from grouping. [T-43; T-D0]

“Conditional gain” does not ask whether a group contains a few similarities. It compares an analysis using the candidate grouping against a null model. The null model must be complexity-matched and must not use that grouping information. Otherwise, if one side has more parameters, more data, or access to outcomes, its advantage may arise from these extra opportunities rather than the grouping itself. Complexity matching is not mechanical parameter counting; an actual design must specify effective flexibility, tuning budgets, and comparison methods for its model class. This explains the research responsibility of implementing fair comparison; it does not claim that the original text specifies one unique complexity measure. [T-43]

The object, scale profile, time window, identity criterion, candidate grouping, and thresholds must all be set down in advance. The scale profile specifies the scale positions of the comparison, the time window its periods, and the identity criterion what continues to count as the same object. Changing boundaries, membership, time, or identity changes the claim being tested. Failed members cannot be removed or a favorable period selected after seeing results while still claiming support for the original grouping. [T-43; T-D0]

The predictive-gain subtype's sole success criterion is “out-of-sample predictive gain”: out-of-sample gain in the selected predictive evaluation. The intervention-gain subtype's sole success criterion is “out-of-sample intervention gain”: out-of-sample gain in the intervention evaluation defined in advance. These cannot be exchanged after seeing results. Predictive discrimination does not automatically show that acting on this grouping improves outcomes; intervention benefit cannot fill in success for an unevaluated prediction task either. Tests of both subtypes are governed by the common discipline of finalization, controls, boundaries, and replication checks. [T-43]

A shared environment is an important competing explanation: similar changes among records in one group may simply reflect exposure to the same weather, equipment, or rules. Sampling procedures may place groups in different locations or imaging conditions; classification bias may favor assigning easily recognized samples to one category; grouping leakage allows outcomes to be predicted, test information, or near-direct proxies for them to enter grouping or training. A nominal training/test split does not automatically eliminate these problems. [T-43]

“Out of sample” means that evaluation information was not used to select, fit, or rescue this confirmatory claim. The specific split must fit the unit of extrapolation in question; near-duplicate records from the same source falling on opposite sides do not constitute independent new sources. After observing out-of-sample gain, the prespecified boundary perturbations must also be tested: does the gain persist under proportionate changes to allowable uncertain boundaries? Perturbation is not arbitrary destruction of the object; which changes remain within the original task and identity criterion must be stated in advance. [T-43; T-41]

Another requirement is checking replication in independent time blocks or locations. Repeated random splits within the same collection conditions cannot automatically be called independent temporal or spatial replication. “Or” means the original text permits proportionate types of replication check; it does not permit selecting a favorable result afterward while concealing other failures. Replication units, rules, and recorded results should match the finalized pre-registration. If a finding holds only at location A, retain the local material for A rather than automatically generalizing it to B. [T-43; T-41]

The minimum positive support in this section is a conjunction: prespecified evaluation metrics and thresholds, out-of-sample gain relative to the null model, robustness to boundary perturbations, independent time-block or location replication, and the test's own eligibility for support. Satisfying only one item is insufficient. In particular, “better than no model” does not mean “better than a complexity-matched null model that does not use grouping information,” and “excellent on the original sample” does not mean “both perturbation and replication checks hold.” [T-43]

If gain does not reach the positive threshold, or perturbation or replication results do not reproduce, the default is that this test is not supported or remains unresolved. This may weaken its extrapolation claim, but does not automatically prove that the grouping is useless, much less that the object does not exist. Only when equivalence or sufficiency tests, proportionate power or sensitivity, and tolerance requirements under the pre-registered null-conclusion rule all pass may a bounded null model be supported or the corresponding grouping-gain test be refuted. The scope of refutation remains limited by the original pre-registration. [T-43; T-41]

If the object, grouping, success criterion, null model, decision rule, threshold, data split, or leakage controls were not fixed before results, the original text requires suspending the test. Suspension concerns eligibility for confirmatory support: information already obtained may be retained as exploratory material, with a separately explicit version or independent test, but cannot be presented as if prespecified. Existing domain methods remain evaluated on their own evidence; absence of a record made under this framework cannot invalidate all knowledge. [T-43; T-41; T-D0]

Passing a grouping-gain test permits, at most, determining the strength of support for grouping gain within the specified scale, time window, and identity criterion, the robustness of that gain to tested boundary perturbations, and the grouping's applicability window. It does not confer a shared will on a group of people, turn a class of devices into a responsible party, or authorize researchers to redistribute resources or act upon members. Grouping gain, mechanisms, intentions, values, and actions each have different evidential and procedural responsibilities. Nor may the formal proofs later in the text replace external material for this section's empirical propositions. [T-43; T-roles]

The formal results in the source are the strength of support for grouping gain, the robustness of that gain to tested boundary perturbations, and its applicability window. “Robust” modifies the gain's performance under listed perturbations; it does not mean that boundaries are now real, unique, or beyond dispute. Changing outcome variables, extrapolation units, or boundary sets requires explaining whether the original support still applies.

Giving a membership list to researchers can establish identity facts supported by the list. If using that list as a predictive feature provides no gain, that finding limits this particular use. Members cannot be required to prove that they improve predictive accuracy before qualifying for recognition, services, or appeal.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    First specify the candidate grouping to be tested, the object, and the scale, time window, and identity criterion; fix in advance the predictive-gain or intervention-gain subtype and its matching success criterion.

  2. 2

    Design a complexity-matched null model that does not use this grouping information, specifying controls for shared environment, sampling, classification bias, and leakage.

  3. 3

    Compute the specified evaluation gain out of sample using the prespecified split, and assess whether the positive criterion is passed according to thresholds and uncertainty rules.

  4. 4

    Test robustness under boundary perturbations allowed in advance, then check replication in proportionate independent time blocks or locations; preserve failures and locally valid scopes.

  5. 5

    Only when all the above conditions and the test's eligibility are met may bounded object identification and the robustness of that gain to tested boundary perturbations be strengthened. Failure defaults to not supported or unresolved; null conclusions are judged by their own criteria.

  6. 6

    Finally retain the limits of scale, time window, and identity criterion; do not infer ultimate existence, shared will, value, responsibility, or permission.

Distinctions to keep clear

Definition of a structural object

Make the candidate object explicit.

≠

Grouping gain

Test its task gain through proportionate comparison and new material.

Predictive-gain subtype

Tests prespecified out-of-sample predictive performance.

≠

Intervention-gain subtype

Tests prespecified out-of-sample intervention gain; neither substitutes as evidence for the other.

Random holdout

A method of splitting data.

≠

Independent time/location replication check

Requires appropriate independent blocks; the name “random split” cannot guarantee it.

Failure to obtain positive support

The current material does not meet the required support.

≠

Support for the null model or bounded refutation

Separately requires a prespecified null rule and adequate testing conditions.

Bounded object identification

Useful at a particular task scale and within a particular window.

≠

Subjecthood and authorization

Cannot arise automatically from grouping gain.

Mathematical teaching construction: initial gain passes, but the boundary-perturbation test may still failTeaching scenario

AssumptionsAll data, trained means, model classes with two parameters each, thresholds, groupings, and perturbation rules are mathematically stipulated. The candidate's and the null model's training sets exclude these four test records, and selection does not inspect test outcomes. The example assumes that the specified membership perturbation falls within boundary uncertainty accepted beforehand, rather than arbitrarily destroying the object.

Suppose two predictors fixed in advance each have two fitted means. The candidate groups by predefined g and is trained to predict 0 and 4; the null model does not use g, instead grouping by another predefined variable z and learning 2 and 2. Four independent teaching test records have Y=(0,0,4,4), g=(0,0,1,1), and z=(0,1,0,1). The candidate mean squared error is MSEg=(0+0+0+0)/4=0; the baseline is MSEN0=(4+4+4+4)/4=4; the gain Δ=4−0=4 exceeds the predefined threshold 1. Next, under a pre-allowed boundary-uncertainty scenario, change the second record's group membership to 1 while keeping the trained predictors and all other inputs unchanged. Candidate predictions become (0,4,4,4), MSEg=(0+16+0+0)/4=4, and Δ=0. Thus, passing the initial gain requirement does not satisfy this perturbation rule, and independent replication remains incomplete.

BoundaryThis demonstrates calculations and the logic of the criteria. Equal two-parameter counts illustrate matching only within the stipulated model classes; they are not a universal complexity criterion. Statistical uncertainty has not been estimated, nor has a formal grouping-gain test been completed.

Conditional-counterfactual teaching example: a predictive marker is not an intervention benefitTeaching scenario

AssumptionsE has a distribution with equal probabilities for 0/1; g=E and Y=E, with no g→Y; do(g) replaces only the g equation without changing E's distribution or the Y equation. These are all teaching causal assumptions, not a measured graph of any real organization.

Let environment E take 0 or 1 with equal probability, with structural equations g=E and Y=E. Under observation, g=Y always holds, so predicting Y from g can be perfectly accurate. If an intervention only replaces the recorded variable g, leaving E and the equation Y=E unchanged, Y remains determined by the original E. This suffices to show that the inference from predictive association to ‘changing the group name changes the outcome’ is invalid.

BoundaryThis does not deny that actually changing the resources, interactions, or environment corresponding to a grouping may have effects; that requires specifying the actual intervention and gathering separate evidence.

A deliberate construction in real research: a wolf/husky classifier that looks at the backgroundDocumented case

Section 6.4 of Ribeiro, Singh, and Guestrin's 2016 paper describes a deliberately constructed bad-classifier experiment: training images of wolves had snowy backgrounds, while those of huskies did not; predictions on separately obtained images also largely followed snow or light backgrounds. The authors explicitly state that they deliberately created this model to study whether people could identify the problem; it must not be retold as an incident accidentally discovered in a real deployed system. This section uses it to illustrate how sampling backgrounds and categories can be entangled: names and some correct predictions are insufficient to establish that a model captures the intended grouping. LIME explanation images are not treated here as a substitute for all the conditions of a grouping-gain test.

SourceRibeiro et al., Why Should I Trust You?, authors' arXiv v3arXiv:1602.04938v3, 2016-08-09; first and second paragraphs of §6.4, PDF page 8, and the Figure11 caption on page 9Reading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsThis genuinely published experiment contains data deliberately selected by its authors. It provides specific research material on sampling-bias risks, not newly fabricated measurements in this lesson. The complexity matching, pre-registration, boundary perturbations, and cross-site replication a grouping-gain test needs have not been audited for it. It is not used to deny the existence of animal categories or to claim that any explanation method can guarantee correctness.

Scope and open questions

This section directly concerns grouping, sampling bias, and extrapolation, and uses a classifier experiment explicitly labeled a deliberate construction in a real paper. Separately, author-constructed mathematical inputs demonstrate gain and the robustness requirement; the two kinds of material are not conflated.

  • Choosing appropriate complexity measures, sets of boundary perturbations, and independent replication units for a specific study requires domain-specific design and original material. This section offers no universal numerical answer.

Why does a grouping outperforming others on a random test set still not establish that the grouping-gain test is complete?

A fair null model, confounding and leakage controls, predefined boundary robustness, independent time-block or site replication, and test eligibility are still required, among other conditions. A random holdout does not automatically satisfy these.

Basis: Chinese source lines 649–653.

After the predictive-gain subtype fails, can the subtype be changed to the intervention-gain subtype upon discovering a favorable intervention metric?

The subtype cannot be changed after the fact while retaining the original confirmatory status. The new lead may be retained and investigated further under an explicit version and independent design.

Basis: Chinese source lines 627 and 653.

Is the example's initial Δ=4 already sufficient?

No. Under the predefined boundary scenario, Δ=0, so the robustness requirement is not met; independent replication and other conditions have not actually been carried out either.

Basis: Teaching-construction calculations and Chinese source line 653.

If no grouping-gain test has been carried out, can one say that an institution documented in archives does not really exist?

No. Reliable archives can support bounded facts about an institution; a grouping-gain test separately asks whether grouping yields gains for the task in question.

Basis: §3.1, Chinese source line 479.

Does one failed cross-site replication prove ineffectiveness everywhere?

No. It limits support for the corresponding extrapolation. Whether a bounded null conclusion is supported depends on predefined rules and testing ability, and the original local facts should also be retained.

Basis: Chinese source line 653.

4.4Specified-Channel Effects and Per-Dimension Boundedness (G2) ​

In briefKnowing that a treatment changed an outcome does not necessarily tell us which route carried the change. The channel-effect question specifically checks the specified channel; once a channel has an effect, each of its performance dimensions still requires separate measurement.

This kind of question is called channel effect for short. Its proposition is as follows: in a formal test whose carrier or channel has been specified in advance, the channel is determined to be a candidate for causally carrying that transition only when the preselected controlled perturbation, controlled intervention, or natural variation meeting identification conditions produces a difference in the specified state transition that exceeds a predetermined threshold. Capacity, delay, reliability, controllability, and loss must be measured separately, channel by channel and dimension by dimension; unmeasured dimensions are not established merely because the proposition holds.

A channel-effect test has two subtypes, and it likewise must preselect only one subtype and one success criterion before results appear (§4.1). For the controlled-identification subtype, what is pre-registered is a controlled means of identification, and its success criterion must be exactly one preselected from “controlled-perturbation effect” and “controlled-intervention effect”; “either perturbation or intervention succeeds” must not be written as a criterion that, after the fact, accepts whichever of the two holds. For the natural-variation subtype, what is pre-registered is natural variation meeting identification conditions, and its only admissible success criterion is “channel effect of natural variation that meets identification conditions.” Both subtypes must first specify the channel, target transition, quantity type and unit, comparative threshold, and dimensions to be measured. The null model is written only for the selected criterion: the preselected perturbation, intervention, or natural variation does not produce a difference in the target transition exceeding the threshold. Criteria not preselected do not enter the success or failure of this test. Boundedness in each dimension separately takes “no difference” or a baseline fixed in advance as its null model.

The question of channel effect does not claim that all causal processes have currently visible channels, nor that all channels are bounded in every dimension. Measuring delay alone does not permit capacity, reliability, controllability, and loss to be declared established along with it. Shifting may be traced further only for quantities of the same type, or quantities with explicit type conversion, units, an accounting boundary, and accounting rules. If the preselected criterion does not produce a difference above the threshold, the default is only to record the positive channel effect as “not supported or unresolved”; this test may be refuted only if it was pre-registered for falsification or a null judgment and the corresponding null-conclusion rule has passed. When common inputs, alternative channels, or measurement protocols can explain the difference, support for the candidate channel should be withdrawn; criteria that were not preselected cannot be used to rescue it, even if their results are favorable. A channel-effect test can locate only candidate causal carrying and the limits on measured dimensions; it cannot create a unified cost across domains, still less turn a carrier into a responsible party.

A channel-effect test tests specified channels and measured dimensions; it is not the sole entry point into causal knowledge. If an eligible comparison identifies the total effect of a treatment but cannot yet distinguish which channel it passes through, the total effect should be retained and the channel marked unresolved; mechanisms must not be fabricated to make up a channel-effect test. If the total effect is near zero, that fact alone cannot negate local processes that offset or compensate for one another; these processes still require independent evidence. When the way the intervention is implemented, common inputs, selection, or measurement conditions change, the current claim is reviewed again; switching afterward to a favorable criterion cannot recover the original confirmatory eligibility.

4.4Note

Understanding this section

4.4 Specified-channel effects and per-dimension boundedness (G2)

Knowing that a treatment changed an outcome does not necessarily tell us which route carried the change. The channel-effect question specifically checks the specified channel; once a channel has an effect, each of its performance dimensions still requires separate measurement.

Chinese source line 659 limits the conclusion to ‘a candidate for causally carrying that transition.’ This does not declare causation simply by drawing an arrow. First specify the carrier or channel, target state transition, and identification design, then test whether the preselected change produces a difference in the target exceeding the threshold. ‘Candidate’ retains competing explanations and withdrawal conditions; evidence for a channel in one transition does not mean it accounts for all changes. [T-44]

The controlled-identification subtype requires exactly one preselected criterion: ‘controlled-perturbation effect’ or ‘controlled-intervention effect.’ In plain terms, a study may predefine an examination of responses to controlled perturbation or effects of controlled intervention, but it cannot try both and then say ‘either success establishes it.’ The specific operational meaning, intensity, object, and comparison must be defined in the plan; the name itself does not guarantee that the manipulation affects only the specified channel. [T-44]

The natural-variation subtype uses natural variation that satisfies identification conditions, with the sole criterion ‘channel effect of natural variation that meets identification conditions.’ ‘Naturally occurring’ does not mean ‘naturally random.’ The actual design must explain where the variation comes from, why it can distinguish the channel effect in question, and which common causes or selection processes might still explain the result. Calling something a ‘natural experiment’ cannot dispense with these identification conditions. Specific assumptions differ across designs; this section provides no universal set of conditions applicable to all natural variation. [T-44]

Both subtypes must fix the channel, target transition, quantity type and unit, comparison threshold, and dimensions to be measured before results are known. The null model concerns only the selected criterion: the perturbation, intervention, or identifiable natural variation does not produce a difference in the target transition exceeding the threshold. Unselected success criteria do not determine the success or failure of this test. Other favorable measured results may honestly be recorded as exploratory findings or separate questions, but cannot rescue the original confirmatory claim. [T-44；T-41]

The five dimensions must be separated individually. Capacity asks how much can be carried, at what rate or limit, under given conditions and within a given window; latency asks how long it takes from which starting point to which endpoint; reliability asks the frequency or probability of agreed success under which trial denominator and conditions; controllability asks which available operations can change the target over what range; loss asks how much of a same-type quantity decreases, transfers, or transforms after crossing a boundary. Each needs its own measurements, errors, and null model or predefined baseline; a single instance of ‘it can get through’ does not establish all five performance dimensions. [T-44]

The title's ‘dimension-by-dimension finitude’ is not an unconditional law of the universe. Chinese source line 663 explicitly does not claim that every channel is finite in every dimension. Conclusions about finite ranges, upper bounds, or limits must concern actual channels and actually measured dimensions. A single latency measurement does not measure maximum throughput, long-term reliability, every controllable state, or loss. Unmeasured items remain unknown; do not write them as zero, infinite, or established. [T-44]

Tracing a ‘transfer’ also requires compatible quantity types. If 10 joules enter and 8 joules leave through a specified outlet, the destination of the remaining 2 joules can be discussed after clearly accounting for the boundary. They need not have disappeared; they may be stored within the boundary or exit elsewhere. If the input is electric charge and the output is a count of information items, the same conservation subtraction cannot be performed directly. Specify conversion relations, units, accounting boundaries, and accounting rules. Money, time, injury risk, and emotional burden do not become directly additive quantities of the same type merely because all are called costs. [T-44]

If common inputs, alternative channels, or measurement protocols suffice to explain a difference attributed to the specified channel, the corresponding channel support should be withdrawn, rather than preserved by switching to a favorable metric. For example, rising temperature can change two sensors together without their transmitting to each other; changes to statistical definitions can also create apparent differences. How the intervention is actually implemented, who is selected, and how common conditions and measurements change can all alter the original identification account. [T-44]

If the preselected criterion produces no difference exceeding the threshold, the default is that the positive channel effect is not supported or unresolved, not automatically that ‘the channel is ineffective.’ The corresponding null conclusion or refutation must be pre-registered and pass qualified equivalence or sufficiency tests, power or sensitivity requirements, tolerance rules, and related conditions. Tests that are too coarse, insufficient exposure, or unsuitable windows may leave the current material unable to distinguish effects. There may also be strong bounded counterevidence, which must be explained according to the actual design; these situations cannot all be written as a definite zero effect. [T-44；T-41]

The reverse direction is equally important: the channel-effect test is not the sole entry point for all causal knowledge. If a qualified comparison identifies a treatment's total effect but cannot yet distinguish intermediate paths, retain the total effect and the unresolved mechanism. Do not invent a mediator to fill in the channel item; nor should a well-grounded total effect be deleted because its mediator remains unknown. The reliability of the total effect still depends on the original design and evidence; ‘mechanism unresolved’ is not a license to waive reviews of confounding and measurement. [T-44；T-domain]

A near-zero total effect also cannot by itself rule out every local process. Two paths may have opposite directions, or compensation may maintain an endpoint quantity. A mathematical sum of zero does not imply that every term is zero. But ‘possible cancellation’ is only a competing hypothesis, not proof that canceling channels actually exist; local processes still require independent evidence. Later, §11.6 also discusses why segment-level effects cannot unconditionally be combined into an effect of the entire chain: common support, timing, and correspondence must be retained. [T-44；T-chain]

Passing a channel-effect test at most locates a candidate causal bearer for a transition and limits in the measured dimensions. A device, procedure, or position transmitting effects within a causal chain does not thereby become a bearer of moral or legal responsibility; a person who actually transmits effects does not automatically bear all responsibility either. Knowledge, control, authorization, duties, and remedies still require separate judgments. Causal localization does not create a unified cost across domains or grant researchers real-world authority to operate. [T-44；T-CVRS]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    First specify the state transition to be explained and the candidate channel; fix the controlled-identification or natural-variation subtype and its uniquely matching criterion before results are known.

  2. 2

    Explain identification conditions for the actual perturbation/intervention or natural variation, controlling explanations based on common inputs, alternative channels, selection, and measurement.

  3. 3

    Compare target differences using the predefined type, units, window, and threshold; the corresponding evidence supports only the selected criterion.

  4. 4

    Measure capacity, latency, reliability, controllability, and loss separately, each with its own baseline; a result in one dimension cannot fill in the others.

  5. 5

    If the positive criterion is not passed, retain unsupported or unresolved status; assess null conclusions independently under predefined rules. A new favorable criterion does not restore the original eligibility.

  6. 6

    If only the total effect is identified, retain it and acknowledge that the channel remains unresolved; if the total effect is near zero, judge local channels only from independent evidence.

  7. 7

    Stop at the candidate causal bearer and measured limits; do not automatically infer responsibility or real-world authority.

Distinctions to keep clear

Total treatment effect

How the target changes overall after a treatment is changed.

≠

Specified-channel effect

Which selected path carries the change requires evidence identifying the channel.

Natural variation

Change not directly manipulated by the researcher.

≠

Satisfying identification conditions

Additional design conditions sufficient to support the causal comparison in question.

One latency measurement

A time result under given conditions.

≠

All performance dimensions are known

Separate evidence for capacity, reliability, controllability, and loss is still needed.

Zero total effect

The overall net change is zero.

≠

No path has any effect

This cannot be inferred from a zero sum; nor can local paths be established by conjecture.

Causal carrier

The object that actually carries the change.

≠

Responsible party

Separate grounds such as a basis for responsibility and standing as a responsible agent are required.

Mathematical construction: opposing paths produce a zero sumTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe equations, common units, and operation domain allowing independent settings of M1/M2 are mathematical assumptions; there are no real channels or experimental samples.

Let structural equations be M1=2X, M2=−2X, Y=M1+M2, with X equal to 0 or 1. Under do(X=0), the equations give M1=M2=Y=0; under do(X=1), M1=2, M2=−2, Y=0. The total effect Y(1)−Y(0)=0, while the two intermediate quantities change by +2 and −2. Under independent operations allowed in this model, setting M1 from 0 to 2 while fixing M2=0 changes Y from 0 to 2, showing that a zero total effect has not erased local effects.

BoundaryRefutes the unconditional inference “the sum is zero ⇒ every term is zero”; it does not establish offsetting real-world paths or confer ability or authorization to manipulate mediators.

Teaching construction: one timing record cannot fill five performance dimensionsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe record and synchronization conditions are teaching inputs, not measurements of real equipment; the example illustrates measurement responsibilities only.

A fictional transmission log records only one message sent at t=0 seconds and received at t=2 seconds, with synchronized clocks and consistent endpoint definitions. This record's delay can be calculated as 2 seconds; without more material, maximum capacity, success probability within an agreed window, reachable control range, and loss rate remain unknown. If intermediate buffering also exists, the relationship between capacity and delay needs an explicit model and cannot be inferred from one number.

BoundaryOne successful record can describe one success, but does not imply 100% long-term reliability, still less complete identification of the channel effect.

An additional observation in the same case: two explanations the authors still could not rule outDocumented case

Section 4.2 uses Gneezy and Rustichini's 2000 daycare-fine study to distinguish behavioral counts from psychological claims. This section additionally checks the opening of the conclusion on printed page 15: after reporting behavior following the introduction and removal of fines, the authors explicitly state that the available data and theory still cannot rule out the two proposed explanations. Pages 10–14 discuss explanations involving information in incomplete contracts and social norms. This new location illustrates the difference between ‘a research report of a treatment effect’ and ‘a uniquely identified intermediate channel.’ The paper did not withdraw all reported observations merely because its mechanism explanations still competed.

SourceGneezy & Rustichini, A Fine is a Price, university-hosted public copy of the original publicationJournal of Legal Studies29(1),2000:1–17; §IV, printed pages 10–14, especially §IV.D, pages 13–14; first paragraph of §V, printed page 15 (PDF page 16)Reading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsThis relies on the authors' explicit statement that explanations remain unresolved; it does not upgrade the study into a formal channel-effect test under this framework, recalculate its total effect, or establish a psychological mechanism. Nor does it generalize to all fines, all people, or current policy. An unknown mechanism does not mean every total-effect claim is reliable; those claims are still evaluated by the original design.

  • Author-constructed conditional counterexample: an instrument changes from milliseconds to seconds but the report does not convert units. A thousandfold apparent numerical decrease does not mean the channel has become faster; review of units and protocols must precede mechanism conclusions.
  • Existing bounded causal knowledge in research is evaluated according to its original design, without requiring prior conversion into a current channel-effect test. This lesson has not fabricated pre-registration or channel tests for historical research.

Scope and open questions

This section addresses total effects versus channel identification, reusing the same original journal publication while adding a precise location for the authors' explicit conclusion that competing mechanisms remain unresolved. A mathematical offsetting model explains the logical boundary without inventing actual offsetting paths.

  • Specific identification assumptions for the natural-variation subtype, indicators for the five performance dimensions, and accounting boundaries depend on the object studied; this section provides no directly reusable universal threshold or cost scale.

If controlled perturbation fails but another intervention succeeds, can the original controlled-identification test count as passing?

No. Judge only by the single preselected criterion; another result may generate a new question, but cannot retrospectively rescue confirmatory eligibility.

Basis: Chinese source lines 661–665.

If a naturally occurring power outage accompanies reduced output, can it directly count as a natural-variation test?

Natural occurrence alone does not confer identification. Actual exposure, common conditions, selection, alternative channels, and measurement must also be examined so the comparison supports the specified channel.

Basis: Chinese source lines 635 and 663.

How should one report a qualified randomized treatment comparison that finds a total effect but does not measure mediators?

Retain the bounded total effect, mark the channel unresolved, and invent no mechanism; also retain the comparison's actual limitations.

Basis: Chinese source line 665.

If the mathematical example's total effect is zero, do both paths have no effect?

No. Changes of +2 and −2 in the two intermediate quantities offset each other; but this is only a conclusion of the given model, and real paths require separate evidence.

Basis: Chinese source line 665 and this lesson's mathematical construction.

Does measuring 2 seconds imply 100% reliability or a capacity of 0.5 items/second?

No. Two seconds is only the delay in this log entry; reliability needs an explicit denominator and conditions, while capacity needs corresponding load/concurrency/window and measurement. Inverse delay is not a universal capacity formula.

Basis: Chinese source lines 633 and 663.

4.5Historical Formation, Current Carriers, and Historical Increments (G3) ​

In brief“The past has an effect” can ask at least three things: how it shaped the present, how the present continues to carry that effect, and what the past adds after the present is already known. The historical-increment question addresses only the third; each needs separate evidence.

Research into the effects of history first distinguishes three questions: how earlier experiences formed the current state; how current carriers retain, update, and continue to affect later outcomes; and whether historical materials still provide additional information or effects given the stated current representation. The first two can hold while the third does not; nor can lack of support for the third establish, in reverse, that the first two hold. The question of historical increment tests only the third; it cannot replace all research into historical causation, learning, accumulation, continuation, or reproduction. The full name of this third question is “historical conditional increment beyond the current representation,” where “the current representation” means the current state as stated on this occasion; where the book speaks of a “historical residual” or a “conditional residual,” it means this same item.

A historical-increment test has two subtypes, and it likewise must preselect only one subtype and one success criterion before results appear (§4.1).

For the subtype of predictive path dependence, the proposition is: if historical variables have been defined before future outcomes are observed, and, after controlling for the stated current state, environment, and measurement protocol, still provide reviewable out-of-sample conditional-increment information for a predetermined outcome, they can support predictive path dependence. Its only admissible success criterion is “historical conditional predictive gain.”

Beyond that conditional increment, the subtype of causal path dependence must also preselect one criterion among history erasure, history recovery, and an equivalent intervention; it supports causal path dependence only when that preselected causal criterion changes the outcome and exceeds the predetermined threshold. The corresponding success criteria are “history-erasure effect,” “history-recovery effect,” and “equivalent-intervention effect,” of which only one may be preselected; it must not wait for results and then select a favorable result from erasure, recovery, or an equivalent intervention.

The null model of both subtypes is that the stated current state already constitutes a sufficient statistic and historical terms provide no conditional increment. The null model of causal path dependence adds one more condition: its own preselected intervention criterion does not change the outcome. Criteria not preselected play no part in success or failure.

The preservation of traces is not the same as their entering later transitions; a predictive gain is not the same as history having causal efficacy, either. If historical variables are defined only after future results have been seen, current-state information is plainly omitted, or a subtype and success criterion have not been uniquely preselected, any one of these suspends the test. If historical terms provide no positive increment after controlling for the current state, environment, and measurement protocol, or if the criterion preselected for the subtype of causal path dependence does not pass the positive threshold, the default record is only “not supported or unresolved”; a corresponding refutation is formed only when the falsification rule or null-conclusion rule fixed in advance has been followed to completion. Other unselected criteria cannot be used to rescue the claim. Passing a historical-increment test permits only the determination of predictive or causal path differences within the pre-registered time window; it does not permit inferences of historical fate, absolute irreversibility, responsibility, or authorization.

Scope of application: predictive path dependence and causal path dependence are this framework's narrow classifications for “historical conditional increments beyond the current representation,” not definitions of all historical causation. Suppose earlier experience H changes current skill S, and S then affects outcome Y. If S already carries the relevant historical information sufficiently, H may add no further predictive information about Y given S. The narrow condition for a historical increment is then not satisfied, but the historical formation process H→S→Y and learning in its general sense may still be supported by independent process materials or a research design. The total historical effect, current carrier, and conditional residual should be reported separately; a historical increment must not be manufactured by omitting known S. 〔Studies 03.03, 04.01–04.04, 24.04, 25.08〕

Intertemporal judgments follow two routes, each stated separately: the carrier-transmission route and the historical-increment route. The carrier-transmission route requires four kinds of material: a measured current state or carrier; grounds for how earlier inputs or changes entered that carrier; the carrier's retention or updating within the declared time window; and longitudinal materials showing its continued effects on predetermined outcomes. Seeing only a lasting outcome, or only the existence of a carrier, cannot confirm the transmission mechanism. A causal claim must additionally compare interruption, replacement, recovery, or natural variation meeting identification conditions under the conditions for causal claims (§2.4), and address common inputs, sustained exposure, selection, attrition, and measurement changes. When there are only correlational materials without the corresponding basis for identification, the conclusion stops at an intertemporal description or a candidate mechanism.

Applying for formal mechanism support for the carrier routes of the conclusion rules below additionally requires the relevant channel and outcome to be supported by an eligible channel-effect test, or by the test of a human empirical hypothesis (§4.2) that the relevant human variable specifies. A “Historical Trace Carriers” test supports only traces within the selected carrier and time window; on its own it cannot satisfy the requirements for subsequent effects or causation. The original test's object, outcome, and time window must cover the claim now being made: a single immediate effect must not be extrapolated to a long-term effect, nor may several separately established local links be treated as a connected chain as a whole. Existing domain evidence still retains its own conclusions and limits under §2.1.1; the separation into routes in this section does not automatically confer on it eligibility as a formal test or as a test of a human empirical hypothesis.

The historical-increment route separately tests, under the requirements of a historical-increment test, conditional increments beyond the current representation, with predictive and causal conclusions still kept separate. Carrier transmission can hold while historical increment is not supported; failure of the positive criterion for historical increment does not establish that carrier transmission holds, either. Known current states must not be omitted to obtain a historical increment, and routes must not be switched after results to rescue the original claim. Each route separately states its grounds, competing explanations, failure conditions, and ceiling on conclusions. Accumulation, continuation, learning, delayed recovery, and intertemporal reproduction cannot acquire support merely by being named.

Historical increments depend on how the current representation is chosen; they must not be treated as an essence of the system independent of representation. Let the complete current state be x_t, the stated representation be z_t=π(x_t), and the retained history be h_t. If history still provides an increment for a future target given z_t, this may be because h_t recovers current differences collapsed by π; that in itself does not establish that the complete dynamics contains an additional history term. Proportionate comparisons should be made among available, task-relevant current carriers, measurement errors, and model complexity. Known current-state information must not be deliberately deleted to manufacture historical gains.

In reality, the complete state is usually unavailable. Thus, “can in principle be expanded into a sufficient state” must not be treated as having already established the absence of historical increments in this case. If the materials support only an increment relative to the stated current state, report it under that representation, target, and time window; when the representation changes, redo the comparison. How much value history has in assisting prediction, how history formed the current carriers, and whether a historical-increment test in the narrow sense receives support are three questions that can have different answers. Appendix C.11 gives an exact example: the current projection has omissions, and historical gains arise as a result.

4.5Note

Understanding this section

4.5 Historical formation, current carriers, and historical increments (G3)

“The past has an effect” can ask at least three things: how it shaped the present, how the present continues to carry that effect, and what the past adds after the present is already known. The historical-increment question addresses only the third; each needs separate evidence.

Chinese source line 669 states these three questions and emphasizes, “The first two can hold while the third does not.” Historical formation asks how earlier experiences change the current state; carrier transmission asks how current records, skills, damage, organizational arrangements, and so on retain or update effects and influence what follows; conditional increment asks what information or effect historical material adds given the stated current representation. The historical-increment test specifically tests the third; it does not provide a single new definition for all historical causation, learning, accumulation, persistence, or reproduction. [T-45]

The distinction is necessary because the same fact can be questioned from different temporal positions. Practice may form a skill, and the skill may change later performance. If the current skill already carries sufficient target-relevant information, adding practice history will not improve prediction. Disappearance of extra predictive information does not erase formation; conversely, “no extra information” cannot establish that the skill formed or transmission occurred, since both causal chains still require their own material. [T-45]

For predictive path dependence, the sole permitted success criterion is “historical conditional predictive gain.” Historical variables must be defined before observing future outcomes; after controlling for the stated current state, environment, and measurement protocol, they must still supply a reproducible out-of-sample conditional increment for the predefined future target. The comparison is between two information sets, not between having or lacking a historical story: the current representation and relevant controls, versus these plus historical variables. Additional accuracy must not result from future-information leakage, opportunities for model selection, or deliberate omission of known current variables. [T-45; T-41]

“Conditional” means asking whether knowing history still helps on top of the current information already known. Here the current state is a stated representation actually available, not an omniscient observer's complete world state. Results must be tied to representation, target, window, error, and comparison method; changing the target or adding current variables may alter the increment. That does not automatically falsify the earlier bounded predictive result; it means the question it answers has a scope. [T-45]

For causal path dependence, in addition to the out-of-sample conditional increment above, exactly one of “history-erasure effect,” “history-recovery effect,” and “equivalent-intervention effect” must be preselected, and the corresponding erasure, recovery, or equivalent intervention must exceed the predefined threshold. Correlational prediction using history cannot simply be labeled causal, nor may all three operations be tried and the most favorable afterward presented as the original criterion. [T-45]

For these causal operations, researchers must explain exactly which carrier/record is erased or recovered, how this is implemented, which current conditions change, and how an identifying comparison is made. The names do not mean that the already-occurred past is literally changed, nor guarantee arbitrary alteration of history while all relevant current conditions remain fixed. If an operation only changes current skill, storage, or damage, its effect may answer the carrier question; whether it additionally satisfies the conditional-increment and selected-operation criteria of causal path dependence must still be tested, not conferred by the word “erasure.” [T-45; T-causal]

The null models for both subtypes include the stated current state being a sufficient statistic for the specified target, with history supplying no further conditional increment. Causal path dependence additionally requires that its own preselected intervention criterion produce no outcome change; unselected operations do not count toward the success or failure of this test. Sufficiency here is target-relative conditional informational sufficiency: it does not require recovering every past detail or imply sufficiency for other tasks. [T-45; T-F1]

If historical variables are defined only after future outcomes have been seen, current-state information is clearly omitted, or subtype and success criterion were not uniquely preselected, the source requires suspension of the test. Suspension does not delete historical records; it prevents packaging this material as predefined confirmation. Exploratory findings can retain their status and motivate an independent test. Omitting known relevant current skill so that practice history appears especially predictive is precisely the increment this section forbids manufacturing. [T-45; T-41]

If history supplies no positive increment after controlling for the relevant current state, environment, and measurement protocol, or if the operation preselected for causal path dependence does not exceed the positive threshold, the default is not supported or unresolved. A bounded refutation or zero conclusion still requires completing the equivalence or sufficiency, power or sensitivity, and tolerance rules fixed in advance. Nonsignificance, small samples, or coarse measurement cannot automatically constitute proof of sufficiency. Favorable results from unselected operations cannot rescue the original test. [T-45; T-41]

The H→S→Y example in Chinese source line 681 uses H for earlier experience, S for current skill, and Y for subsequent outcome. H may affect Y through S; once sufficient S is given, H adds no predictive information, while the total historical effect still exists. The conditional question answered by controlling for a mediator differs from the total-effect question. More observational controls are not automatically better: choose them according to the estimation target and causal design instead of adding every measurable variable to the model. [T-45; T-causal]

The carrier-transmission route needs four kinds of positive material: measurement of the current carrier or state; how earlier inputs or changes entered it; how it was retained or updated within the declared window; and longitudinal material on its continued influence on the predefined outcome. Merely observing that a file remains or an outcome persists cannot complete all four links. A file may never be used; a persistent outcome may result from uninterrupted external exposure; a carrier with the same name at two times may have been replaced. [T-45]

A further claim of causal carrier effects requires a proportionate comparison, such as interruption, replacement, restoration, or natural variation with identification conditions, addressing common inputs, continued exposure, selection, attrition, and measurement change. Association without corresponding identification grounds stops at cross-time description or a mechanism candidate. Not every question requires an experiment, but the adopted historical reconstruction, observational, or comparative design must disclose what it can and cannot distinguish. [T-45; T-causal]

Applying for formal mechanism support through the carrier routes of the conclusion rules below also requires a corresponding qualified channel-effect test, or the test of a human empirical hypothesis that the human variable specifies, covering the channel and outcome. A “Historical Trace Carriers” test supports only trace retention in the selected carrier and window; it cannot alone satisfy the requirements for subsequent effects or causation. This requirement concerns the route of formal support; domain research may still have bounded conclusions under its own design and does not lose its original grounds merely because it did not use this book's testing methods. [T-45; T-H5; T-domain]

Coverage cannot exceed the original test: an immediate effect is not automatically long-term, nor is short-window retention automatically reproduction across periods. Several separately supported local links cannot directly be combined into a complete same-case chain: an upstream change must actually reach the object, state, and time to which the next link can respond. A total effect identified by a qualified comparison can be retained without first exhausting every microscopic mechanism; add the corresponding connections only when seeking a more specific propagation explanation. [T-45; T-causal]

The carrier-transmission and historical-increment routes must each independently state evidence, competing explanations, failure conditions, and conclusion ceilings. Carrier support with the historical increment unsupported is a possible combination; failure of a historical-increment test does not imply carrier support. Failure of increment cannot justify relabeling the same material “carrier-route success” and automatically closing the original inquiry. If independent carrier evidence exists, honestly report a different proposition without switching the original question. [T-45]

Chinese source line 689 further expresses representation dependence as x_t, z_t=π(x_t), and h_t: x_t is the model's complete current state, π compresses it into the stated representation z_t, and h_t is retained history. If π merges different current states that affect the future, history may distinguish those merged states, producing historical gain conditional on z_t. Yet the complete-state dynamics may not actually require an additional historical term. This is a competing explanation that must be examined, not proof that the real world necessarily lacks memory. [T-45; T-C11]

Make proportionate comparisons of current-carrier availability, measurement error, and model complexity. Coarse measurement of relevant current variables may let history serve as a proxy; greater fitting freedom for the history model may also create an unfair advantage. Conversely, complete real-world states are usually unavailable; “can in principle be expanded into a sufficient state” cannot substitute for case-specific evidence to declare no historical increment. Honestly record how much current information can be obtained, when it is obtained, and whether its use is permitted. [T-45]

Appendix C.11 gives an exactly calculable two-queue example. The complete current pair of queues determines the next state, while the current mean merges different allocations; the historical initial mean helps reduce error caused by this merging. The two positive errors in the original manuscript are not accidental performance of fitting software, but minimum risks over the complete constructed state domain under specified weights and squared loss. This lesson shows why the conditional mean is optimal, two particular trajectories, and calculated values for four input sets, without treating artificial enumeration as real-world samples. [T-C9; T-C11]

Three practical conclusions may therefore differ: history-assisted prediction is useful; how history formed the current carrier has an independent explanation; and whether a historical-increment test in the narrow sense meets formal-support requirements remains a separate judgment. Any positive historical-increment test permits determining only predictive or causal path differences within the pre-registered window, not historical destiny, absolute irreversibility, responsibility, or real-world authorization. With insufficient data, identify precisely which question remains unresolved instead of concluding “history determines everything” or “the present suffices, so the past is irrelevant.” [T-45]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    First separate historical formation, continued current-carrier effects, and conditional increment beyond the stated current representation, avoiding one kind of evidence answering all three questions.

  2. 2

    For a historical-increment test, define historical variables, current representation, controls, target, window, and the unique criterion of one of the two subtypes before outcomes; fix comparison rules and data splits.

  3. 3

    Compare out-of-sample target performance using current information alone and with history added; examine omitted known current states, measurement error, leakage, and model complexity.

  4. 4

    Beyond conditional increment, causal path dependence requires identification and an above-threshold effect for its selected erasure/recovery/equivalent intervention; unselected operations cannot be used to rescue it.

  5. 5

    The carrier route separately checks input entry, retention/updating, longitudinal consequences, and proportionate causal comparisons; formal mechanism support additionally requires a channel-effect test or a specified test of a human empirical hypothesis covering the object, outcome, and window.

  6. 6

    Formally, a projection merging current states can generate historical predictive increment. This counterexample refutes the unconditional inference that “increment must come from additional memory in the complete dynamics,” not real-world memory.

  7. 7

    Report only bounded combinations supported by current material; failure of a historical-increment test neither cancels historical formation nor automatically establishes a carrier mechanism, and positive support generates neither destiny nor authorization.

Distinctions to keep clear

Historical formation

How earlier experience changes the current state.

≠

Historical conditional increment

What history adds once the current representation is given.

Current-carrier transmission

A retained/updated state continues to affect consequences.

≠

Traces of historical trace carriers

Only traces in the selected carrier and window; does not independently establish subsequent effects.

Predictive path dependence

Out-of-sample predictive increment for the predefined future target.

≠

Causal path dependence

Also requires the corresponding effect of a preselected causal operation; prediction cannot establish it by proxy.

Complete state x_t

A candidate sufficient state in the model.

≠

Stated representation z_t

Information actually stated, possibly merging current differences.

Carrier supported and historical increment unsupported

A combination that may have independent grounds.

≠

Historical increment unsupported, therefore carrier supported

Logically invalid; positive evidence for the carrier is missing.

The state can theoretically be expanded

A formal modeling possibility.

≠

No historical increment remains in this case

Requires real material; it does not automatically follow from a possibility.

Mathematical teaching construction: the total historical effect and the conditional residual can be separatedTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe distribution, structural equations, domain of operations, and sufficient measurement are all teaching assumptions; this is not an actual experiment on human training.

Let H equal 0 or 1 with equal probability, skill S=H, and outcome Y=10S, and assume that H can be intervened on while the other equations remain unchanged. do(H=0) gives Y=0, and do(H=1) gives Y=10, so the total effect within the model is 10. Given S, Y is uniquely determined, and the minimum squared prediction error using S and using (S,H) is 0 in both cases. Thus a formation chain H→S→Y and no additional predictive quantity from H given S can coexist.

BoundaryWhether controlling for a mediator is appropriate in reality depends on the estimation target; this construction does not certify actual learning, qualification as a historical-increment test, or permission to intervene.

Expanding a mathematical example from the book: how omissions in a current projection produce a historical incrementTeaching scenario

AssumptionsUniformity applies to the original initial states, not to means, states after the first round, or distinct input fibers; the numbers are rounded from exact fractional calculations over a finite artificial domain. Squared loss, absence of noise, symmetric service, and availability of the inputs are all stipulated.

Following Appendices C.9/C.11, let the initial state (q1,q2) range over the 961 ordered combinations in {0,…,30}², with each initial state weighted 1/961. There are no new tasks in any round, and service actually follows F(q1,q2)=(max(q1−5,0),max(q2−5,0)); this is not merely an uncertain upper bound of ‘at most 5’. Let h be the initial mean, z the mean after the first round, and Y the mean after the second round. Trajectory A: (0,20)→(0,15)→(0,10), with h=10, z=7.5, and Y=5; trajectory B: (10,15)→(5,10)→(0,5), with h=12.5, z=7.5, and Y=2.5. The same z merges different values of Y, while h distinguishes these two trajectories. For any input V and output a, E[(Y−a)²|V]=Var(Y|V)+(a−E[Y|V])²; the second term is nonnegative, so prediction by the conditional mean attains the minimum loss on that fiber. Advancing each original initial state individually and preserving its original weight gives the following minimum MSEs for the four input types: z: 0.579016561; (z,h): 0.271143397; complete current two-queue state x: 0; (x,h): 0 (rounded to 9 decimal places). History improves the coarse representation but no longer improves the already complete current queues.

BoundaryThis is mathematical risk, not prediction error in a real service system or empirical evidence of a historical increment. Distinguishing the means in one case does not establish that history is fully sufficient for every sample; the MSE of (z,h) over the whole domain remains greater than 0.

Apollo 13: earlier ground operations, the damaged state during flight, and the later failureDocumented case

The section ‘Preflight Damage to Tank Wiring’ in NASA's investigation report of June 15, 1970 records prolonged heating during the special detanking operations of March 27–28; the investigation concluded that the protective switches most probably welded closed under a 65-volt DC load. Subsequent tests supported the finding that overheating could severely damage wire insulation, which the report connected with the later risk of a short circuit. This reuses the accident but adds a focus on how earlier operations left a physical state that continued to have effects, rather than examining only inputs on the day of the accident. The report also retains probabilistic wording about the ignition mechanism and the limitation that telemetry could not establish every detail.

SourceNASA, Report of Apollo13 Review BoardReport dated 1970-06-15; Chapter 5, ‘Preflight Damage to Tank Wiring’, printed pages 5-9—5-11 (PDF pages 175—177); ignition assessment on 5-6 (PDF page 172), and telemetry limitations on 5-8 (PDF page 174)Reading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsThis is a bounded historical causal judgment formed by the investigation from logs, telemetry, tests, and reconstruction, not a historical-increment study testing additional historical increments while holding the complete pre-failure state fixed. No comparative result establishes whether a historical increment holds or fails in this case, nor can it be said that the damaged state was fully known at the time. This lesson does not reassign individual responsibility.

What does not follow

  • Counterexample from the source: in C.11, the historical mean can supplement the current mean, but the complete current queues already determine the future; historical gain alone does not establish an additional historical term in the complete dynamics.
  • Author-constructed conditional counterexample: H, S, and Y are mutually independent, with no causal arrow from H to S or from S to Y; H has no predictive increment given S, yet the claimed transmission through a carrier is also absent. Failure of a historical-increment test therefore cannot establish the carrier route.
  • Author-constructed conditional counterexample: a file has been preserved for years but never subsequently read or used. Its existence and persistence alone do not establish that it changed a decision.
  • Author-constructed conditional counterexample: deliberately leaving a known, available skill unmeasured and then obtaining predictive improvement from practice history cannot secure qualified support from a historical-increment test through that artificial omission.
  • Author-constructed conditional counterexample: treating recollections classified after an outcome as a prior historical variable risks carrying future information back into the past; the corresponding confirmatory test should be paused, and the materials' actual timing preserved.
  • Failure of the formal carrier route or historical-increment route does not automatically revoke well-supported historical research within a domain; likewise, this lesson does not retrospectively certify an actual accident reconstruction as a formal historical-increment test.

Scope and open questions

This section involves actual historical formation and physical carriers. It uses newly checked material on preflight damage in the NASA investigation while preserving uncertainty in the reconstruction, and uses an explicit mathematical model to distinguish total effects, carriers, and conditional residuals.

  • The complete current state is usually unavailable in reality; specific historical predictive value and causal paths require data proportionate to the task. This lesson has not conducted a historical-increment test on Apollo 13 controlling for the current representation.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    Practice did form a skill, but current skill predicts the next score equally accurately. Does this mean history never played a role?

  2. 2

    If a test of predictive path dependence has passed, can causal path dependence be recorded?

  3. 3

    If a “Historical Trace Carriers” test establishes that an archive persists, does that directly support a claim that it changes subsequent action?

  4. 4

    Two queues both have a current mean of 7.5. What are their respective next means?

  5. 5

    Can the original table be reproduced by reassigning equal weights to the distinct states after the first round?

  6. 6

    Since all history can theoretically be packed into a state, must the historical increment fail to hold in this case?

  7. 7

    If a historical-increment test has not passed, can the carrier route be declared to have passed instead?

Practice did form a skill, but current skill predicts the next score equally accurately. Does this mean history never played a role?

No. The formation process and additional information given skill are different questions; the total historical effect can be realized through current skill.

Basis: Chinese source, lines 643 and 681; teaching structural equations.

If a test of predictive path dependence has passed, can causal path dependence be recorded?

No. Causal path dependence additionally requires proportionate identification and threshold results for a preselected erasure, recovery, or equivalent intervention.

Basis: Chinese source, lines 673—679.

If a “Historical Trace Carriers” test establishes that an archive persists, does that directly support a claim that it changes subsequent action?

No. Evidence of reading or entry into transitions, longitudinal effects, and proportionate comparisons is required; the formal carrier route also needs support from a specified channel-effect test or test of a human empirical hypothesis covering the corresponding claim.

Basis: Chinese source, lines 683—685.

Two queues both have a current mean of 7.5. What are their respective next means?

A is 5 and B is 2.5; the mean omits the current allocation. The initial means of 10 and 12.5 distinguish these two examples, but history plus the mean is still not fully sufficient over the entire domain.

Basis: Chinese source, Appendix C.11, line 4978, and the complete calculation.

Can the original table be reproduced by reassigning equal weights to the distinct states after the first round?

No. The weight of 1/961 for each of the 961 original initial states must be preserved; when several initial states converge on the same current state, their probabilities must be added.

Basis: Chinese source, Appendix C.11, line 4978.

Since all history can theoretically be packed into a state, must the historical increment fail to hold in this case?

No. The representation actually available in this case is not an omniscient state; comparisons should follow the stated representation, target, and window, and be retested when the representation changes.

Basis: Chinese source, lines 689—691.

If a historical-increment test has not passed, can the carrier route be declared to have passed instead?

The judgment cannot be changed automatically. If independent carrier evidence exists, a separate bounded conclusion may be drawn, but its evidence, competing explanations, and stopping point must be explicit.

Basis: Chinese source, lines 643 and 687.
