4.6Representational Closure and Object or Intervention Conversion (G4) ​

In briefAn aggregate representation may describe the current total correctly yet omit the composition that determines the next step or the response to a particular intervention. A scale-closure test must first specify which failure or conversion is being tested; closure itself can also be a valuable result.

This kind of question is called scale closure for short. A scale-closure test has two subtypes, and it likewise must preselect, before results appear, only one subtype and one success criterion for that subtype (§4.1); only when the preselected criterion exceeds the predetermined threshold or tolerance is the corresponding test supported. The two subtypes answer different questions.

The closure-failure subtype tests whether excluded scale variables still provide a conditional increment given the variables retained at the target scale. It permits three success criteria: “conditional-increment information,” “conditional predictive gain,” and “conditional intervention gain”; each test may preselect only one. Its null model is that, under the preselected criterion, the excluded scale variables provide no conditional increment beyond the threshold given the retained variables.

The subtype for object or intervention conversion tests whether the object or the intervention is converted under scale transformation (§3.4). It permits five success criteria: “noncommutation of object dynamics,” “noncommutation of intervention,” “failure of the identity criterion,” “change in effective relations,” and “change in intervention response”; each test likewise may preselect only one. The first two criteria say that scale transformation does not commute with object dynamics or with intervention, that is, a different order of the two gives a different result; the third says that the target mapping does not satisfy the identity criterion fixed in advance. The null model is also written only for the selected item: object dynamics commute, or interventions commute, or the target mapping satisfies the identity criterion fixed in advance, or effective relations do not change beyond tolerance, or intervention responses do not change beyond tolerance. The five must not be combined into a fallback formulation under which “any one holding counts.”

General correlation, unconditional coupling, similar narratives, and omitted variables at the same scale are all insufficient to support a positive conclusion from a scale-closure test. The test is suspended if exactly one subtype and success criterion were not preselected before results, or if any of the following was not fixed in advance: the mapping required by scale transformation and by the epistemic constraint “Testing Cross-Scale Transfer” (§4.8.5), the comparison models, the positive threshold, the null-conclusion rule, the requirements for statistical power or sensitivity, and the tolerance. When the positive criterion passes, the closure-failure subtype determines only closure failure within the pre-registered variables, metrics, scales, and time window; the subtype for object or intervention conversion determines only the preselected conversion candidate within the pre-registered mapping, identity criterion, scales, and time window. When the positive criterion does not pass, the default record is only “not supported or unresolved.” Only when the equivalence or sufficiency test, the requirements for statistical power or sensitivity, and the tolerance in the null-conclusion rule actually pass may the closure-failure subtype determine “closure within the limits of the criterion,” and the subtype for object or intervention conversion determine “the preselected conversion was not detected.” Merely being “not statistically significant,” or not passing the positive threshold, does not permit direct determination of closure, absence of object conversion, or equivalence of interventions. Unselected criteria must not be used for rescue, nor for refutation. Passing a scale-closure test does not mean that higher scales are truer, more important, or have greater authority to act.

This kind of question maintains a symmetrical research interest in closure and nonclosure. Supporting closure within a specified scope under a stated test can show that a concise representation is already sufficient for the current task; detecting nonclosure shows that the representation, task, or scope of operations needs revision. “Supported” and “null conclusion supported” are only evidential states relative to the preselected factual assertion, not rankings of the quality of a method or of theoretical progress.

Comparisons of scale closure must specify the targets, horizons, environments, and admissible operations relative to which closure is assessed. Sufficiency for prediction under ordinary conditions does not guarantee continued sufficiency under a new intervention; the same macro-level state may respond differently to the same operation because of differences in the composition collapsed by the representation. After the representation is found to be insufficient, necessary variables may be added, composition or history retained, the set of actions limited, the horizon shortened, or the use narrowed; there is no need to recover all micro-level details. Closure holding can itself be a successful result of an effective macro-level description; emergence, aggregation, omissions at the same scale, and cross-boundary transmission do not universally require closure failure.

Example of intervention sufficiency: two micro-level states A₁ and A₂ both have probability 0.2 of entering B under natural evolution, so merging them into A may be sufficient for this predictive task. Under a particular intervention, their probabilities of entering B are 0.8 and 0.1, respectively. The macro-level intervention outcome then depends on the share p of A₁, with probability 0.1+0.7p. One can then try adding only p rather than recovering all micro-level details. This teaching construction distinguishes predictive closure from intervention closure; it does not establish that real-world systems necessarily take these values. 〔Study 05.06〕

4.6Note

Understanding this section

4.6 Representational closure and object or intervention conversion (G4)

An aggregate representation may describe the current total correctly yet omit the composition that determines the next step or the response to a particular intervention. A scale-closure test must first specify which failure or conversion is being tested; closure itself can also be a valuable result.

Lines 695—697 of the Chinese source distinguish the closure-failure subtype from the subtype for object or intervention conversion. The closure-failure subtype asks whether variables excluded by the scale representation still provide a predetermined conditional increment once the retained variables are given; the subtype for object or intervention conversion asks whether a selected conversion difference arises between scale transformation and dynamics, intervention, object identity, or related features. Neither is established merely by observing that two levels are ‘related’; each has explicit comparisons, thresholds, and stopping points. [T-46]

The closure-failure subtype permits three success criteria, one of which each test must preselect: ‘conditional-increment information’ asks whether excluded scale variables increase the specified conditional information; ‘conditional predictive gain’ asks whether they improve specified conditional predictive performance; ‘conditional intervention gain’ asks whether they improve specified intervention-evaluation performance. Information, prediction, and intervention are not the same metric; a positive result on one cannot count as success on another. The null model concerns only the selected criterion: given the retained variables, the excluded scale variables provide no corresponding increment above the predetermined threshold. [T-46]

The subtype for object or intervention conversion permits five criteria, again with only one preselected. ‘Noncommutation of object dynamics’ asks whether advancing the dynamics and then converting differs from converting first and then advancing proportionate target dynamics; ‘noncommutation of intervention’ asks whether the order of intervention and conversion makes a difference; ‘failure of the identity criterion’ asks whether the target mapping no longer satisfies the identity criterion fixed in advance; ‘change in effective relations’ asks whether the effective relation changes beyond tolerance; ‘change in intervention response’ asks whether the intervention response changes beyond tolerance. Each requires named mappings and actual objects; the five cannot be combined into a fallback of ‘something is bound to differ’. [T-46]

Null models for the subtype for object or intervention conversion likewise match the preselected criteria one to one: object dynamics commute, interventions commute, the target mapping satisfies the identity criterion, the effective relation stays within tolerance, or the intervention response stays within tolerance. Unselected criteria neither rescue nor refute this test. For example, if a preselected change in relations does not meet the threshold and the identity criterion is later found not to hold, that issue should be recorded separately and accurately; the original claim about relations cannot be reclassified as having passed. [T-46]

Scale transformation (§3.4) and the epistemic constraint ‘Testing Cross-Scale Transfer’ (§4.8.5) require specifying the source and target scales, retained/changed/lost variables, the type of transformation, errors, scope of applicability, comparison targets, and competing explanations. Without this inspectable bridge, repeated terms and similar narratives are merely parallel descriptions. ‘Testing Cross-Scale Transfer’ does not require the scale-closure proposition to be true first; rather, a scale-closure test must pass this constraint. This avoids wrongly making ‘cross-scale research can be conducted’ depend on ‘cross-scale failure must first be found’. [T-D3；T-E5]

General correlation, unconditional coupling, similar narratives, and omitted variables at the same scale are insufficient to support a positive conclusion from a scale-closure test. The key is what the declared scale transformation discards and whether it still changes the selected target conditional on the variables already retained. If the original model has merely omitted a variable at the same scale, analyze that omission first; do not label it cross-scale closure failure merely to fit the terminology. [T-46]

A test is paused if a unique subtype/criterion was not specified before results, or if the mapping required by scale transformation and by ‘Testing Cross-Scale Transfer’, the comparison model, positive threshold, null-conclusion rule, power or sensitivity requirement, and tolerance were not fixed in advance. This prevents observing a difference first and then changing the scale, identity criterion, or threshold to guarantee success. Reasonable exploration may remain exploration, and existing domain results retain their standing according to their designs, but a nonexistent confirmatory pre-registration cannot be backfilled. [T-46；T-41；T-domain]

If the positive criterion passes, the closure-failure subtype determines only closure failure within the pre-registered variables, metrics, scales, and window; the subtype for object or intervention conversion determines only the selected conversion candidate within the predetermined mapping, identity criterion, scales, and window. Failure to pass the positive criterion defaults to unsupported or unresolved. Only when pre-registered equivalence/sufficiency tests and the power/sensitivity and tolerance requirements actually pass may the closure-failure subtype determine criterion-bounded closure, or the subtype for object or intervention conversion determine that the preselected conversion was not found. Nonsignificance is not proof of closure, much less of equivalence across all interventions. [T-46]

This makes both closure and nonclosure researchable outcomes. If a concise representation is already sufficient for the current task, criterion-bounded closure supports continuing to use it; if nonclosure is detected, then consider revising the representation or narrowing its uses. ‘Supported’ and ‘null conclusion supported’ are relative to the preselected factual assertion: when the assertion is ‘closure failure’, ‘null conclusion supported’ may favor retaining the concise model. They are not rankings of methodological quality, theoretical progress, or the superiority of scales. [T-46]

Sufficiency must be relative to the target, horizon, environment, and permitted operations. A representation sufficient for prediction under natural evolution may become insufficient under an added intervention, because the compositions merged into the same macroscopic state may respond differently. When insufficiency is found, one can add necessary variables, retain composition or history, restrict the set of actions, shorten the horizon, or narrow the use; recovering every microscopic detail is unnecessary. Conversely, emergence, aggregation, same-scale omissions, and cross-boundary transmission do not universally presuppose closure failure; a well-closed model can still correctly represent cross-boundary effects. [T-46；T-D3]

The A1/A2 probability example at the end of this section addresses only a specified one-step target. Under natural evolution, both have probability 0.2 of entering B, so predicting ‘whether B is reached at the next step’ need not distinguish composition. After intervention, the probabilities become 0.8 and 0.1, making the mixture response 0.8p+0.1(1−p)=0.1+0.7p, where p is the share of A1. Adding p alone answers this mixture's one-step probability, but does not specify how p itself subsequently updates, how other target blocks change, or whether other interventions remain applicable. [T-46；T-461]

Subsection 4.6.1 further supplies exact formal closure and approximate error bounds, explaining why static queries, one-step targets, multistep dynamics, and intervention operations must be separated. Mathematical criteria can establish relationships in a given model; they cannot dispense with measurement, mappings, samples, and the positive and null-conclusion criteria for a real-world scale-closure test. Crossing scales does not automatically expand authority to act within the scope of jurisdiction and authorization either. [T-461；T-E5]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    First declare the mapping M and source/target scales, target, horizon, environment, and permitted operations, explicitly identifying retained and excluded variables.

  2. 2

    Fix in advance the closure-failure subtype or the subtype for object or intervention conversion and a single success criterion; establish a matching null model, comparison method, positive and null thresholds, sensitivity, and tolerance.

  3. 3

    Check the selected increment conditional on retained variables, or compare the selected order of dynamics/intervention, identity criterion, relation, or response; do not substitute general correlation.

  4. 4

    Passing the positive gate supports only the corresponding closure failure or conversion candidate; failure leaves the instance unsupported/unresolved, and a null conclusion requires independently completing every gate.

  5. 5

    Use the result to choose whether to enrich the representation, restrict operations, shorten the horizon, or retain an already sufficient concise model; do not equate higher scales or positive statuses with superiority.

  6. 6

    Separate formal models, empirical support, and actual authority; the construction in this section demonstrates logic only and does not automatically certify real scale-closure tests.

Distinctions to keep clear

Closure-failure subtype

Excluded scale variables still provide the selected increment given the retained variables.

≠

Subtype for object or intervention conversion

Under the selected mapping, dynamics, operations, the identity criterion, relations, or responses exhibit the selected change.

General correlation

Two quantities change together.

≠

Conditional increment

Beyond the information already retained, an excluded variable still increases the quantity being asked about.

One-step prediction under normal conditions

Sufficiency for the specified target under natural evolution.

≠

Closure under all interventions/over multiple steps

Operations and composition updates require separate tests; they cannot be inferred in succession from the former.

Null conclusion supported

Bounded support for the null model of the preselected assertion.

≠

Methodological failure

The two are not equivalent; bounded closure may support a concise representation.

Mathematical teaching construction from the book: the intervention response of the same macrostate A changes with its compositionTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe probabilities, two constituent types, and operation are teaching assumptions from the original text, with p∈[0,1]; there is no empirical estimation or fitting of unknown parameters.

Let p=P(A1|A) and 1−p=P(A2|A). Under natural conditions P(B|A1)=P(B|A2)=0.2, so P(B|A)=0.2p+0.2(1−p)=0.2. Under the selected intervention the two probabilities are 0.8 and 0.1, so P(B|A,intervention)=0.1+0.7p. At p=0,0.5,1 these are 0.1,0.45,0.8 respectively. Knowing A without knowing p cannot yield the same intervention probability for all mixtures; adding p can restore this time point’s one-step target.

BoundaryThis concerns only a one-step probability for target B; without a full transition kernel or a rule for updating p, closure cannot be declared for the entire projected process and all operations.

Teaching model

Source example: under ordinary conditions, A₁ and A₂ each have probability 0.2 of entering B. Under the specified intervention, these become 0.8 and 0.1 respectively.

0%25%50%75%100%
Ordinary prediction0.200
Specified intervention0.450

Calculation: 0.8 × p ＋ 0.1 × (1 − p) ＝ 0.450. The ordinary result stays the same, but the intervention response changes with the internal composition.

All values come from the formal teaching example in the source; they are not real measurements. Adding p helps answer this specified question only. It does not automatically resolve long-term evolution or other interventions.

Actual experiment: overall density and local congestion patterns on the same circular trackDocumented case

Sugiyama et al.’s 2008 paper reports arranging 22 cars on a circular track with a circumference of 230 meters. They initially traveled at nearly uniform spacing, after which stop-and-go waves emerged. Figure 3 compares the initial scene with the scene after 3 minutes, and Figure 4 gives vehicle trajectories. The bounded inference here is that an aggregate description such as a fixed number of cars divided by track length can remain unchanged while local traffic patterns change. Thus ‘the overall-density statistic is correct’ must be separated from ‘this information suffices to answer questions about local congestion or the next response’.

SourceSugiyama et al., Traffic jams without bottlenecks, published version in a university repositoryNew Journal of Physics 10 (2008) 033001, 2008-03-04; printed p. 4 experimental setup and Figure 2, p. 5 Figure 3 and description, p. 6 Figure 4 (PDF pages 6–8)Reading scope: Read

Scope and limitsThe original experiment is actual traffic research; separating aggregate description from target sufficiency is this guide’s bounded interpretation of its setup. No conditional-information, predictive, or intervention comparison was repeated under the current scale-closure test; the experiment is not declared to have passed a test of the closure-failure subtype or of the subtype for object or intervention conversion, and one circular-track experiment does not establish nonclosure for all roads or all macroscopic representations.

Scope and open questions

This section involves empirical sufficiency questions and uses the published circular-track experiment to illustrate the distinction between aggregate records and local targets; experimental observations are not automatically converted into formal closure judgments.

If the closure-failure subtype’s predictive-gain criterion fails but an information measure is significant, may ‘supported’ be added to the original test?

No. The judgment must follow the single preselected criterion; other findings may form separate questions.

Basis: Chinese source lines 695–701.

Is ‘null conclusion supported’ necessarily a bad result?

No. When the positive assertion being tested is failure of closure, qualified null support can support the sufficiency of a simpler representation for the bounded task.

Basis: Chinese source line 703.

At p=0.5, what are the natural and intervention probabilities of reaching B?

Natural: 0.2; intervention: 0.1+0.7×0.5=0.45. This includes no rule for p’s evolution at the next time point.

Basis: Chinese source line 707 and 4.6.1, line 713.

Does adding p complete closure over arbitrarily many steps?

No. Updating p itself and other retained variables, complete target probabilities, and the corresponding conditions for every permitted operation are still needed.

Basis: Chinese source line 713.

Does good macroscopic closure rule out emergence or cross-boundary effects?

That inference is invalid. Closure is a property of a specific representation relative to a task, not a universal condition negating the existence of those processes.

4.6.1Formal Closure, Approximate Closure, and Empirical Eligibility ​

In briefThe formal question of closure is whether the same simplified state can determine the same next simplified state. Approximate closure adds a question: how does per-step error accumulate over the required horizon?

In a deterministic model, let the source state space be X, the representation be π:X→Y with Y=π(X), and the one-step dynamics be F:X→X. A macro-level update F̄:Y→Y satisfying π∘F=F̄∘π exists if and only if any two source states with the same representation still have the same representation after updating. This condition is an exact closure criterion within the model. If it holds throughout the state domain, commutation over multiple steps under fixed dynamics follows by induction; if it holds only at a few visited states, it cannot be extrapolated to closure over the entire domain. Sufficiency for a static query cannot replace this dynamic condition, either.

When multiple operations are admissible, the specific version of each operation should be stated and its update under state projection tested. If a macro-level operation does not determine its corresponding micro-level implementation, it is also necessary to check whether the various admissible implementations yield identical macro-level responses or responses within tolerance. A stochastic model must test the conditional transition probabilities to each target state or target block; identical means alone are insufficient to establish closure of the distribution. Adding a particular composition proportion can repair a one-step prediction at a specified time, but does not automatically supply an update law for that proportion itself, nor closure under every operation.

Approximate closure must be stated together with an error quantity, initial conditions, targets, an operation set, and a horizon. Suppose the per-step error under state projection is at most ε, and the Lipschitz constant of the proposed macro-level update on the relevant region does not exceed L. Starting from the same initial representation, the error at step t is then at most ε∑_{j=0}^{t−1}L^j; this bound requires the premises to hold at every step. When L<1, a uniform upper bound ε/(1−L) is available; when L=1, the bound is tε; when L>1, the error bound may increase rapidly. A one-step mean error or a short-term fitting error must not be substituted directly into this state-by-state, step-by-step bound.

These proofs provide structure under stated conditions; they do not provide support for any real-world scale-closure test. Measurement, mapping, samples, operations, and error conditions must still be checked empirically, with testing carried out separately against the positive criterion and the null-conclusion criterion. A formal proof of exact closure and failure to detect a deviation in limited data are evidence of two different statuses; without sufficient sensitivity, the latter remains unresolved.

4.6.1Note

Understanding this section

4.6.1 Formal Closure, Approximate Closure, and Empirical Qualification

The formal question of closure is whether the same simplified state can determine the same next simplified state. Approximate closure adds a question: how does per-step error accumulate over the required horizon?

Chinese source line 711 gives a source-state domain X, a representation π:X→Y with Y=π(X), and deterministic one-step dynamics F:X→X. Exact closure requires a macroscopic update F̄:Y→Y such that π(F(x))=F̄(π(x)) for every x. The left side advances at the source level before aggregating; the right aggregates first and then advances at the macro level. Only equality allows the macro representation to update independently. Taking Y as the actually attainable image avoids imposing irrelevant conditions on representations without sources. [T-461; T-C8]

Explicit proof of necessity: if such an F̄ exists, choose any π(x)=π(x′). Then π(F(x))=F̄(π(x))=F̄(π(x′))=π(F(x′)). The same current representation cannot split into two different next representations; otherwise the same input would require F̄ to output two values simultaneously, so no such function exists. This is a logical contradiction independent of sample size or fitting algorithm. [T-461; T-C8]

Explicit proof of sufficiency: conversely, suppose π(x)=π(x′) always implies π(F(x))=π(F(x′)). For each y∈Y, define F̄(y) as π(F(x)) for any source state satisfying π(x)=y. Since the condition ensures that all such x give the same value, the definition does not depend on the representative chosen. Since Y=π(X), each y has a source; F(x) remains in X, so the output is also in Y. Thus π∘F=F̄∘π holds. [T-461; T-C8]

If this condition holds over the whole state domain for fixed F, multistep closure follows by induction: at t=0, π∘F⁰=π=F̄⁰∘π; if π∘Fᵗ=F̄ᵗ∘π, then π∘Fᵗ⁺¹=(π∘F)∘Fᵗ=F̄∘π∘Fᵗ=F̄ᵗ⁺¹∘π. Finding no conflict in a few visited states cannot replace the whole-domain premise: future trajectories may reach unchecked states sharing a representation but differing in response. [T-461; T-C8]

Sufficiency for a static query cannot substitute for dynamical closure. If the current question asks only for the sum of two queues, retaining the sum is of course exact; under service saturation, however, different allocations with the same sum can update to different sums. The target has changed from ‘the current total’ to ‘the next-step total’. This is a task change, not a mathematical contradiction; the static recovery of the proposition ‘Task Recovery’ (§4.18.1) and the dynamical closure of the proposition ‘Closure under Dynamics and Admissible Interventions’ (§4.18.2) each have their own conditions. [T-461; T-D3; T-C9]

If multiple operations are permitted, specify the source update F_u for each operation version u and test the projection condition separately. A proof for natural F cannot directly be applied to F_u. If one macroscopic operation name admits several microscopic implementations, check whether they produce the same macroscopic response or responses within tolerance. If an operation is feasible only in some collapsed states, check common implementability or restrict the domain. A shared operation name does not eliminate these differences. [T-461; T-C8]

Following Appendix C.8, this guide develops the case of a finite stochastic system with a given partition; comparing means alone is insufficient. For any two states in the same source block, compare the sums of conditional transition probabilities into each target block. Equality defines a macroscopic transition kernel independent of hidden composition. Accidental equality for one initial mixture may fail when the mixture changes. Nor can ‘the same probability of reaching B’ be expanded into ‘the same distribution over all target blocks’; the example in 4.6 therefore claims only one-step sufficiency for the specified target. [T-461; T-C8]

Approximate closure first fixes a metric d, ε≥0, L≥0, operations, operating range, initial state, and horizon. Every step must satisfy the projection-deviation bound d(π(F(x)),F̄(π(x)))≤ε; the macroscopic update must satisfy the Lipschitz condition d(F̄(y),F̄(y′))≤L·d(y,y′) at the comparison points involved. These are bounds for every relevant state and step, not a single average error; all points used by the actual and macro trajectories must remain within the range where the premises hold. [T-461; T-C8]

Let the actual projection be π(x_t), the macro-model state be y_t, and e_t=d(π(x_t),y_t), starting from the same initial representation with e_0=0. The triangle inequality separates ‘one-step projection deviation’ from ‘existing error amplified by the macro update’: e_{t+1}≤d(π(F(x_t)),F̄(π(x_t)))+d(F̄(π(x_t)),F̄(y_t))≤ε+Le_t. Starting from e_0=0 gives e_1≤ε and e_2≤ε+Lε; induction gives e_t≤ε∑_{j=0}^{t−1}L^j. [T-461; T-C8]

For 0≤L<1, the geometric sum is (1−Lᵗ)/(1−L), so e_t≤ε/(1−L) at times satisfying the premises; for L=1, e_t≤tε; for L>1, e_t≤ε(Lᵗ−1)/(L−1), and the bound may grow rapidly. These are upper bounds, not assertions that actual error must attain them. Nonzero initial error adds Lᵗe_0; changing per-step error or L requires rewriting the recursion rather than mechanically applying the fixed formula. [T-461; T-C8]

Adding a composition proportion may repair a one-step probability at one time without supplying that proportion’s own update. The approximate formula also cannot be applied directly from a short-run average fitting error. Leaving the operating range, changing operations, or encountering omitted errors requires rechecking premises. With only finite empirical material and insufficient sensitivity, ‘no departure yet detected’ remains unresolved; it is not a mathematical proof of exact closure. [T-461]

This subsection establishes conditional relations within a model and does not provide support for any real-world scale-closure test. Actual applications still require independent checks of measurement, source-to-target mapping, samples, operation implementation, and error conditions, with testing carried out separately against the positive criterion and the null-conclusion criterion. Proof of exact closure, finite-domain enumeration, numerical estimation, and real-world testing each retain their own status; numerical checking adds no real-world observations and creates no authority to act. [T-461; T-form]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Necessity: the same represented input into a single F̄ must yield the same output, so its projections after source-level updating must agree.

  2. 2

    Sufficiency: define F̄ by the common next projection of source states sharing a representation; the image condition ensures total definition, and agreement within each fiber ensures unambiguity.

  3. 3

    Multiple steps: with fixed dynamics over the whole domain, start at t=0 and repeatedly apply the commutation relation to obtain any nonnegative integer number of steps.

  4. 4

    Operation/stochastic branches: test each permitted operation and microscopic implementation separately; for a finite stochastic system with a given partition, test every target block’s probability, not just the mean.

  5. 5

    Approximation: the triangle inequality, per-step ε bound, and Lipschitz condition give e_{t+1}≤ε+Le_t; with e_0=0 the recursion yields a geometric sum.

  6. 6

    Boundary: all premises must hold throughout the required horizon and operating range; mapping the mathematical conclusion to reality, measurement, and test eligibility require separate evidence.

Distinctions to keep clear

Static sufficiency

The current representation can answer a static target.

≠

Dynamical closure

The same representation determines the same next representation, requiring update conditions.

Equal means

The numerical expectations are equal.

≠

Distributional closure

For this guide’s finite stochastic system under a given partition, each target block has equal probability, a stronger condition than preserving the mean.

Error upper bound

A limit that cannot be exceeded when the premises hold.

≠

Actual error

May be smaller or even zero; an upper bound cannot be treated as a measured curve.

Uniform per-step bound

Holds for every state and step involved.

≠

Short-run average fit

A small average does not guarantee a small value at any individual point or subsequent step.

Proof within a model

Derived for a specified domain, mapping, and dynamics.

≠

Qualification for a real-world scale-closure test

Requires separate checks of specific empirical material and of the positive and null-conclusion criteria.

Mathematical teaching construction: a static total cannot advance independentlyTeaching scenario

AssumptionsQueues, service equations, absence of arrivals, and deterministic operations are all stipulated; no actual queueing effect is estimated.

Let X be pairs of nonnegative integer queues, π(q1,q2)=q1+q2, and let F subtract the actually serviceable min(q,5) at each position. Both x=(0,6) and x′=(3,3) have π=6; F(x)=(0,1) gives π=1, whereas F(x′)=(0,0) gives π=0. If a macro function F̄ existed, F̄(6) would have to equal both 1 and 0, a contradiction. These two states witness failure of exact closure, although π still answers the current total accurately.

BoundaryOther representations or dynamics may be closed; a counterexample targets only the specified π and F.

Mathematical teaching construction: identical one-step error bounds, different multistep guaranteesTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe same metric, statewise projection error ≤0.1, and the corresponding Lipschitz conditions hold throughout every relevant step; model and trajectories remain in the operating range.

Let ε=0.1 and e0=0, comparing fixed L=0.5,1,2. The geometric-sum upper bounds for t=1 through 4 are: L=0.5: (0.1,0.15,0.175,0.1875), with long-run uniform bound 0.2; L=1: (0.1,0.2,0.3,0.4); L=2: (0.1,0.3,0.7,1.5). Values follow from B_{t+1}=0.1+LB_t and B0=0; they are conditional guarantees, not three actual error trajectories.

BoundaryThis does not establish that these L or ε exist in reality; L>1 says only that the bound can amplify, not that every actual error grows exponentially.

Scope and open questions

This subsection specifically states formal conditions for deterministic/stochastic closure and error propagation; explicit proofs and mathematical counterexamples directly address its content. A real-world story need not be used as evidence that model premises hold. The actual empirical example retains its bounded status in the parent section.

  • The mathematical conclusions have been proved under the stated premises; whether any actual system meets the whole-domain, operation, and per-step-error conditions requires independent empirical material, and this guide provides no such certification.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    Why do two source states sharing a representation but yielding different next representations make F̄ impossible to define?

  2. 2

    Why is agreement of the next representation within each fiber also sufficient?

Why do two source states sharing a representation but yielding different next representations make F̄ impossible to define?

A function can give only one output for the same input; the two conflicting requirements already constitute a counterexample.

Basis: Proof of necessity.

Why is agreement of the next representation within each fiber also sufficient?

The common value can define that macrostate’s update; every macrostate has a source, and choosing a different representative does not change the result.

Basis: Proof of sufficiency and Y=π(X).

If all visited states agree, can closure be claimed for any future?

No. Uncovered compatible states or operations may split; whole-domain conditions or an explicit valid subdomain and reachability are required.

Basis: Chinese source lines 685 and 713.

Why do random 0/2 in A and constant 1 in B have equal means without distributional closure?

A assigns 0.5 each to 0 and 2; B assigns 1 to 1. Target-block probabilities differ, and the mean 1 erases that distinction.

Basis: Chinese source line 713 and the counterexample.

With ε=0.1 and L=2, must the fourth-step error be 1.5?

No; 1.5 is an upper bound while the premises hold, and actual error can be smaller.

Basis: The recursion and teaching values.

Can a training mean error of 0.1 be used directly as ε=0.1?

No. A uniform bound for the relevant states and steps is required, along with Lipschitz and operating-range conditions.

Basis: Chinese source line 715.

4.7A Fictional Set of Formal Tests ​

In briefThese four fictional cards are not four experimental reports. They place the preceding evidential responsibilities of the four empirical questions in one setting to examine how the questions connect and how they cannot substitute for one another.

The following four small examples serve only to show how pre-registration works. They describe a fictional transport model with multiple layers, cite no external observations, and constitute no empirical support for any proposition of the four empirical questions.

Example one (grouping-gain test, predictive-gain subtype). The candidate object consists of several interconnected groups of units. The boundary, state variables, time window, scale profile, identity criterion, grouping method, and a null model of comparable complexity are fixed in advance; only “out-of-sample predictive gain” is selected as the success criterion, and its metric and threshold are fixed. If the candidate grouping is effective only in the training sample, or if the gain disappears after a slight boundary perturbation, example one fails; limited grouping-gain support within this time window is obtained only if the result is also reproduced in independent time blocks.

Example two (channel-effect test, controlled-identification subtype). For example one's candidate object, a transmission channel and a target state transition are specified in advance, only “controlled-perturbation effect” is selected as the success criterion, and the channel is then blocked under controlled conditions. Even if the blockage changes the target transition by more than the threshold, the channel can be determined only as a candidate for causal carrying. Suppose only delay is measured in this example; then capacity, reliability, controllability, and loss remain unknown and cannot be established along with example two.

Example three (historical-increment test, predictive path dependence). First define the historical variable “backlog in the preceding three rounds,” select only “historical conditional predictive gain” as the success criterion, then control for the current queue, environmental inputs, and measurement protocol. If the historical term still provides an out-of-sample conditional increment for the next round's outcome, predictive path dependence may be determined; without an intervention for history erasure or history recovery, this must not be raised to causal path dependence.

Example four (scale-closure test, closure-failure subtype). Before results, select only the closure-failure subtype and only “conditional-increment information” as the success criterion; fix in advance the micro-level and aggregated scales, the scale transformation between them, the retained variables, the excluded variables, the metric, and the threshold. Closure failure within this time window is determined only if the excluded local temporal sequence, given the aggregate variables, provides a conditional increment above the threshold under that criterion. A predictive or intervention gain must not be substituted after results are seen, nor may the result be rewritten as object conversion under the subtype for object or intervention conversion.

These examples show that the four tests can raise further questions for one another, but cannot replace one another. Passing example one does not guarantee that example two's channel is effective; passing example two does not guarantee example three's historical effect; and passing example three does not guarantee example four's scale-closure failure.

4.7Note

Understanding this section

4.7 A Fictional Set of Formal Tests

These four fictional cards are not four experimental reports. They place the preceding evidential responsibilities of the four empirical questions in one setting to examine how the questions connect and how they cannot substitute for one another.

Chinese source line 721 says outright that the examples “cite no external observations.” Examples one to four demonstrate pre-registration within a fictional multilayer transport model, not an actual organization, engineering accident, or collected dataset. Readers can learn what each must ask and how it can fail, but cannot add the four to an empirical-support inventory. Conditional results expressed with “if” and “suppose” do not imply actual occurrence. [T-47]

These are teaching abbreviations, not four formal tests with every item and all evidence materials supplied. Full eligibility still follows §4.1: two record sections, finalization before evidence, evidence mode, data splits, the four outcome statuses, departure disclosure, and evidence that corresponds to real material, among other requirements. When example one lists only some object elements, for example, that does not permit permanent omission of the relations R and interfaces I of a structural object. Actual research must still explain these under the object's full definition. Parameters, samples, or measurement precision absent from the original must remain unspecified, not invented for the author. [T-47；T-41；T-D0]

Example one (grouping-gain test, predictive-gain subtype) asks about predictive grouping gain for a candidate group of units. Fix beforehand the candidate group, boundary/state variables/time window/scale profile/identity criterion, grouping method, complexity-matched null model without that grouping information, the single criterion “out-of-sample predictive gain,” and its metric and threshold. Excellent training-set performance means only fit to those data, not out-of-sample gain. Loss of gain after a slight boundary perturbation fails the predetermined robustness requirement; replication in independent time blocks is another requirement selected by this example. Read the “failure” of example one in the original with the preceding section as noncompletion of positive-support conditions, not automatic proof of the null model. [T-47；T-G1]

If example one passes under the teaching premise that all conditions hold, it yields only bounded grouping-gain support within the corresponding window. It does not show aligned intentions within the group or identify which route caused the target change. Using this candidate object to pose the question of example two next is a continuation of research, not automatic completion of the causal identification of a channel effect by grouping-gain performance. [T-47；T-G1]

Example two (channel-effect test, controlled-identification subtype) first specifies a channel and target transition, selects only “controlled-perturbation effect,” and uses controlled blockage as the perturbation. Only if a proportionate design excludes shared-input, alternative-channel, selection, and measurement explanations, and blockage produces a target-transition difference exceeding the threshold, does the channel receive candidate causal-carrier status. “Different before and after blockage” cannot be cut out of those complete comparison conditions and treated as sufficient causal proof in every situation. [T-47；T-G2]

Example two specifically assumes only delay was measured. Readers must retain one positive result alongside four gaps: delay is measured; capacity, reliability, controllability, and loss remain unknown. Unknown is neither 0 nor infinity, nor proof that the channel has no effect. Evidence of producing an effect and the extent of measurement across performance dimensions are separate matters. [T-47；T-G2]

Example three (historical-increment test, predictive path dependence) predefines “backlog in the preceding three rounds” as its historical variable and selects only “historical conditional predictive gain.” Controlling the current queue, environmental inputs, and measurement protocol, it asks whether that variable adds out-of-sample predictive information about the next round's target. The study must specify which times “the preceding three rounds” includes and how they are summarized. This section supplies no such calculation rule; it cannot be claimed already set down as an actual data item. [T-47；T-G3]

If example three obtains a proportionate conditional increment, it determines only predictive path dependence. No qualified causal erasure or recovery operation is supplied here. §4.5 also permits causal path dependence to use one uniquely preselected equivalent intervention, but this likewise requires additional causal conditions and a selected outcome exceeding its threshold. This example cannot upgrade to causal path dependence merely because a channel-effect test found a channel or the predictive path dependence subtype supplies predictive gain. Nor should its mention only of erasure/recovery be misread as §4.5 removing the equivalent-intervention route. [T-47；T-G3]

Example three also retains a representational boundary: if the current queue already sufficiently carries the relevant historical information, an additional historical variable may add no gain. That does not negate how the past formed the backlog or how the current carrier continues to act. Conversely, historical predictive information may supplement insufficiently measured current differences. Do not deliberately omit a known current queue to manufacture gain, or infer an established carrier backward from a zero increment. [T-G3]

Example four (scale-closure test, closure-failure subtype) asks only about “conditional-increment information” in closure failure. Before results, fix micro and aggregate scales, mapping M, retained and excluded variables, the metric, and threshold; then ask whether excluded local timing carries conditional information exceeding the threshold given the aggregate variables. Conditional information is not general correlation. An unfavorable result cannot prompt replacement with predictive or intervention gain, or a jump to object conversion under the subtype for object or intervention conversion. [T-47；T-G4]

If example four does not pass its positive criterion, its own null rule still governs; it cannot automatically be called “aggregation is closed.” Corresponding equivalence/sufficiency, sensitivity, and tolerance conditions can support bounded, criterion-specific closure. Without that material, the result remains unresolved. This example has neither an actual results section nor power testing, so this explanation invents no final “supported” or “null conclusion supported” states for the four items. [T-41；T-G4]

The final sentence is the section's key point: the four tests can suggest subsequent questions for one another but do not substitute for one another. Useful grouping does not guarantee that the selected channel is effective; an effective channel does not guarantee historical increments beyond the current representation; historical gain relative to one representation does not guarantee that variables excluded by the selected scale mapping satisfy the information criterion of the scale-closure test. The latter two may concern different variables, representations, windows, and targets. Similar names do not create automatic inference. [T-47]

This separation does not prevent the same material from supporting several different facts, but specify exactly which step it supports and retain the shared-source relationship rather than counting independent reviews repeatedly. When one test is unresolved, other independently grounded conclusions may remain; only higher-level claims actually dependent on that gap must stop. The cards clarify local responsibilities, rather than requiring the world to traverse grouping gain→channel effect→historical increment→scale closure as universal mandatory stages. [T-47；T-missing；T-source]

Example one's teaching conclusion should be called “bounded grouping-gain support within the corresponding window.” It creates no fact of candidate-unit existence and supplies no evidence in place of example two's channel effect, example three's additional historical information, or example four's representational closure. Independently established object facts remain on their original grounds if any one item fails.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    First label examples one to four as fictional teaching tests, without external observations or empirical truth assigned to them.

  2. 2

    Example one fixes in advance a predictive grouping comparison and checks out-of-sample performance, boundaries, and independent time blocks. At most it answers bounded grouping-gain support.

  3. 3

    Example two separately fixes the channel and controlled perturbation to identify candidate causal carriage. Retain the measured delay alongside the four unknown dimensions in this example.

  4. 4

    Example three separately fixes the preceding-three-round historical variable and conditional prediction rules, controlling the current queue and other relevant information. Predictive support does not replace causal operations.

  5. 5

    Example four separately fixes the cross-scale mapping and single conditional-information criterion; neither changing the criterion nor switching to object conversion is allowed.

  6. 6

    Passing one item does not directly complete the next, and failure limits only conclusions actually dependent on it. Formal results and null judgments still require complete pre-registration and actual material.

Distinctions to keep clear

Four questions in one setting

Share object clues while separately asking about grouping/channels/history/scale.

≠

One evidence package settles four conclusions

Each still needs its own relevant material and criterion.

Positive-support failure in example one

Effective only on training samples, or robustness/review conditions unmet.

≠

Supported null model

Requires a separate null-conclusion rule and qualified test.

Measured delay in example two

Observations exist only for that dimension.

≠

Other dimensions unknown

The channel's effect does not automatically fill them in.

Predictive path dependence in example three

Out-of-sample historical increment beyond the current representation.

≠

Causal path dependence

Additionally requires a preselected qualified causal operation and effect.

Conditional-information criterion in example four

One test under a fixed scale mapping.

≠

Prediction/intervention criterion or conversion subtype

Cannot replace the original claim after results.

Teaching construction: a channel can have an effect while historical residuals remain zeroTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe structural equations, distribution of H, control operation, and current information set (S,c) are artificial assumptions, without noise or omissions. No formal pre-registration of example two or example three was executed.

Use artificial equations to isolate the logic: historical H is equally likely 0/1, and current state S=H. A controllable channel switch c∈{0,1} gives next-step Y=S+c. Holding S fixed, changing c from 0 to 1 changes Y by 1, so the within-model channel effect is nonzero. Given (S,c), Y is uniquely determined, and adding H contributes no predictive information. Thus the channel effect that example two concerns can coexist with zero additional historical information of the kind example three concerns.

BoundaryIt refutes only “a channel effect necessarily implies an additional historical increment”; it does not establish the result of any actual channel-effect test or historical-increment test.

Teaching construction: cards with numbers must still retain material statusTeaching scenario

Assumptions2 seconds and both cards are teaching assumptions, not observed values reported by the original.

Suppose one illustrative card for example two reads “delay=2 seconds,” while another reads “delay unknown.” If the former is merely a constructed assumption, it still cannot become an actual measurement. The latter honestly retains an unknown without denying a possible channel effect. Using the former in an actual test requires separate material on clocks, starting and ending points, logs, and comparison conditions.

BoundaryNo actual channel experiment is conducted, and invented numbers do not fill the original test's results record.

  • Author-constructed conditional counterexample: an artificial simulation is run one thousand times, then examples one to four are said to have one thousand real-world reviews. Computational repetition does not create external observations.
  • This section provides no actual samples, effect sizes, numerical thresholds, evidence and analysis materials, or final outcome states. Explanation must not disguise these missing items as executed research.

Scope and open questions

This section explicitly explains the original book's pre-registration demonstration in a fictional model and makes no claim about effects in actual cases. Adding an external accident cannot turn fictional cards into real tests. Publicly specified conditional constructions and a complete separation of responsibilities directly explain the content.

  • Actual data for examples one to four, numerical thresholds, comparison results, and complete analysis materials are not provided in the original. Their teaching purpose does not require inventing them.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    After example one passes, what must example two still examine?

  2. 2

    If example two measures only delay, should reliability be recorded as 0 or 100%?

  3. 3

    When is the preceding-three-round backlog variable defined? Why not select the most favorable three rounds afterward?

  4. 4

    Is example three's historical predictive gain sufficient to support causal path dependence?

  5. 5

    What if example four's information criterion lacks support but its predictive criterion performs well?

  6. 6

  7. 7

    In the teaching equation Y=S+c, why does H add no information once S and c are known?

After example one passes, what must example two still examine?

A channel, single perturbation criterion, proportionate identification comparison, and target difference are still required. Useful grouping prediction does not establish effectiveness of that channel.

Basis: Chinese source lines 697–701 and 731.

If example two measures only delay, should reliability be recorded as 0 or 100%?

Neither. The material supplies no reliability value. Retain unknown status and explain the missing trial denominator, conditions, and success definition.

Basis: Chinese source line 725; §4.4.

When is the preceding-three-round backlog variable defined? Why not select the most favorable three rounds afterward?

Define it before seeing future outcomes and specify the window/calculation rule. Post-result selection changes the confirmatory question and may introduce selection or leakage.

Basis: Chinese source line 727; §4.5.

Is example three's historical predictive gain sufficient to support causal path dependence?

No. A uniquely preselected erasure, restoration, or equivalent intervention and corresponding causal-identification/threshold conditions are also required. This example lacks that material.

Basis: §4.5, Chinese source lines 673–679.

What if example four's information criterion lacks support but its predictive criterion performs well?

Retain the original information-criterion result and label the predictive discovery as another question or exploration. The original success conditions cannot be replaced afterward.

Basis: Chinese source line 729.

Does repeated execution of a fictional model increase the count of real empirical support?

No. It can test code or within-model relations, but creates no external observation.

Basis: Chinese source line 721; §4.17.2.

In the teaching equation Y=S+c, why does H add no information once S and c are known?

Current information already uniquely determines Y. Adding H cannot further distinguish the answer to this target, although c's within-model effect on Y remains 1.

Basis: The explicit structural equations in this section.

4.8The Five Epistemic Constraints (E1–E5) ​

In briefThese five constraints govern “on what grounds we judge”: clarify the object, visible scope, and whether observation participates; retain competing explanations; and test cross-scale connections.
4.8Note

Understanding this section

4.8 The five epistemic constraints (E1–E5)

These five constraints govern “on what grounds we judge”: clarify the object, visible scope, and whether observation participates; retain competing explanations; and test cross-scale connections.

The original parent section at Chinese source lines 733–734 contains only a heading, without additional body text. What follows is navigation to five independent subsections, not a new empirical law. The “Constraint on Object Declaration” limits object declarations; “Observation Position and Model Limits” limits what records and models can see; “Conditional Observational Participation” requires an actual causal channel for observational participation; “Retaining Competing Explanations and Residuals” compares competing explanations that would alter judgment and retains residuals; “Testing Cross-Scale Transfer” checks cross-scale transfer. [T-Eintro；T-E1；T-E2；T-E3；T-E4；T-E5]

These epistemological and methodological constraints first govern analysts' reasoning. Following a methodological rule does not automatically cause a real mechanism to occur. Complete items, coherent explanations, and cross-scale diagrams cannot replace specific evidence. Conversely, insufficient material on one item should limit only conclusions actually dependent on it, rather than declare the whole world unknowable. [T-roles；T-missing]

The five constraints are not a checklist for mechanically increasing costs. Locate gaps in the object's items by inference rather than expanding material endlessly. Do not demand more viewpoints when the representation already suffices for the current task. Do not invent competing explanations merely to reach a count when none is reasonable. Transfer testing also does not require first finding scale-closure failure. Each subsection specifies when to add evidence, narrow, retain, or stop. [T-E1；T-E2；T-E4；T-E5]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    First identify the object, observation, and comparison grounds required by the current claim.

  2. 2

    Review the distinct responsibilities of the five constraints without treating methodological compliance as mechanism evidence.

  3. 3

    Limit gaps locally while retaining independently established bounded conclusions.

Distinctions to keep clear

Methodological constraint

Specifies how analysis remains grounded and within bounds.

≠

Law of the world

A normative method cannot directly imply that an object must behave that way.

What does not follow

  • This parent section is only chapter navigation and cannot replace the independent explanations in the five subsections below.
  • The number of methodological rules does not accumulate empirical support or authorize collecting personal information or undertaking real interventions.

Scope and open questions

The original parent section contains only a heading; its applicable content is navigation among five subsection responsibilities. No unrelated empirical story is forced onto the navigation.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    After all five are checked off, has the actual mechanism been proved?

  2. 2

    Must every question add observational perspectives?

After all five are checked off, has the actual mechanism been proved?

No. Every specific assertion still requires material and identification conditions. Completed methodology does not automatically establish facts about the object.

Basis: §2.2 and the five subsections.

Must every question add observational perspectives?

No. “Observation Position and Model Limits” explicitly assesses sufficiency for the specific task rather than mechanically seeking more perspectives.

4.8.1Constraint on Object Declaration (E1) ​

In briefFirst clarify whom, which period, which scope, and what you are judging; then ask whether the material is sufficient. Identify the specific effects of missing items rather than invalidating evidenced facts along with them.

For the current judgment, this constraint requires the object, scope, scale, time window, necessary variables, and the object's identity conditions to be made clear; comparative claims must also specify the corresponding baseline or null model. When an item is missing, state which inferred conclusion it limits and how; independently established source facts must not be canceled merely because an item is missing from the format. When the seven elements of a structural object (§3.1) are incomplete, the analyst's grouping must not be declared an objective structure. Ordinary facts, textual meanings, and mathematical proofs are still reviewed under their own evidence and burden of argument.

4.8.1Note

Understanding this section

4.8.1 Constraint on Object Declaration (E1)

First clarify whom, which period, which scope, and what you are judging; then ask whether the material is sufficient. Identify the specific effects of missing items rather than invalidating evidenced facts along with them.

Chinese source line 737 requires explicit specification of the object, scope, scale, time window, necessary variables, and identity. An object is more than a name: should an institution with the same name be compared by the same standards before and after restructuring? Can one week's logs represent the entire year? Are individual averages, organizational aggregates, and regional totals answering the same question? These matters must be stated first; otherwise apparently consistent statements may refer to different objects. [T-E1; T-D0]

Comparative claims separately declare a baseline or null model. For example, “faster processing” must specify faster than which process, under which identical task and window. A receipt record only establishes that a record exists at a particular time; a control group need not be invented merely to state this limited fact. A null model belongs to the definition of a specific comparison. It should not be inserted into the seven elements of a structural object (§3.1) and used to declare that all facts must first pass the same test. [T-E1; T-D0; T-41]

The key is to locate gaps relative to inferences. If a log gives dates and items but no identity criterion across years, it may still support “this item was recorded on this day” while failing to support “the same mechanism operated throughout ten years.” Where scale or boundaries are missing, an analyst's convenient grouping cannot directly be declared an objective structure; this does not make sourced people, events, or texts vanish. [T-E1; T-missing]

Ordinary facts, textual meaning, and mathematical proofs are reviewed under their respective responsibilities. Textual interpretation checks versions, context, and argument; mathematical propositions check domains, assumptions, and derivations; empirical effects check objects, design, and material. A complete mathematical counterexample cannot be required to undergo real-world sampling before its logical force is recognized; nor can the rigor of mathematical expressions perform measurement for an empirical object. [T-E1; T-form]

The constraint on object declaration thus guards against both upgrading “I drew a boundary” into “it is an entity” and overreaching from “one field is blank” to “all material is invalid.” Supplementing information should focus on the inference actually disputed, not endlessly expand collection. Actual adoption also requires separate checks of necessity, protection, and permissions. [T-E1; T-missing]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Specify the object, scope, scale, window, variables, and identity criterion of the current judgment.

  2. 2

    If claiming comparative advantage or difference, separately list a matching baseline or null model.

  3. 3

    For each gap, identify the inference it blocks while preserving sourced facts that do not depend on it.

  4. 4

    Continue review under the distinct responsibilities for ordinary facts, textual interpretation, formal proof, and empirical effects.

Distinctions to keep clear

Object declaration

Makes the object in question locatable.

≠

Grouping gain

Still requires the corresponding empirical comparison; it cannot follow from a grouping's name.

Comparison baseline

Bound to a specific comparative claim.

≠

Any ordinary fact

Not every source record requires first establishing a formal test.

A locally missing item

Limits inferences that depend on it.

≠

All material is invalid

Does not automatically follow.

Teaching construction: one record can support a small fact without supporting a broad comparisonTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe log's reliability and content are teaching assumptions; no actual document A or institution exists.

Suppose a reliable teaching log explicitly records “document A received on day 5,” but provides no completion time, alternative process, or records for other months. Within the assumptions, one may say that A was received; one cannot say that processing was faster than process B or that all months were the same. Missing comparative and extrapolation material limits the latter two questions without canceling the first.

BoundaryIn reality, the log's source, terminology, and record-generation process require checking; assumed reliability cannot be treated as empirical certification.

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleConstructed conditional counterexample: because it is unknown whether an institution meets an identity criterion after restructuring, someone declares that evidenced documents issued before restructuring do not exist. This wrongly cancels independent facts through an intertemporal gap.

What it limitsLimits the unconditional chain of inference addressed in this section while preserving evidenced, bounded conclusions.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari, On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation

Teaching counterexampleConstructed conditional counterexample: dividing a list into three color groups and then claiming three objective mechanisms have been identified. Color labels supply no evidence of grouping gain.

What it limitsLimits the unconditional chain of inference addressed in this section while preserving evidenced, bounded conclusions.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari, On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation

What does not follow

  • Constructed conditional counterexample: because it is unknown whether an institution meets an identity criterion after restructuring, someone declares that evidenced documents issued before restructuring do not exist. This wrongly cancels independent facts through an intertemporal gap.
  • Constructed conditional counterexample: dividing a list into three color groups and then claiming three objective mechanisms have been identified. Color labels supply no evidence of grouping gain.
  • Scope, scale, and the identity criterion also cannot be changed after seeing results to accommodate them without retaining a version record.

Scope and open questions

This section concerns rules for object declaration and evidential responsibilities. Explicit teaching records separate the logic. There is no specific empirical-mechanism claim, so unrelated historical stories are not attached as supposed proof of the rules.

  1. 1

    Without data from another process, can an existing receipt log still be confirmed?

  2. 2

    If a structural object lacks an identity criterion, which conclusions are especially affected?

  3. 3

    Can a mathematical counterexample undermine the unconditional logical inference it targets without a real-world experiment?

Without data from another process, can an existing receipt log still be confirmed?

The log's own provenance may support a limited fact of receipt; it cannot establish comparative process quality.

Basis: Chinese source line 737.

If a structural object lacks an identity criterion, which conclusions are especially affected?

Comparisons depending on the same object across periods or changes are especially affected. The specific effect must still be explained claim by claim, without indiscriminately canceling other evidenced facts.

Basis: Chinese source line 737 and §3.1.

Can a mathematical counterexample undermine the unconditional logical inference it targets without a real-world experiment?

Yes, provided the model's premises and derivation hold; whether reality satisfies that model requires separate evidence.

Basis: §2.1.2。

4.8.2Observation Position and Model Limits (E2) ​

In briefEvery observation reveals some things and leaves others unseen. Whether to look again depends on whether the omission could change the answer to the current task.

Observation positions, measurement channels, and model choices limit what is visible; one record must not be treated as the object's entire state. Nor does this constraint presuppose that every specific task must add perspectives. Whether a representation is sufficient depends on the target, horizon, environment, and admissible operations. Invisibility is not the same as nonexistence. When blind spots relevant to the task are substantial, evidence should be added, the use narrowed, or the judgment kept unresolved; whether probing is possible still requires comparing risks, time windows, and authorization.

4.8.2Note

Understanding this section

4.8.2 Observation Position and Model Limits (E2)

Every observation reveals some things and leaves others unseen. Whether to look again depends on whether the omission could change the answer to the current task.

Chinese source line 741 says, in translation, “One kind of record cannot be treated as the object's entire state.” Position affects who and which stages can be reached; the measurement channel determines what is recorded; model choice determines which differences are preserved. A customer-service phone line covers only callers; an instrument measures only its designed quantities; an aggregate model may not retain positional differences. These scopes require item-by-item checking. “We have data” cannot bypass how those data were generated. [T-E2; T-measure]

But the constraint “Observation Position and Model Limits” does not presume that every task needs an additional viewpoint. If the current question asks only for a recorded total of like items, a reliable, complete aggregate table may suffice; if the question changes to which position is overloaded, that same total may be insufficient. Sufficiency depends on objectives, deadlines, environment, and permitted operations. More observations are not inherently better, and extra information may add cost, delay, or privacy burdens. [T-E2; T-D3]

“Invisibility is not the same as nonexistence” limits inference from a blank record to negation in the world. Treating absence as counterevidence requires reasons to expect that the event would generate a record, that the record would be preserved, and that it could be found in this search. Conversely, invisibility is not evidence of existence either. Mark unknown or unobservable states; “it may be hidden” cannot exempt every conjecture from testing. [T-E2; T-evidence; T-source]

When task-relevant blind spots are substantial, three justified responses are available: supplement with proportionate evidence, narrow the use, or remain unresolved. For example, inability to identify affected positions can halt a claim of harmlessness across the whole domain while preserving facts about measured positions. Supplementing evidence need not mean collecting more personal information; it may mean adjusting the question, using public aggregates, or obtaining credible review. The choice is constrained by protection, costs, and authorization. [T-E2; T-evidence]

Whether probing is permitted is a separate decision. A high-risk operation does not automatically gain permission because “trying it will tell us”; waiting may also miss a window or cause harm. Compare known risks, reversibility, deadlines, and authorization, choosing proportionate protection or evidence collection under current evidence. “Observation Position and Model Limits” must not be misread as requiring permanent inaction or complete knowledge before action. [T-E2]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Record observational positions, measurement channels, models, and data-generation processes.

  2. 2

    Compare observed information with the current objective, deadline, environment, and operations to assess whether blind spots are relevant.

  3. 3

    Do not infer nonexistence directly from lack of a record, or existence from possible invisibility.

  4. 4

    If blind spots materially affect the task, supplement evidence, limit use, or remain unresolved; probing separately requires checking risk windows and permissions.

Distinctions to keep clear

Bounded record

Measurement may be accurate while covering only a portion.

≠

Invalid record

Lack of complete knowledge alone does not justify this judgment.

More viewpoints

Sometimes improve task information.

≠

Additional viewpoints are required every time

The original text explicitly makes no such presumption.

Invisible

The material cannot provide an answer.

≠

Nonexistent / already existent

Both conclusions require corresponding evidence.

Mathematical teaching construction: the same total has different sufficiency for two questionsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe states and queries are constructed; the quantities are of the same kind, and the recorded total is error-free.

Counts at two positions may be (4,6) or (0,10), both totaling 10. If only the total is asked, the representation 10 suffices. If the question is “does the first position contain any quantity,” the two states give different answers, so the representation 10 is insufficient. Adding positional observations must be justified by the latter task's requirements, not by the belief that finer data are inherently more advanced.

BoundaryNo actual institution is simulated, and this does not establish the necessity of, or authorization for, collecting personal details in reality.

NASA investigation: what an electrical test can establish, and what it still cannot seeDocumented case

Determinations (4), in the continuation of item 7 on printed page 5-13 of the Apollo 13 investigation report, states that an external 500-volt withstand test could not reveal the extent of possible internal insulation damage. It showed only that, with the relative wire positions at the time of the test, that potential could be withstood without breakdown. This section adds attention to the measurement channel and current use: a test can produce a genuinely valid bounded result while not covering the full internal state.

SourceNASA Apollo 13 Review Board report1970-06-15, Chapter 5, item 7 continued, Determinations (4), printed 5-13, PDF p. 179Reading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsThis is the report's limitation on a particular electrical test, not a universal claim that withstand testing is invalid. The passage is not extended into the entire accident mechanism or any individual's prior knowledge, nor does it require unlimited testing for every task.

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleConstructed conditional counterexample: an aggregate table completely answers “what is the total,” yet private details about every person are demanded before that total is accepted. This confuses task sufficiency with reconstruction of the entire state.

What it limitsLimits the unconditional chain of inference addressed in this section while preserving evidenced, bounded conclusions.

What it limitsLimits the unconditional chain of inference addressed in this section while preserving evidenced, bounded conclusions.

Teaching counterexampleConstructed conditional counterexample: a single test detects no damage, and all internal equipment states are directly inferred to be intact. The conclusion exceeds the measurement channel.

What it limitsLimits the unconditional chain of inference addressed in this section while preserving evidenced, bounded conclusions.

What does not follow

  • Constructed conditional counterexample: an aggregate table completely answers “what is the total,” yet private details about every person are demanded before that total is accepted. This confuses task sufficiency with reconstruction of the entire state.
  • Constructed conditional counterexample: a system does not record offline activities, and the absence of logs is taken to mean that offline activities never occurred. The record-generation conditions do not support this denial.
  • Constructed conditional counterexample: a single test detects no damage, and all internal equipment states are directly inferred to be intact. The conclusion exceeds the measurement channel.

Scope and open questions

This section directly addresses actual measurement limits. The original NASA report's qualification of a specific electrical test illustrates bounded validity, while a mathematical example shows that not every question requires another viewpoint.

If the total is correct but positions are unknown, which answers can still be retained?

The answer about the total may be retained; position-dependent judgments are limited, and whether to supplement evidence depends on the task.

Basis: Chinese source line 741 and the teaching counterexample.

Why does failure to find a log not always refute an event?

First check whether this kind of event should have left a record, whether that record should have been preserved, and whether this search should have found it; otherwise absence may reflect a channel blind spot.

Basis: §2.7.1, Chinese source line 375.

May risky probing be conducted directly to fill a blind spot?

No. Probing requires comparing risks, windows, and authorization; the need for more evidence does not automatically confer permission to operate.

Basis: Chinese source line 741.
