4.8.3Conditional Observational Participation (E3) ​

In briefObservation, naming, or rating sometimes enters an object's environment for action, but “a change occurred after observation” is insufficient. “Conditional Observational Participation” requires finding the actual connection and explaining what would happen without this kind of observation.

Only when observation, naming, scoring, or publication enters into actual causal coupling with the object does it count as observational participation. Temporal order alone, or a mechanism story that “being observed changes the object,” is insufficient to pass this constraint; a specific channel must be located, and a counterfactual comparison established: what happens without observation, what happens under a different observation, or what happens when the channel is blocked.

4.8.3Note

Understanding this section

4.8.3 Conditional Observational Participation (E3)

Observation, naming, or rating sometimes enters an object's environment for action, but “a change occurred after observation” is insufficient. “Conditional Observational Participation” requires finding the actual connection and explaining what would happen without this kind of observation.

The limiting phrase in Chinese source line 745 is “Only when ... enters into actual causal coupling.” An analyst privately writing a name does not automatically change the studied object merely through naming. A testable candidate for participation arises when, for example, a platform displays a rating, an institution adopts a classification, or an observation device changes measured conditions. One must still record what information or operation traveled through which channel, reached whom, and caused what change when. [T-E3; T-causal]

Temporal order is one necessary check, but not sufficient proof. Behavioral change after publication may result from simultaneous policy, environmental, or sample changes; “people care about evaluations” is only a possible mechanism. Locate the actual channel, then establish counterfactual comparisons involving no observation, alternative observation, or blockage. Whether using experiments, natural variation, or another design, disclose identification conditions and limits. [T-E3; T-causal]

The three comparisons serve different purposes: a no-observation condition compares the presence and absence of the observational arrangement; alternative observation compares different display, notification, or measurement methods; blockage compares outcomes when the signal cannot arrive or cannot continue to act. This does not require dangerously removing oversight or protection to obtain a control, nor does it mean every object can safely undergo these operations. Research design and eligibility for actual implementation require separate arguments. [T-E3]

The target of participation may be behavior, expression, material distribution, or subsequent feedback. A change in one target cannot settle every target. Sending a notice does not mean it was received; receipt does not mean behavior changed; and behavioral change does not automatically support a psychological explanation. Actual causal coupling may occur through physical or informational paths; it does not assign intentions to devices, platforms, or statistical indicators. [T-E3; T-H4]

Thus neither the unconditional claim that all observation changes objects nor the view that observers are absolutely external is acceptable. “Conditional Observational Participation” requires a conditional, fallible judgment: if a channel does not reach its target, alternative inputs explain the difference, or the comparison lacks identification, retain a candidate or unresolved status. Further action involving publication and feedback also requires separate checks of protection, permissions, and consequences. [T-E3; T-causal]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Define the specific version of observation, naming, rating, or publication and the target change.

  2. 2

    Locate the channel through which it actually reaches the object and enters subsequent processes.

  3. 3

    Use proportionate no-observation, alternative-observation, or blockage comparisons to distinguish shared conditions and selection explanations.

  4. 4

    Determine only the supported scope of participation. Separate receipt, behavioral change, and psychological mechanisms; actual operations require separate permission checks.

Distinctions to keep clear

Temporal succession

Observation comes first, change follows.

≠

Causal participation

Also requires actual coupling and an identifiable counterfactual.

Signal published

An output record exists.

≠

Object responded

Requires checking arrival, receipt, and subsequent change.

Effect of a platform rating

Information and rules produce effects through channels.

≠

The platform has intentions

An effect cannot directly justify personification.

Conditional-counterfactual teaching example: isolated records versus records entering decisionsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsIsolation, display, the threshold, and the response rule are all stipulated; this does not pretend that real people's responses to scores all follow this pattern.

Suppose the same teaching score R has two channels. Channel A writes R into an offline, isolated archive that, by assumption, has no path to the next action. Channel B displays R to a decision-maker, with the stipulated behavioral rule A=1 if and only if R reaches the threshold. Channel A has no behavioral channel under the assumptions; channel B can change A in a comparison that crosses the threshold. This shows that participation depends on channels and response rules, rather than on ‘the score exists.’

BoundaryIn reality, actual reception and behavioral differences still require testing. An assumed rule cannot replace empirical research or user consent.

A real randomized experiment: how prior ratings enter the environment for subsequent ratingsDocumented case

Muchnik, Aral, and Taylor's 2013 Science paper reports randomly assigning new comments on a social-news website to a positive-vote, negative-vote, or control group. The paper explains that users see a comment's current score alongside the comment. The experiment thus makes visible prior ratings the channel of change, rather than merely comparing naturally occurring high and low scores. The paper reports that prior ratings changed subsequent rating behavior. This section concerns ratings actually entering the environment for later observation and choice; it does not generalize ‘a researcher is watching’ into an all-purpose reflexivity claim.

SourceMuchnik et al., Social Influence Bias: A Randomized Experiment, public copy of the original publicationScience341(6146),2013-08-09:647–651; comment-display and random-vote-assignment paragraphs on printed page 647, explanation of randomized comparison on page 648; public abstract (PDF pages 2–3)Reading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsOnly the platform display, randomized operation, and reported behavioral effects described in the original publication are used. Data and supplementary material were not recalculated, current formal eligibility as a “Power, Mediation, and Reflexivity” test or a channel-effect test was not checked, and individual users' subjective motives are not inferred. This does not authorize manipulating ratings on real platforms.

Read the case and sources

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleConstructed conditional counterexample: a researcher names historical photographs offline; the names are neither published nor entered into any channel affecting the objects. The word “naming” alone cannot establish that the objects' behavior at the time was changed.

What it limitsLimits the unconditional chain of inference addressed in this section while preserving evidenced, bounded conclusions.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari, On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation

Teaching counterexampleConstructed conditional counterexample: task difficulty decreases at the same time that evaluation scores are published. Increased output cannot be attributed entirely and directly to score publication; simultaneous changes should be compared.

What it limitsLimits the unconditional chain of inference addressed in this section while preserving evidenced, bounded conclusions.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari, On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation

What does not follow

  • Constructed conditional counterexample: a researcher names historical photographs offline; the names are neither published nor entered into any channel affecting the objects. The word “naming” alone cannot establish that the objects' behavior at the time was changed.
  • Constructed conditional counterexample: task difficulty decreases at the same time that evaluation scores are published. Increased output cannot be attributed entirely and directly to score publication; simultaneous changes should be compared.
  • When the actual channel is unknown, do not fill the gap with a reflexivity story; nor may a control be fabricated because a particular manipulation is ethically impermissible.

Scope and open questions

This section directly discusses observations or ratings entering an object. It uses the original randomized-rating study to check the actual display channel and comparison, retaining the distinction between behavioral effects and psychological explanations.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    If an object changes after being named, can this be determined to be observational participation?

  2. 2

    If a score is published but nobody receives it, has it been established that the score changed behavior?

  3. 3

    If an actual experiment finds a change in aggregate subsequent ratings, can one say that every person psychologically conformed?

If an object changes after being named, can this be determined to be observational participation?

No. Temporal order alone is insufficient; locate an actual causal channel and an appropriate counterfactual comparison.

Basis: Chinese source line 745.

If a score is published but nobody receives it, has it been established that the score changed behavior?

No. Publication, arrival, reception, and behavioral effects each require evidence.

Basis: Chinese source line 745 and channel requirements.

If an actual experiment finds a change in aggregate subsequent ratings, can one say that every person psychologically conformed?

No. Aggregate behavioral effects, individual psychological mechanisms, and heterogeneity are different questions.

Basis: The original publication's scope of support and this section's causal limitations.

4.8.4Retaining Competing Explanations and Residuals (E4) ​

In briefA good explanation must do more than make sense: it must specify which other explanations it genuinely conflicts with, which evidence remains unexplained, and allow new evidence to change the judgment.

In an explanation, competing accounts that the materials permit and that are sufficient to change the judgment should be compared, and counterexamples and unexplained residuals retained. What the competing explanations dispute must be specified: the size of an effect, its mechanism, contextual meaning, the scope of extrapolation, or normative premises. In the comparison, the evidential requirements, judgments about sources, and tests used to support or weaken one explanation must be applied equally to the explanations competing with it, including the explanation the analyst favors and explanations written in this framework’s terms. Where the standard has been relaxed for one side, or that side has been allowed to add auxiliary conditions to accommodate exceptions, the other sides must be given the same latitude; the added conditions must themselves have independent grounds and must not be added merely to explain a known failure (§16.3). Where the threshold for accepting materials of the same kind differs, a reason that does not depend on the conclusion to be established must be stated, for example that the two kinds of reports differ in how hard they are to observe, or that the conclusions differ in use and risk (§1.5.2). This requirement constrains the standard; it does not require the sides to reach the same conclusion, nor that their evidence carry equal weight.

Compatible explanations can each bear responsibilities at different layers. When several compatible explanations together account for a set of phenomena, state which phenomena and conditions each bears; a counterexample must not be reassigned to another explanation after the fact, and the baseline of comparison must not move with the results.

Whether or not an explanation is compatible with others, its failure conditions must be able to occur under the rules of determination or interpretation actually adopted. If an explanation reads opposite outcomes, and both the assent and the denial of the persons concerned, as support, then none of these outcomes and statements can be counted as support for it; this does not entail that the explanation is false, nor that the denial of the persons concerned is counterevidence. The analyst must separately state an observation that is obtainable in reality and is not reinterpreted under the same rule, as its failure condition; where none can be stated and the explanation is used for a strong judgment, the item “contrary conditions” in the strong-judgment kit is treated as missing (§13.5).

When no reasonable competing explanation is available, one must not be fabricated merely to fill a quota, but the scope of the search and failure conditions must still be stated. Openness, love, complexity, or a sense of theoretical wholeness cannot fill gaps in evidence. How competing explanations that have not yet been distinguished limit action must be judged in conjunction with harm, reversibility, external obligations, and current permissions.

4.8.4Note

Understanding this section

4.8.4 Retaining competing explanations and residuals (E4)

A good explanation must do more than make sense: it must specify which other explanations it genuinely conflicts with, which evidence remains unexplained, and allow new evidence to change the judgment.

Chinese source line 749 requires comparing competing accounts ‘that the materials permit and that are sufficient to change the judgment.’ Evidence-permitted excludes arbitrary, groundless imagination; sufficient to change the judgment excludes irrelevant details. The strongest opposing account should address the same object, target, and evidence, rather than serving as an obviously absurd stand-in that lets one's own explanation win easily. [T-E4]

First clarify the point of dispute. The parties may disagree about effect size, the operative mechanism, a text's meaning in context, the populations to which results generalize, or the value premises underlying action. Effect-size evidence cannot automatically resolve a dispute about normative justification, and interpretation of word meanings cannot replace causal identification. If one account concerns upstream formation and another downstream execution, they may be compatible; there is no need to eliminate one merely to manufacture a binary choice, but state which phenomena and conditions each bears; a counterexample must not be reassigned to another explanation after the fact. [T-E4；T-roles]

A counterexample is material that limits a claim; a residual is what a model or explanation has yet to explain. Residuals may arise from measurement error, omitted variables, changes in the domain of application, or model error. They are not automatically positive evidence for another grand theory. Retain their location, magnitude or content, and timing, and specify which subsequent evidence might distinguish their causes. Do not delete records that fail to match expectations after seeing results. [T-E4；T-evidence]

If there is no reasonable competing explanation, do not invent one to meet a quota. Honestly state the scope of material searched or checked, why existing alternatives are insufficient, and the conditions under which the explanation could fail. ‘None found yet’ must not become ‘no alternative exists anywhere.’ Conversely, failure to distinguish mechanisms does not cancel established observations or bounded total effects independent of those mechanisms. [T-E4；T-causal]

Openness, love, complexity, and a sense of theoretical wholeness cannot fill evidence gaps. They may influence question selection or normative discussion, but when channels, comparisons, or textual grounds are absent, these words cannot turn unresolved matters into proven ones. ‘Complex’ is also no reason to regard arbitrary conclusions as equally reliable; claims must still be limited by the strength of support. [T-E4]

How unresolved explanations constrain action depends on consequences, rather than a blanket rule. Some reversible, low-risk measures may be appropriate under multiple explanations; some irreversible decisions with high potential harm rely more heavily on certainty about mechanisms and protection. External obligations, the current window, and authority must also be checked. Incomplete knowledge does not automatically imply complete inaction, and urgency does not justify ignoring unknowns. [T-E4]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Determine whether competing accounts address the same disputed point and are permitted by the evidence.

  2. 2

    Distinguish effects, mechanisms, context, extrapolation, and normative premises; compatible levels may coexist.

  3. 3

    Retain counterexamples and residuals, specifying which conclusions they limit and what subsequent evidence could distinguish explanations.

  4. 4

    If there is no reasonable alternative, report the search scope and failure conditions; do not fabricate competition.

  5. 5

    Judge the implications of unresolved matters for action by harm, reversibility, external obligations, and authority.

Distinctions to keep clear

Competing mechanisms

Different accounts of the cause of the same effect.

≠

Compatible levels

Upstream formation and downstream execution may be described simultaneously.

Unexplained residual

A difference not yet explained by the current model.

≠

Another theory is established

This does not follow from the former alone.

No alternative found in a search

A result within the stated scope.

≠

No alternative exists

The conclusion cannot automatically be expanded.

Mathematical teaching construction: identical observations can correspond to different causal explanationsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe equations, distribution, and operation form constructed causal models, not real data; other variables are omitted to isolate the logic.

Let U be 0/1 with equal probability, with T=U during observation. Model A sets Y=T; model B sets Y=U. Both therefore produce only (T,Y)=(0,0) or (1,1) observationally, with identical association. If do(T=1) is allowed while U's distribution is unchanged, model A always gives Y=1, whereas model B still gives Y=0 half the time. The models thus agree on observations but differ under the specified intervention.

BoundaryThis indicates which new comparisons might distinguish the accounts; it neither authorizes an intervention nor claims that reality must be one of the two models.

Competing explanations in the same rating study: quality or prior influence?Documented case

On printed page 647, the 2013 rating paper above notes that an item receiving high scores both in the past and in the future may reflect prior evaluations influencing later judgments, or simply the item's initially high quality. The study therefore randomly changes initial ratings, making conditions such as quality comparable across groups by design. This additional location shows that the two explanations dispute the cause of rating associations; it does not count a single record that ‘the platform has high scores’ as two independent pieces of evidence.

SourceMuchnik et al., Science2013The ‘distinguishing influence from uninfluenced agreement’ paragraph on printed page 647 and the paragraph on comparability of randomized groups on page 648; PDF pages 2–3Reading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsThis illustrates how the paper raises and distinguishes a substantive competing-explanation question. It does not claim that randomization removed every possible limitation, check supplementary material, or establish all individual psychological mechanisms. It shares the same study as the case for ‘Conditional Observational Participation’ (§4.8.3) and cannot count cumulatively as independent replication.

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleAuthor-constructed conditional counterexample: because an existing model leaves errors, claiming that those errors must be caused by ‘love’ or ‘wholeness’ lacks discriminating evidence.

What it limitsLimits the unconditional chain of inference addressed in this section while preserving evidenced, bounded conclusions.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari, On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation

Teaching counterexampleAuthor-constructed conditional counterexample: one account says earlier training formed a skill, while another says the current skill supports performance, and a forced choice is imposed. They may be different links in the same chain.

What it limitsLimits the unconditional chain of inference addressed in this section while preserving evidenced, bounded conclusions.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari, On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation

Teaching counterexampleAuthor-constructed conditional counterexample: supplying a claim wholly incompatible with the time and object as a competitor just to provide two viewpoints is not a genuine stress test.

What it limitsLimits the unconditional chain of inference addressed in this section while preserving evidenced, bounded conclusions.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari, On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation

What does not follow

  • Author-constructed conditional counterexample: because an existing model leaves errors, claiming that those errors must be caused by ‘love’ or ‘wholeness’ lacks discriminating evidence.
  • Author-constructed conditional counterexample: one account says earlier training formed a skill, while another says the current skill supports performance, and a forced choice is imposed. They may be different links in the same chain.
  • Author-constructed conditional counterexample: supplying a claim wholly incompatible with the time and object as a competitor just to provide two viewpoints is not a genuine stress test.

Scope and open questions

This section involves a real competing-explanation question, reusing the original quality-versus-social-influence dispute in the rating paper and explicitly noting dependence on the same source. A separate mathematical construction demonstrates discriminating evidence.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    If one explanation concerns formation and another execution, must one be eliminated?

  2. 2

    If no competing explanation can currently be found, should one be invented to complete the table?

  3. 3

    Can an unexplained residual directly establish another grand mechanism?

  4. 4

    If observations in both models satisfy T=Y, does that prove that T causes Y?

If one explanation concerns formation and another execution, must one be eliminated?

Not necessarily. First check whether they genuinely dispute the same conclusion; compatible explanations can each bear responsibilities at different layers, but which phenomena and conditions each bears must be stated.

Basis: Chinese source line 749.

If no competing explanation can currently be found, should one be invented to complete the table?

No. State the checked scope, current limitations, and failure conditions.

Basis: Chinese source line 749.

Can an unexplained residual directly establish another grand mechanism?

No. Residuals require further discrimination among explanations involving measurement, omissions, models, and so on; they cannot be filled in with an unsupported mechanism.

Basis: Chinese source line 749.

If observations in both models satisfy T=Y, does that prove that T causes Y?

No. Teaching model B produces the same observations through common U, but gives a different do(T) result.

Basis: The explicit equations in this section.

4.8.5Testing Cross-Scale Transfer (E5) ​

In briefResults obtained at one scale must be transferred with their mapping and conditions of applicability. A wider observational reach does not confer wider authority, and cross-scale testing need not wait for proof that the macro representation fails.

Cross-scale transfer must pass the tests that scale transformation (§3.4) requires: of the mapping, invariants, changed items, lost items, error, competing explanations, and residuals. The only inferential premise of this constraint is a single definition, that of scale transformation. The two epistemic constraints “Constraint on Object Declaration” (§4.8.1) and “Retaining Competing Explanations and Residuals” (§4.8.4), together with the conditions for evidence (§2.5) and the conditions for analogy (§2.6), are all method requirements here: they do not enter the acyclic graph that inferential premises form (§2.3), nor masquerade as additional empirical causes. This constraint does not depend on the proposition of scale closure being true; conversely, every scale-closure test must pass this constraint. Expansion of observational scope does not imply expansion of authorization scope; the axis of jurisdiction and authorization must not be extrapolated automatically along with the other scale axes.

4.8.5Note

Understanding this section

4.8.5 Testing cross-scale transfer (E5)

Results obtained at one scale must be transferred with their mapping and conditions of applicability. A wider observational reach does not confer wider authority, and cross-scale testing need not wait for proof that the macro representation fails.

Chinese source line 759 limits the hard inferential prerequisite of cross-scale transfer testing to scale transformation (§3.4). Scale transformation supplies a mapping from source to target scale; this constraint tests the invariants, changes, losses, errors, competing explanations, and residuals in that connection. Any claimed invariant must specify the transformations under which it is preserved. One cannot merely write ‘the same structure’ without telling readers how variables and units correspond. [T-E5；T-D3]

For example, mapping individual records to regional means may preserve weighted totals while losing location, distribution, and extreme values; moving from one day to one year may change event aggregation, time windows, and identity requirements. The mapping must specify the task, horizon, environment, and permitted operations. Correct current statistics do not guarantee sufficiency for future evolution or targeted intervention. When losses are found, necessary variables may be added or uses narrowed; recovering all microscopic information is not the default requirement. [T-E5；T-D3]

The constraint on object declaration (§4.8.1), ‘Retaining Competing Explanations and Residuals’ (§4.8.4), the conditions for evidence (§2.5), and the conditions for analogy (§2.6) serve here as method requirements. The constraint on object declaration checks the object, ‘Retaining Competing Explanations and Residuals’ checks competition and residuals, the conditions for evidence check evidential support, and the conditions for analogy prevent smuggling through shared words or similar diagrams. They cannot masquerade as additional empirical causes or be inserted alongside scale transformation as hard inferential prerequisites in the stated acyclic inference graph. These method requirements must still be carried out carefully: ‘not included in that graph’ does not mean they may be omitted. [T-E5；T-analogy；T-evidence]

Cross-scale transfer testing does not depend on the proposition of scale closure (§4.6) being true, but every scale-closure test must pass cross-scale transfer testing. That is, a valid mapping and test come first; afterward one may find closure failure, support bounded closure when the null-conclusion criterion is sufficient, or remain unresolved. Reversing this and requiring scale-closure failure to be found before cross-scale transfer testing can pass prejudges an open test as necessarily yielding nonclosure, creating an improper circularity. [T-E5；T-G4]

Expanding scale also requires preventing a leap from factual scope to authority scope. Statistics covering an entire city do not authorize an analyst to modify every resident's records or direct every institution. Authorization on the axis of jurisdiction and authorization must be independently specified, and cannot expand automatically when spatial, aggregation, or organizational axes expand. Facts, model usability, normative reasons, and actual operational authority are established separately. [T-E5；T-SP]

Genuine cross-domain analogy also cannot replace bridging with similar words. Analogy may help propose channels and counterexamples to examine; empirical support for relations in the target domain still requires target-domain evidence. Cross-scale transfer testing allows a concise representation to transfer successfully, and also allows correct source-scale conclusions to be retained while limiting their use at the new scale. It is not a rule that rejects every transfer. [T-E5；T-analogy]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    State the source/target scales of the scale transformation and the mapping, what is preserved, changed, or lost, units and errors, and the domain of application.

  2. 2

    Use the constraint on object declaration, retaining competing explanations and residuals, the conditions for evidence, and the conditions for analogy as methodological checks, without conflating them with empirical causes or hard inferential prerequisites.

  3. 3

    After testing the mapping and task, judge closure, nonclosure, or unresolved status separately; do not presuppose that a positive scale-closure result must hold.

  4. 4

    If actual adoption is involved, independently check the scope of jurisdiction and authorization and normative procedures; do not infer expanded authorization from expanded observational reach.

Distinctions to keep clear

Hard inferential prerequisite: scale transformation

Provides the mapping that cross-scale transfer testing is to test.

≠

Method requirements

Constrain how the examination is conducted; they remain mandatory but do not masquerade as additional empirical causes.

Cross-scale transfer testing

First check bridging and the scope of support.

≠

Positive scale-closure result

Support for closure failure/transformation that a particular test may obtain, not a prerequisite of cross-scale transfer testing.

Observational scope

Which scales of facts can be studied.

≠

Scope of jurisdiction and authorization

Who may take which actions on which objects is checked separately.

Mathematical teaching construction: weights are also part of scale mappingTeaching scenario

AssumptionsGroup sizes, means, same-type indicators, and absence of missing data are all teaching assumptions; no real population data are provided.

Two groups have 1 and 3 members, with indicator means of 0 and 4 respectively. The overall mean is (1×0+3×4)/(1+3)=3, not 2 from simply averaging the two group means. If the target question is precisely ‘the equally weighted average of the two group means,’ however, 2 is correct. The two values need not mean that one calculation is wrong; the target units and weights differ. An overall mean of 3 also does not mean every individual has a value of 3.

BoundaryNo properties of real groups or allocation rules are presumed, and statistical weights certainly do not generate administrative authorization.

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleAuthor-constructed conditional counterexample: assigning an accurate citywide mean to every neighborhood. An aggregate quantity cannot be reversed into every local value.

What it limitsLimits the unconditional chain of inference addressed in this section while preserving evidenced, bounded conclusions.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari, On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation

Teaching counterexampleAuthor-constructed conditional counterexample: assuming that access to data throughout a domain confers authority to modify or act throughout it. Observation and operation require different authorizations.

What it limitsLimits the unconditional chain of inference addressed in this section while preserving evidenced, bounded conclusions.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari, On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation

Sourced counterexampleSource boundary: cross-scale transfer testing does not depend on a positive scale-closure result being true; ‘first prove nonclosure’ cannot be made the entry requirement for all transfer studies.

What it limitsLimits the unconditional chain of inference addressed in this section while preserving evidenced, bounded conclusions.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari, On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation

What does not follow

  • Author-constructed conditional counterexample: assigning an accurate citywide mean to every neighborhood. An aggregate quantity cannot be reversed into every local value.
  • Author-constructed conditional counterexample: assuming that access to data throughout a domain confers authority to modify or act throughout it. Observation and operation require different authorizations.
  • Source boundary: cross-scale transfer testing does not depend on a positive scale-closure result being true; ‘first prove nonclosure’ cannot be made the entry requirement for all transfer studies.
  • Analogical similarity only generates questions; it cannot replace target-domain evidence. Without a mapping, only side-by-side description is possible.

Scope and open questions

This section explains methodological dependencies and responsibilities in cross-scale transfer. A mathematical construction with explicit weights suffices to show nonequivalence between mappings; unrelated real incidents are not added as a substitute for bridging evidence in the target domain.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    Must cross-scale transfer testing wait for a scale-closure test to establish closure failure before it can be performed?

  2. 2

    If method requirements are excluded from the acyclic inference graph, may they be skipped?

  3. 3

    In the example, which is wrong: 2 or 3?

  4. 4

    Does being able to view citywide data mean one can change citywide rules?

Must cross-scale transfer testing wait for a scale-closure test to establish closure failure before it can be performed?

No. The hard prerequisite of cross-scale transfer testing is scale transformation; scale-closure tests, conversely, must pass cross-scale transfer testing. Transfer testing may yield bounded closure, failure, or unresolved status.

Basis: Chinese source line 759.

If method requirements are excluded from the acyclic inference graph, may they be skipped?

No. They still constrain how a study can hold; they simply do not masquerade as hard inferential prerequisites or empirical causes.

Basis: Chinese source line 759.

In the example, which is wrong: 2 or 3?

The equally weighted average of the two group means is 2; the overall mean across all individuals is 3. Clarify the target unit and weights first.

Basis: The openly stated calculation in the teaching construction.

Does being able to view citywide data mean one can change citywide rules?

No. Authorization within the scope of jurisdiction and authorization and normative/operational responsibilities must be checked independently; they cannot expand with observational scale.

Basis: Chinese source line 759.

4.9Evidential Status of Human-Experience Clauses ​

In briefThis section separates ‘an account of human experience is appealing’ from ‘specific facts have external evidence.’ ‘Meaning and Coordination,’ ‘Power, Mediation, and Reflexivity,’ and ‘Historical Trace Carriers’ each pose testable questions, but no label can complete the testing for a case.

The three human-domain clauses “Meaning and Coordination,” “Power, Mediation, and Reflexivity,” and “Historical Trace Carriers” (§7.1) are empirical hypotheses awaiting testing. The specific factual assertions for all three are tested against their objects and evidence. Under this procedure, eligibility for formal support belongs only to specific tests that have completed the pre-registration and outcome record under §4.2 and met the corresponding criteria; definitions, the descriptions of the human variables, and the framework's own formulations are not external empirical support. Without eligible records of external tests, the record of empirical evidence is empty, and the evidential status is “awaiting evidence from a specific test.”

Thus, “Meaning and Coordination” needs to be tested case by case: preselect only one outcome family among resources, action, or coordination, and test the differences that meaning arrangements make. “Power, Mediation, and Reflexivity” also needs to be tested case by case: preselect only one outcome family among evidence coverage, safety of expression, object behavior, or reflexive response, then establish the channel through which position, mediation, or disclosure conditions act, together with the counterfactual comparison. “Historical Trace Carriers” must preselect only one carrier family, one specific carrier within it, and one durability criterion. Only if the family to which that carrier belongs matches the selected subtype, the historical event, baseline, trace observables, threshold, and durability time window were all fixed before results, and the selected criterion has passed, may candidate traces within the specified carrier and time window be determined, and the predefined historical variable be submitted as a candidate to a historical-increment test.

Historical conditional increments beyond the current representation, and the corresponding repair window, are handled separately by a historical-increment test and the conclusion rule “Historical Effects, Path Differences, and Repair Windows” (§4.12.1). Historical effects transmitted by current carriers and general effects of intervention timing obtain independent grounds under §4.5 and §6.10, respectively. Protection, harm reduction, or repair actions separately go through the conclusion rule “Normative Bridging” (§4.14.1), explicitly stated normative premises, and operational procedures. Clause names, internal definitions, or this framework's own narrative cannot complete the specific tests on behalf of these three clauses.

Understanding this section

4.9 Evidential status of the human-experience clauses

This section separates ‘an account of human experience is appealing’ from ‘specific facts have external evidence.’ ‘Meaning and Coordination,’ ‘Power, Mediation, and Reflexivity,’ and ‘Historical Trace Carriers’ each pose testable questions, but no label can complete the testing for a case.

Chinese source line 763 calls the three human-domain clauses “Meaning and Coordination,” “Power, Mediation, and Reflexivity,” and “Historical Trace Carriers” (§7.1) “empirical hypotheses awaiting testing.” This means they are a kind of question that may be asked, not universal laws already proved by one experiment. “Meaning and Coordination” asks how meaning arrangements affect resources, action, or coordination; “Power, Mediation, and Reflexivity” asks how position, mediation, or publicity conditions affect evidence, expression, behavior, or reflexive response; “Historical Trace Carriers” asks whether a historical event leaves a persistently observable difference in a specified carrier. Their shared human subject matter does not give them a shared success criterion. [T-49; T-42]

Two judgments must be maintained together. First, judge particular facts by their objects and proportionate evidence: an existing study may have reliable results without adopting Xikari's pre-registration. Second, the formal support eligibility this procedure gives to a specific test has its own requirements for prior records and testing. Existing results cannot be used to retrospectively fill in “prior selection” and claim this eligibility. The former judges material from real research; the latter judges the scope determined under this procedure. Failure to obtain the latter does not erase the former. [T-49; T-42; T-domain]

When no record of a qualified external test exists, the record of empirical evidence is empty. This means only that this formal support record is empty; the evidential status is “awaiting evidence from a specific test,” meaning evidence from a specific test is still needed. It does not mean “nothing of this kind has ever happened in the world” or “the hypothesis has been refuted.” An abstract hypothesis awaiting evidence and the four outcome statuses of a specific test occupy different levels. “Supported,” “null conclusion supported,” “not supported or unresolved,” and “not yet evaluated” must be determined according to the pre-registration of the particular test and actual material; an empty record cannot automatically become a zero conclusion. [T-49; T-41; T-42]

The “Meaning and Coordination” test uniquely preselects one outcome family to specify what the meaning arrangement is expected to explain. If the question concerns action choice, predefine candidate meaning arrangements, comparison conditions, action outcomes, and thresholds. A favorable finding in resource allocation or coordination may become another question but cannot retrospectively rescue the original action criterion. The three corresponding success criteria are “effect of the meaning arrangement on resource allocation,” “effect of the meaning arrangement on action choice,” and “effect of the meaning arrangement on coordination outcomes.” Qualified support stops at a conditional orientation anchor within the specified scope; shared vocabulary or aligned action does not establish identical inner states, genuine consent, or a common will. [T-49; T-42; T-H]

The four outcome families of “Power, Mediation, and Reflexivity” ask different questions: evidence coverage concerns which material can be seen; expression safety concerns risks or constraints on expression; object behavior concerns behavioral responses under mediation or publicity conditions; reflexive response concerns responses caused when observation, naming, scoring, or publication enters the object through actual channels. The corresponding success criteria are, respectively, “effect of position or mediation on evidence coverage,” “effect of position or mediation on the safety of expression,” “behavioral response to mediation or publicity,” and “reflexive response to observation or publication.” A difference in one family does not automatically establish the other three; words such as “a platform exists” or “there is power” cannot fill in channels, comparisons, and counterfactuals. [T-49; T-42; T-E3]

“Historical Trace Carriers” locks carrier identity before asking what trace it leaves. The five permitted families are institutional or textual record, role or organizational arrangement, habit or practice, trauma record, and collective memory carrier. These are categories for preselection, not an exhaustive account of every way history exists. The selected carrier family must match the subtype; the selected specific carrier must be exactly one and not empty, not a list of candidate carriers from which a survivor is eventually chosen. [T-42; T-49]

The “Historical Trace Carriers” test must also uniquely preselect one durability criterion: “stays above the threshold over the pre-registered window,” “detected again across pre-registered windows,” or “persists after the event or exposure ends.” Historical event, baseline, observable quantity, threshold, and persistence window are fixed before outcomes. Finding an old document initially establishes only that it was found; specific trace support under this procedure additionally requires explaining its connection to the specified event, its reference baseline, the quantity that persists, and the preselected criterion it satisfies. [T-49; T-42]

Passing a “Historical Trace Carriers” test stops at “candidate traces within the specified carrier and time window.” It permits handing a predefined historical-variable candidate to a historical-increment test for further inquiry, but does not pass the historical-increment test on its behalf. Past formation of a current carrier, the carrier's continued effect on the future, and additional historical increment given the stated current representation are three distinct questions. The first two may draw on independent formation or carrier-effect evidence under §4.5; only the third is the narrow question of the historical-increment test. When the current carrier sufficiently holds the relevant information, the historical residual can be zero while the carrier effect remains nonzero. [T-49; T-G3]

Repair timing must also remain distinct. Claiming that earlier or later intervention changes recoverability within a specific window requires the general repair-timing evidence of §6.10. A further claim that historical increment beyond the current representation produces the repair window corresponding to the conclusion rule “Historical Effects, Path Differences, and Repair Windows” (§4.12.1) also requires the matching branches of the historical-increment test and of this rule. Benefits of early intervention cannot all be retrospectively treated as support for “Historical Trace Carriers” or a historical increment; absence of additional historical increment cannot negate independently supported possibilities for repair or harm reduction either. [T-49; T-repair; T-C4]

These limits do not impose a general ban on protection until a complete empirical mechanism is established. Protection, harm reduction, and repair proceed separately through the conclusion rule “Normative Bridging” (§4.14.1), explicit normative premises, current itemized authorization, and operational procedures, judged by specific risks, duties, evidence, and reversibility. However strong an empirical description, it cannot alone establish who must bear a burden or who has authority to act. “Action Uptake and Classification of Responsibility” is a rule for classifying uptake and responsibility, “Institutional Write-Back” is a classification rule, and “Open-Ended Undertaking” is a normative boundary; none becomes one of the three kinds of empirical hypothesis addressed here merely by being listed among the six human-domain clauses. [T-49; T-42; T-H; T-C12]

For existing literature, first preserve what its authors actually did and how far it supports conclusions, then explain which question of a human empirical clause it can inform through external material or research leads. If no qualified specific test is established here, do not fabricate a formal test, finalization time, or evidence record; this does not prevent serious explanation of the literature's own findings. Questions beyond the standard list may still be asked and tested through proportionate research procedures; the original question must not be forcibly changed to obtain a favorable label. [T-42; T-domain]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    First distinguish the empirical roles of “Meaning and Coordination,” “Power, Mediation, and Reflexivity,” and “Historical Trace Carriers” from the classificatory or normative roles of “Action Uptake and Classification of Responsibility,” “Institutional Write-Back,” and “Open-Ended Undertaking.”

  2. 2

    Consult external material first for particular facts; separately assess the strength of literature-based facts and formal-support eligibility under this procedure.

  3. 3

    For the tests of “Meaning and Coordination” and “Power, Mediation, and Reflexivity,” uniquely preselect an outcome family, corresponding criterion, and comparison conditions; do not choose the best result afterward.

  4. 4

    For the “Historical Trace Carriers” test, uniquely preselect a family, matching specific carrier, and durability criterion; fix event/baseline/quantity/threshold/window in advance.

  5. 5

    Only after the corresponding specific test satisfies every condition may its bounded result be determined; empty records, unresolved status, and qualified zero conclusions are not interchangeable.

  6. 6

    Obtain separate evidence for traces, current-carrier effects, historical increment beyond the current representation, and repair timing; separately check norms, permission, and procedures for protection and intervention.

Distinctions to keep clear

The three empirical hypotheses

Organizes testable questions; it is not already true as a whole.

≠

A specific test

Has an object, criterion, window, record, and actual test result.

Facts from external research

Judge actual results through domain evidence.

≠

Formal eligibility under this procedure

Requires this procedure's prior and outcome discipline; it cannot be filled in retrospectively.

Empty support record

No qualified record has entered this support list.

≠

Qualified zero conclusion

Separately requires prior zero rules and proportionate sensitivity and tolerance.

Candidate trace of historical trace carriers

A carrier retains a difference within a window.

≠

Future effects or historical increment

Require subsequent causal grounds or grounds from a historical-increment test, respectively.

Empirical support

Strengthens a bounded description or explanation.

≠

Real-world intervention

Also requires normative premises, itemized authorization, operational procedures, and normative bridging; it is not obtained automatically.

Mathematical teaching construction: separate carrier effects from historical residualsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe binary distribution, S=H, Y=S, and intervention replacing only S are all constructed model stipulations; current information includes S, with no omitted noise.

Let H∈{0,1} have equal probabilities, current carrier state S=H, and future target Y=S. Observationally Y=H, making history and future appear perfectly aligned. But given S, Y is already determined, so additional H no longer reduces prediction error. If the constructed structural equations intervene only by forcing S to 0 or 1, Y becomes 0 or 1 accordingly; the current-carrier effect within the model remains 1. This shows that “a carrier transmits the past” and “additional historical information beyond the current representation” can differ.

BoundaryThere is no actual pre-registration of a “Historical Trace Carriers” test or historical-increment test, measurement, or human experiment; the example establishes only logical nonequivalence of the two kinds of conclusion.

Teaching construction: a revision record selected in advanceTeaching scenario

AssumptionsR17, R18, and the rule event are teaching fictions; they illustrate only the relationships among the necessary items, without fabricating observed differences.

Suppose a study first selects the single record R17 from the institutional or textual record family. The historical event is a rule revision; the preselected criterion is “persists after the event ends,” with a field change, prerevision baseline, threshold, and subsequent window predefined. If proportionate material meets the selected conditions, a candidate trace in R17 within that window may be discussed. Whether anyone actually acts under the new rule still requires execution material. If R17 fails, R18 cannot replace it after outcomes to close the R17 case.

BoundaryNot a real institutional record; confers no positive eligibility on any “Historical Trace Carriers” test, nor derives learning or repair directly from a record change.

The 2013 rating experiment: separate external behavioral evidence from formal eligibility as a “Power, Mediation, and Reflexivity” testDocumented case

Muchnik, Aral, and Taylor published a randomized experiment in Science in 2013 examining how existing ratings on a social-news aggregation website affected subsequent rating behavior. They reported that prior ratings influenced rating behavior, with asymmetric herding effects for positive and negative influence. This section focuses on evidential roles: the actual study can supply external material for the questions of “Power, Mediation, and Reflexivity” about mediation/publicity conditions and object behavior; its own results remain understood under its actual experimental design. We have not thereby completed the full pre-registration and outcome record of a “Power, Mediation, and Reflexivity” test under this framework, nor presented a retrospective mapping as the study's prior selection for this clause.

SourceMuchnik, Aral, Taylor, Science 341(6146):647–651 (2013), original abstract indexed in PubMedPMID 23929980; 2013-08-09; DOI 10.1126/science.1240466; first three sentences of the Abstract and subsequent qualifications.Reading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsThe same study as in the preceding lesson, not a second independent review; only its randomized research topic and reported rating-behavior differences are used, without inferring participants' full psychology, expression safety, or current platform conditions.

What does not follow

  • Source boundary: definitions, descriptions of the human variables, proposition names, and the framework's own narrative cannot serve as external empirical support.
  • Source boundary: the tests of “Meaning and Coordination” and “Power, Mediation, and Reflexivity” prohibit selecting the most favorable outcome family afterward; the test of “Historical Trace Carriers” prohibits searching across carriers or criteria for a surviving result.
  • Constructed conditional counterexample: examining four outcomes, selecting the sole significant one, and calling it “preselected” does not meet actual prior finalization; correct computation does not repair the record's status.
  • Constructed conditional counterexample: a carrier preserves an old difference, but every subsequent decision explicitly ignores it, and the teaching stipulation excludes any other transmission or effect channel between that carrier and the future target. A trace does not imply an effect on that target.
  • Constructed conditional counterexample: current state S fully preserves the information in history H relevant to the target, so H adds no information conditional on S; this does not mean S has no effect.
  • Boundary of support from real material: behavioral differences in the 2013 rating experiment cannot establish every person's inner consent, expression safety, all power mechanisms, or eligibility for formal support as a “Power, Mediation, and Reflexivity” test under this framework.
  • This lesson has not actually established a new specific test, executed an intervention, or obtained real reader-effect data; methodological explanation and review of existing literature do not pretend those tasks have been completed.

Scope and open questions

This unit concerns methodological judgment. Actual sources support only the listed facts; the diagram and teaching construction each retain their own status.

  • To turn an existing study into a new confirmatory specific test under this procedure, which prior records, main criterion, versions, splits, evidence, and analysis outputs remain missing? This lesson does not assume they have been supplied.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    Does absence of a record of a qualified specific test mean that meaning or power has never had an effect in reality?

  2. 2

    If the “Meaning and Coordination” test preselected action choice but only resource allocation improves, can the original criterion be marked as passed?

  3. 3

    If the “Power, Mediation, and Reflexivity” test finds behavioral differences after public ratings, can expression immediately be called safer?

  4. 4

    May the “Historical Trace Carriers” test list three archives as the selected carrier and choose the most persistent one?

  5. 5

    Why does passing trace retention not mean passing a historical-increment test?

  6. 6

    If carrier effects have evidence but there is no additional historical increment, can protection still be discussed?

  7. 7

    In the model Y=S, S=H, why does historical association not establish conditional historical increment?

Does absence of a record of a qualified specific test mean that meaning or power has never had an effect in reality?

No. What is empty is this formal support record; particular facts are still judged by external material. It is neither an empty world nor a qualified zero conclusion.

Basis: §4.9, Chinese source line 763; §4.2.

If the “Meaning and Coordination” test preselected action choice but only resource allocation improves, can the original criterion be marked as passed?

An unselected family cannot rescue the original criterion. Retain the original result; the new finding may become exploration or a new research question.

Basis: §4.2, Chinese source lines 637–643.

If the “Power, Mediation, and Reflexivity” test finds behavioral differences after public ratings, can expression immediately be called safer?

No. Object behavior and expression safety are different outcome families, each requiring proportionate material.

Basis: §4.2, “Power, Mediation, and Reflexivity” row; §4.9.

May the “Historical Trace Carriers” test list three archives as the selected carrier and choose the most persistent one?

No; there must be a unique specific carrier matching family and subtype, with one durability criterion separately fixed in advance.

Basis: §4.2, Chinese source lines 640–643.

Why does passing trace retention not mean passing a historical-increment test?

Trace retention asks about persistent differences in a carrier; a historical-increment test additionally asks whether history supplies an increment after controlling for the stated current state, environment, and so on. Their targets and conditions differ.

Basis: §4.9, Chinese source line 765; §4.5.

If carrier effects have evidence but there is no additional historical increment, can protection still be discussed?

Yes, through normative bridging (§4.14.1) and explicit normative premises, itemized authorization, and operational procedures, according to current risks, duties, and material. A gap in the historical-increment test is not a general ban on all protection, and an effect does not directly confer authority to intervene.

Basis: §4.9；§4.14.1。

In the model Y=S, S=H, why does historical association not establish conditional historical increment?

Unconditionally H and Y agree, but conditional on S, Y is already determined; adding H cannot improve prediction error that is already zero.

Basis: The explicit mathematical assumptions in this lesson.

4.10The Twelve Conclusion Rules (C1–C12) ​

In briefThe twelve conclusion rules are not twelve laws established by the same kind of evidence, but twelve output rules with scopes, premises, and stopping positions. This section first teaches how to read these rules before their individual development.

Each conclusion rule delimits which conclusions can be drawn according to its own definitions, empirical basis, additional conditions, or normative and procedural premises; those of its branches that rely on formal tests must obtain the support of the corresponding tests. Each rule below is written under the same items: Grounds, Conditions, Can conclude, Cannot conclude, and Must also meet. “Grounds” lists the inferential premises, that is, the hard premises that enter the inferential acyclic graph (§2.3). “Must also meet” lists the method requirements, which determine whether a conclusion may be released but do not serve as empirical causes. Domain restrictions and objects of application are explained separately in the body. Minimum evidence, key counterexamples, and failure boundaries are presented together, group by group, in the table after each group.

The twelve conclusion rules (§4.11 to §4.14) do different argumentative work. In four places the work is mainly to record the outcomes within specified limits already supported by the corresponding empirical tests, adding a scope of use: the three rules “Grouping Gain and Its Robustness to Boundary Perturbation,” “Carrying and Channel Constraints,” and “Scale Closure and Object Conversion,” and the historical-increment route of “Historical Effects, Path Differences, and Repair Windows.” Six rules must also combine separately listed mechanism, temporal, or domain conditions: “Effective Feedback and Feedback-Mediated Learning,” “Load, Capacity, and Recovery,” “Local Improvement and Cross-Boundary Spillover,” “Observation Channels and Reflexive Responses,” “Human Uptake and Intertemporal Reproduction,” and “Institutional Write-Back.” The basic pattern of “Variation–Differential Retention–Reproduction” depends on separately obtained evidence of variation, differential retention, and reproduction. “Normative Bridging” is a check on normative procedure. Placing these in one sequence does not turn them into empirical laws of the same kind; nor does the same material, used in a formal test and cited again in a conclusion rule, constitute a second piece of independent support.

4.10Note

Understanding this section

4.10 The twelve conclusion rules (C1–C12)

The twelve conclusion rules are not twelve laws established by the same kind of evidence, but twelve output rules with scopes, premises, and stopping positions. This section first teaches how to read these rules before their individual development.

Chinese source line 773 says that the twelve conclusion rules “do different argumentative work.” Placing them in one sequence can create the illusion that once a formal test passes, all subsequent conclusions follow in sequence. This section first separates that misunderstanding: some rules record bounded results supported by existing tests; others additionally connect mechanisms, timing, or domain conditions; others test evolutionary patterns requiring independent evidence; the last checks how description may lawfully enter normative choice. Each has its own grounds for holding. [T-410]

When reading each conclusion rule, look first at its first four items. ‘Grounds’ specifies the required hard premises; ‘Conditions’ states what object correspondence, quantity mapping, temporal, or mechanism material is also needed; ‘Can conclude’ bounds what can be said; ‘Cannot conclude’ states what still cannot follow even when all the conditions of the rule are met. These four items publicly structure responsibilities; filling them does not automatically make them true. Subsequent grouped evidence tables add minimum evidence, key counterexamples, and failure boundaries; reading four headings cannot replace these substantive conditions. [T-410; T-C123]

‘Grounds’ enters an acyclic inference graph to express dependencies within an argument; this is not equivalent to a real-world causal graph. A definition such as the structural object (§3.1) can be a hard premise for determining an object without thereby causing an event in the world. The method requirements listed under ‘Must also meet’ are evidential or procedural requirements affecting whether the corresponding conclusion may be issued under this framework; the conditions for evidence, the conditions for causal claims, and the like cannot be treated as newly discovered empirical causes. Domain restriction further specifies the kinds of objects to which a rule applies: the conclusion rule ‘Human Uptake and Intertemporal Reproduction’ (§4.13.3), for example, specifically addresses structures involving human action, care, maintenance, or institutional implementation. Inferential edges, methodological constraints, scopes of applicability, and real-world channels should be drawn and explained separately. [T-410；T-role；T-C1011]

The first category mainly carries results already supported by the corresponding empirical tests into an explicit scope of use: ‘Grouping Gain and Its Robustness to Boundary Perturbation’ (§4.11.1) reads the grouping-gain test and records its result; ‘Carrying and Channel Constraints’ (§4.11.2) reads the channel-effect test and records specified carrying and measured channel constraints; ‘Scale Closure and Object Conversion’ (§4.12.3) reads the scale-closure test and records bounded results under the selected scale mapping; of ‘Historical Effects, Path Differences, and Repair Windows’ (§4.12.1), only the ‘historical-increment route’ belongs to the route here that relies on the historical-increment test. This is not another independent experiment under a conclusion rule, much less a direct inference from the name of the corresponding empirical question to a conclusion. Objects, scales, windows, identity, mappings, and additional conditions must still correspond. [T-410；T-C123；T-C4；T-C6]

The qualifier in ‘Historical Effects, Path Differences, and Repair Windows’ is especially important: the current-carrier-effect route and the general intervention-timing route stand on their own evidence and do not universally require a historical increment beyond the current representation. Reading line 773 of the Chinese source as ‘all conclusions of this rule must pass a historical-increment test’ removes the two independent routes that the source explicitly preserves. Conversely, a claim of an additional historical residual cannot use ‘carrier effects’ to evade the burden of the historical-increment test. Branch names here determine the question being asked and the evidential responsibilities. [T-410；T-C4]

The second category, namely the six rules ‘Effective Feedback and Feedback-Mediated Learning,’ ‘Load, Capacity, and Recovery,’ ‘Local Improvement and Cross-Boundary Spillover,’ ‘Observation Channels and Reflexive Responses,’ ‘Human Uptake and Intertemporal Reproduction,’ and ‘Institutional Write-Back,’ requires its respective additional mechanism, temporal, or domain conditions. For example, a channel-effect test showing that a channel has an effect is insufficient to establish effective feedback: a return channel, timing, the items changed, and comparisons with no return or blocking are also needed. A further claim of learning requires corresponding route evidence such as retention of updates, repeated use over multiple rounds, and task comparisons. ‘Load, Capacity, and Recovery’ additionally asks about commensurate demand and capacity and accumulation over time; ‘Local Improvement and Cross-Boundary Spillover’ about constrained relations between objects and consequences outside boundaries; ‘Observation Channels and Reflexive Responses’ examines whether observations arrive and reflexive responses occur; ‘Human Uptake and Intertemporal Reproduction’ separates human uptake from intertemporal routes; and ‘Institutional Write-Back’ distinguishes acceptance, changes in institutional elements, and actual implementation. This lists the directions of responsibility; full conditions are developed in each subsequent independent subsection. [T-410；T-C123；T-C57；T-C9；T-C1011]

The basic pattern of ‘Variation–Differential Retention–Reproduction’ (§4.13.1) separately examines variation, differential outcomes in comparable environments, retention or reproduction entering the next round, repeated rounds, and competing explanations such as drift. It uses the basic state terms (§3.2) to define the question of change but cannot establish the pattern directly from the definition of the basic state terms, nor does it universally require a channel-effect test as a prerequisite for the basic pattern; a channel-effect test is added only when a specific retention or reproduction mechanism is further claimed. A single instance of persistence is not evidence of reproduction across multiple rounds, and ‘being retained’ does not automatically mean better or more normatively justified. [T-410；T-C8]

The conclusion rule ‘Normative Bridging’ (§4.14.1) is not another empirical mechanism but a check in normative procedure. Facts can indicate what a proposal might do; alone, they cannot decide what ought to be pursued, who has authority to implement it, or how to stop and correct errors. An analytical recommendation for deliberation should disclose normative premises, evidence, and the price to be paid, without pretending that authorization for actual implementation has already occurred. A bounded recommendation entering actual adoption must satisfy this rule's requirements for explicit normative premises, protection floors, itemized authorization, and records such as those of the four-step operational procedure. Possessing only the overreach-prohibiting function of the normative premise ‘Explanation Does Not Confer Authority to Act’ (§14.3) cannot itself generate a positive proposal. [T-410；T-C12]

The same material may play different roles at different positions in an argument, but its source identity cannot multiply with its citation count. An experimental result first supports a channel-effect test and is then used in the conclusion rule ‘Carrying and Channel Constraints’ (§4.11.2) to bound a channel conclusion; it remains that same result, and this rule has not become a second independent review. Independence depends on the actual relationships among samples, measurements, analyses, and sources; writing another file or changing a number cannot create an independent source. [T-410；T-source]

Conclusion rules help insufficiencies stop at the right point. With a channel-effect test but without the return conditions, one may retain a channel effect but cannot additionally claim effective feedback; with one feedback event but without multiround task evidence, one may retain feedback without calling it learning; missing a historical-increment test blocks only the branch explicitly dependent on additional historical quantities and does not revoke an existing carrier route. Conversely, meeting every descriptive conclusion rule does not automatically establish value, stage, responsibility, or authority to act. Each subsequent conclusion rule must be judged through its own items and counterexamples, rather than automatically upgraded in the order in which the rules are listed. [T-410；T-C123；T-tree]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    First identify whether the output requested here is a bounded test result, an additional mechanism condition, an independent pattern test, or a check in normative procedure.

  2. 2

    Read the first four items of the rule, then the method requirements under ‘Must also meet’ and grouped evidence/counterexamples/failure boundaries.

  3. 3

    Verify actual support for the hard premises; do not treat nodes in a dependency graph or method requirements as empirical causes.

  4. 4

    Connect objects, variables, units, scales, windows, and additional conditions within the same case; output only conclusions actually permitted by the full conditions.

  5. 5

    Trace the common sources of the materials; reuse can support a new position in an argument but does not increase the number of independent reviews.

  6. 6

    When a gap appears, stop only the branch that actually depends on it and preserve existing independent conclusions; actual adoption follows a separate normative and authorization procedure.

Distinctions to keep clear

Grounds

A hard premise required for an argument to hold.

≠

Real-world causation

An event or channel relationship requiring empirical identification, which cannot be supplied by a dependency edge.

Method requirements that must also be met

Method requirements bounding the use of evidence and the issuing of conclusions.

≠

Empirical cause

A condition that actually changes the target and requires proportionate materials.

Domain restriction

Defines the category of objects to which a rule applies.

≠

Established mechanism

Belonging to this domain does not mean every causal condition already holds.

Reuse of the same material

May support different bounded claims in two positions.

≠

Independent review

Requires actually independent sources or designs, not relabeling.

Historical-increment route of ‘Historical Effects, Path Differences, and Repair Windows’

Evidence from the corresponding historical-increment test is indispensable.

≠

Carrier/timing route of ‘Historical Effects, Path Differences, and Repair Windows’

Uses its own corresponding evidence; a historical-increment test is not universally added.

Analytical recommendation

Disclose normative premises, evidence, and the price to be paid for deliberation.

≠

Actual adoption

Must satisfy the full procedure of normative bridging and current authorization.

Logical teaching construction: a conjunctive condition cannot lose a conjunctTeaching scenario

AssumptionsP, Q, and R are logical propositions introduced to explain a conditional; a specific conclusion rule also has its full definitions and methodological requirements.

Let P mean ‘qualified evidence of an effect exists for the specified channel’, Q mean ‘additional conditions concerning return, timing, and proportionate comparisons hold’, and R mean the feedback conclusion to be determined here. Suppose the conclusion rule gives (P and Q)→R. P alone does not deductively imply R, because assigning P true, Q false, and R false still makes that conditional true. This counterexample demonstrates only why additional conditions cannot be deleted; it does not replace empirical argument for a feedback mechanism.

BoundaryWhat is proved is that R cannot be inferred from the given conditional and P; it does not prove that every feedback process lacking qualification is absent in reality.

Teaching construction: citing one material twiceTeaching scenario

AssumptionsE and F are illustrative labels; no claim is made that such an experiment actually exists.

Suppose a single experimental material E records a channel comparison. Argument A uses E to form a channel-effect test result; argument B uses that same E and a mapping of quantities in ‘Carrying and Channel Constraints’ to bound its output. The evidence lineage still contains only one E; if E's measurement is refuted, both A and B may be affected. Saving B as a second report cannot eliminate the common source; if B also uses independent material F, the parts supported by E and F should be labeled separately.

BoundaryThis illustrates source dependence without denying that the same genuine material may have multiple legitimate uses or asserting that any two articles must lack independence.

What counterexamples change

Sourced counterexampleBoundary in the source: the twelve conclusion rules are not a collection of empirical laws of the same type; being placed in one sequence cannot justify a uniform way of establishing them.

What it limitsDistinguish different ways in which claims are established.

Sourced counterexampleBoundary in the source: method requirements determine whether a conclusion may be issued, but do not thereby become empirical causes of events.

What it limitsDo not turn method requirements into empirical causes.

Sourced counterexampleBoundary in the source: citing the same material again in a formal test and a conclusion rule does not constitute a second independent source of support.

What it limitsAvoid double-counting independent support.

Teaching counterexampleAuthor-constructed conditional counterexample: a channel does change the output, but no return route exists; a channel effect is not the same as effective feedback having formed.

What it limitsA channel effect alone is insufficient to infer feedback.

What does not follow

  • Boundary in the source: the twelve conclusion rules are not a collection of empirical laws of the same type; being placed in one sequence cannot justify a uniform way of establishing them.
  • Boundary in the source: method requirements determine whether a conclusion may be issued, but do not thereby become empirical causes of events.
  • Boundary in the source: citing the same material again in a formal test and a conclusion rule does not constitute a second independent source of support.
  • Author-constructed conditional counterexample: a channel does change the output, but no return route exists; a channel effect is not the same as effective feedback having formed.
  • Author-constructed conditional counterexample: a one-time state update was neither retained nor used again; merely changing a file's title to ‘learning’ cannot produce a learning result.
  • Author-constructed conditional counterexample: a choice prolongs persistence, but explicit protective obligations or current authority prohibit it; a descriptive advantage cannot alone determine what ought to be done.
  • This section explains how to read and route conclusion rules; it reports no new real-world effect and does not attach an accident story to confer empirical truth on every conclusion rule.

Scope and open questions

This section explains the roles of conclusion rules and how to read them; it contains no independent historical event or new empirical claim. It explains directly through an accurate comparison of the source's branches, a counterexample in conditional logic, and an evidence-lineage construction, rather than replacing subsequent item-by-item tests with an unrelated real-world story.

  • Whether any conclusion rule holds in a specific case must be judged separately against its object, materials, and complete branch conditions; this section does not fabricate actual case results.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    What are the first four items of a conclusion rule? Is reading them sufficient?

  2. 2

    If the conditions for evidence appear under ‘Must also meet,’ does that mean they cause the object to change?

  3. 3

    Must the basic pattern of ‘Variation–Differential Retention–Reproduction’ first have a channel-effect test?

  4. 4

    Do all conclusions of ‘Historical Effects, Path Differences, and Repair Windows’ depend on a historical-increment test?
