What are the first four items of a conclusion rule? Is reading them sufficient?

‘Grounds,’ ‘Conditions,’ ‘Can conclude,’ and ‘Cannot conclude’; the method requirements under ‘Must also meet’ and corresponding evidence, counterexamples, and failure boundaries must also be read, and actual materials checked.

Basis: Chinese source, §4.10, line 771, and the subsequent format of each conclusion rule.

If the conditions for evidence appear under ‘Must also meet,’ does that mean they cause the object to change?

No. It is a method requirement concerning evidence; actual causes separately require mechanisms and proportionate evidence.

Basis: Chinese source, line 771.

Must the basic pattern of ‘Variation–Differential Retention–Reproduction’ first have a channel-effect test?

Not universally. The basic pattern must independently satisfy variation, differential outcome, and retention, entry into the next round, repeated rounds, and competition with drift explanations; only the specific-mechanism branch adds a channel-effect test.

Basis: Chinese source, §4.13.1, lines 900—912.

Do all conclusions of ‘Historical Effects, Path Differences, and Repair Windows’ depend on a historical-increment test?

No. The branch explicitly claiming a historical increment beyond the current representation requires a historical-increment test; the current-carrier or general intervention-timing route stands on its own materials.

Basis: The ‘historical-increment route’ in line 773 of the Chinese source; §4.12.1.

If the same experiment is cited in a channel-effect test and in ‘Carrying and Channel Constraints,’ does the number of independent supports become two?

No. The number of citation positions increases, but the source remains the same material; their common dependency must be preserved.

Basis: Chinese source, line 773; §2.7.1.

If P and Q imply R and P holds, why can R not be announced?

A consistent assignment with P true, Q false, and R false exists, showing that P alone is insufficient; Q and the remaining conditions of the rule must also actually be checked.

Basis: The explicit logical construction in this section.

Once every descriptive conclusion rule is met, may the most effective proposal be implemented?

Implementation is not automatic. The proposal's objectives, protective obligations, scope of authorization, stopping and error correction, and related matters must still be checked under normative bridging (§4.14.1); actual adoption should also be distinguished from analytical recommendations offered solely for deliberation.

Basis: Chinese source, §4.14.1, lines 973—981.

4.11Group 1: Objects, Carrying, and Feedback ​

In briefThis group answers three respective questions: how much support this candidate grouping receives, what carries a specified change, and how returned information changes a later process. The questions are related but do not replace one another.
4.11Note

Understanding this section

4.11 Group one: objects, carrying, and feedback

This group answers three respective questions: how much support this candidate grouping receives, what carries a specified change, and how returned information changes a later process. The questions are related but do not replace one another.

Lines 775—776 of this parent section in the Chinese source contain only a group heading, with no additional empirical proposition. The three conclusion rules each have an independent body: ‘Grouping Gain and Its Robustness to Boundary Perturbation’ (§4.11.1) determines bounded grouping-gain support from a candidate structural object and grouping-gain support; ‘Carrying and Channel Constraints’ (§4.11.2) determines specified channels and measured constraints from the structural object and the channel effect; ‘Effective Feedback and Feedback-Mediated Learning’ (§4.11.3) determines feedback from effective feedback, the channel effect, and additional return conditions, and further distinguishes two learning routes. The heading groups them to facilitate comparison of responsibilities; it does not make an earlier rule automatically imply a later one. [T-intro；T-C1；T-C2；T-C3]

When reading this group, repeatedly ask three questions: what does the grouping add over a proportionate baseline; which target transition does the channel affect, and which dimensions remain unmeasured; and does the return cause a subsequent change, and then enter retention and use? The object, quantities, scales, windows, and comparison conditions of each question must connect; one story cannot silently supply a missing segment. [T-C1；T-C2；T-C3]

Lines 821—825 at the group's end in the Chinese source put the three items' minimum evidence, key counterexamples, and failure boundaries in one table. The table is part of the complete source scope for this lesson. The units below explain their respective items, and the lesson on §4.11.3 additionally explains how to read across the whole table. Readers need not master all subsequent mechanisms at once, but should first preserve the distinction among candidate grouping, candidate causal carrying, effective feedback, and feedback-mediated learning as different outputs. [T-table]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Recognize that this parent section serves only navigation; do not invent a fourth empirical proposition.

  2. 2

    Read the four items and the method requirements under ‘Must also meet’ of the three rules separately in their original order.

  3. 3

    Finally, use the evidence table at the group's end to check each item's counterexamples and stopping points; do not treat a horizontal juxtaposition as an automatic inferential chain.

Distinctions to keep clear

Placement in the same group

Facilitates comparison of three kinds of work.

≠

Automatic sequence of establishment

Passing an earlier item does not supply the conditions of a later one.

What does not follow

  • This parent section replaces none of its subsections; all three are delivered as separate independent objects.
  • ‘Feedback’ in the group name does not imply that all feedback is learning, improves outcomes, or requires persistent traces.

Scope and open questions

The parent section contains only a grouping title, making it appropriate for source navigation and explanation of relationships; real-world facts are embedded in the relevant subsections, without creating an extra case proposition at the title level.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    If the conclusion rule ‘Grouping Gain and Its Robustness to Boundary Perturbation’ supports a grouping, may a channel within it be declared effective?

  2. 2

    Does this group heading provide an additional real-world law?

If the conclusion rule ‘Grouping Gain and Its Robustness to Boundary Perturbation’ supports a grouping, may a channel within it be declared effective?

No. The channel-effect test corresponding to ‘Carrying and Channel Constraints’ and channel-identification materials are still required.

Basis: §4.11.1—4.11.2。

Does this group heading provide an additional real-world law?

No; it organizes three conclusion rules whose substantive text and evidence are in the subsections.

Basis: Chinese source, lines 775—776.

4.11.1Grouping Gain and Its Robustness to Boundary Perturbation (C1) ​

In briefThis conclusion rule turns ‘we grouped things this way’ into a bounded identification judgment that can be compared and overturned. It measures the scope within which this grouping is useful; it does not declare that the world has only this one natural boundary.

Grounds: structural object (§3.1); grouping gain (§4.3).

Conditions: The grouping-gain test relied on has completed pre-registration and obtained support. The candidate object, the null model, the evaluation threshold, the extrapolation unit, and the boundary-perturbation plan have all been fixed in advance.

Can conclude: within that scale, time window, identity criterion, and extrapolation unit, how strong the support for grouping gain is, how robust that gain is to the boundary perturbations tested, and the window in which the candidate grouping applies.

Cannot conclude: that limited grouping-gain support is an ultimate ontological verdict; that whether grouping-gain support has been obtained is the overall threshold for an object's existence; that the object has a natural boundary, is a unified subject, has a common target, or is at a stage described by the seven state prototypes (§8.3); the value of persistence, the allocation of responsibility, or authorization for choice or action.

Must also meet: Constraint on Object Declaration (§4.8.1); Retaining Competing Explanations and Residuals (§4.8.4); conditions for evidence (§2.5).

The derivation proceeds in this order: first, the candidate object is fixed according to the seven elements of a structural object, without presupposing that the grouping yields a gain; next, the out-of-sample gain obtained in the same grouping-gain test relative to a null model of comparable complexity is read; finally, boundary perturbation and independent review are combined to determine the strength of support and the applicable window.

4.11.1Note

Understanding this section

4.11.1 Grouping gain and its robustness to boundary perturbation (C1)

This conclusion rule turns ‘we grouped things this way’ into a bounded identification judgment that can be compared and overturned. It measures the scope within which this grouping is useful; it does not declare that the world has only this one natural boundary.

Chinese source line 783 limits the conclusion to ‘within that scale, time window, identity criterion, and extrapolation unit’. The structural object (§3.1) first specifies the candidate object, including such elements as boundaries, variables, relations, interfaces, scale, window, and identity; entering a candidate does not pre-establish its effectiveness. The grouping-gain test (§4.3) then tests under conditions fixed in advance whether the candidate grouping adds predetermined out-of-sample explanatory or intervention results relative to a complexity-matched null model that does not use that grouping information. This rule reads this actual support and determines the strength of support for grouping gain, its robustness to the tested boundary perturbations, and the grouping’s applicability window. [T-C1; T-D0; T-G1]

‘The grouping-gain test relied on has completed pre-registration and obtained support’ does not count merely because a test name is attached. It must actually meet §4.1’s support-eligibility requirements, including finalization before evidence, evidence mode, completion as finalized, a passed positive criterion, and references to evidence and analysis outputs that correspond to real material. An attractive grouping discovered in exploration can be studied further, but backdating cannot make it completed confirmatory support. Existing domain studies retain their conclusions on their actual evidence and are not erased for not using this framework. [T-C1; T-contract]

This rule’s conditions each prevent a change of question: fixing candidate S* prevents choosing the best of many partitions; fixing a complexity-matched null model prevents winning merely through greater model flexibility; fixing evaluation thresholds and extrapolation units prevents lowering standards or expanding populations after results; fixing the boundary-perturbation plan prevents selecting only adjustments that preserve the result. The grouping-gain test’s shared environment, sampling/classification bias, and grouping leakage must also be handled; these responsibilities already in the pre-registration of the formal test cannot be dropped. [T-C1; T-G1]

Out-of-sample gain asks ‘Does it still work on new material?’; boundary perturbation asks ‘Is support retained under slight changes to the boundary?’; review in independent time blocks or locations asks ‘Does it occur only under the original conditions?’ These address overfitting, boundary fragility, and local contingency separately; a beautiful training plot cannot handle them all. The original text promises no particular sample size or universal threshold; values must follow the predetermined task, and this guide does not add a universal passing score on the author’s behalf. [T-C1; T-G1; T-table]

Bounded strength of support for grouping gain is not a mysterious entity score. Reports should specify the grouping-gain subtype, measure, amount of support and uncertainty, boundary perturbations and independent blocks where support persists, and the scale, time window, and identity criterion under which it may be used. The predictive-gain and intervention-gain subtypes cannot be interchanged after results; even a stable predictive grouping does not directly establish a unified goal, shared will, or natural boundary for all members. [T-C1; T-G1]

The row for this rule in the concluding table gives three important counterexamples: gain disappears in independent blocks, slight boundary perturbation breaks it, or the null model absorbs all the gain. When these occur, downgrade or stop current support under the prior rules. Failure at the positive criterion usually means only that this test is ‘not supported or unresolved’, not that the null model is proved; a qualified null conclusion still needs its independent null-conclusion rule. Returning to candidate-grouping status beyond the tested scale, time window, and identity criterion without new testing also does not invalidate all material from the original window. [T-table; T-G1]

This rule’s prohibited extensions also include the stages described by the seven state prototypes (§8.3), value of continued existence, responsibility, choice, and authority to act. A statistically identifiable group of people does not become a unified moral subject because researchers cluster them; a stable organizational unit does not thereby deserve preservation at any cost. Empirical grouping, subject standing, stage classification, and normative decisions each have other evidence and procedures. [T-C1]

The constraint on object declaration under ‘Must also meet’ requires object and scale declarations, ‘Retaining Competing Explanations and Residuals’ requires proportionate competing explanations and residuals, and the conditions for evidence require sources and support scope. These method requirements help assess a conclusion publishable under this rule; they are not additional empirical factors causing the studied objects to group. Actual clustering research can illuminate ‘useful grouping and its limits’, but analogy alone cannot tick off every item and test in this rule. [T-C1; T-E]

In v2, this rule is renamed ‘Grouping Gain and Its Robustness to Boundary Perturbation’. Always ask of its output: which outcome, which matched null model, which boundary perturbations, which window, and which extrapolation unit? It cannot be compressed into an object-strength score that decides whether a group is real or whether a member should be included.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    First fix the candidate object in advance according to the elements of a structural object, without presupposing grouping effectiveness in its definition.

  2. 2

    Verify the same grouping-gain test’s support eligibility, single subtype, null model, out-of-sample target, and controls.

  3. 3

    Read actual gain, then check predetermined boundary perturbations and independent review, marking uncertainty and failure points.

  4. 4

    Within the same scale, time window, identity criterion, and extrapolation unit, determine bounded identification strength, robustness of that gain to the tested boundary perturbations, and its applicability window.

  5. 5

    Retain the separate threshold for null conclusions; do not infer subjects, goals, stages, value, or authority from this rule’s conclusions.

Distinctions to keep clear

Candidate object (structural object)

Specifies what is to be studied.

≠

Bounded support under this rule

Additionally requires the corresponding grouping-gain comparison and review.

Attractive training grouping

May merely reflect fitting or display effects.

≠

Out-of-sample and boundary support

Require new material, perturbations, and independent review.

Robustness of the gain to tested boundary perturbations

Usable within the specified task and perturbations.

≠

A unique natural boundary

This rule makes no such ontological ruling.

Grouping identification

A bounded result in an empirical task.

≠

Shared will / responsible party

Cannot arise directly from grouping.

Mathematical teaching construction: a gain value leaves other evidentiary responsibilitiesTeaching scenario

AssumptionsAll numbers are teaching assumptions; prediction vectors are assumed fixed before these targets were revealed, without claiming that they are actual out-of-sample observations.

Given four artificial test targets y=(0,0,2,2) and two prediction vectors fixed beforehand, p=(0,0,2,2) and q=(1,1,1,1), mean squared errors are MSE(p)=0 and MSE(q)=(1+1+1+1)/4=1. Thus p is lower than q by 1 under this loss. This calculation shows one scoring comparison only; it supplies no training provenance, complexity matching, candidate-leakage control, perturbation robustness, or independent review, and cannot establish this rule’s conclusion.

BoundaryValid conditional arithmetic is not actual qualification as a grouping-gain test, much less proof of natural object boundaries.

Gene-expression clustering in 1998: useful similarity structure is not a natural treeDocumented case

Eisen et al.’s 1998 PNAS paper organizes microarray gene data by similarity of expression patterns and reports that many genes with similar functions cluster together. Its introduction explicitly states that expression patterns have no underlying tree like that of sequence evolution; the dendrogram represents expression similarity. The results also compare clustering after randomly permuting the original data. This section uses it to show that actual research can provide material on grouping’s uses and controls, while a tree in a figure does not prove natural object boundaries.

SourceEisen et al., Cluster analysis and display of genome-wide expression patternsPNAS 95(25):14863–14868, 1998-12-08; introduction paragraph beginning ‘Whereas no such underlying tree exists…’; first paragraph of RESULTS and Figure 3 description; the ‘provisional attribution’ qualification in the third-to-last paragraph of DISCUSSION.Reading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsThe 1998 study is not retrospectively entered as a grouping-gain test of this framework or a case under this rule, nor claimed to have completed all this rule’s advance-finalization, out-of-sample, or boundary-perturbation requirements; it is not used to definitively diagnose functions of unknown genes.

What does not follow

Scope and open questions

This unit concerns methodological judgment. Actual sources support only the listed facts; the diagram and teaching construction each retain their own status.

  • A specific study must provide the actual candidate grouping’s scope, measures, thresholds, perturbation plan, and independent-review material; this guide generates no new empirical test.

Why does this rule’s conclusion not automatically hold when all items of candidate S* are complete?

The structural object only fixes the candidate; qualified out-of-sample gain, boundary robustness, and independent review under the corresponding grouping-gain test are also required.

Basis: Chinese source lines 779–789; §4.3.

If a result does not recur in an independent time block, can one directly say the object does not exist?

No. Limit this test’s support under predetermined rules; null or ontological conclusions are not the default substitute.

Basis: Chinese source line 823; §4.3, line 653.

Can a population cluster with excellent predictive performance represent a shared will?

No; this rule grants neither a unified subject, goals, nor actual consent.

Basis: Chinese source line 785.

Can artificial p with MSE=0 satisfy this rule?

No. Only a score difference is supplied here; other necessary design and material are absent.

Basis: This guide’s mathematical construction and Chinese source lines 749 and 789.

4.11.2Carrying and Channel Constraints (C2) ​

In brief‘Carrying and Channel Constraints’ asks which channel carries a specified change and requires clarity about what is transmitted, its units, and which performance dimensions have actually been measured. It does not permit every ‘cost’ to be merged into a universal total.

Grounds: structural object (§3.1); channel effect (§4.4).

Conditions: The channel-effect test relied on has been pre-registered and has obtained support. When shifting is discussed, the source and target quantities must be of the same type or have an explicit type conversion. The quantities' units, equality criteria, time window, and accounting boundary, together with the conversion mapping or accounting rules, have all been fixed in advance. Capacity, delay, reliability, controllability, and loss are stated channel by channel and dimension by dimension; unmeasured dimensions remain unknown.

Can conclude: candidate causal carrying for a specified state transition; the limits on the channel within the measured types, units, time windows, and dimensions. Shifting may be traced only when the conditions for quantities of the same type and for mapping are satisfied.

Cannot conclude: that quantities of different types or nonconvertible quantities can be merged into a unified cost; that boundedness measured in one dimension can be generalized to all dimensions or all channels; that a carrier or channel is automatically the responsible party or the bearer of costs; that conservation across domains can be inferred from the occupation of resources.

Must also meet: Constraint on Object Declaration (§4.8.1); Retaining Competing Explanations and Residuals (§4.8.4); conditions for causal claims (§2.4); conditions for evidence (§2.5).

This derivation holds only for the specified channel, target transition, and measured dimensions. Quantities of the same type can be traced through equality of units; quantities of different types must go through explicit conversion or an accounting mapping. Unmeasured dimensions and quantities outside the boundary remain unknown; they must not be recorded as conserved, vanished, or costs already shifted.

4.11.2Note

Understanding this section

4.11.2 Carrying and Channel Constraints (C2)

‘Carrying and Channel Constraints’ asks which channel carries a specified change and requires clarity about what is transmitted, its units, and which performance dimensions have actually been measured. It does not permit every ‘cost’ to be merged into a universal total.

Chinese source line 797 permits determining only ‘candidate causal carrying for a specified state transition’ and constraints in measured dimensions. The structural object (§3.1) fixes the object in question; a qualified channel-effect test (§4.4) identifies the specified channel’s role in the target transition; this rule then places that conclusion within quantity types, units, windows, and accounting boundaries. If a treatment has a total effect but its channels remain indistinct, retain the total effect without inventing a mechanism to fill out this rule. Identifying one channel also does not mean every channel of that object has been studied. [T-C2; T-G2]

Causal carrying requires proportionate controlled perturbation, controlled intervention, or natural variation with identification conditions, following the single preselected criterion and threshold. Temporal sequence or two numbers rising and falling together is insufficient; shared inputs, alternative channels, and measurement protocols may explain differences. The channel-effect test on which this rule relies must have obtained support, and the original result’s target, object, and window must cover the present use; one instantaneous comparison cannot establish all long-term performance. [T-C2; T-G2; T-contract]

The five dimensions answer different questions: capacity is how much of a same-type quantity can pass under specified conditions; latency is the time from input to the relevant output; reliability is the frequency or probability of success across specified opportunities, tasks, and conditions; controllability asks whether permitted interventions can change the state or transition in question; loss is the difference or loss between input and corresponding quantifiable output within the declared accounting boundary. These only indicate explanatory directions; actual measurements require denominators, units, tasks, protocols, and scope. If only latency is measured, record only latency, leaving the other four unknown. [T-C2; T-G2]

Discussing ‘transfer’ first requires checking types. 1000 joules and 1 kilojoule are different units of the same energy and admit a definite conversion; 3 hours and 20 yuan are different quantity types and cannot directly add to 23 units of ‘cost’. Even declaring an hourly price yields a monetary valuation under a particular accounting mapping, not a discovery that time and money are physically conserved; it also cannot erase unpriced care, opportunities, or risks. [T-C2; T-measure]

Matching units is still insufficient: disclose whose quantity it is, its start and end points, time window, stock changes, external inputs, measurement error, and flows beyond the boundary. Accounting for conservable physical quantities must be established under the relevant domain laws and complete inflow/outflow conditions; this rule cannot infer cross-domain conservation from ‘resources were occupied’. Without mappings or boundaries, at most describe observed inputs, occupation, losses, or candidate constraints; do not assert that costs have been transferred to a specified person. [T-C2; T-table]

Redundant channels especially remind us to distinguish the effect asked about. Cutting c1 alone may leave the target unchanged because c2 fully compensates. This leaves unsupported the claim that ‘cutting c1 must change the target under the current substitution conditions’, but does not alone establish that c1 never had any local effect. Identifying local transmission and compensation requires additional measurements and design; nor may ‘there might be compensation’ rescue a failed predetermined criterion. [T-table; T-G2]

Carriers and responsibility are different types. Equipment, programs, or positions may transmit resources or execute instructions; moral, legal, or institutional responsibility depends on subject standing, knowledge, control, authorization, conduct, oversight, and applicable rules. The busiest or most visible person, or the one bearing losses, does not automatically become the primary responsible party; identifying causal channels confers no authority to allocate costs or require unlimited burden-bearing. [T-C2; T-human]

The row for this rule in the concluding table lists minimum evidence: a qualified channel-effect test, quantity types and mappings, channel-by-channel and dimension-by-dimension measurements, accounting boundaries, and windows; counterexamples include redundant substitution, unlike quantities without mappings, and differences explained by shared inputs. It requires specifying which conclusion is blocked rather than blanket claims that ‘data establish a transfer’ or ‘one missing item means nothing is known’. The constraint on object declaration, retaining competing explanations and residuals, the conditions for causal claims, and the conditions for evidence under ‘Must also meet’ remain evidentiary responsibilities, not empirical causes. [T-C2; T-table]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Use the structural object to fix the object, and a qualified channel-effect test with matching target/window to identify the specified channel.

  2. 2

    State source and target quantity types, units, identity criteria, accounting boundaries, and time window.

  3. 3

    Track quantities of the same type through unit identities; compare unlike quantities only under an explicit conversion or accounting mapping, retaining its limits.

  4. 4

    Measure capacity, latency, reliability, controllability, and loss separately for each channel; do not fill unknowns with zero or infinity.

  5. 5

    Check shared inputs, redundant compensation, and measurement changes; determine only the supported scope and separate carrying from responsibility.

Distinctions to keep clear

Same type, different units

Can be compared through actual conversion relations.

≠

Unlike quantities

Require an explicit conversion or accounting mapping first.

A channel has an effect

Proportionate identification exists for a specific target transition.

≠

All performance dimensions are known

The five dimensions require separate measurement; an effect cannot fill them all in.

Occupation or loss

Described within explicitly defined quantities and boundaries.

≠

Unified cross-domain cost

This rule supplies neither a universal unit nor conservation.

Causal carrying

Executing, transmitting, or maintaining the change in question.

≠

Responsible party

Requires independent subject standing and grounds for responsibility.

Mathematical teaching construction: separate conversion, valuation, and unmeasured dimensionsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe account values and 10 yuan per hour are teaching assumptions; J/kJ conversion is a unit definition. No actual wages or budgets were surveyed.

In artificial accounts, A records energy of 1000 J and B records 1 kJ; the unit identity 1 kJ=1000 J makes them equal. Separately, labor is 3 hours and spending is 20 yuan. If the teaching accounting rule ‘10 yuan per hour’ is explicit, valuation gives 3×10+20=50 yuan. The 50 is a total under that rule, not a measured universal cost, and does not mean that duration, emotion, or rights have been exhausted by money.

BoundaryUnit conversion does not establish that a resource actually transferred from A to B; corresponding paths, boundaries, and inflow/outflow evidence are still required.

Mathematical teaching construction: a target remains unchanged with redundant channelsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe max structure, binary states, and permitted interventions are explicit artificial assumptions, not observations of an actual network.

Let binary channels be c1,c2 and target Y=max(c1,c2). Changing (1,1) to (0,1) leaves Y at 1; changing (1,0) to (0,0) changes Y from 1 to 0. This shows that an intervention’s target effect on the same channel depends on the other route’s state. In actual research, failure of the first comparison cannot be followed by a covert switch to the second to rescue the original preselected result.

BoundaryThis shows only conditional dependence and the possibility of compensation; it grants no actual channel qualification as a channel-effect test.

Mars Climate Orbiter, 1999: same-type quantities still require correct unit interfacesDocumented case

NASA’s Phase I investigation report of November 10, 1999 states that ground-based SM_FORCES output should have been in N·s but was reported in lbf·s; subsequent navigation processing therefore underestimated the corresponding effect by approximately a factor of 4.45. This section adds the observation that even when both numbers represent impulse, successful interface formatting does not establish consistent interpretation of the quantity; units and conversions must travel downstream with the values.

SourceNASA Mars Climate Orbiter Mishap Investigation Board Phase I Report§4 MCO Root Cause, printed p. 16/PDF 16; §5 Contributing Cause No. 1, printed p. 17/PDF 17; report dated 1999-11-10.Reading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsThe same case as in Part One is reused, not a new independent validation; 4.45 is the approximate factor used by the report. This guide neither determines all personnel responsibility from the unit issue alone nor claims to have completed a channel-effect test of the framework.

What does not follow

  • Counterexamples in the original text: full replacement by redundant channels or differences explained by shared inputs limit the original effect claim for the specified channel.
  • Counterexample in the original text: unlike quantities without a mapping cannot be retrospectively recognized as a transfer of the same cost.
  • Boundary in the original text: latency material alone cannot establish that capacity, reliability, controllability, and loss were measured.
  • Constructed conditional counterexample: both backup channels are open and Y=max(c1,c2); closing c1 while holding c2=1 leaves Y=1. One ineffective blockage cannot establish the absence of all local processes.
  • Constructed conditional counterexample: directly adding 3 hours and 20 yuan into 23 cost units defines no interpretable quantity.
  • Real-case boundary: MCO’s unit inconsistency for the same impulse type does not mean all comparisons across quantities are impossible; proportionate conversion is precisely a necessary part of feasible tracking.

Scope and open questions

This unit concerns methodological judgment. Actual sources support only the listed facts; the diagram and teaching construction each retain their own status.

  • Definitions, denominators, and windows for measurement of a specific channel's five dimensions must come from the actual object. This lesson generated no such field data.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    If latency has been measured at 2 seconds, may reliability also be entered as 100%?

  2. 2

    Why can 1000 J and 1 kJ be compared, while 3 hours and 20 yuan cannot directly be added?

  3. 3

    Does an unchanged target after closing a channel prove that the channel never had any effect?

  4. 4

    Is the most visible executing device or person necessarily the responsible party?

If latency has been measured at 2 seconds, may reliability also be entered as 100%?

No. Reliability requires a success definition, an opportunity denominator, and data under the corresponding conditions. Unmeasured dimensions remain unknown.

Basis: Chinese source lines 795–803.

Why can 1000 J and 1 kJ be compared, while 3 hours and 20 yuan cannot directly be added?

The former quantities are of the same type and permit unit conversion; the latter are heterogeneous and require explicit accounting or conversion rules, which do not create physical conservation.

Basis: Chinese source lines 771, 775, and 803.

Does an unchanged target after closing a channel prove that the channel never had any effect?

No. Redundant compensation may exist, but this also does not license declaring an effect without evidence. Separate local and conditional comparisons are required.

Basis: Chinese source line 824; §4.4, line 665; the artificial max model.

Is the most visible executing device or person necessarily the responsible party?

Not automatically. Causal carriage, eligibility for responsibility, informed control, and authorization rules require separate arguments.

Basis: Chinese source line 799; §7.2.4–7.2.5.

4.11.3Effective Feedback and Feedback-Mediated Learning (C3) ​

In briefA returned signal counts as effective feedback in the sense of this rule only if it actually changes a subsequent process. Calling it feedback-mediated learning additionally requires tracing how an update remains and how later tasks call upon it. One observed change is far from sufficient.

Grounds: effective feedback (§3.3); channel effect (§4.4).

Conditions: The basic branch, that is, effective feedback, must have a return channel, temporal order, the item that is subsequently changed, and a counterfactual comparison with no return or a blocked channel; effective feedback requires only a change in at least one subsequent state, probability, or constraint, and need not leave a durable historical trace. The carrier route, that is, carrier learning, separately checks under §4.5 the carrier of the update, the retention or updating rules, subsequent invocation over multiple rounds, a comparison on a predetermined task, and the corresponding causal evidence. The historical-increment route, that is, historical-increment learning, additionally requires a historical-increment test, updates that can be retained, repeated rounds, and a comparison on a predetermined task.

Can conclude: The basic branch may determine effective feedback, its time lag, and the item it changes. When the carrier route's conditions hold, candidate feedback-mediated learning may be determined within the specified updates, task, and time window. With an additional historical-increment test, updates that can be retained, and repeated rounds, candidate historical-increment feedback-mediated learning may be determined.

Cannot conclude: that a feedback entry point or proof of receipt is effective feedback; that one state update is learning, repair, or positive improvement; that a direction of value or authorization to act can be inferred directly from facts about feedback or learning.

Must also meet: Retaining Competing Explanations and Residuals (§4.8.4); conditions for causal claims (§2.4); conditions for evidence (§2.5).

The basic branch first uses a channel-effect test to identify the return channel as a candidate causal carrier, then, under the definition of effective feedback, compares the situation with a return against that with no return or a blocked channel. The carrier route must trace how updates are retained, how they are invoked in subsequent rounds, and how they affect the predetermined task, checking longitudinal and causal materials under §4.5; sufficiency of the current state does not negate this route. The historical-increment route additionally requires a historical-increment test to show an increment beyond the current representation. The two kinds of evidence cannot substitute for one another.

This rule has three branches. The basic branch: a return channel, changes in subsequent states or transitions, and a blocking counterfactual comparison. The carrier route: additional evidence, as §4.5 requires, of an update carrier, invocation over multiple rounds, and task outcomes. The historical-increment route: an additional historical-increment test, with updates that can be retained, repeated rounds, and an out-of-sample comparison on a predetermined task.

4.11.3Note

Understanding this section

4.11.3 Effective feedback and feedback-mediated learning (C3)

A returned signal counts as effective feedback in the sense of this rule only if it actually changes a subsequent process. Calling it feedback-mediated learning additionally requires tracing how an update remains and how later tasks call upon it. One observed change is far from sufficient.

Chinese source line 809 explicitly states that “effective feedback requires only a change in at least one subsequent state, probability, or constraint, and need not leave a durable historical trace.” The grounds of the basic branch are effective feedback (§3.3) and channel effect (§4.4): the definition of effective feedback defines return and subsequent change, while a qualified channel-effect test identifies candidate causal carriage by the specified return channel. A feedback entry point, acknowledgment, or statement establishes only the corresponding message process, not a changed target transition. Effective feedback does not universally require a historical-increment test either. [T-C3；T-D2；T-feedback]

The basic branch, that is, effective feedback, must connect prior state/output, returned signal, channel, receiving position, the items subsequently changed, and temporal order, then compare no-return or blocked-channel conditions. The issue is not drawing a circular arrow but whether return causes a subsequent difference exceeding the threshold for the specified object and window. Shared inputs producing both the signal and change, changed measurement protocols, or change preceding the signal may undermine the explanation; the comparison must address these conditions. [T-C3；T-feedback]

A brief but properly identified change may also be effective feedback. An artificial controller, for example, receives a current deviation and adjusts the next step, then does not retain the signal. It can satisfy a within-model return effect without providing learning across periods. Absence of long-term traces does not invalidate all feedback, and a persistent archive does not establish that feedback changed the target. [T-C3；T-feedback]

Beyond feedback, the carrier route, that is, carrier learning, requires a locatable update carrier, retention or continuing-update rules, actual use across multiple later rounds, and predetermined task comparisons. A carrier may be a state, parameter, rule, memory, or structure; the key is whether the update enters subsequent tasks and produces reviewable differences. Archiving without use, changing only proxy scores without affecting the target, or a task's coincidental one-time success does not complete this learning mechanism. [T-C3；T-learning]

Causal claims on this carrier route still require interruption, replacement, recovery, or comparisons meeting identification conditions, addressing shared inputs, ongoing training, selection, attrition, and measurement changes. Original channel-effect test results and longitudinal material must cover the task and window now claimed; immediate effects cannot be promoted into years-long extrapolations. Claims of transfer or improved prediction require proportionate independent-task or out-of-sample comparisons. If only repeated success is observed and the mechanism remains unidentified, a domain judgment of ordinary learning may remain without claiming completion of the formal feedback-mediated mechanism. [T-G3；T-learning]

The historical-increment route is the original text's fixed “historical-increment” learning branch; its name alone does not put all learning within it. Besides retainable updates, repeated rounds, and out-of-sample comparisons on predetermined tasks, it requires an eligible historical-increment test supporting an additional historical conditional increment beyond the current representation. Predictive path dependence and causal path dependence remain distinct; a predictive residual alone does not supply its own causal explanation. [T-C3；T-G3]

The two learning routes are not stronger/weaker personalities or higher/lower stages. When current parameters fully retain what was learned, complete training history may add no target-predictive information conditional on those parameters, while carrier-mediated learning remains supported by independent process and task evidence. This permits neither deliberately omitting known parameters to manufacture a historical increment nor renaming a failed predetermined historical-increment test as the carrier route to erase failure. Independent carrier evidence may support a separate, explicitly bounded conclusion. [T-C3；T-G3；T-learning]

“Learning” is not synonymous with improvement. Disclose the predetermined task, comparison baseline, and actual results, then separately assess costs, harms, and net benefit. Incorrect rules may also be retained, repeatedly used, and change task performance; effective feedback may even amplify bias. Changing targets after failure requires explaining the new target's reasons and procedure, retaining failure and costs under the old target, and not rewriting history through a retrospective target. [T-C3；T-learning]

The evidence table at the group's end aligns three questions: “Grouping Gain and Its Robustness to Boundary Perturbation” examines the object's definition, the grouping-gain test, out-of-sample gain, boundaries, and independent review; “Carrying and Channel Constraints” examines the channel-effect test, quantities and mappings, dimension-specific data, and accounting boundaries; “Effective Feedback and Feedback-Mediated Learning” examines return, timing, blockage, and the items changed, then adds material for its learning route. They share no overall “sufficient evidence” score. Failure of the first returns to a candidate grouping; insufficient mapping under the second stops at inputs/occupancy or candidate limitations; insufficient learning evidence under the third stops at independently supported effective feedback. [T-table]

The three counterexamples in this rule's row of the table block different points: signal arrival without a changed transition lacks basic-feedback support; unretained or unused updates lack learning-route support; differences explained by shared inputs or proxy indicators prevent confirmation of the corresponding mechanism. Missing a historical-increment test blocks only the historical-increment route, not independently supported carrier-mediated learning. Without return or subsequent change, say only that a signal arrived; “not yet measured” cannot be rewritten as “proved to have no effect.” [T-table；T-C3]

Neither basic feedback nor learning automatically supplies a value direction or authority for real action. Recording a mechanism's existence does not mean it should be reinforced, or that someone must undergo training or bear costs. “Retaining Competing Explanations and Residuals,” the conditions for causal claims, and the conditions for evidence address competing explanations, causal identification, and material credibility here; real adoption still requires corresponding norms, protection, authorization, and procedures. [T-C3；T-C12]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Fix in advance the return channel, receiving position, temporal sequence, target items, and comparison rules; identify the corresponding effect through a qualified channel-effect test.

  2. 2

    Compare subsequent differences with return versus no return/blockage, distinguishing signal arrival from effective feedback.

  3. 3

    For carrier-mediated learning, add the update location, retention or continuing updating, use across rounds, task outcomes, and corresponding causal evidence.

  4. 4

    For an additional claim of historical increment beyond the current representation, add a historical-increment test and out-of-sample comparisons on predetermined tasks, preserving the prediction/causation distinction.

  5. 5

    Narrow claims item by item for counterexamples such as shared inputs, unused updates, and proxy indicators. A missing condition stops the branch actually dependent on it.

  6. 6

    Assess stability, net benefits, transfer, and authority separately; none follows automatically from the labels feedback or learning.

Distinctions to keep clear

Signal arrival

An input or acknowledgment has appeared.

≠

Effective feedback

Return actually causes a subsequent change in state, probability, or constraint.

Effective feedback

A single bounded change is allowed, without a long-term trace.

≠

Carrier-based learning

Additionally requires retainable updates, use across rounds, and task comparisons.

Carrier-based learning

Current state may sufficiently carry what was learned.

≠

Historical-increment learning

Additionally requires support from a historical-increment test for an increment beyond the current representation.

Learning mechanism

Updates enter tasks and change outcomes.

≠

Net benefit or transfer

Requires separate evaluation of costs, harms, and target scope.

Mathematical teaching construction: one effective return requires no long-term memoryTeaching scenario

AssumptionsExact equations, no noise or saturation, identical initial values, and reset/no-memory conditions are all teaching assumptions. Deviation is a signed dimensionless quantity.

Artificially set deviation x=1, return control u=−kx, and next step x′=x+u. For k=0.5, x′=0.5; with blocked return k=0, x′=1, a difference of −0.5. Further stipulate that an external reset sets x=1 next round and the controller stores no information from this round. The return still changes the next step without providing learning retained across rounds. With k=3 instead, x′=−2 and squared deviation is 4, exceeding the blocked-return value 1.

BoundaryNot a recommendation for actual control gain or an empirical channel-effect test. It only shows that feedback, traces, and improvement are nonequivalent.

Mathematical teaching construction: retained parameters can carry learning while historical residuals remain zeroTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe constant target 1, update rule, storage and repeated use, untrained baseline, and output equal to θ are artificially specified. Future tasks have no undeclared changes or noise.

Fix task target 1 and initial parameter θ0=0; after error return, update θn+1=θn+0.5(1−θn). The first three updates give θ1=0.5, θ2=0.75, θ3=0.875; squared task errors are 0.25, 0.0625, and 0.015625. Suppose θ3 is then saved and repeatedly used for the same fixed task without further training. Compared with the no-update baseline θ=0, subsequent squared error falls from 1 to 0.015625. Given current θ3 and the target, output and error are already determined; complete training history adds no information.

BoundaryIllustrates the logical distinction between carrier and residual, without claiming completion of an actual test as this rule or the historical-increment test requires. It cannot be extrapolated to changing targets, independent transfer, or actual net benefits.

AlphaGo Zero, 2017: an actual research entry point for updates entering the next task roundDocumented case

The abstract of Silver and colleagues' 2017 paper reports training a neural network through self-play to predict moves and winners. The updated network improves tree search and enters the next self-play iteration; the authors also report game results against existing AlphaGo. This section uses that bounded fact to show why studying learning requires seeing updates used in subsequent tasks, not merely a preserved record.

SourceSilver et al., Mastering the game of Go without human knowledge, Nature 550:354–359PMID 29052630; 2017-10-18; DOI 10.1038/nature24270; original abstract sentences 5–8, especially training predictions, the next iteration, and the final game-results sentence.Reading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsThis lesson read the original abstract and does not claim review of all code, supplementary experiments, or mechanism ablations. No channel-effect test, historical-increment test, or complete case under this rule was constructed under this framework. General algorithmic learning is not directly equated with historical increments beyond the current representation, nor extrapolated to real social benefits.

Scope and open questions

This unit concerns methodological judgment. Actual sources support only the listed facts; the diagram and teaching construction each retain their own status.

  • Determining a learning study to be a formal branch of this rule still requires item-by-item review of the relevant channel-effect test, update retention/use, and task comparisons; a historical-residual claim also requires the corresponding historical-increment test. An abstract cannot fill those gaps.

Is one feedback event necessarily ineffective if it leaves no long-term trace?

No. Basic feedback may hold if the specified return causes a qualified subsequent change relative to no return/blockage. Learning adds conditions such as retention and use.

Basis: Chinese source lines 785 and 817; §6.2.

If a record is updated but never read afterward, is that enough to call it learning?

No. Carrier-mediated learning requires updates actually entering multiple later task rounds, with proportionate outcome and causal evidence.

Basis: Chinese source lines 785 and 817–825; §6.3.

Can carrier-mediated learning exist without a historical-increment test?

It can, but the carrier route's material must be independently completed. Absence of a historical-increment test does not automatically establish that route.

Basis: Chinese source lines 817–825; §4.5.

Why is feedback effective but not improving when x=1 and k=3?

Return changes the next step from 1 under blockage to −2, so there is an effect. Yet with target 0, squared error increases from 1 to 4.

Basis: This lesson's artificial model, not advice for actual control.

After θ3 is retained, why may training history supply no additional predictive information?

Subsequent output is determined by current θ3. Conditional on it, complete history cannot further reduce uncertainty for this fixed task.

Basis: This lesson's artificial updating and use assumptions.

Does one learning success establish cross-context transfer or net benefit?

No. New task scope, support conditions, costs, and harms require separate evaluation.

Basis: §6.3, Chinese source lines 1404–1410.

AlphaGo Zero, 2017: an actual research entry point for updates entering the next task round

4.12Group 2: History, Load, Scale, and Spillovers ​

In briefThis group asks separately about historical effects, load, scale representation, and effects beyond boundaries. They often occur in one case, but words such as “long-term,” “whole,” and “overloaded” cannot replace the material each requires.
4.12Note

Understanding this section

4.12 Group II: history, load, scale, and spillover

This group asks separately about historical effects, load, scale representation, and effects beyond boundaries. They often occur in one case, but words such as “long-term,” “whole,” and “overloaded” cannot replace the material each requires.

Chinese source lines 827–828 are a group heading, without an additional independent empirical law. “Historical Effects, Path Differences, and Repair Windows” (§4.12.1) distinguishes historical formation, current carriers, additional historical information, and repair timing. “Load, Capacity, and Recovery” (§4.12.2) distinguishes immediate gaps, carrier-mediated accumulation, and historical-increment accumulation. “Scale Closure and Object Conversion” (§4.12.3) distinguishes scale-closure failure from preselected object/intervention conversion. “Local Improvement and Cross-Boundary Spillover” (§4.12.4) distinguishes crossing object boundaries, crossing scales, and model closure. Each of the four following subsections provides its own complete explanation; the parent summary cannot replace it. [T-intro；T-C4；T-C5；T-C6；T-C7]

The shared reading principle is to identify the branch actually claimed, then check the channels, time, representation, quantities, or accounting definitions it truly depends on. A historical-increment test is required only when historical information beyond current state is explicitly claimed. Scale transformation and cross-scale transfer testing are added only for actual cross-scale movement, and a corresponding scale-closure test only for explicit closure-failure or conversion claims. A branch with fewer conditions cannot be chosen afterward to erase an original test failure, but independently supported narrower conclusions may remain. [T-C4；T-C5；T-C7；T-G3]

The table at Chinese source lines 887–894 compares evidence, counterexamples, and stopping points for the four rules. Its final paragraph especially notes that same-scale transmission can have real cross-boundary effects, and well-closed models can represent them. The group is not a chain in which “longer history, greater load, and higher scale make harm increasingly inevitable”; it comprises four sets of separately testable responsibilities. [T-table；T-C7]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Distinguish the parent heading from its four independent subsections.

  2. 2

    Specify each branch and its object, time, quantities, and mapping, avoiding automatic addition of irrelevant thresholds.

  3. 3

    Use the closing table to check counterexamples and failure points, retaining existing independent evidence.

Distinctions to keep clear

Multiple questions in one case

Permit separate study of history, load, scale, and spillover.

≠

One concept handles everything

Similar names do not complete other rules.

What does not follow

  • The parent section adds no proposition about actual effects and completes no subsection's explanation in its place.
  • Cross-boundary does not always mean cross-scale; cross-boundary effects do not first require proof of model closure failure.

Scope and open questions

The original parent section contains only a heading, so navigation and separation of responsibilities are used without forcing a factual case onto the title.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    If a measure in one district affects another, is a scale-closure test immediately required?

  2. 2

    Do all long-term effects require a historical-increment test?

If a measure in one district affects another, is a scale-closure test immediately required?

Not immediately. First examine the actual cross-boundary channel. Check scale transformation and cross-scale transfer testing only for actual cross-scale movement, and require a scale-closure test only for the further claim of closure failure or conversion.

Basis: §4.12.4。

Do all long-term effects require a historical-increment test?

No. A current carrier's effects across periods follow their own material; increments beyond the current representation carry the responsibility of the historical-increment test.

Basis: §4.12.1—4.12.2；§4.5。

4.12.1Historical Effects, Path Differences, and Repair Windows (C4) ​

In briefThis conclusion rule does not reduce historical influence to one kind of “residual,” nor understand repair as returning to yesterday. First specify which object or function is to be repaired, then compare how intervention timing affects attainability and costs.

Grounds: basic state terms (§3.2). The historical-increment route additionally requires historical increment (§4.5); the current-carrier route and the intervention-timing route obtain the corresponding evidence under §4.5 and §2.4.

Conditions: On the historical-increment route, historical variables must be defined before future results appear, with the stated current state, environment, and measurement protocol all controlled; the predictive and causal subtypes must not be conflated. Evidence for general historical formation and for the effects of current carriers is obtained through the separate routes set out in §4.5. Discussion of a repair window additionally requires a target identity criterion or target functional criterion made public in advance (§3.2), comparisons of intervention at different times, and the corresponding causal identification; a historical-increment test is added only when an additional historical residual is claimed.

Can conclude: The historical-increment route may determine predictive or causal historical increments within the pre-registered time window and under the current representation. The current-carrier route may determine limited historical effects according to its own materials. With an additional target identity criterion or target functional criterion, timing comparisons, and the corresponding basis for identification, a conditional repair window may be determined; this does not require the outcome to retain a historical residual beyond the current representation.

Cannot conclude: that the preservation of traces is a historical effect; that a predictive gain is causation or irreversibility; that path differences are fate, progress, decline, responsibility, or regression to an earlier stage; that repair can be claimed while the target identity criterion or target functional criterion has not been made public.

Must also meet: Constraint on Object Declaration (§4.8.1); Retaining Competing Explanations and Residuals (§4.8.4); conditions for causal claims (§2.4); conditions for evidence (§2.5).

Evolution is first classified by the basic state terms; historical effects cannot be inferred from a definition. The current-carrier route checks formation, retention, invocation, and subsequent outcomes. The historical-increment route looks separately at the predictive gain for predictive path dependence or the causal basis for causal path dependence. A repair window compares, for interventions at different times, whether the target identity criterion or target functional criterion made public in advance can be attained, and at what price; it bears the corresponding responsibility of a historical-increment test only when it also claims a historical residual beyond the current representation.

4.12.1Note

Understanding this section

4.12.1 Historical Effects, Path Differences, and Repair Windows (C4)

This conclusion rule does not reduce historical influence to one kind of “residual,” nor understand repair as returning to yesterday. First specify which object or function is to be repaired, then compare how intervention timing affects attainability and costs.

Chinese source line 831 separates the grounds: the basic state terms (§3.2) handle classification of evolution; the historical-increment route additionally requires a historical-increment test; the current-carrier route and the intervention-timing route stand on §4.5 and causal-evidence rules respectively. The basic state terms can identify what kind of change occurred in states, relations, boundaries, or identity; their definitions alone cannot prove that the past caused the present. This rule's first task is to assign separate responsibilities to “change occurred” and “what caused the change.” [T-C4; T-D1]

Historical formation asks how earlier experiences entered the current state; the carrier route continues by asking how that state preserves, updates, and calls upon information and affects later outcomes. Longitudinal records showing co-persistence may still fail to distinguish the transmission mechanism. Shared inputs, continued exposure, selection, attrition, and measurement changes must be addressed. The channel-effect test or specified test of a human empirical hypothesis required for a formal carrier mechanism must also cover the corresponding object, outcome, and window; a trace under “Historical Trace Carriers” itself cannot substitute for subsequent effects. [T-C4; T-G3]

The historical-increment route defines historical variables before future outcomes, controls for the stated current states, environment, and measurement protocols, and then examines the predictive increments of predictive path dependence or the causal conditions of causal path dependence. Better prediction is not an actionable causal path, still less irreversibility. If the current state has absorbed the relevant historical information, the residual may disappear. This limits only the claim of an additional increment: it neither denies carrier effects nor, conversely, provides evidence for them. [T-C4; T-G3]

Repair begins by disclosing a target identity criterion or target functional criterion (§3.2). The target identity criterion specifies what object identity is to be recovered or established; the target functional criterion specifies the functional target to be reached. They must be explicit before results, not selected afterward because a result looks favorable. Repair may change components, relations, interfaces, or carriers; it is not equivalent to reversing history or restoring the original configuration. A recovered function may be acknowledged within limits. Remaining deficits in other functions do not negate it, but this local success cannot establish recovery of the entire former object and all consequences for life. [T-C4; T-repair; T-load]

“There is a repair window” is stronger than “improvement followed one measure.” It requires comparing attainability and costs of interventions at different times under the same disclosed objective, with proportionate causal identification: did early and late groups differ initially in severity, did other changes occur in between, and which resources or permitted actions changed? A single success supplies, at most, material on that process and outcome. It does not automatically identify a window's boundaries, much less prove absolute impossibility at a later, untested time. [T-C4; T-repair; T-causal]

Ordinary differences in repair timing may be carried entirely by the current state. For example, after current damage reaches a threshold, the permitted repair operation may cease to work: this is a model of present constraints and intervention timing. The responsibilities of a historical-increment test arise only with the further claim that additional historical records change outcomes beyond the same stated current representation. This distinction both prevents all delayed recovery from being mislabeled a historical residual and prevents “the current state is sufficient” from erasing the actual formation process. [T-C4; T-G3]

The counterexamples in this rule's row of the group's concluding table target failure to distinguish formation from effects, absorption of residuals into current states, and lack of stable differences across intervention times. Absence of a historical-increment test blocks only additional historical increments; without causal material, historical causation cannot be claimed; without a target identity criterion or target functional criterion and timing evidence, a repair window cannot be claimed. Explicit counterevidence, non-observation, and insufficient precision must still be recorded separately. Not every unsuccessful attempt means permanent irreparability. [T-table]

This rule also prohibits turning path differences into fate, progress, decline, responsibility, or regression between stages. Even if a particular intervention is known to be more effective, whether its target is justified, who may decide, who bears the costs, and who has authority to implement it require independent normative and procedural judgments. The constraint on object declaration, retaining competing explanations and residuals, the conditions for causal claims, and the conditions for evidence under “Must also meet” require object declaration, competing explanations, and evidential identification; they do not replace these value and permission questions. [T-C4; T-repair; T-C12]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    First specify the type of change through the basic state terms; classification must not replace causation.

  2. 2

    Specify formation, current carriers, and increments beyond the current representation separately; obtain proportionate material for each.

  3. 3

    To call something repair, disclose a target identity criterion or target functional criterion, the object, population, supporting conditions, and persistence window in advance.

  4. 4

    To call something a repair window, compare target attainability and costs of interventions at different times, checking causal identification.

  5. 5

    Add a historical-increment test only for claims of an additional historical residual, distinguishing prediction from causation; assess normative targets and authorization separately.

Distinctions to keep clear

Trace formation

A carrier preserves differences.

≠

Historical effects

Require proportionate material showing formation or subsequent effects.

Current carrier

May take up all relevant historical information.

≠

Additional historical quantity

Asks what remains after conditioning on the stated current representation.

One repair

A result occurs under a specified target and support.

≠

Repair window

Also requires comparison and identification across different times.

Functional repair (target functional criterion)

A specific function reaches its prespecified target.

≠

Complete restoration of the former state

Is not necessary for every repair and does not follow from a local function.

Mathematical teaching construction: current damage suffices to produce differences in repair timingTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe state domain 0–4, evolution, repair threshold, permitted operation, target, and clock are all artificially specified; only this same operation and fixed target are compared here.

Set artificial damage d0=0. Without intervention, d increases by 1 each step, capped at 4. The same repair operation R(d) sets d to 0 when d≤2 and leaves d unchanged when d≥3. The prespecified target functional criterion is “d≤1 one further step after intervention.” Intervening at τ=1 or 2 gives 0 after R and 1 at the next step, meeting the target. At τ=3, R(3)=3 and the next step gives 4, failing the target. Given current d and the operation, the next step is determined; additional history is unnecessary.

BoundaryThis only shows that a conditional window can be explained by a current carrier; it supplies no real damage threshold, diagnosis of irreversibility, or actual status as a historical-increment test or under this rule.

Apollo 13 carbon-dioxide removal modification: functional repair can change an interfaceDocumented case

Item 46 of the NASA report records that engineers developed and tested a method for adapting command-module LiOH canisters to the lunar module's air-cleaning system. The crew built the modification, after which carbon-dioxide partial pressure fell. After additional canisters were fitted, it remained within the reported range for the rest of the return journey. This section adds attention to function and configuration: a new adaptation can take up a bounded air-treatment function without restoring the original configuration.

SourceNASA Apollo 13 Review Board report1970-06-15; item 46, Modification of LM Carbon Dioxide Removal System, Findings (c)–(e) and Determination, printed 5-34/PDF 200.Reading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsThis historical action is not retroactively entered as a prior Xikari pre-registration, nor does one modification establish a general repair window. It does not mean that the original lunar-landing mission or all spacecraft systems were restored. Reusing the same report as earlier lessons adds no independent source.

What does not follow

  • Original-text counterexample: a current state absorbs all historical residuals, limiting only the historical increment without canceling an independent carrier route.
  • Original-text counterexample: intervention times show no stable differences; a window cannot be determined from an “early good, late bad” narrative.
  • Original-text boundary: when a target identity criterion or target functional criterion was not disclosed, a favorable outcome selected afterward cannot establish repair.
  • Constructed conditional counterexample: one successful repair with no comparison to other times cannot determine the last possible repair time.
  • Constructed conditional counterexample: in an artificial Markov damage model, early and late intervention outcomes are fully determined by current damage; a window does not require an additional historical increment.

Scope and open questions

This unit concerns methodological judgment. Actual sources support only the listed facts; the diagram and teaching construction each retain their own status.

  • Specific repair targets, comparison times, costs, and external support must be determined for the actual task; this lesson proposes no real-world intervention deadline without identification.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    Do all branches of this rule require a historical-increment test?

  2. 2

    Can recovery of only one function count as bounded repair?

  3. 3

    Why can a single success not determine a repair window?

  4. 4

    Why does the artificial τ=3 case fail the target?

Do all branches of this rule require a historical-increment test?

No. The additional historical-increment route requires a historical-increment test; carrier effects and ordinary timing effects rely on their respective material.

Basis: Chinese source lines 831–841.

Can recovery of only one function count as bounded repair?

Yes, if accurately stated within the prespecified target functional criterion, supporting conditions, and window. Returning to the old configuration is not required, and the claim must not expand into complete recovery.

Basis: §6.10, Chinese source line 1502; §6.6.

Why can a single success not determine a repair window?

Without comparisons of attainability/costs across intervention times and proportionate identification, competing explanations such as differences between early and late objects cannot be excluded.

Basis: Chinese source lines 833–841.

Why does the artificial τ=3 case fail the target?

At intervention d=3; R leaves it unchanged, and the next step gives 4, exceeding the requirement of 1 in the target functional criterion. This is not caused by an unstated historical residual.

Basis: The artificial equations in this lesson.
