4.12.2Load, Capacity, and Recovery (C5) ​

In briefThis conclusion rule first compares demand and capacity of the same type, at the same position and time, then asks whether this gap leaves subsequent effects. Busyness, gaps, cumulative damage, and delayed recovery must not be collapsed into one conclusion.

Grounds: structural object (§3.1); channel effect (§4.4).

Conditions: The basic branch, that is, the instantaneous branch, must have definitions of demand and capacity of the same type, units or a conversion mapping, measurement within the same time window, and distribution across positions. The carrier route, that is, carrier accumulation, must trace under §4.5 how load enters the current state of damage or capacity, the process of accumulation or recovery across time windows, and its subsequent effects, and must satisfy the channel-effect test's requirements for the channel. The historical-increment route, that is, historical-increment accumulation, additionally requires a historical-increment test and a locatable historical carrier.

Can conclude: The basic branch may determine an instantaneous load–capacity shortfall at a specified time window and position. When the carrier route's conditions hold, candidate cumulative damage or candidate delayed recovery may be determined within that carrier, time window, and outcome. With an additional historical-increment test, candidate historical-increment accumulation or delayed recovery beyond the current representation may be determined.

Cannot conclude: that load necessarily accumulates monotonically, or that overload necessarily causes collapse; that demand and capacity of different types can be subtracted directly; that an instantaneous shortfall automatically proves durable damage; that a need for recovery directly generates an obligation of sacrifice for a named subject.

Must also meet: Constraint on Object Declaration (§4.8.1); Retaining Competing Explanations and Residuals (§4.8.4); conditions for causal claims (§2.4); conditions for evidence (§2.5).

The basic branch first fixes the types and units of demand, capacity, replenishment, loss, and the time window, uses a channel-effect test to confirm the carrying channel, then compares the immediate shortfall and the positions of spillover within the same time window. Accumulation and delayed recovery both require materials spanning time windows: the carrier route identifies under §4.5 how historical load formed the current state, how that state is maintained or recovers, and how it affects subsequent outcomes; the historical-increment route separately uses a historical-increment test to test increments beyond the current representation. Sufficiency of the current state is compatible with a carrier explanation, but cannot replace evidence of the carrier's formation process and of causation.

This rule has three branches. The basic branch: a demand–capacity mapping for quantities of the same type, and measurement within the same time window. The carrier route: additional evidence, as §4.5 requires, of a current carrier, accumulation or recovery across time windows, and subsequent effects. The historical-increment route: an additional historical-increment test, with a historical carrier and subsequent differences in capacity or recovery.

4.12.2Note

Understanding this section

4.12.2 Load, Capacity, and Recovery (C5)

This conclusion rule first compares demand and capacity of the same type, at the same position and time, then asks whether this gap leaves subsequent effects. Busyness, gaps, cumulative damage, and delayed recovery must not be collapsed into one conclusion.

Chinese source line 849 limits the basic output to “an instantaneous load–capacity shortfall at a specified time window and position.” The structural object (§3.1) fixes the object and the channel-effect test (§4.4) locates carrying channels; comparable demand, available capacity, replenishment, loss, and windows must be declared first. Demand measured in items cannot be directly subtracted from capacity measured in hours. If tasks take different amounts of time, task composition or a proportionate conversion is also needed. Calling both totals “capability” does not make them comparable quantities of the same type. [T-C5; T-C2]

The basic branch, that is, the instantaneous branch, requires measurements within the same window and at each position. Sufficient daily capacity may coexist with a peak gap in one hour; sufficient institution-wide capacity may coexist with one location unable to access idle resources. Capacity must also distinguish peak from sustained levels, alternative channels, and replenishment; maximum short-term performance cannot be treated as all-day sustainable capability. Positional distribution is not decoration on an overall average: it determines which demands can actually be taken up. [T-C5; T-load]

An immediate gap does not mean permanent damage. Capacity may expand simultaneously, demand may fall, and tasks may queue, reroute, or stop within permitted deadlines; a resolved gap may leave no subsequent difference. Claims of collapse, damage, or delayed recovery require independent criteria for that outcome and evidence across windows. “Demand exceeds capacity” cannot deduce every bad outcome. [T-C5; T-table; T-load]

The carrier route, that is, carrier accumulation, traces how load enters a current damage or capacity state, how it accumulates, persists, or recovers across windows, and how it affects later outcomes. This explanation requires a specific carrier and causal comparison, addressing continued shared inputs, replenishment changes, or measurement changes. Poor long-term outcomes alone do not mean that earlier load caused damage; nor does the current state's explanatory power for later outcomes excuse omission of material on how historical load formed it. [T-C5; T-G3]

The historical-increment route, that is, historical-increment accumulation, additionally requires a historical-increment test and a locatable historical carrier, asking whether historical quantities beyond the current representation still explain later differences in capacity or recovery. If the current damage state already carries past information sufficiently, the historical increment may be zero while the carrier route independently holds. Conversely, lack of positive support from a historical-increment test does not establish any specific damage carrier; neither kind of evidence can pay the other's evidential burden. [T-C5; T-G3]

Recovery must also specify what recovered: apparent output, recovery measured by the target identity criterion or target functional criterion, internal reserves, or personnel rest and recuperation may differ. Temporary premises, external assistance, or auxiliary equipment may produce real, bounded functional recovery; continued support does not automatically mean failure. But persistence, expiry, and replacement arrangements must be explained, and unexperienced peaks or maintenance cycles cannot count as verified. Failure after a new shock cannot erase an earlier success that was accurately bounded. [T-load]

The original text prohibits deriving a named subject's obligation to sacrifice directly from recovery needs. A position's current ability to carry more does not imply unlimited obligation. Costs, stopping rights, alternative routes, existing duties, and protective conditions require separate judgments. This rule describes resources and processes; it does not decide for normative bridging (§4.14.1) who must continue to bear the burden, or diagnose malice directly from a high burden. [T-C5; T-C12; T-human]

The stopping points in this rule's row of the group's concluding table are local: where types, units, windows, or channels are insufficient, describe only bounded resource states; without cross-window evidence, do not claim a cumulative mechanism; without a historical-increment test, block only the historical-increment route. Simultaneous capacity expansion, incomparable demand and capacity, absence of later differences after a gap resolves, and continued shared inputs explaining outcomes are counterexamples that materially change conclusions, not merely a vague claim that “things are complicated.” [T-table]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Fix the types, units, common window, and positions of demand, capacity, replenishment, and loss, and check the channels identified by the channel-effect test.

  2. 2

    First determine instantaneous gaps and their distribution, distinguishing peak/sustained capability and alternative resources that can actually be accessed.

  3. 3

    If claiming accumulation or delayed recovery, add formation of the current carrier, persistence/recovery, subsequent effects, and causal comparison.

  4. 4

    If claiming historical quantities beyond the current representation, additionally require a historical-increment test and a historical carrier; branches cannot rescue one another after the fact.

  5. 5

    Specify recovery targets, support, and deadlines, separately checking costs, duties, stopping rights, and actual permissions.

Distinctions to keep clear

Instantaneous shortfall

Demand of the same type exceeds available capacity in the current window.

≠

Persistent damage

Requires evidence of a carrier across windows and subsequent effects.

Overall capacity

Total resources under a particular aggregation.

≠

Position-accessible capacity

Must actually be accessible at that time and position.

Output recovery

A function or quantity has reached its target.

≠

Recovery of internal reserves

Personnel, spare parts, funds, and so forth require separate measurement.

Recovery is needed

Identifies a resource or functional problem.

≠

Someone must sacrifice

Obligation cannot follow from description alone.

Mathematical teaching construction: a short-term backlog can be clearedTeaching scenario

AssumptionsHomogeneous tasks, deterministic arrivals, work-conserving service, arrival before service, the ability to serve all remaining tasks, no dropping, and no other losses are all stipulated.

Suppose arrivals precede service each round, with queue q0=0 and qt+1=max(0,qt+dt−ct). In each of the first three rounds, 3 items arrive and 2 are actually served whenever tasks are present, giving q1=1, q2=2, and q3=3. In the fourth round, no new items arrive and actual service can handle up to 3, clearing the queue to 0. The model contains only a pending-task count, without damage or worker-fatigue variables, so these values cannot establish actual damage. They only refute the logical claim that ‘instantaneous overload inevitably causes continuing collapse.’

BoundaryClearing the queue does not mean actual personnel margins or service quality have recovered; no actual channel-effect test, historical-increment test, or study under this rule has been conducted.

Mathematical teaching construction: averages conceal locationsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsHomogeneous item counts, capacity in the same window, and nontransferability are explicit teaching conditions.

Two stations can each serve 4 items during the same hour; their demands are 8 and 0, with no transfer between stations during that hour. Total demand 8 equals total capacity 8, but the first station is short by 4 while the second has 4 idle. An average of 4 items per station cannot establish that neither has a shortfall. If transfers are subsequently allowed, their latency, price to be paid, and feasibility must be added separately to the new model.

BoundaryThis does not claim that any real stations have this distribution or automatically attribute responsibility for locational differences to anyone.

Apollo13 consumables: demand and support can change during the processDocumented case

The NASA report records that after the accident, margins for consumables such as water and LiOH initially appeared tight. When power use in the lunar module was reduced, heat production and cooling-water demand decreased accordingly, improving the resource situation. This section adds an observation about the demand side and supporting conditions: an initially tight situation cannot be directly extrapolated into inevitable depletion in every later period. Track actual load reduction, replenishment, and remaining tasks.

SourceNASA Apollo 13 Review Board report1970-06-15; final paragraph on printed 4-48/PDF155 (critical consumables and powerdown); this lesson uses only that paragraph's assessment of resources.Reading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsThis is the same report as in the case for §4.12.1 but a different factual point, not independent repeated evidence. Historical success does not prove that any future system can be saved by reducing load, and it is not listed as a formal case under this rule.

What does not follow

  • Original-text counterexample: simultaneous capacity expansion can absorb demand; load need not accumulate monotonically.
  • Original-text counterexample: no subsequent difference remains after the gap resolves; an instantaneous gap does not automatically establish damage.
  • Original-text counterexample: continued shared inputs explain long-term outcomes; persistence alone cannot establish a historical-carrier effect.
  • Author-constructed conditional counterexample: two locations have demand (8,0) and capacity (4,4). If transferring service is prohibited or impossible within the window, equal total capacity still leaves a shortfall of 4 at the first location.
  • Author-constructed conditional counterexample: a constructed queue first builds a backlog of 3 and is then cleared by sufficient service, with no damage state; backlog does not mean inevitable collapse.

Scope and open questions

This unit concerns methodological judgment. Actual sources support only the listed facts; the diagram and teaching construction each retain their own status.

  • Whether actual load produces lasting damage, the capacity at each location, and when support expires require separate cross-window measurements; the constructed queue in this lesson cannot supply those data.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    Can a shortfall be obtained directly by subtracting service hours from the number of items demanded?

  2. 2

    Why can overload still occur when total capacity equals total demand?

  3. 3

    Once the queue is cleared, can complete recovery be declared?

  4. 4

    Does the lack of a historical-increment test cancel existing evidence for carrier-based accumulation?

Can a shortfall be obtained directly by subtracting service hours from the number of items demanded?

No. First supply compatible conversions, such as time per task, and common-window conditions.

Basis: Chinese source lines 823, 827, and 855.

Why can overload still occur when total capacity equals total demand?

Resources may be unavailable at the required location or time; the constructed (8,0)/(4,4) case still has a shortfall of 4 at the first location.

Basis: §6.6, Chinese source line 1456, and the teaching example.

Once the queue is cleared, can complete recovery be declared?

Only that queue target can be confirmed; internal margins, quality, sustainability of support, and other aspects require separate measurement.

Basis: §6.6, Chinese source lines 1456–1460.

Does the lack of a historical-increment test cancel existing evidence for carrier-based accumulation?

It does not cancel a carrier route that genuinely has independent support; it only limits the additional historical-increment route.

Basis: Chinese source lines 833 and 890.

4.12.3Scale Closure and Object Conversion (C6) ​

In briefThis conclusion rule first requires a clear choice between ‘the representation omits useful information’ and ‘the mapping changes the object or intervention relation,’ followed by testing under one criterion fixed in advance. Finding no difference and having evidence supporting closure are different things.

Grounds: scale transformation (§3.4); scale closure (§4.6).

Conditions: Before results, preselect only one of the closure-failure subtype and the subtype for object or intervention conversion, and select only one success criterion from those that subtype admits; the scale transformation from the source scale to the target scale, together with the retained items, changed items, lost items, error, comparison models, positive threshold, and tolerance, have all been fixed in advance. To determine single-scale closure within specified limits, or that the preselected conversion was not detected, the equivalence or sufficiency test, the requirements for statistical power or sensitivity, and the tolerance in the null-conclusion rule must be fixed before results and must actually pass.

Can conclude: for the closure-failure subtype, single-scale closure failure within the pre-registered variables, metrics, scales, and time window; for the subtype for object or intervention conversion, object conversion or intervention conversion within the pre-registered mapping, identity criterion, scales, and time window. The two are determined separately. When the positive criterion does not pass, the default record is only “not supported or unresolved.” Only when the pre-registered equivalence or sufficiency test and the requirements for statistical power, sensitivity, and tolerance have all passed may “closure within the limits of the criterion” be determined for the closure-failure subtype, or “the preselected conversion was not detected” for the subtype for object or intervention conversion; these conclusions must not be extrapolated to unselected criteria.

Cannot conclude: that general correlation, unconditional coupling, or omissions at the same scale can support the conclusion of a scale-closure test; that the two subtypes can be combined after the fact; that within one subtype the success criterion can be changed after the fact, or unselected criteria used for rescue; that a result “not statistically significant,” or one not passing the positive threshold, is directly single-scale closure, absence of object conversion, or equivalence of interventions; that a wider scale range makes an explanation truer or authorization greater; that the use of the same term proves that the objects or the interventions are the same.

Must also meet: Retaining Competing Explanations and Residuals (§4.8.4); Testing Cross-Scale Transfer (§4.8.5); conditions for evidence (§2.5).

The closure-failure subtype separately tests conditional increments from excluded scale variables. The subtype for object or intervention conversion tests only its preselected item: noncommutation of object dynamics, noncommutation of intervention, failure of the identity criterion fixed in advance, change in effective relations, or change in intervention response. The scale-closure test that this rule cites must have fixed both one subtype and one success criterion before results; switching is prohibited after results, whether between subtypes or within one subtype.

4.12.3Note

Understanding this section

4.12.3 Scale closure and object conversion (C6)

This conclusion rule first requires a clear choice between ‘the representation omits useful information’ and ‘the mapping changes the object or intervention relation,’ followed by testing under one criterion fixed in advance. Finding no difference and having evidence supporting closure are different things.

Chinese source line 861 specifies scale transformation (§3.4) and scale closure (§4.6) as its grounds. Scale transformation defines the transfer: source/target scales, mapping M, retained, changed, and lost items, errors, and so forth. A scale-closure test addresses the uniquely selected subtype and criterion. This rule does not permit combining claims such as ‘more accurate prediction,’ ‘a different object,’ and ‘a different intervention’ after seeing results, then declaring success whenever any one looks favorable. [T-C6；T-D3；T-G4]

The closure-failure subtype asks whether excluded-scale variables still provide a conditional increment given the retained variables at the target scale. The three permitted criteria are ‘conditional-increment information,’ ‘conditional predictive gain,’ and ‘conditional intervention gain’; only one may be preselected. General correlation or unconditional coupling is insufficient because neither answers ‘how much is added after retained quantities are known.’ Same-scale omissions do not automatically become cross-scale questions merely by being called local details. [T-C6；T-G4]

The subtype for object or intervention conversion asks about a transformation under the predefined mapping. Its five criteria are ‘noncommutation of object dynamics,’ ‘noncommutation of intervention,’ ‘failure of the identity criterion,’ ‘change in effective relations,’ and ‘change in intervention response.’ They ask whether dynamics commute with mapping, whether intervention commutes with mapping, whether the target representation satisfies the identity criterion fixed in advance, whether effective relations change, and whether intervention responses change. Preselect exactly one; the five cannot serve as an after-the-results ‘any success will do’ fallback. [T-C6；T-G4]

This rule's conditions must fix M(SP0→SP1), retained/changed/lost items, error quantities, comparison models, positive thresholds, and tolerances together before results are known. The scale description must also retain the status of all nine axes and their respective applicability. In particular, wider observational scope cannot automatically expand the scope of jurisdiction and authorization. A name appearing at two scales does not prove that the object or intervention version is the same; how a source operation is implemented at the target scale requires an actual mapping. [T-C6；T-D3；T-SP]

When the positive criterion passes, the closure-failure subtype determines closure failure only within the pre-registered variables, metrics, scales, and windows; the subtype for object or intervention conversion determines only a candidate for the preselected object/intervention transformation. Failing the positive criterion defaults to ‘not supported or unresolved.’ Determining criterion-bounded closure or no detected preselected transformation additionally requires all three requirements—equivalence or sufficiency testing, power or sensitivity, and tolerance—to have been fixed beforehand and actually passed. Nonsignificance does not replace these three requirements. Null conclusions also concern only the selected criterion, not permanent equivalence of all objects or operations. [T-C6；T-G4；T-table]

Support for closure and support for nonclosure are both informative results: the former indicates that the concise representation suffices for the task/operation/horizon in question; the latter suggests adding variables, revising the representation, or narrowing its use. They do not rank theoretical progress, nor is either a prerequisite for the other. Testing positive closure failure does not require first establishing closure, and obtaining a null conclusion does not require first establishing failure. A representation sufficient for routine prediction may be insufficient under a new intervention; it must not be reused across tasks without justification. [T-G4；T-table]

Formal models can express noncommutation precisely. If two source states with the same representation yield different representations after updating, no deterministic macro function based only on that representation can determine the next step. If πF=F̄π holds across the entire domain, exact closure holds within the model. This is a conditional proof, not a scale-closure test in reality. Empirical work still requires measurements, sampling, permitted operations, errors, and eligibility evidence; seeing no difference at a few visited points cannot replace a proof over the full domain. [T-formal]

The row for this rule in the table at the end of the group lists key cases: current retained quantities are sufficient; gains arise only from same-scale omissions or complexity; mapping commutes with dynamics/intervention; or sample sensitivity is insufficient. If the conditions are incomplete, no criterion was preselected, post hoc rescue occurs, or results do not replicate, return to the source scale's scope of support. If neither the positive criterion nor the null-conclusion rule passes, remain unresolved. Returning does not deny every macro description; it simply refuses to treat current deficiencies as a completed transfer. [T-table]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Fix in advance the mapping of the scale transformation, source and target scales, retained/changed/lost items, errors, identity criterion, and permitted operations.

  2. 2

    Preselect exactly one of the closure-failure subtype and the subtype for object or intervention conversion, and one of its criteria, defining comparison models and positive/null rules.

  3. 3

    Conduct the selected positive test and the qualified null-conclusion criteria separately; nonsignificance cannot substitute for closure.

  4. 4

    Limit outputs to the predefined variables, criterion, scales, windows, and operations, without expanding them to unselected criteria.

  5. 5

    Separate within-model proofs of commutation from real-world eligibility; different scales do not automatically increase reality, value, or authority.

Distinctions to keep clear

Closure-failure subtype

The increment from excluded-scale quantities conditional on retained variables.

≠

Subtype for object or intervention conversion

Object or intervention transformation under the preselected mapping.

The positive criterion did not pass

The matter may be unresolved or the current claim unsupported.

≠

Qualified zero conclusion

All three null-conclusion criteria have actually passed, limited to the selected criterion.

Within-model proof of closure

The equations satisfy commutation over the entire domain.

≠

No difference observed in limited empirical evidence

Sensitivity requires separate checking; this cannot replace a full-domain proof.

Cross-boundary effects

Transmission between objects.

≠

Closure failure

The representation is insufficient for the target/operation; this is a different question.

Mathematical construction: two dynamics under the same aggregationTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe source domain, projection, two dynamics, and exact calculations are constructed mathematical objects; statistical sampling and real-world noise are not specified.

On source domain X=the nonnegative real pairs, let π(a,b)=a+b. For the first dynamics, F(a,b)=(a,2b), x=(1,0) and x′=(0,1) both map to 1; after updating, πF(x)=1 and πF(x′)=2, so no deterministic F̄ can answer both. For the second dynamics, G(a,b)=(a/2,b/2), every (a,b) satisfies πG=(a+b)/2; choosing Ḡ(s)=s/2 gives commutation across the whole domain. The two results depend entirely on the dynamics and target representation, and do not become identical because both are called ‘aggregation.’

BoundaryThe first is within-model nonclosure/noncommutation and does not automatically qualify as an empirical conclusion of the closure-failure subtype or the subtype for object or intervention conversion; the second does not prove closure for any real model.

The 2008 circular-track experiment: global density cannot substitute for a local traffic targetDocumented case

Sugiyama et al.'s original paper describes 22 cars on a 230-meter circular track, initially traveling approximately uniformly before stop-and-go waves emerged. Neither track length nor car count changed as a result. This section adds an observation about representational use: describing global density by car count/track length and describing whether traffic is stopping at each location have different informational requirements. Average density alone cannot answer the latter target.

SourceSugiyama et al., Traffic jams without bottlenecks—experimental evidence for the physical mechanism of the formation of a jamNew Journal of Physics10(2008)033001; experimental setup/Fig2 on printed page 4, Fig3 and adjacent text on printed page 5, Fig4 on printed page 6; PDF6–8.Reading scope: Read

Scope and limitsThis reuses the same study as §4.6 and is not an independent replication. It analyzes task representation only; it does not claim that the paper performed this framework's preselection for a scale-closure test and its null-conclusion criterion, or infer from local fluctuations that all traffic models fail to close.

What does not follow

  • Source counterexample: gains from same-scale omissions or complexity cannot alone be determined to be cross-scale support from a scale-closure test.
  • Source counterexample: if insufficient sample or measurement sensitivity causes the positive criterion not to pass, that does not also support closure.
  • Source boundary: favorable results on unselected criteria cannot rescue a claim; neither subtype nor its internal criterion may be switched after the fact.
  • Author-constructed formal counterexample: with π(a,b)=a+b and F(a,b)=(a,2b), (1,0) and (0,1) both initially have representation 1, but next yield 1 and 2 respectively, so there cannot be just one F̄(1).
  • Author-constructed formal boundary: with F(a,b)=(a/2,b/2), πF=π/2 gives exact closure; aggregation does not imply inevitable closure failure.

Scope and open questions

This unit concerns methodological judgment. Actual sources support only the listed facts; the diagram and teaching construction each retain their own status.

  • Determining which operations and horizons a particular real representation suffices for still requires appropriate measurements and positive/null tests; neither the circular-track story nor a mathematical model can settle all of it.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    If the closure-failure subtype's information criterion fails but its intervention criterion performs well, can the original conclusion be changed?

  2. 2

    If no conversion is detected, when may a bounded finding that no conversion was found be determined?

  3. 3

    Why do F's two states suffice to refute deterministic closure under this projection?

  4. 4

    Does G's exact closure prove that there are no cross-boundary effects?

If the closure-failure subtype's information criterion fails but its intervention criterion performs well, can the original conclusion be changed?

No. Unselected criteria cannot rescue the claim after the fact. They may be pursued as exploration or a new study, retaining the original result.

Basis: Chinese source lines 863–871.

If no conversion is detected, when may a bounded finding that no conversion was found be determined?

Every corresponding requirement of the null-conclusion rule fixed in advance—equivalence/sufficiency, power/sensitivity, and tolerance—must actually pass, without extrapolation to unselected criteria.

Basis: Chinese source lines 863–865.

Why do F's two states suffice to refute deterministic closure under this projection?

F̄ can give only one value for input 1, but the two source states require 1 and 2, a contradiction.

Basis: §4.6.1 and the mathematical example.

Does G's exact closure prove that there are no cross-boundary effects?

No. Closure concerns the relation between representation and dynamics; transmission between objects is another question, and ‘Local Improvement and Cross-Boundary Spillover’ (§4.12.4) can hold within a closed model.

Basis: Chinese source lines 861 and 894.

4.12.4Local Improvement and Cross-Boundary Spillover (C7) ​

In briefThis conclusion rule requires tracing real channels to examine the effects of local changes beyond a boundary. Crossing an administrative line does not automatically make a process cross-scale; finding an effect does not automatically establish harm, an externality, or someone's obligation to compensate.

Grounds: channel effect (§4.4). Claims that actually cross scales additionally require the mapping that scale transformation (§3.4) and Testing Cross-Scale Transfer (§4.8.5) require; claims of closure failure, object conversion, or intervention conversion further require the corresponding scale-closure test (§4.6).

Conditions: The local target, the object boundary, the time window of impact, and the variables outside the boundary have all been stated; a channel-effect test locates the cross-boundary channel; between the local change and the outcome outside the boundary there are temporal order, a mechanism bridge, and a blocking or substitution counterfactual comparison. Crossing an object boundary or an administrative boundary does not automatically constitute a change of scale; when scales are actually crossed, the check is made separately under scale transformation and Testing Cross-Scale Transfer. A corresponding scale-closure test is carried out separately only when closure failure, object conversion, or intervention conversion is further claimed. Using the word “externality” requires stating the costs and benefits and who bears or receives them. These must be specified within the institutional or accounting arrangements at issue.

Can conclude: When the mechanism bridge and the counterfactual comparison hold, cross-boundary spillover accompanying local improvement, together with its distribution across positions, may be determined; it is called an externality only when an additional institutional or accounting definition is available.

Cannot conclude: that every local improvement necessarily harms a larger scale; that cross-boundary correlation is a spillover mechanism; that something can be called an externality without an institutional or accounting definition; that finding a spillover automatically assigns compensation, responsibility, or an action plan.

Must also meet: Retaining Competing Explanations and Residuals (§4.8.4); conditions for causal claims (§2.4); conditions for evidence (§2.5); and, when scales are actually crossed, Testing Cross-Scale Transfer (§4.8.5).

First measure the predetermined improvement in the local target, then trace outputs, risks, resource occupation, or signals outside the boundary along the channel specified by the channel-effect test, using proportionate comparisons to separate a common shock from a cross-boundary effect. When the statement is cross-scale, specify the mapping that scale transformation and Testing Cross-Scale Transfer require; when it concerns scale-closure failure or object conversion, also provide the evidence of the corresponding scale-closure test. A model with sound closure can also represent cross-boundary effects correctly; inadequacy of a model must not be made a necessary condition for the existence of an effect. Whether the costs and benefits at issue count as externalities is further determined by the institutional or accounting definition.

Conclusion RuleMinimum EvidenceKey CounterexamplesFailure Boundary
Historical Effects, Path Differences, and Repair WindowsThe historical-increment route requires a historical-increment test and control of the current representation; the carrier route obtains evidence under §4.5; a repair window requires a target identity criterion or target functional criterion, timing comparisons, and the corresponding causal basisCarrier formation or subsequent effects have not been distinguished; the residual is absorbed by a sufficient current state; intervention timing makes no stable differenceAbsence of a historical-increment test blocks only additional historical increments; without causal evidence, do not call it historical causation; without a target identity criterion or target functional criterion and a timing basis, do not call it a repair window

Scale Closure and Object ConversionEverything that scale transformation and Testing Cross-Scale Transfer require, complete; a preselected subtype and criterion; competing explanations and the corresponding review. A positive conclusion requires a record that the preselected criterion passed; a null conclusion requires records of passing the corresponding equivalence or sufficiency, statistical power or sensitivity, and tolerance requirements; the two routes are established separately, neither being a premise for the otherRetained variables form a sufficient statistic; the gain comes from omissions at the same scale or from model complexity; the scale transformation commutes with dynamics or intervention, and the mapping is stable; insufficient sample or measurement sensitivity prevents the positive criterion from passing but cannot support the null conclusion eitherReturn to the source scale if the conditions are incomplete, the subtype or criterion was not preselected, an unselected criterion is used for rescue, or the result cannot be reproduced; remain unresolved if neither the positive criterion nor the null-conclusion rule passes
Local Improvement and Cross-Boundary SpilloverLocal variables and variables outside the boundary; the channel specified by a channel-effect test, temporal sequence, and counterfactual comparison; for a cross-scale claim, additionally scale transformation and Testing Cross-Scale Transfer; for a claim of closure failure or object conversion, additionally a scale-closure test; for an externality, additionally an institutional or accounting definitionBlocking the channel has no effect; a common shock explains the difference; the claimed cost does not fall within that accounting definitionWithout cross-boundary causation, determine only correlation or an accounting gap; closure holding does not negate spillover; without the corresponding definition of where costs and benefits fall, the classification as an externality is not obtained

Crossing boundaries, crossing scales, and whether a model has closure answer different questions. Transmission at the same scale can have real effects. So can cost shifting across administrative boundaries. Synchronized changes caused by a common cause cannot become cross-boundary effects through correlation alone. Existing domain evidence is retained according to its research design. When the formal mechanism route of the conclusion rule “Local Improvement and Cross-Boundary Spillover” is used, check the channel, mapping, and accounting conditions actually required by the level claimed. 〔Studies 04.05, 20.07, 26.02, 28.02〕

4.12.4Note

Understanding this section

4.12.4 Local improvement and cross-boundary spillover (C7)

This conclusion rule requires tracing real channels to examine the effects of local changes beyond a boundary. Crossing an administrative line does not automatically make a process cross-scale; finding an effect does not automatically establish harm, an externality, or someone's obligation to compensate.

Chinese source line 875 distinguishes three levels of requirements: a basic cross-boundary mechanism depends on channel effect (§4.4); genuinely cross-scale claims additionally require scale transformation (§3.4) and cross-scale transfer testing (§4.8.5); a further claim of closure failure or object/intervention transformation then requires the corresponding scale-closure test (§4.6). These levels answer different questions and cannot be compressed into one sequence of checkpoints every case must pass. A complete micro-level or single-scale model can also accurately represent cross-boundary transmission; closure failure is not necessary for an effect to exist. [T-C7；T-table]

First fix in advance the local target, object boundary, effect window, and variables outside the boundary to clarify what ‘improvement’ and ‘external effect’ ask. Reduced local waiting, lower financial spending, and increased output are different outcomes. One cannot switch to a favorable local metric after seeing results while ignoring external time, risk, or resource use. A specific improvement must also be confirmed against predefined targets and appropriate comparisons, not merely inferred from better local numbers after a measure is implemented. [T-C7]

A cross-boundary mechanism requires the channel specified by the channel-effect test, temporal order, mechanism bridge, and appropriate counterfactuals such as blocking or alternative conditions. Two areas improving or worsening together may reflect common demand, weather, or policy; synchronization alone cannot establish that one caused the other. Conversely, cross-boundary transmission can occur between two objects at the same scale. Bridging actual objects and quantities matters more than ‘macro/micro’ slogans. [T-C7；T-causal]

Crossing object boundaries means transmission between two previously delimited objects or jurisdictions; crossing scales means changes to scale axes and mappings, such as observation/aggregation, time, or organization. Closure asks whether the retained representation suffices to describe a specified target or operation. An administrative boundary change need not change the scale used, and expanded research coverage does not automatically expand the scope of jurisdiction and authorization. Identically named indicators or matching units still require consistency in objects, time points, and accounting definitions. [T-C7；T-D3；T-SP]

‘Externality’ is a more specialized classification than general spillover. The source requires specifying costs, benefits, and their attribution within institutional or accounting arrangements: who receives the local benefit, who bears which actual cost, and whether those are included in the accounting arrangement used. A change outside the boundary cannot be declared an economic externality merely because it is ‘outside.’ Conversely, appropriate existing evidence of cost attribution cannot be dismissed merely because the model closes. [T-C7]

Neither direction nor distribution can be stipulated in advance. Local improvement may accompany harmful spillovers, beneficial spillovers, offsetting effects, or no identifiable change; traffic rerouting may also come with capacity expansion or improved management. Report by specific location, variable, and window. An unchanged overall average must not become a claim that every road or person is unharmed, and an additional burden somewhere must not become a claim that all local improvements inevitably harm larger scales. [T-C7；T-table]

The table at the end of the group requires different evidence for each of the group's four rules: history/repair, load/recovery, the positive and null-conclusion criteria for scale, and cross-boundary mechanisms/accounting. Counterexamples specific to this rule include channel blocking having no effect, common shocks explaining differences, or claimed costs falling outside the given accounting definition. Without cross-boundary causation, determine only association or an accounting gap; without an externality definition, that classification is not obtained. Established closure does not refute spillovers. [T-table]

Discovering spillovers still does not automatically determine compensation, responsibility, or a plan of action. Descriptive effects, actual harm, grounds for responsibility, allocation rules, and implementation authority require separate judgments. Evidence may support an analytical recommendation with explicit normative premises, prices to be paid, and alternatives, but actual adoption still requires procedures such as normative bridging (§4.14.1). When empirical questions remain incompletely distinguished, the action ceiling must also account for risk, reversibility, external obligations, and current authority, rather than uniformly requiring either doing nothing or immediate intervention. [T-C7；T-E4；T-C12]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Fix in advance the local target, object boundary, window, and outside-boundary variables, and confirm the claimed local improvement.

  2. 2

    Use a channel-effect test, timing, mechanism bridges, and blocking/alternative comparisons to identify cross-boundary effects and rule out common shocks.

  3. 3

    Add scale transformation and cross-scale transfer testing only when the claim is genuinely cross-scale; add a scale-closure test when closure failure or transformation is explicitly claimed.

  4. 4

    Calling something an externality additionally requires institutional or accounting definitions of how costs and benefits are assigned; not every change outside a boundary should be so named.

  5. 5

    Report direction and limits for each position, separately checking compensation, responsibility, norms, and authorization; do not move straight from discovery to execution.

Distinctions to keep clear

Cross-boundary

Effects between two objects or jurisdictions.

≠

Cross-scale

A change in representation or scale axis and its mapping.

Spillover

An effect beyond a boundary through an actual crossing channel.

≠

Externality

Defined separately by institutional/accounting allocation of costs and benefits.

Adequate closure

The representation can describe the dynamics or operations in question.

≠

No cross-boundary effect

Not synonymous with closure: a complete model can include transmission.

Local improvement

A predefined indicator improves at a particular location.

≠

The larger scale must suffer

No such universal necessity holds.

Mathematical teaching construction: a closed model can still include cross-boundary effectsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsTasks are homogeneous, transfer has no loss or delay, 0≤u≤a, and no other inputs exist; rules and targets are mathematical stipulations. Additional pending tasks at B are not automatically real-life harm.

Let pending tasks at two stations at the same time be (a,b)=(8,2). Under an artificial rule, transfer u=3 items from A to B: F_u(a,b)=(a−u,b+u), giving (5,5). If the local target is reducing A's pending tasks, it improves by 3; B's pending tasks increase by 3. The complete two-component state exactly determines both outcomes, and the total mapping π=a+b also satisfies πF_u=π, remaining 10. Cross-object transmission can therefore coexist with exact closure.

BoundaryNo empirical eligibility as a channel-effect test or under this rule is established. Externality status additionally requires definitions of costs, benefits, and accounting assignment; whether transfer is warranted separately requires norms and authorization.

Teaching counterfactual: two locations changing together need not transmit effects to each otherTeaching scenario

AssumptionsOnly common input E exists, with no direct or indirect A-to-B channel: these are explicit teaching assumptions.

Suppose a common external variable E raises demand at both A and B, with no channel whatsoever from A to B. Demands change together, but blocking the supposed A→B channel would not change B; correlation cannot supply a cross-boundary mechanism. This structural stipulation rules out a faulty inference; it does not prove that any real areas are unconnected.

BoundaryWhether a real system involves a common cause or cross-boundary effect must be identified from material; a stipulated setting cannot replace investigation.

London's 2004 monitoring report: rerouting, traffic volume, and congestion are different indicatorsDocumented case

TfL's second-year report records reduced congestion inside the charging zone; total vehicle-kilometers increased on the boundary Inner Ring Road, but overall congestion did not worsen accordingly. The report also emphasizes improved traffic management and completion of some roadworks as background conditions, and notes varying changes across sections and directions of the ring road. This lesson therefore requires separate measurement of the local target, traffic outside the boundary, congestion, and distribution, without presupposing that local improvement must create greater congestion.

SourceTransport for London, Central London Congestion Charging: Impacts Monitoring, Second Annual ReportApril 2004; Overview, printed pp.1–2/PDF pp.5–6; §2.5, printed pp.14–15/PDF pp.18–19; §3.7 and Table 3.5, printed pp.31–32/PDF pp.35–36, especially passages on the small congestion reduction, management/roadworks context, and differences among road sections.Reading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsA bounded conclusion of the official monitoring report at that time, not proof of no harm to every place/population or a channel-effect test or scale-closure test under this framework. Concurrent management and roadworks changes must be retained; all changes cannot be attributed to charging alone. No current charging-policy or travel advice is provided.

What does not follow

  • Source counterexample: a common shock produces simultaneous changes at two locations; this does not directly establish a cross-boundary effect.
  • Source counterexample: if the original difference persists after blocking or replacing a channel, reassess the specified mechanism.
  • Source boundary: without a definition of cost/benefit assignment, do not call it an externality; detecting spillover does not automatically determine compensation or responsibility.
  • Constructed formal counterexample: F_u(a,b)=(a−u,b+u) on the full state (a,b) completely specifies changes at two locations while including cross-boundary task transfer; model closure does not exclude spillover.
  • Real-material boundary: TfL reported increased total traffic on the boundary ring road without worsening overall congestion, which does not support “local improvement necessarily makes the boundary more congested”; it also does not prove absence of harm at every location or for every consequence.

Scope and open questions

This unit concerns methodological judgment. Actual sources support only the listed facts; the diagram and teaching construction each retain their own status.

  • This lesson does not redo causal estimation or externality accounting for London policy; specific cost-benefit and responsibility proposals still require explicit objects, accounting, and normative grounds.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    Does crossing administrative jurisdictions necessarily cross scales?

  2. 2

    Can an exactly closed model represent spillover?

  3. 3

    Does increased traffic outside the boundary necessarily mean worse congestion?

  4. 4

    Can an observed effect immediately be classified as an externality with compensation assigned?

  5. 5

    Does no overall worsening establish that nobody was harmed?

Does crossing administrative jurisdictions necessarily cross scales?

Not necessarily. Two objects may still be registered at the same scale, involving only a boundary crossing; add a mapping only when scale actually changes.

Basis: Chinese source lines 851–853 and 894.

Can an exactly closed model represent spillover?

Yes. The constructed F_u(a,b) example exactly determines both locations' states while including transfer.

Basis: Chinese source line 885 and the mathematical example.

Does increased traffic outside the boundary necessarily mean worse congestion?

Not necessarily; capacity, management, and other conditions also matter. Measure congestion and its distribution independently.

Basis: This lesson's historical TfL report and the conditions of the two rules ‘Load, Capacity, and Recovery’ and ‘Local Improvement and Cross-Boundary Spillover.’

Can an observed effect immediately be classified as an externality with compensation assigned?

No. An externality requires institutional/accounting assignment of costs and benefits; compensation additionally requires grounds concerning responsibility and normative procedures.

Basis: Chinese source lines 877–881.

Does no overall worsening establish that nobody was harmed?

No. Differences across locations, populations, variables, and times must be preserved.

Basis: Chinese source line 879 and TfL §3.7's account of local variation.

4.13Group 3: Patterns of Evolution, Observation, Human Uptake, and Institutional Write-Back ​

In briefThese conclusion rules move from multiround changes to observation participation, human uptake, and institutional response. All require seeing that the process actually connects; each differs in which conditions must connect and how far its conclusions extend.
4.13Note

Understanding this section

4.13 Group Three: evolutionary patterns, observation, human uptake, and institutional write-back

These conclusion rules move from multiround changes to observation participation, human uptake, and institutional response. All require seeing that the process actually connects; each differs in which conditions must connect and how far its conclusions extend.

Chinese source lines 896–897 contain only the group heading, without an additional empirical proposition. The four subsections are “Variation–Differential Retention–Reproduction” (§4.13.1), “Observation Channels and Reflexive Responses” (§4.13.2), “Human Uptake and Intertemporal Reproduction” (§4.13.3), and “Institutional Write-Back” (§4.13.4). They may occur in the same case; one label cannot complete testing for the other three. [T-intro; T-C8; T-C9; T-C10; T-C11]

The basic pattern of “Variation–Differential Retention–Reproduction” does not universally require a channel-effect test as a hard premise, but independently requires evidence for variation, differential outcome, and retention, entry into the next round, repetition, and competition with drift; a specific mechanism separately adds a channel-effect test. Formal mechanism routes for the conclusion rules “Observation Channels and Reflexive Responses,” “Human Uptake and Intertemporal Reproduction,” and “Institutional Write-Back” each require a channel-effect test and their own conditions. The human-domain clauses “Action Uptake and Classification of Responsibility” and “Institutional Write-Back” (§7.1) supply typology and classification, respectively, not extra empirical causes of human action or institutional change. [T-C8; T-C9; T-C10; T-C11]

The table at the end of the group places minimum evidence, counterexamples, and failure boundaries alongside each rule: one change need not constitute selection, repeated stimulation need not be persistence of one effect, staff scheduling need not produce actual continuity, and rewriting institutional elements need not mean execution. Each following unit preserves these distinctions; the parent section helps navigation and does not replace close reading of the subsections. [T-table]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Identify the output in question through the four subsections.

  2. 2

    Distinguish basic patterns, specific channels, human typologies, and institutional execution.

  3. 3

    Check gaps item by item using the group-end table; one success is not common support for all four.

Distinctions to keep clear

Rules in the same group

Related but with different evidential responsibilities.

≠

The same kind of law

Being listed among the twelve conclusion rules cannot unify their grounds for holding.

What does not follow

  • The parent section serves navigation only and adds no empirical regularity.
  • Multiround repetition, persistence, and reproduction are not synonyms; examine transmission and competing explanations separately.

Scope and open questions

The parent section has no independent substantive proposition and serves only as section navigation; relevant actual facts appear in the subsections.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    Must the basic pattern of “Variation–Differential Retention–Reproduction” first have a channel-effect test?

  2. 2

    Are the two human-domain clauses “Action Uptake and Classification of Responsibility” and “Institutional Write-Back” additional empirical causes in this group?

Must the basic pattern of “Variation–Differential Retention–Reproduction” first have a channel-effect test?

Not universally; it independently requires evidence of variation, differential outcome, retention, and the like. A claim of a particular retention/reproduction mechanism separately adds a channel-effect test.

Basis: Chinese source lines 900–912.

Are the two human-domain clauses “Action Uptake and Classification of Responsibility” and “Institutional Write-Back” additional empirical causes in this group?

No. They are, respectively, an operational typing requirement and a classification requirement for institutional write-back.

Basis: Chinese source lines 916–918 and 950–958.

4.13.1Variation–Differential Retention–Reproduction (C8) ​

In briefThis conclusion rule does not call every change selection. It requires identifiable variation, comparable differential outcomes, and differences actually entering later rounds, while competing with explanations such as drift.

Grounds: basic state terms (§3.2).

Conditions: Variation means that distinguishable variations and their sources are defined before results. A differential outcome means that differences in outcomes exceeding a threshold occur in comparable environments. Retention means that those differences enter the next round and can be reviewed across repeated rounds. Random drift, common external causes, sampling bias, and one-time shocks are compared as competing explanations. A claim about a specific carrying mechanism additionally requires a channel-effect test (§4.4).

Can conclude: When variation, differential outcome, retention, entry into the next round, repeated rounds, and comparison with random drift as a competing explanation all hold, a variation–differential retention–reproduction pattern may be determined within the specified environment; a specific carrying mechanism is determined only with an additional channel-effect test.

Cannot conclude: that all evolution is explained by selection; that a single case of persistence or a single sample difference is differential retention; that what is retained is better, more advanced, or more justified; that systemic selection is a subject's choice, collective governance, or authorization.

Must also meet: Retaining Competing Explanations and Residuals (§4.8.4); conditions for causal claims (§2.4); conditions for evidence (§2.5).

This rule tests a pattern and requires independent evidence; it cannot be proved directly from a definition or the framework's narrative. The basic pattern branch requires variation, differential outcome, retention, entry into the next round, repeated rounds, and comparison with random drift as a competing explanation to hold together; the specific mechanism branch additionally requires a channel-effect test to locate the retention or reproduction channel. It describes systemic selection, not an acting subject's intentional choice, still less authorization for governance.

This rule has two branches. The pattern branch: variation, differential outcome, retention, the next round, repeated rounds, and comparison with random drift as a competing explanation. The mechanism branch: an additional channel-effect test, with a specified retention or reproduction channel and perturbation or natural variation of the channel.

4.13.1Note

Understanding this section

4.13.1 Variation–differential retention–reproduction (C8)

This conclusion rule does not call every change selection. It requires identifiable variation, comparable differential outcomes, and differences actually entering later rounds, while competing with explanations such as drift.

Chinese source line 910 makes clear that this rule “tests a pattern and requires independent evidence.” The basic state terms (§3.2) serving as its grounds supply only the language for classifying evolution; “a change occurred” cannot define variation, differential outcome, and retention into existence. The pattern branch requires variation, differential retention, next-round continuity, and repeated results each to have a location in actual material; the mechanism branch additionally requires a channel-effect test and evidence for specific carrying channels. [T-C8; T-D1]

“Variation” means distinguishable variation and its source defined beforehand. Researchers must specify the unit for identifying differences, which changes belong to the same type, and where variation comes from; they cannot wait for one type to win and arbitrarily rename it the only type worth studying. Observation error, changes in sample composition, and replacement of a measurement protocol cannot directly be treated as new variation in the object. [T-C8; T-measure]

“Differential outcome” requires differences in outcome exceeding a threshold in comparable environments. Environment, opportunities, observation window, and evaluation definitions must be sufficiently comparable to judge whether differences concern the types in question. High and low values in one sample may reflect random drift, sampling bias, common external causes, or a one-off shock; “more happened to remain” cannot retrospectively establish a necessary adaptation mechanism. [T-C8; T-table]

“Retention” does not merely mean an individual lives a long time: the difference in question must enter the next round and be reproducible across repeated rounds. Biological research may examine inheritance by descendants; organizational research may examine actual continuity of rules, capabilities, or practices. Cross-domain use needs explicit mappings; similar wording does not imply the same mechanism. If external inputs recreate differences each round without retaining those from the previous round, repeated appearance does not establish reproduction. [T-C8; T-D3]

The basic pattern simultaneously requires variation, differential outcome, retention, entry into the next round, repeated rounds, and comparison with random drift as a competing explanation. These are conjunctive conditions; strong material for one cannot fill a missing other. “Comparison with random drift as a competing explanation” means proportionate repetition, probability models, or comparative designs examining how far random change can explain the result, not merely listing drift at the end of a report. Do not force unreasonable alternatives, but seriously address the key alternative processes explicitly required by this pattern. [T-C8; T-E4]

The mechanism branch additionally requires a channel-effect test locating a retention or reproduction channel, with grounds such as channel perturbation or natural variation satisfying identification conditions. Confirming retention of a difference across rounds need not mean knowing every molecular, institutional, or resource mechanism; conversely, knowing a channel exists does not replace the complete pattern of variation, differential outcome, and retention. Absence of a channel-effect test limits the specific-mechanism output, without automatically canceling independent pattern evidence. [T-C8; T-table]

Those retained reproducing more in this environment does not mean they are better, more advanced, or more justified. “System selection” describes differential retention, not conscious choice by a subject, collective governance, or real-world authorization. Even researchers setting an experimental environment cannot personify all selection outcomes within it as what the system itself wants. [T-C8]

The row for this rule in the group-end table lists common inputs simultaneously producing differences, failure of differences to enter the next round, drift already providing a sufficient explanation, and ineffective perturbation of a reproduction channel as key counterexamples. These limit the pattern or particular mechanism, rather than defeating all evolutionary knowledge at once. If material supports only change or a one-time difference, preserve exactly that level; do not use the full name “Variation–Differential Retention–Reproduction” to add proof a bounded observation has not obtained. [T-table]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Use the basic state terms to delimit the change question; predefine the units, types, and sources of variation.

  2. 2

    Test D and its threshold in comparable environments and windows; do not directly treat sampling fluctuations as selection.

  3. 3

    Check R, entry into the next round, and repetition, excluding appearances recreated solely by continuing common inputs.

  4. 4

    Compare alternatives such as drift; determine a bounded pattern only when variation, differential outcome, retention, and related requirements hold together.

  5. 5

    A specific carrying-mechanism claim separately requires a channel-effect test; retention outcomes do not imply value, subject intentions, or governance authorization.

Distinctions to keep clear

Change

A difference in state or type.

≠

Differential-retention pattern

Also requires variation, differential outcome, retention, the next round, repetition, and competing explanations.

Individual persistence

An object continues to exist.

≠

Reproduction

The difference in question enters later rounds.

Pattern support

Knowing how differences are retained within a bounded environment.

≠

Specific-mechanism support

Separately requires a specified channel and proportionate grounds from a channel-effect test.

Retained more often

Describes outcomes in that environment.

≠

More justified or ought to be selected

Requires independent normative grounds.

Mathematical teaching construction: retention rules determine changes in sharesTeaching scenario

AssumptionsDeterministic continuous shares, replication weights of 2 and 1, and the retention rule are all teaching stipulations, with no real-world observations.

Let there be two artificial types A/B, with A's share p. Explicitly stipulate that each round A produces 2 successors and B produces 1, with types fully retained and no drift, immigration, capacity constraints, or environmental change. The next-round share is p′=2p/[2p+(1−p)]=2p/(1+p). Starting from p0=1/2 gives p1=2/3, p2=4/5, and p3=8/9. This follows from the stipulated replication difference and retention rule; if the share is forcibly reset to 1/2 each round, growth in share across rounds does not hold.

BoundaryThis cannot establish actual biological or organizational selection; still less can growth in share imply that A is more deserving of retention.

Mathematical teaching construction: a random increase is not a selection mechanismTeaching scenario

AssumptionsTwo independent identically distributed draws with probabilities of 1/2 each are artificial assumptions.

If the next generation consists of only two independent draws, each with A/B probabilities of 1/2, the probability that both are A is (1/2)²=1/4. There is no replication advantage for A in this result, yet in one occurrence A's share will be 1. Distinguishing this random fluctuation from systematic differential retention requires proportionate repetition, models, and error judgments.

BoundaryThis 1/4 is not a real-world drift probability, nor does it show that any adequately studied selection result can be attributed to chance.

The 2008 E. coli long-term evolution study: distinguishing emergence, descendant expansion, and mechanistic explanationDocumented case

The 2008 paper by Blount, Borland, and Lenski reports that a citrate-utilizing variant appeared in one population of a long-term experiment, and its descendants subsequently became numerically dominant while coexisting with another type. The authors checked phenotypes and DNA markers to rule out external contamination as the explanation for the variant, and also examined preserved samples from different generations. This shows that establishing variant identity, descendants, and temporal materials involves separate work; a single change in turbidity does not complete the conclusion.

SourceBlount、Borland、Lenski，PNAS105(23):7899–7906Online 2008-06-04, journal issue 2008-06-10; DOI10.1073/pnas.0803151105; final paragraph of the Introduction; first paragraph of Results, ‘Evolution of Cit+ Function in Population Ara-3’, and paragraphs adjoining Fig1—2.Reading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsOnly the source's facts about variant identity, descendants, and samples are used; the complete evolutionary data are not recalculated, nor is formal qualification under this rule, as a channel-effect test, or as a historical-increment test backfilled under this framework. No claim is made that the variant represents universal progress or that this paper identified every subsequent mechanism.

What does not follow

  • Source counterexample: common external causes generate differences simultaneously each round; repeated appearance alone cannot establish reproduction of those differences.
  • Source counterexample: if differences do not enter the next round or drift suffices to explain them, the pattern conditions remain incomplete.
  • Source boundary: without a channel-effect test, do not claim a specified mechanism; one instance of persistence is not variation–differential retention–reproduction and does not imply that those retained are better or more justified.
  • Mathematical counterexample: with equal A/B probabilities, two independent unbiased draws yield two As with probability 1/4; a one-time increase in A's share does not rule out drift.
  • Mathematical boundary: deterministic reproduction coefficients of 2 versus 1 can increase A's share; if each round resets to equal proportions, the new difference is not transmitted to the next round.

Scope and open questions

This unit concerns methodological judgment. Actual sources support only the listed facts; the diagram and teaching construction each retain their own status.

  • Thresholds, the range of repetition, drift models, and mechanism evidence for a specific pattern must be determined separately for the object of research; this lesson does not replace actual testing with teaching shares.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    Why does seeing more A in one round not directly establish variation–differential retention–reproduction?

  2. 2

    The pattern can be supported, but the specific carrying channel remains unknown. What should be done?

  3. 3

    Why does the artificial p0=1/2 become 2/3 in the next round?

  4. 4

    Does being retained more mean being more advanced or more normatively justified?

Why does seeing more A in one round not directly establish variation–differential retention–reproduction?

The source of variation, comparable environments, entry into the next round, repetition, and competing explanations such as drift are still required; a single fluctuation cannot discharge all these responsibilities.

Basis: Chinese source, lines 902—912.

The pattern can be supported, but the specific carrying channel remains unknown. What should be done?

Retain the bounded pattern; without a corresponding channel-effect test, do not determine a specific mechanism or invent a channel.

Basis: Chinese source, lines 880, 888, and 962.

Why does the artificial p0=1/2 become 2/3 in the next round?

A's successor weight is 1 and B's is 1/2, totaling 3/2; A's share is 1/(3/2)=2/3.

Basis: The explicit replication equation in this lesson.

Does being retained more mean being more advanced or more normatively justified?

No. Replication differences in an environment are descriptive outcomes; normative choice requires a separate argument.

Basis: Chinese source, line 906.
