4.15Combined Conditions and Evidence Routes ​

In briefThese three conditional trees resemble route maps: starting from an evidenced point, each move toward a stronger conclusion requires corresponding additional material. The “+” signs do not mean that putting several names together automatically establishes a mechanism.

Several common routes that combine formal tests with additional conditions can be drawn as the following condition trees:

Grouping-gain test + bridge between object and variables + channel-effect test └─ Candidate channel on which the specified form of organization depends ├─ + Return channel and blocking counterfactual comparison │ └─ Effective feedback │ ├─ + Current update carrier + invocation over multiple rounds and task comparison (§4.5) │ │ └─ Candidate carrier-transmission feedback-mediated learning │ └─ + Historical-increment test + updates that can be retained + repeated rounds │ └─ Candidate historical-increment feedback-mediated learning └─ + Scale-closure test (closure-failure subtype, or subtype for object or intervention conversion) + mapping required by scale transformation and Testing Cross-Scale Transfer └─ Candidate closure failure, or candidate object or intervention conversion

Channel-effect test + demand–capacity mapping for quantities of the same type └─ Candidate instantaneous overload ├─ + Current carrier + accumulation or recovery across time windows and causal comparison (§4.5) │ └─ Candidate carrier-transmission cumulative damage or delayed recovery └─ + Historical-increment test + historical carrier └─ Candidate historical-increment cumulative damage or delayed recovery beyond the current representation

Basic state terms + variation + differential outcome + retention + next round + repeated rounds + comparison with random drift as a competing explanation └─ Variation–differential retention–reproduction pattern ├─ + Channel-effect test → specified retention or reproduction mechanism └─ + Historical-increment test → candidate historical path across rounds

The three trees depict several common combinations of routes, not the minimum premises of each conclusion rule; what each rule and each mechanism requires is governed by the grounds, conditions, and further requirements it states for itself (§4.11–§4.14, Part 6). For example, when no grouping gain is claimed, effective feedback is determined under §4.11.3 and §6.2 and does not presuppose a grouping-gain test; the conclusion rule “Scale Closure and Object Conversion” (§4.12.3) rests on a scale transformation and one scale-closure test (§4.6), and presupposes neither a grouping-gain test nor a channel-effect test. Listing only the names of formal tests does not constitute sufficient conditions for a mechanism to hold; the corresponding additional conditions, method requirements, bridging evidence, and limits of application must also hold. When conditions are complete, determine limited results under the specific conclusion rule; when conditions are incomplete, identify what is missing and which conclusions it blocks, without withdrawing content that already has independent grounds. Even if every test in a particular set of tests of the four empirical questions passes, this does not imply a stage described by the seven state prototypes (§8.3), nor direction, value, responsibility, choice, or authorization; these conclusions each require their own classification conditions, normative conditions, and procedural conditions.

4.15Note

Understanding this section

4.15 Composition Conditions and Evidence Routes

These three conditional trees resemble route maps: starting from an evidenced point, each move toward a stronger conclusion requires corresponding additional material. The “+” signs do not mean that putting several names together automatically establishes a mechanism.

Chinese source line 989 calls these “condition trees”; line 1014 immediately limits them: “Listing only the names of formal tests does not constitute sufficient conditions for a mechanism to hold”. The trees depict several common combinations of routes, not the minimum premises of each conclusion rule, and cannot be interpreted apart from the specific rules. For example, omitting repetition of all method requirements, preselected criteria, task comparisons, and the valid scopes of tests does not remove those responsibilities. Each arrow points only to a bounded result that may be determined once the complete conditions are met. [T-415; T-contract]

The first tree begins with a grouping-gain test, an object/variable bridge, and a channel-effect test. The grouping-gain test supports conditional gain from the candidate grouping for a given task; the channel-effect test supports the effect of a specified channel. The object bridge makes the two bodies of material genuinely connect on the same object, variables, scale, window, and outcome. They cannot be joined merely because both say “organization” or “effect.” If objects differ, units are incompatible, or an upstream output is not the downstream input, the combined conclusion of a “candidate channel dependent on the specified organization” is not obtained. [T-415; T-G1; T-G2; T-chain]

Along the first return route, effective feedback requires additional checks of the return channel, temporal order, the items changed, and no-return or blockage counterfactuals. Feedback need only change at least one subsequent state, probability, or constraint; it need not leave a persistent historical trace and does not automatically mean something good or beneficial. Moving further toward learning, the carrier branch adds a current update carrier, retention or updating rules, subsequent use across multiple rounds, prespecified task comparisons, and causal evidence covering that window. “Feedback occurred” cannot replace “it was later actually used and changed task outcomes.” [T-415; T-C3; T-history]

Historical-increment feedback learning additionally requires a historical-increment test, retainable updates, repeated rounds, and prespecified out-of-sample task comparisons. The historical-increment test asks whether history retains a conditional increment given the stated current representation; predictive and causal forms cannot be mixed. When the current state already carries all relevant historical information, carrier learning may still have independent grounds. Lack of support in the historical-increment test blocks only the historical-increment route; it neither establishes the carrier route nor denies learning in general. Routes must not be switched after seeing results to rescue a claim, and known current states must not be deliberately omitted to manufacture an increment. [T-C3; T-history]

Another branch of the first tree combines a scale-closure test (closure-failure subtype, or subtype for object or intervention conversion) with the mappings required by scale transformation and “Testing Cross-Scale Transfer”. The “or” in the parentheses denotes different routes according to a preselected subtype: the closure-failure subtype asks about conditional increments from excluded scale variables; the subtype for object or intervention conversion asks about object or intervention conversion. It does not mean either can rescue success if it happens to “look significant.” Source and target scales, mappings, losses, comparison models, one preselected criterion, thresholds, and null-conclusion rules are required. Method requirements are not empirical causes; crossing scales does not make higher scales truer or automatically confer wider permissions. [T-415; T-G4; T-D3]

The second tree moves from a channel-effect test and a mapping of demand/capacity of the same type to a candidate instantaneous overload. Matching types includes appropriate types, units, time windows, and accounting positions; total monthly capacity cannot answer whether a particular node is congested during a particular hour. Further claims of cumulative damage or delayed recovery require a current carrier, how load enters its state, accumulation/recovery across windows, subsequent effects, and proportionate causal comparison. An instantaneous gap itself proves neither persistent damage nor inevitable collapse. [T-415; T-C5]

The historical-increment branch of the load tree additionally requires a historical-increment test and a locatable historical carrier, addressing extra historical quantities beyond the current representation. If current damage sufficiently explains subsequent recovery, an evidenced carrier recovery process may still be supported, but this is not a positive result of the historical-increment test. A carrier's existence does not prove subsequent effects, and a positive result of the historical-increment test cannot replace evidence for a specific carrier, window, and bridge. Current mechanisms, historical formation, and conditional residuals are three questions that may have different answers. [T-history; T-C5]

The third tree begins with basic state terms plus variation, differential outcome, retention, the next round, repeated rounds, and competition from drift, permitting a variation–differential retention–reproduction pattern within a bounded environment to be determined. Basic state terms define a minimal grammar of change; they do not prove that the pattern has occurred in the world. Variation must be distinguished in advance, differences in outcome are checked under comparable conditions, and retention is checked as entry into later rounds and rechecked. Competing explanations include drift, shared external causes, sampling, and a one-time shock. A channel-effect test is not imposed on the basic pattern; it is added only when a specified retention/reproduction channel is claimed. A historical-path candidate across rounds additionally requires a historical-increment test of the relevant type, but retention still does not imply superiority, a subject's intentions, or governance authorization. [T-415; T-C8]

Composition also has three noninterchangeable kinds of success: whether functional conversions give the same final answer; whether causal effects connect within jointly supported conditions in the same cases; and whether tasks can be jointly executed under shared resources. Positive average effects on every local edge do not guarantee a positive whole-chain effect; individual feasibility of every task does not guarantee joint feasibility before the same deadline. Conversely, when an existing design independently identifies a bounded total effect, every microscopic process need not first be exhausted before that effect can be retained. Additional connections are needed only when added uses—manipulating mediators, transferring across domains, or assigning responsibility—actually depend on them. [T-chain; T-composition]

Gap reports should be localized: identify the missing item, the branch it blocks, and narrower conclusions that retain independent support. Without multi-round evidence, stop at effective feedback; a missing historical-increment test does not erase evidenced carrier learning; without examining drift, a one-time difference cannot be determined to be a “Variation–Differential Retention–Reproduction” pattern. Even when conditions are complete, determine only the bounded result under the specific conclusion rule. Even if a set of tests of the four empirical questions all pass, stage classification under the seven state prototypes (§8.3), direction, value, responsibility, choice, and authorization still require their own conditions. “All empirical questions passed” cannot become a universal closure stamp. [T-415; T-C12]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    First choose the bounded result in question and find a corresponding route through the three trees, while taking its prerequisites from what its conclusion rule itself states.

  2. 2

    Check each test's actual eligibility and correspondence of objects, variables, scales, outcomes, and windows—not just its name.

  3. 3

    Supply the return, carrier, multi-round, comparable-quantity, scale-mapping, variation, differential-outcome, retention, or other conditions and method requirements genuinely required by that branch.

  4. 4

    Distinguish current-carrier transmission from historical increments beyond the stated current representation; do not automatically apply a historical-increment test because a label contains “learning” or “cumulative.”

  5. 5

    Check joint responses, interfaces, temporal order, and resource constraints; local effects and individual feasibility do not automatically establish composition.

  6. 6

    When incomplete, explain local blockages and independent results still retained; even when complete, determine only conclusions bounded by the conclusion rule.

  7. 7

    Stages, values, responsibility, and actual adoption follow separate classification, normative, and procedural routes; they do not follow from the trees.

Distinctions to keep clear

Complete list of test names

Listing labels such as grouping-gain test and channel-effect test.

≠

Composition conditions satisfied

Valid evidence, corresponding objects, and complete additional conditions and method requirements.

Effective feedback

Return causes changes in subsequent states or transitions.

≠

Feedback-mediated learning

Additionally requires retention, multi-round use, and prespecified task comparisons.

Carrier transmission

The current state preserves information and continues to exert effects.

≠

Historical conditional increment

An additional quantity remains given the stated current representation.

Average edge effect

The population average for each local channel.

≠

Whole-chain effect

Requires support from joint responses in the same cases or an independently qualified design.

Individually feasible

One task can be completed alone.

≠

Joint feasibility

Can also be satisfied simultaneously under shared resources and deadlines.

System selection

A pattern of variation, differential retention, and reproduction.

≠

Subject choice or authorization

Cannot be obtained automatically from the pattern.

Original mathematical counterexample expanded: positive edge means, zero whole-chain effectTeaching scenario

AssumptionsExact structural equations, equal weighting of two types, and separation of direct intervention on m from natural transmission; entirely a formal construction from the original text.

Let type s be 0 or 1 with equal probability, with binary treatment a and mediator m, m(a)=a(1−s), and y(a,m)=sm. When s=0, treatment changes m from 0 to 1, but y remains 0. When s=1, m is 0 for every a; directly setting m could change y, but this is not a change actually brought about by a. Thus the average effect of treatment on m is (1+0)/2=1/2, and the average effect of directly setting m on y is (0+1)/2=1/2. Yet the natural chain gives y(a,m(a))=sa(1−s)=0, so the whole-chain effect is 0 for both types.

BoundaryThis does not estimate effects in real populations. It only refutes unconditional multiplication, not total effects identified by independently qualified designs.

Original mathematical counterexample expanded: shared deadline and capacityTeaching scenario

AssumptionsUnit tasks are indivisible, capacity units are identical across periods, there are no other resources, and advance processing is unavailable. Changing the deadline is only a conditional counterfactual, not actual authorization.

Tasks A and B each occupy one complete time period and must both finish before the end of period one. Period-one capacity is only 1, so required capacity 2 exceeds available capacity 1, and any schedule completes at most one task. Each is feasible alone; jointly they are infeasible. If period-one capacity becomes 2, they can finish in parallel. If valid grounds permit moving B's deadline to period two and period-two capacity is 1, they can finish sequentially. Merely increasing period-two capacity while retaining both original deadlines cannot repair the period-one constraint violation.

BoundaryThis does not establish real demand, capacity, or permission to delay; later resources cannot offset an earlier time limit.

Mathematical teaching construction: history transmitted through the current stateTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe equations and intervention semantics are artificially specified; the stated current state actually includes S, measured precisely.

Let a binary historical input H first form S=H, with future Y=S and no other path or noise. Intervening on H changes Y through S, and current S also determines Y. But given S, Y is already determined, so knowing H additionally does not improve prediction. Historical formation, current-carrier effects, and “historical increment conditional on S” may therefore respectively be present, present, and zero. If only correlation is observed and these structural equations are unknown, this causal conclusion is not yet available.

BoundaryThis model is not treated as actual learning or a historical-increment test, nor does it permit deliberately omitting a known S from real-world analysis.

1999 MCO: interface requirements exist, but connections still need verificationDocumented case

NASA's Phase I investigation report records that ground-based SM_FORCES outputs should have used N·s under the interface specification, but actually provided lbf·s. Downstream navigation used the data according to the expected units, which the report identified as the accident's root cause. This section adds the observation that an object/variable bridge must check actual delivery and use: an interface document and functional names at both ends do not mean that quantities are interpreted consistently along the actual chain.

SourceNASA MCO Mishap Investigation Board Phase I Report1999-11-10; §4 MCO Root Cause, printed p. 16/PDF 16; §5 Cause No. 1, printed p. 17/PDF 17.Reading scope: Partly read

This lesson uses only the interface facts explicitly recorded in the report; it does not claim that every local component was independently effective, certify eligibility for grouping-gain or channel-effect tests under this framework, or derive all responsibility and governance authorization.

Scope and open questions

This unit concerns methodological judgment. Actual sources support only the listed facts; the diagram and teaching construction each retain their own status.

  • The three conditional trees are evidence routes, not new tests actually conducted in this lesson; real-world composition still requires object bridges, joint material, and the respective conditions.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    If grouping gain and channel effect both have research support, can they immediately be combined into the same organizational channel?

  2. 2

    If effective feedback is evidenced but there is no material on multi-round use, where should the conclusion stop?

  3. 3

    If the current carrier is sufficient and the historical-increment test is not supported, can we say that learning does not exist?

  4. 4

    If both average edge effects are 1/2, must the whole chain equal 1/4?

  5. 5

    Can sufficient capacity in period two recover a period-one deadline?

  6. 6

    Must the basic pattern of “Variation–Differential Retention–Reproduction” first have a channel-effect test?

If grouping gain and channel effect both have research support, can they immediately be combined into the same organizational channel?

No. An object/variable bridge, corresponding windows and outcomes, and the additional conditions of the specific rules are still required.

Basis: Chinese source lines 991–1014.

If effective feedback is evidenced but there is no material on multi-round use, where should the conclusion stop?

Retain bounded effective feedback; the learning branch remains a candidate or insufficiently evidenced.

Basis: Chinese source lines 993–998; “Effective Feedback and Feedback-Mediated Learning” (§4.11.3).

If the current carrier is sufficient and the historical-increment test is not supported, can we say that learning does not exist?

No. Carrier learning may be supported by independent evidence of retention, use, tasks, and causation. A failed historical-increment test also cannot establish carrier learning in reverse.

Basis: §4.5。

If both average edge effects are 1/2, must the whole chain equal 1/4?

No. In the equally weighted type counterexample, the actual total chain effect is 0 because different types carry the effects of the two segments.

Basis: §2.4.2; Appendix C.12.

Can sufficient capacity in period two recover a period-one deadline?

No, unless the deadline itself is independently and validly changed; later resources do not alter the original period's constraints.

Basis: Appendix C.12.

Must the basic pattern of “Variation–Differential Retention–Reproduction” first have a channel-effect test?

No. Variation, differential outcome, retention, the next round, repeated rounds, and competing explanations require independent evidence; a channel-effect test is added only for claims of a specific mechanism.

Basis: Chinese source lines 1009–1012.

4.16Scope and Stopping Points of Empirical Judgments ​

In briefThis section requires each conclusion to stop where the evidence can actually reach. Stopping does not mean refusing all judgment; it means precisely stating what is known, what holds only within a model, and which gaps cannot yet be crossed.

Empirical judgments provide descriptions and limited explanations, constrained by the object, scale, time window, evidence, and extrapolation unit. Specific factual assertions under the four empirical questions must be tested through specific tests; conclusion rules record existing results or combine mechanism conditions; conditional formal propositions provide proofs under formal premises; and real-world mechanisms still require independent case evidence. Definitions, identifiers, examples, and the framework's internal descriptions cannot determine whether an empirical proposition holds in the world. Further evaluation of value, responsibility, sacrifice, choice, or how the situation should be handled requires adding human-domain typing, normative reasons, and the four-step operational procedure (§14.6). Empirical conclusions must not bypass these responsibilities on their own.

4.16Note

Understanding this section

4.16 Scope and Stopping Points of Empirical Judgments

This section requires each conclusion to stop where the evidence can actually reach. Stopping does not mean refusing all judgment; it means precisely stating what is known, what holds only within a model, and which gaps cannot yet be crossed.

Chinese source line 1018 limits empirical judgments as “constrained by the object, scale, time window, evidence, and extrapolation unit”. A conclusion should simultaneously specify its object, representation and granularity, temporal scope, evidential material, and intended population or task for generalization. Writing only “verified” erases these limits. The same evidence may support a narrow proposition without supporting a broader one. [T-416; T-evidence]

The four empirical questions, the conclusion rules, and the conditional formal propositions have different roles. The four empirical questions organize testable specific factual claims that specific tests must answer; conclusion rules record established results or combined mechanism conditions, requiring corresponding eligibility in particular branches; conditional formal propositions provide proofs under given state domains, mappings, targets, operations, and logical premises. The conclusion rule “Normative Bridging” is also a check on normative procedure; it must not be treated as an empirical mechanism merely because it is listed among the conclusion rules. These classifications mark responsibilities, not certification of all three categories by the same experiment or truth rule. [T-416；T-roles；T-C12]

Both the power and the boundaries of formal proof must be retained. If premises and derivation are valid, a within-model conclusion does not disappear because no real-world experiment has been performed; one exact counterexample also suffices to refute the unconditional inference it targets. Applying it to reality requires separate evidence for measurements, variable mappings, state domains, errors, and operational conditions. Repeated computation of the same constructed model does not continually add independent empirical samples; numerical enumeration also covers only the finite domain and precision actually specified. [T-formal]

Definitions, numbering, examples, and internal explanations cannot determine whether a real mechanism exists. Defining a process as ‘learning’ does not establish that it actually retains updates, uses them across multiple rounds, or produces a historical conditional increment. Recording a table as a test likewise does not establish that its requirements have substantively passed. Conversely, historical archives and existing studies not recorded in this framework may still support domain conclusions under their own designs; eligibility for formal tests cannot become a universal standard of truth for all knowledge. [T-416；T-domain]

Stopping points must also distinguish ‘not studied,’ ‘evidence unresolved,’ and ‘an appropriately supported null conclusion.’ Failure to meet a positive criterion usually permits only unsupported or unresolved status. If equivalence/sufficiency rules, sensitivity, and tolerances fixed in advance have not actually passed, no significant difference cannot be rewritten as zero effect. Failure of an identification assumption should narrow explanations depending on it, without canceling descriptions or bounded total effects that have other independent grounds. [T-instance；T-estimand]

Extrapolation requires appropriate bridging. A study sample is not the whole world, its original window is not forever, and an average result is not every individual's result. When adding objects, uses, interventions, or horizons, ask whether the original comparison still covers them. Shared words, identical indicators, or visual similarity cannot transplant causal conclusions. Nor must every microscopic mechanism be exhausted before retaining a narrow result identified by a qualified design. [T-evidence；T-estimand；T-analogy]

For further evaluations of value, responsibility, sacrifice, choice, or action, the source requires adding human-domain classification, normative reasons, and the four-step operational procedure (§14.6). The six human-domain clauses (§7.1) are not an undifferentiated set of axioms about human nature: “Action Uptake and Classification of Responsibility” and “Institutional Write-Back” classify, “Meaning and Coordination,” “Power, Mediation, and Reflexivity,” and “Historical Trace Carriers” require evidence from specific tests, and “Open-Ended Undertaking” has a normative-boundary role. Recommendations for deliberation and actual adoption remain separate; the latter additionally requires passing normative bridging, the protection floor, the scope of authorization, and operational procedures in full. Empirical correctness itself grants no authority to decide for people. [T-416；T-roles；T-C12；T-task]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Separate the proposed conclusion into descriptive, causal, formal, classificatory, and normative/action components.

  2. 2

    For the empirical component, specify the object, scale, window, evidence design, and unit of extrapolation.

  3. 3

    For the formal component, state its premises, proof, and whether mapping to the real object has been checked, retaining its conditional status.

  4. 4

    Under the specific test and conclusion rule, distinguish supported, unsupported or unresolved, appropriately supported null conclusions, and unevaluated status; do not replace testing with a title.

  5. 5

    Narrow only conclusions affected by the gap; retain other independent grounds.

  6. 6

    When value or action conclusions are needed, add the corresponding human-domain, normative, and procedural responsibilities; otherwise stop at the existing description and bounded explanation.

Distinctions to keep clear

Factual truth

Whether a specific claim holds in the world.

≠

Current evidence status

Whether available evidence can support the claim.

Proof within a model

Established by the stated premises and derivation.

≠

Real-world mechanism

Mappings of quantities, domains, operations, and so on, plus independent case evidence, are still required.

Domain conclusion

Retains its grounds and scope under the original research design.

≠

Eligibility for a formal test

Requires this framework's pre-registration in advance and its testing requirements.

No positive support

The positive criterion has not been met, or uncertainty remains.

≠

Support for a null conclusion

Predefined null rules, sensitivity, and tolerance have actually passed.

A grounded narrow conclusion

Limited to specified objects, horizons, and targets.

≠

Unconditional extrapolation

Expanding objects, tasks, or scope without bridging.

Mathematical teaching construction: how far a proof reaches, and why a changed task requires recheckingTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe state space contains these two states, numbers are exact reals, and there is no measurement error; both task and representation are constructed assumptions.

Let state x=(x1,x2), representation π(x)=x1+x2, and task q(x)=2(x1+x2). Define r(z)=2z; then for every specified state, r(π(x))=2(x1+x2)=q(x), a complete algebraic proof. If actual use changes to q′(x)=x1, states (1,0) and (0,1) both have π=1 but require answers 1 and 0 respectively. The same r′(1) cannot supply two different answers, so q′ cannot be recovered from π alone.

BoundaryThe first proof remains valid; the second task does not satisfy its premises. Whether real variables actually correspond through these equations still requires evidence; calculation cannot replace investigation.

Teaching construction: a scope statement for a qualified conclusionTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe study, location, and results are entirely hypothetical; no real data are supplied.

Suppose a fictional study measures an output difference between schemes A and B only for selected equipment, in a specified load range, at site A during one month. An appropriate statement retains these qualifications and uncertainty. Directly rewriting it as ‘A applies to all equipment and is always better’ adds four kinds of unsupported claims: object, time, load, and value. Extended research questions may be proposed, but they cannot be backfilled as already verified.

BoundaryThis exercises scope statements. It neither claims that this study exists nor prescribes the same design for every real study.

The 2018 replication project: denominators and success criteria must not disappearDocumented case

Camerer et al. replicated 21 systematically selected social-science experiments published in Nature and Science during 2010–2015. The original abstract reports that 13 met the metric of a significant result in the same direction as the original study; other replication metrics produced different counts. This section adds the point that results must be reported with their selected study set and criterion. The fraction 13/21 cannot be renamed the proportion of true propositions in all of social science.

SourceAbstract of Camerer et al.'s original paper, as hosted by PubMedNature Human Behaviour2:637–644, published online 2018-08-27, DOI10.1038/s41562-018-0399-z; first two paragraphs of the Abstract.Reading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsOnly the original abstract and bibliographic information were read; the 21 experiments were not individually redone. The fraction 13/21 is not the truth rate of all studies, and missing this criterion does not directly prove a zero effect or misconduct. This is the same study as S-4-1, not independent evidence; this section only adds questions about scope and metrics.

Scope and open questions

This unit concerns methodological judgment. Actual sources support only the listed facts; the diagram and teaching construction each retain their own status.

  • Whether any real mechanism satisfies the premises of the corresponding conditional formal proposition or the requirements of the corresponding tests and conclusion rules requires separate evidence about the object; this lesson does not replace those tests with a teaching model.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    If a formal proposition has been proved, has it thereby been established that a real system satisfies it?

  2. 2

    In the mathematical sum-representation example, why does changing the target to x1 fail?

  3. 3

    Are all older studies invalid if they have not been converted into this framework's formal tests?

  4. 4

    Does a 13/21 result under one replication measure mean that only 62% of an entire discipline is true?

  5. 5

    If experimental results are reliable, can one directly require someone to sacrifice?

If a formal proposition has been proved, has it thereby been established that a real system satisfies it?

No. The proof's conditional conclusion holds, but whether the real system's variables, domain, operations, and errors conform still requires independent verification.

Basis: §2.1.2 and Chinese source line 1018.

In the mathematical sum-representation example, why does changing the target to x1 fail?

The same representation value 1 corresponds to different answers 1 and 0; a single input cannot recover two target values. This is insufficient information after the task changes.

Basis: The explicit algebra and two-state counterexample in this lesson.

Are all older studies invalid if they have not been converted into this framework's formal tests?

No. Retain domain conclusions under their original designs. Eligibility for a formal test cannot be granted automatically, but neither does its absence negate existing grounds.

Basis: §2.1.1。

Does a 13/21 result under one replication measure mean that only 62% of an entire discipline is true?

No. The denominator is that selected study set and the metric is that replication criterion; neither covers all studies or directly defines factual truth.

Basis: The original P-Camerer abstract and this section's extrapolation boundary.

If experimental results are reliable, can one directly require someone to sacrifice?

No. Value, responsibility, protection, and bounded procedures each have their own requirements; empirical conclusions do not themselves create obligations or authority to act.

Basis: Chinese source line 1018; normative bridging (§4.14.1).

4.17Common Method Constraints ​

In briefThe ‘laws’ here are methodological constraints that analysis should follow, not natural laws about how the world necessarily operates. They must also face a question in return: after actual use, do they really reduce errors and improve understanding at a proportionate cost?

Method constraints govern how analysts construct, check, and use models; they do not claim how the world necessarily works. They may be questioned and revised; whether they are useful must be assessed by comparing the errors they actually reduce, the understanding they add, and the costs of using them.

4.17Note

Understanding this section

4.17 Common method constraints

The ‘laws’ here are methodological constraints that analysis should follow, not natural laws about how the world necessarily operates. They must also face a question in return: after actual use, do they really reduce errors and improve understanding at a proportionate cost?

Chinese source line 1022 explicitly states that methodological constraints govern how analysts construct, check, and use models and ‘do not claim how the world necessarily works’. This section therefore adds no new empirical causal mechanism; it requires model use to retain boundaries of tasks, evidence, and authority. [T-417]

The three numbered subsections respectively require joint declaration of task and representation, traceability of material identity and scope of support, and separate establishment of facts, values, and eligibility to act. The fourth subsection then subjects the rules themselves to evaluation: they may be challenged and revised, and cannot escape comparison by calling themselves rigorous. [T-417]

Following rules can make analysis more transparent, but transparent records alone do not prove a judgment true or a method beneficial on balance. The source identifies actual error reduction, gains in understanding, and costs of use as comparative responsibilities. Without an appropriate comparison, one may describe only intended uses and verified local results. [T-eval]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    First distinguish methodological requirements governing analysis from empirical propositions describing the world.

  2. 2

    Use the three laws to check task, material, and actual-adoption boundaries.

  3. 3

    Separately design a comparison with a common task and budget to evaluate the method's own benefits and prices to be paid.

Distinctions to keep clear

Methodological constraint

Govern the construction, checking, and use of analysis.

≠

Law of the world

Factual claims about how an object operates.

Process transparency

Records are traceable.

≠

The method is effective on balance

Actual comparisons of errors, understanding, and costs are still required.

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleTeaching counterexample: a report is complete in every item but has an incorrect core calculation. Completeness cannot settle correctness.

What it limitsCompleteness does not establish correctness.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari, On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation

What does not follow

  • Source boundary: a method may be challenged and revised; rule names do not confer universal correctness.
  • Teaching counterexample: a report is complete in every item but has an incorrect core calculation. Completeness cannot settle correctness.

Scope and open questions

The parent section locates and navigates the methodology; specific sources, constructions, and evaluation plans are developed independently in the four subsections.

  2. 2

    Is a complex set of rules sufficient proof that it is worth adopting?

Are the common method constraints new empirical root propositions?

No. They govern the use of analytical methods, without claiming how the world necessarily operates.

Basis: Chinese source line 1022.

Is a complex set of rules sufficient proof that it is worth adopting?

No. Actual errors, understanding, and costs must be compared.

Basis: Chinese source lines 998 and 1038–1040.

4.17.1Tasks and Representations Must Be Declared Together (CMC1) ​

In briefTo judge a representation, first ask what it is for. Omitting details need not impair the task, and retaining many details need not suffice for dynamic prediction or intervention.

Objects, layering, coarse and fine scales, and target variables all need to be stated together with the task, observation position, horizon, environment, and use. A conversion must check what is retained, collapsed, omitted, and added; it must not be presumed lossless, nor may it be claimed conversely that every conversion necessarily causes a task-relevant loss. Whether the target representation suffices to recover an answer, advance dynamics, or evaluate admissible interventions is tested separately; whether different orders of conversion are equivalent is also tested separately. The distinctions on which the task depends must be retained. Recovering every detail unconditionally is unnecessary.

4.17.1Note

Understanding this section

4.17.1 Tasks and representations must be declared together (CMC1)

To judge a representation, first ask what it is for. Omitting details need not impair the task, and retaining many details need not suffice for dynamic prediction or intervention.

Chinese source line 1026 requires binding objects, stratification, scale granularity, and target variables to the task, observational position, horizon, environment, and use. Judging ‘is this summary sufficient?’ must include the target: answering a static question, predicting several steps of evolution, and comparing a permitted operation may require different distinctions. [T-law1]

A transformation must separately state what it preserves, which states it merges, which variables it omits, and which estimates or assumptions it adds. Losslessness cannot be presumed, nor can the reverse claim that all compression causes task-relevant loss. If the target requires only a total, that total may suffice; if the target depends on an individual's location, the total may merge different answers. The method seeks to retain distinctions necessary for the task in question, not recover every task-irrelevant detail. [T-law1；T-F1]

Recovery of static answers, closure under natural dynamics, and closure under permitted interventions are different tests. A representation sufficient to answer the current total does not thereby determine the next period's total; that task also asks whether merged states update into the same representation. When new actions are allowed, action implementability and macro outcomes of different micro implementations may also need rechecking. [T-law1；T-F2]

Transformation order also cannot be presumed equivalent based on names. Rounding before adjustment may differ from adjusting before rounding; some mappings do commute on a bounded domain. Fix the actual versions of both operations, the input domain, and the final target before comparing them. One noncommuting example must not be expanded into ‘no transformations ever commute.’ [T-law1；T-G4]

Changes in horizon, environment, or use justify rechecking; they do not automatically establish that the old representation was always wrong. Supported success on the old task may remain, with distinctions required by the new task added. Variable measurement, error, information-acquisition timing, and operational permission in real models still need independent checks; formal sufficiency does not mean timely availability. [T-formal; T-law1]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    State task, object, representation, target, observation position, environment, horizon, and use together.

  2. 2

    List what is preserved, merged, omitted, and additionally assumed.

  3. 3

    Separately test static recovery, dynamic progression, permitted operations, and conversion order.

  4. 4

    Add only distinctions necessary for the current task; recheck corresponding responsibilities after changes.

Distinctions to keep clear

Information loss

Different source states are merged.

≠

Task loss

Merged states require different task answers.

Static sufficiency

The current query is recoverable.

≠

Dynamic / operational sufficiency

The representation also determines results after updates or permitted interventions.

More detail

More variables are preserved.

≠

Fit for use

Still requires proportionate task, horizon, error, and acquisition conditions.

Mathematical teaching construction: losing detail need not mean losing the taskTeaching scenario

AssumptionsBinary finite states, exact observation, and a deterministic single query.

Let the state set be {(0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)}, with representation π storing only the sum of the two numbers. For counting task q=x1+x2, output π directly, correctly in all four states. For q′=x1, π=1 corresponds to both (0,1) and (1,0), so π cannot uniquely answer. Preserving the first component as an additional distinction supports q′; failure on one task does not imply that all compression is useless.

BoundaryA model illustration, not measurement of real-world data-compression quality.

Mathematical teaching construction: order must be calculatedTeaching scenario

AssumptionsReal-valued inputs and exact arithmetic; the two functions are defined in the stated versions.

Let R(x)=floor(x) round downward and A(x)=x+0.6. At x=0.6, R(A(x))=floor(1.2)=1, whereas A(R(x))=0+0.6=0.6, so the two compositions differ. Changing operations or restricting the domain requires rechecking; one difference cannot establish that all mappings fail to commute.

BoundaryOnly noncommutativity of functions; it neither automatically certifies a real-world scale-closure test nor grants intervention permission.

A 2016 classifier study: changing the evaluation use changes the rankingDocumented case

In §6.1–6.2, Ribeiro and colleagues explain that two classifiers trained on 20 newsgroups had opposite accuracy rankings on the original data split and on a separately constructed evaluation set of religious websites. This section focuses on the relationship between evaluation material and the intended task: scores on the original split cannot be treated without explanation as performance in another environment.

SourceRibeiro, Singh, and Guestrin, original paper v3arXiv:1602.04938v3, 2016-08-09; §6.1 and opening of §6.2, PDF page 7.Reading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsThe authors' particular experiment, not a universal rule for all classifiers or environmental changes; the same paper as the earlier §6.4 case, not an independent replication. Different experimental passages are used here, without obtaining eligibility for a formal scale-closure test under this framework.

Scope and open questions

This unit concerns methodological judgment. Actual sources support only the listed facts; the diagram and teaching construction each retain their own status.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    Is keeping only a total necessarily unscientific?

  2. 2

  3. 3

Is keeping only a total necessarily unscientific?

Not necessarily; it may suffice for counting but fail for a task depending on individual position.

Basis: Chinese source line 1026 and the teaching construction.

Does recoverability of the current query guarantee prediction after intervention?

No. Check closure separately for the actual permitted operations, implementation, and updates.

Basis: “Closure under Dynamics and Admissible Interventions” (§4.18.2) and §4.6.1.

Why do R and A differ in order in the example?

Adding first gives 1.2, then rounding gives 1; rounding first gives 0, then adding gives 0.6.

Basis: The explicit functions and input.

4.17.2The Status of Materials and Scope of Support Must Be Traceable (CMC2) ​

In briefThe same material may be carefully recalculated and yield new understanding; processing it ten times does not make ten independent observations. Reports, simulations, and execution results likewise support only their respective levels.

Reports, observations, model beliefs, and formal proofs retain their respective statuses. So do simulation outputs and execution receipts. Each inference specifies the new information, premises, and rules it uses; processing the same data again must not be counted as a new independent observation. A simulated state can become the starting point of the next simulation, but recursive depth alone cannot add empirical support or raise a capability level. New computations or proofs can improve understanding of existing materials, but their gains come from inspectable arguments and must not be packaged as new real-world samples.

4.17.2Note

Understanding this section

4.17.2 The status of materials and scope of support must be traceable (CMC2)

The same material may be carefully recalculated and yield new understanding; processing it ten times does not make ten independent observations. Reports, simulations, and execution results likewise support only their respective levels.

Chinese source line 1030 lists reports, observations, model beliefs, formal proofs, simulation outputs, and execution receipts, requiring preservation of their distinct statuses. A report is someone else's organization and judgment of material; an observation is a record under a protocol; a belief is a model's judgment; a proof is a derivation under premises; a simulation runs a specified model; a receipt documents an operation only within what it actually records. These can support one another but cannot be exchanged without labeling. [T-law2; T-evidence]

Every inference should identify new information, reused premises and rules, and what the conclusion adds to its inputs. Recalculating raw data, redrawing plots, or changing algorithms may reveal errors, boundaries, or better proofs: these are real gains in knowledge. The source remains the same dataset and cannot count as multiple independent empirical datasets. [T-law2; T-formal]

Recursive simulation can use one round's state as the next round's input, lengthening the model trajectory; recursion depth itself cannot increase real-world support or capability level. The model world is still generated by the given equations; adding steps may expose consequences within the model or accumulate error, and must be recorded separately from new real-world measurements. [T-law2; T-F5]

Independence also concerns shared raw data, the same samples, common measuring equipment, model-training material, and personnel procedures. Two reports with different authors may cite the same observation. Source counts are not independent-evidence counts; identify overlaps and differences, reducing the force of mutual corroboration where necessary without erasing the original value of individual materials. [T-law2; T-evidence]

Execution receipts must not be overextended either. Successful sending differs from the recipient understanding; editing a draft differs from an operating rule taking effect. A recommendation report can indeed propose a recommendation without establishing that it was implemented or effective long-term. Conversely, failure to find implementation evidence does not make an attributable recommendation text nonexistent. [T-law2; T-writeback]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Label each item's generation process, version, time, and observational or model status.

  2. 2

    For every conversion, state new information, premises and rules, and the support ceiling.

  3. 3

    Identify shared original material; do not count repeated computation as independent observation.

  4. 4

    Check separate grounds for simulation outputs versus new real-world records, and recommendations versus actual execution.

Distinctions to keep clear

Reprocessing

New computation or interpretation of the same material.

≠

Independent observation

Requires corresponding grounds for data generation and independence.

Extending a simulation

Recursive progression of model states.

≠

Increased empirical support

Requires genuinely new material or proportionate testing.

Making a recommendation

The report text exists.

≠

Implementation and effects

Separately check actions, execution, and outcomes.

Mathematical teaching construction: more rows, no more independent samplesTeaching scenario

AssumptionsExplicit mechanical duplication of the same two records, without a new measurement process.

Let two original observations be 0 and 2, with mean 1. Copy each five times to create ten rows; the mean remains (5×0+5×2)/10=1. The new table has ten rows but only two original records; whether those two are independent requires separate examination of the original measurement design. Repeated display may support checking or formatting, but cannot be called ten new measurements. If actual repeated measurements exist, reassess them by their real dependencies rather than row counts alone.

BoundaryNot a real data analysis, and not a claim that all repeated measurement is uninformative.

The report's recommendations and their subsequent implementation therefore cannot automatically be combined from the same text. Does running the same simulation to step 1000 provide 1000 real-world tests?

No. It produces a trajectory of the given model; real-world testing requires independent material and an appropriate comparison.

It has value: the gain comes from checkable reasoning, but cannot be relabeled a new real-world sample.

No. Recommendation text and actual execution require different material.

4.17.3Facts, Values, and Eligibility to Act Are Established Separately (CMC3) ​

In briefKnowing how to do something, its being worth doing, and permission to do it are three different questions. The reverse also holds: a target worth protecting does not automatically make an unverified mechanism true.

Facts, predictions, formal feasibility, and technical capability cannot by themselves generate value, responsibility, or authority to act. An analytical recommendation needs to disclose normative targets, evidence, the price to be paid, and dissent; real-world adoption additionally requires valid permissions, a protection floor, implementation resources, and conditions for stopping and remedy. Normative premises constrain choice; they cannot in turn prove empirical mechanisms true.

4.17.3Note

Understanding this section

4.17.3 Facts, values, and eligibility to act are established separately (CMC3)

Knowing how to do something, its being worth doing, and permission to do it are three different questions. The reverse also holds: a target worth protecting does not automatically make an unverified mechanism true.

Chinese source line 1034 confines facts, predictions, formal feasibility, and technical capability to their respective roles. Facts address current conditions or relations; predictions give conditional consequences; formal feasibility supplies possible actions within a model; technical capability states what can be implemented. None alone produces value rankings, responsibility, or authority to act. [T-law3; T-formal]

Analytical recommendations should disclose normative targets, evidence, prices to be paid, and objections. A recommendation may say “under this target and these constraints, option A is more suitable,” without presenting a conditional evaluation as a value-neutral necessity or prohibiting supported deliberation merely because execution permission is still absent. [T-law3; T-C12]

Real-world adoption separately requires valid permission, a protection floor, implementation resources, stopping, and remedy. Sufficient resources do not mean authority; authorization does not mean technical feasibility. Permission must cover the actual action, object, territory, and duration. An application or recommendation cannot itself turn pending review into approval to implement. [T-law3; T-J]

Normative premises constrain permissible choices; they do not establish an empirical mechanism's truth in reverse. For example, explicitly targeting protection of a population does not establish that an intervention will provide it; proportionate material on effects, risks, alternatives, and distribution is still needed. Weaker empirical grounds require revising the proposal and its uncertainty, not lowering the evidence requirements because the target is important. [T-law3; T-C12]

Responsibility and sacrifice also require assessment by specific human positions and independent grounds; “the system needs it” or “it is more efficient” cannot forcibly assign uptake to someone. Existing bounded responsibilities are not universally canceled by this distinction either; state their source, scope, duration, and safe handoff. The methodological boundary prevents both unauthorized additional burdens and unsupported exemptions from independent duties. [T-N]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    List separately what facts, predictions, formal feasibility, and technical capability each support.

  2. 2

    Specify the normative targets, evidence, prices to be paid, and objections of an analytical recommendation.

  3. 3

    Real-world adoption separately requires permission, protection, resources, stopping, and remedy.

  4. 4

    Normative grounds do not establish empirical truth in reverse; empirical changes should return to deliberation over the proposal.

Distinctions to keep clear

Able to implement

Technology and resources permit it.

≠

Authorized to implement

Permission and duties cover the actual action.

Worth protecting

An explicit normative commitment.

≠

The measure actually works

Requires independent empirical grounds.

Recommendation conditions

An evaluation for deliberation.

≠

Actual adoption

Execute within bounds only after every necessary condition is substantively met.

Teaching construction: three cards for target, capability, and permissionTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe system, list, and target are fictional; no real personal data are included and no disclosure was made.

A fictional system can already generate candidate lists: the capability card. Its user wants to reduce omissions: the target card. Whether disclosure to a particular recipient is allowed, for which use, and for how long is a separate permission-and-protection question. The three cards may independently be present or absent. Even with an explicit target and permission, list accuracy needs independent evaluation; good intentions and permission do not determine it.

BoundaryProvides no actual authorization or advice on interventions concerning individuals; specific information-processing rules require verification against the actual institutional arrangements.

The Belmont Report: consent and justice responsibilities beyond scientific benefitsDocumented case

Part C of the 1979 Belmont Report separates informed consent into information, comprehension, and voluntariness, and separately discusses risk-benefit assessment and subject selection. The point here is that these requirements each have their own reasons: potential research benefits do not automatically make being informed and voluntary factual.

Effects cannot be inferred from a target; check the actual mechanism, risks, and distributional consequences.

If an algorithm can generate a result, may it be published externally?

Capability alone cannot justify the conclusion; publication separately has requirements for permission, protection, use, and duration.

Basis: This section and the scope of jurisdiction and authorization.

Must a recommendation for deliberation pretend execution permission has already been obtained?

It need not and must not. Disclose norms, evidence, prices to be paid, and objections while retaining its status as a recommendation.

4.17.4Method Effectiveness and Evaluation of the Framework ​

In briefTesting a case and testing whether a whole framework is worth using involve different denominators and questions. Even if every case makes sense, ask what the framework adds over professional or simpler methods and how much extra it costs.

The four empirical questions organize empirical testing; their number does not establish sufficient coverage. The twelve conclusion rules organize the use of results; their completeness does not establish real-world reliability. Testing whether the entire framework is worth using should involve a separate comparison with common targets, common materials, and a common budget: compared with an adequate specialist method or a simpler approach, whether the framework reduces substantive errors, preserves necessary distinctions, and improves explanation or decision-making, and whether its costs are proportionate. Without such a comparison, only its intended uses and the local results already checked may be stated. In that case, the evidential status of the framework’s net gain on the task concerned is “awaiting evidence from comparison”; the number of times it has been used, users’ approval, and the number of studies written with this framework do not change that status. Studies written with the help of a tool based on this framework (for example an AI tool) are not themselves such a comparison: they can supply records of misuse and candidates awaiting testing; when such studies are the party being evaluated in a comparison, the evaluation standards, the comparator, and the reviewers must be independent of the tool and of its developers and maintainers. Materials used to revise this book can be used to check whether a revision has removed the errors it targeted; they cannot then serve as independent evidence that the revised framework is better overall (§2.1.1, Appendix C.3).

The effect in a single test, the rate at which one of the empirical questions applies within a particular set of objects, and the framework's net gain on a specified task are three different empirical targets. Sampling units, scopes of extrapolation, and evaluation rules must each be stated; a batch of successful cases or a large volume of reading materials must not be treated as proof of universal effectiveness. To evaluate what this framework added in a given analysis, take as the comparator an equally careful specialist practice or close reading that does not use this framework’s terms; the comparator must have actually been carried out or be open to checking: distinctions that the work being read, the domain method, or close reading could have obtained anyway are not recorded as the framework’s gain (§2.7.1). Only what has actually improved in the respects listed in the previous paragraph is recorded as gain; a judgment that has merely changed without becoming better does not count.

4.17.4Note

Understanding this section

4.17.4 Method effectiveness and framework evaluation

Testing a case and testing whether a whole framework is worth using involve different denominators and questions. Even if every case makes sense, ask what the framework adds over professional or simpler methods and how much extra it costs.

Chinese source line 1038 explicitly states that the number of empirical questions does not establish adequate coverage and that the completeness of the conclusion rules does not establish real-world reliability. Many questions, cards, publications, or successful cases show only the scale of organized content; whether the method helps users reduce substantive errors remains an independent empirical question. [T-eval]

Fair comparison first fixes common targets, material, and budgets. Comparators should be adequate professional methods or simpler alternatives, not deliberately weak baselines. Declare users' training, experience, accessible information, time and tool limits, and the tasks and evaluation rules; otherwise improvements due to extra information or time may be miscounted as framework effects. [T-eval; T-evidence]

Evaluation cannot ask only whether forms are complete or users like the method. The source requires asking whether substantive errors decrease, necessary distinctions are preserved, explanation or decisions improve, and costs are proportionate. Tasks can record types of misjudgment, important boundaries missed, calibration or answer quality, time spent, and learning costs; these are evaluation proposals made here but not implemented. Specific metrics and weights must be disclosed beforehand, and no existing educational effect is claimed. [T-eval]

Three empirical targets must be separated. The effect in a single test asks about a bounded difference for a particular object, treatment, and outcome; the rate at which one of the empirical questions applies within a particular set of objects asks which objects qualify under specified sampling and criteria; the framework's net gain asks about differences in outcomes and costs on common tasks between use of this framework and a control. Their sampling units may respectively be individuals/objects, candidate objects, and tasks or users; denominators, extrapolations, and evaluations cannot be borrowed across them. [T-eval]

Collecting only successful cases changes the applicability-rate denominator; giving easy tasks to people familiar with the framework and hard tasks to controls mixes in differences in personnel and tasks. A study could retain the complete task set and records of failures/withdrawals in advance, balance personnel and tasks through a reasonable design, use blinded scoring, and disclose uncertainty. Whether randomization, matching, or another design is appropriate depends on the actual tasks; no actual recruitment, assignment, or testing took place here. [T-eval；T-evidence]

Net gain also requires explicit evaluation objectives; heterogeneous quantities such as errors, minutes, and risks to rights cannot be added without explanation. If weighted loss is used, the weights are choices for this evaluation and should have units, reasons, sensitivity analysis, and noncompensable protection floors. A method that makes fewer errors but takes more time may yield different conclusions for different uses; ‘more comprehensive’ is not proof of superiority without cost. [T-eval；T-law3；T-C2]

Without a proportionate comparison under common objectives, materials, and budgets, claims should stop at intended uses, inspectable public derivations, and supported local results. The present section-by-section explanation, structural validation, graphic checks, and independent content reading each serve a purpose, but they have not established learning gains for real readers or net gain of the framework relative to professional methods. The former remain unevaluated, and the evidential status of the latter is “awaiting evidence from comparison”; neither is zero-benefit or proven effective. [T-eval]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Select separately among individual effects, applicability rates, and the framework's net benefits; do not mix denominators.

  2. 2

    For framework evaluation, fix in advance common tasks, materials, budgets, user conditions, and adequate controls.

  3. 3

    Predetermine metrics for substantive errors, necessary distinctions, understanding/decisions, and costs, explaining weights and hard protective constraints.

  4. 4

    Use a proportionate design to address differences in personnel, difficulty, information, and training, retaining failures and uncertainty.

  5. 5

    If the comparison has not been performed, report only intended uses and checked local results; do not fabricate effects.

Distinctions to keep clear

Number of successful cases

The local facts studied.

≠

Applicability rate of one of the empirical questions

Requires a predetermined object set and an appropriate denominator.

Applicability rate

Which objects satisfy the criteria in question.

≠

Differences in task outcomes and costs relative to adequate controls.

Complete materials/rules

Completeness of organization or recording.

≠

Evaluation plan

Proposed metrics and design.

≠

Evaluation results

Data and analyses obtained after actual completion.

Mathematical teaching construction: the same errors and time, different cost weightsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsAll errors have equal weight, both methods use the same task and materials, and neither violates an independent protection floor; all numbers and weights are artificial stipulations.

Suppose a common budget ceiling is 60 minutes, with fictional method A producing 4 equally weighted errors in 40 minutes and B producing 6 in 20 minutes. The evaluation loss is L=错误数+λ×分钟 (L = error count + λ × minutes), where λ has units of equivalent error cost per minute. At λ=0.05, A=6 and B=7; at λ=0.1, both are 8; at λ=0.2, A=12 and B=10. Which method is more suitable depends on disclosed task-cost weights, not on the word ‘more meticulous’.

BoundaryNo experiment was conducted. Harms to rights or different error types are not automatically converted into minutes; actual weights and hard constraints must be stated separately.

Teaching construction: fix the denominator of an applicability rate firstTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe numbers 100 and 10 and the unevaluated statuses are teaching stipulations, not actual object statistics from this book.

Suppose the predetermined set contains 100 candidate objects, of which only 10 successful cases are displayed. The success proportion among displayed cases is 10/10; the applicability rate across the complete set cannot be determined from this because the remaining 90 have not been evaluated. Only after evaluating the complete set or a proportionate sample by uniform criteria, while retaining unevaluated statuses, may an estimate for the declared population be reported.

BoundaryThe 90 unevaluated objects are not treated as failures, and no inference is made about the framework's actual applicability rate.

A 2016 comparison of explanation methods: separately evaluating tasks of useDocumented case

In §6.2, Ribeiro and colleagues set up a separate task of ‘choosing the classifier that generalizes better’, comparing greedy and LIME explanations and random/submodular instance selection. Each condition limited both the number of words in each explanation and the number of documents viewed to 6, randomized algorithm positions and instance order, and recorded choices. This provides a bounded example of an actual method-evaluation design.

SourceRibeiro and colleagues' original paper, v3§6.2, PDF pages 7—8, especially the continuation on page 8 and Figure9; version dated 2016-08-09.Reading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsThis is the authors' experiment on a specific task, not an evaluation of this framework, and it does not establish that every training, computation, or implementation cost was fairly accounted for. Its results are not transferred into actual reader effects of this explanation. Reusing the same paper as the case in §4.17.1 does not constitute independent verification.

Can organizing 100 papers prove the framework's net benefits?

No. The volume of material is not a controlled evaluation under common tasks and budgets.

Basis: Chinese source, lines 1038—1040.

If all 10 displayed cases succeeded, may all 100 candidates be called applicable?

No. The remaining 90 are unevaluated; unevaluated objects also cannot directly be counted as failures.

Basis: The teaching example of denominators.

What are the losses for A and B when the cost weight λ=.1?

A=4+.1×40=8 and B=6+.1×20=8; the tie applies only under the stipulated weights and conditions.

Basis: Teaching construction.

This explanation has been read and validated; does that prove readers necessarily learn better?

No. Checking content and comparing actual learning effects are different tasks.

Basis: Chinese source, lines 1038—1040, and the scope not actually carried out in this lesson.

4.18Conditional Formal Propositions ​

In briefThis group of propositions turns questions such as ‘is the summary sufficient?’, ‘can the next step be advanced?’, and ‘can a qualified action be selected now?’ into provable conditions. Their certainty comes from stated premises, not from attaching the same labels to the real world.

The following propositions hold within explicitly stated mathematical objects. They provide checkable conditions for representation, conversion, and action, not unmeasured laws of reality. When they are applied in reality, variable mappings, assumptions, errors, and scope of application must additionally be checked under §2.1.2; proving that a function exists does not guarantee that it is computable, available in time, implementable, or authorized for adoption.

4.18Note

Understanding this section

4.18 Conditional formal propositions

This group of propositions turns questions such as ‘is the summary sufficient?’, ‘can the next step be advanced?’, and ‘can a qualified action be selected now?’ into provable conditions. Their certainty comes from stated premises, not from attaching the same labels to the real world.

Line 1044 of the Chinese source explicitly states that the following propositions ‘hold within explicitly stated mathematical objects’. State domains, representations, targets, dynamics, permitted operations, and error conditions are all part of the argument. The first five conditional formal propositions respectively address static task recovery, closure of dynamics and interventions, common feasible actions, preservation of the same task through successive conversions, and approximate error propagation; they cannot replace one another. [T-418]

A formal proof supplies ‘if these conditions hold, the conclusion holds’, or a two-way characterization of conditions. A counterexample can directly refute the unconditional inference it targets even without a real-world experiment; whether a real object satisfies the conditions still requires measurement, variable mappings, and error materials. The number of exhaustive checks within a model cannot be counted as a real-world sample size. [T-formal]

The existence of a set-theoretic function, computability, computation within budget, timely data availability, practical implementability, and authority to adopt it are separate judgments. A recovery function can be mathematically unique while the actual system uses an incorrect rule; original materials may be preserved but fail to arrive when a decision is made. The formal conclusion is not thereby invalidated, nor does responsibility for application disappear. [T-formal；T-F4A]

The numbers, states, and actions in this lesson are mathematical constructions with labeled assumptions; arrows in the figures represent functions or conditional relationships, not actual causal evidence. Real adoption must still comply with corresponding norms, protections, and bounded authority; in particular, the set of qualified actions in the proposition “Common Feasible Actions under Information Constraints” (§4.18.3) cannot itself generate actual authorization. [T-F3A；T-C12]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Specify the mathematical objects, domains, targets, and premises.

  2. 2

    Use a proof or explicit counterexample to determine the conclusion within the model.

  3. 3

    For real-world application, separately check variables, measurement, errors, availability, and the range of operations.

  4. 4

    Continue checking implementation resources, authority, and protections under the corresponding conclusion rules.

Distinctions to keep clear

Formal conclusion

A logical result under stated premises.

≠

Real-world qualification

Evidence that a real object satisfies the premises and testing requirements.

Function existence

There is a mathematical mapping.

≠

Practical usability

Also requires algorithms, time limits, inputs, implementation, and authority.

What counterexamples change

Sourced counterexampleBoundary in the source: formal propositions are not unmeasured real-world laws.

What it limitsSeparate formal existence from responsibility for real-world use.

Scope and open questions

This unit presents conditional propositions within explicitly specified mathematical objects, using complete public proofs and mathematical constructions. Real cases cannot certify premises in their place, so historical events are not forcibly matched to them, and no existing test of a real case is claimed.

The proof guarantees a conditional relationship; whether the real object's quantities, domains, and operations match the premises still requires materials.
