4.18.1Task Recovery (F1) ​

In briefSomeone seeing only the same summary must give the same answer. If that summary merges states that should receive different answers, even the smartest decoder cannot distinguish them using the summary alone.

Let X be a nonempty state domain, with representation π:X→Y and Y=π(X), and target q:X→V. A decoder g:Y→V using only the representation and satisfying q=g∘π exists if and only if π(x)=π(x′) always implies q(x)=q(x′). When this condition holds, g is unique on Y. In other words, states for which the current task requires different answers cannot be merged by the same representation. See Appendix C.6 for the proof and for bounds on scalar recovery error on a finite state domain.

4.18.1Note

Understanding this section

4.18.1 Task recovery (F1)

Someone seeing only the same summary must give the same answer. If that summary merges states that should receive different answers, even the smartest decoder cannot distinguish them using the summary alone.

Let X be nonempty, π:X→Y with Y=π(X), and the target q:X→V. Y includes only representation values that actually occur. For y, the fiber X_y={x:π(x)=y} comprises all source states merged by the same representation. g can read only y; it cannot secretly read source-state numbers, identity labels, or undeclared history. The question is when q=g∘π holds. [T-F1；T-F1A]

Necessity: if q=g∘π, take any π(x)=π(x′)=y; then q(x)=g(y)=q(x′). Thus if a fiber contains two target answers, every deterministic decoder reading only y faces a conflict. This is an information-level impossibility, not something solved by replacing the operator with a more skilled one. [T-F1A]

Sufficiency: if q is constant on every fiber, define g(y) as that fiber's common target value. Y=π(X) makes every fiber nonempty; constancy makes the definition unambiguous. For any x, g(π(x)) is exactly q(x), so recovery holds. Uniqueness: every y has a source state x, and any feasible g must equal q(x), so g is unique on the actual image Y; extended representation points that never actually occur are not constrained by this result. [T-F1A]

This does not require π to be one-to-one. Multiple states can safely be merged as long as their answers to the current target agree; a change of target requires another check. Existence also does not guarantee an algorithm that always halts on an infinite domain, still less finite running time, data availability, or actual authority. Formal ‘losslessness’ is always relative to a specified task, not recovery of every detail of the world. [T-F1；T-formal]

The appendix gives an exact finite-scalar approximation bound. Add the assumptions that X is finite, q is real-valued, g may output any real number, and the loss is worst-case absolute error over the full domain. Let a_y and b_y be the minimum and maximum target values on a fiber. Any output c satisfies |b_y−a_y|≤|b_y−c|+|c−a_y|, so at least one endpoint has error ≥(b_y−a_y)/2. Choosing the midpoint c=(a_y+b_y)/2 puts every fiber value between the endpoints, yielding error ≤ half the range, attained at the endpoints. Hence the optimal full-domain worst-case error is (1/2)max_y(b_y−a_y). [T-F1A]

Thus, given ε≥0, a decoder with full-domain error ≤ε exists if and only if every fiber's range is ≤2ε. Finiteness guarantees the existence of endpoints and the maximum; arbitrary real-valued output makes the midpoint available. Infinite domains, vector targets, integer-only outputs, average loss, and nonuniform probabilities all require new analysis; half the range cannot be treated as a universal information-loss score across domains. [T-F1A]

The appendix also gives the answer for a binary target, zero-one loss, and a uniform distribution over finitely many states: if each fiber contains n_y0 zeros and n_y1 ones, selecting the majority label produces min(n_y0,n_y1) errors, so the minimum error rate is Σ_y min(n_y0,n_y1)/|X|. Randomized output produces a convex combination of the error counts of the two fixed labels and cannot improve on the smaller one. This optimizes average classification error; it does not replace the preceding worst-case absolute error or estimate frequencies in a real population. [T-F1A]

Terms used here

π and Y: representation and its actual image§C.6
π:X→Y is a deterministic representation, with Y=π(X).
X_y: representation fiber§C.6
For any y∈Y, the preimage X_y={x:π(x)=y} is called a representation fiber.
q and g: target and decoder§4.18.1
q:X→V is the target; g:Y→V is a decoder using only the representation. Task recovery requires q=g∘π.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Necessity: the same π value enters the same g, so its q values must agree.

  2. 2

    Sufficiency: define g by the common q value on each nonempty fiber, obtaining q=g∘π.

  3. 3

    Uniqueness: every y has a source, and any recovery function must take this common value at y.

  4. 4

    In the finite-scalar setting, the triangle inequality on the two endpoints gives the half-range lower bound; choosing each fiber's midpoint attains it.

  5. 5

    In the binary uniform case, choose the majority label on each fiber and sum the minimum error counts; randomization cannot improve on the endpoints of the convex combination.

  6. 6

    Bound each conclusion to its own domain, output restrictions, and loss; check its real-world correspondence separately.

Distinctions to keep clear

Recover the source state

Distinguish all x.

≠

Recover the current target

Distinguish only states with different q values.

Uniqueness on the actual image

The task fixes g's value at every actual y.

≠

Uniqueness on an extended domain

Representation points that never occur are not constrained by this conclusion.

Worst-case absolute error

The half-range problem for a finite real-valued target.

≠

Average classification error

The majority-label problem for a binary target, specified distribution, and zero-one loss.

Mathematical teaching construction: optimal recovery of a finite scalar targetTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe five states constitute the entire domain; targets are exact real numbers, outputs may be any real numbers, and loss is worst-case absolute error.

Partition five states into A={x1,x2,x3} and B={x4,x5}, with q values 0,2,4,10,12 respectively. A has range 4; setting g(A)=2 yields errors 2,0,2. B has range 2; setting g(B)=11 yields errors 1,1. The worst error over the domain is 2, and A’s endpoints force any output to have error at least 2, so this is optimal. Tolerance ε=1.5 is unattainable; ε=2 is attainable.

BoundaryThis is not an estimate of empirical measurement error; average loss or restricted outputs require recalculation.

Mathematical teaching construction: another loss for a binary taskTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThis is a separate artificial binary task: five uniform finite states, zero-one loss, and deterministic or independently randomized output.

Now take five uniformly distributed states: labels in fiber A are 0,0,1 and in fiber B are 1,1. Outputting 0 for A misclassifies only one state, and outputting 1 for B misclassifies none, so the minimum average error rate is 1/5. Exact recovery within A remains impossible; only one error in this finite domain does not mean correctness at every state.

Boundary1/5 is not a real classifier’s error rate and must not be conflated with scalar error 2 in the preceding construction.

What counterexamples change

Sourced counterexampleCounterexample boundary in the source: exact recovery is impossible when one fiber has different q values; secretly reading labels is no longer decoding based only on π.

What it limitsThe same input cannot determine two task answers.

Teaching counterexampleMathematical boundary: merging different states through compression need not lose the task, provided q agrees.

What it limitsTask recovery does not require full-state recovery.

Sourced counterexampleBoundary in the source: half the range applies only under the listed assumptions of a finite scalar target, arbitrary real-valued output, and worst-case absolute error; it does not automatically generalize.

What it limitsLoss and output conditions cannot be omitted.

Scope and open questions

Real cases cannot certify premises in their place, so historical events are not forcibly matched to them, and no existing test of a real case is claimed.

Check your understanding

If π is not injective, must exact recovery fail?

Not necessarily; recovery remains possible if q is constant within each fiber.

Basis: Proof of sufficiency.

Why emphasize that Y is the actual image?

It ensures every fiber is nonempty, definitions have sources, and the recovery map is unique on Y; an extended domain has no such uniqueness guarantee.

Basis: Chinese source line 1048.

If the target values in A are 0, 2, and 4, what is the optimal worst-case error?

2, attained by midpoint output 2; the two endpoints give the lower bound.

Basis: Appendix C.6 and the construction.

After restricting outputs to integers, is the optimal error for targets 0 and 1 still .5?

No. Any integer output has worst-case error at least 1, attained by 0 or 1; the premise permitting arbitrary real outputs has changed.

Basis: Counterexample boundary.

Two-way proof and finite scalar error bound of the proposition “Task Recovery” (Appendix C.6)Different responsibilities for formal existence and real-world usability (§2.1.2)

4.18.2Closure under Dynamics and Admissible Interventions (F2) ​

In briefWhether a summary can update forward by itself depends on whether states merged by the summary still yield the same summary after one step. Natural evolution doing so does not mean added interventions do so too.

Let F:X→X be deterministic one-step dynamics. A macro-level update F̄ satisfying π∘F=F̄∘π exists if and only if any two source states with the same representation still have the same representation after updating. If this condition holds throughout the state domain, evolution over any finite number of steps under fixed dynamics commutes. When the admissible actions form a set U, this condition must hold separately for every F_u. Check whether each action can be implemented across the relevant source states sharing a representation. Check the different micro-level implementations as well. Sufficiency for static recovery does not automatically satisfy closure under dynamics or closure under intervention; a stochastic model must also compare the complete transition probabilities to target blocks. See Appendix C.8 for the proof.

4.18.2Note

Understanding this section

4.18.2 Closure under Dynamics and Admissible Interventions (F2)

Whether a summary can update forward by itself depends on whether states merged by the summary still yield the same summary after one step. Natural evolution doing so does not mean added interventions do so too.

Continue with nonempty X and π:X→Y=π(X), and fixed deterministic one-step dynamics F:X→X. Macroscopic closure requires F̄:Y→Y such that π(F(x))=F̄(π(x)) over the whole domain. The left side updates in the source domain and then summarizes; the right updates using only the summary. Agreement gives the macrostate a deterministic update independent of hidden detail. [T-F2; T-F2A]

The two-way proof applies the proposition “Task Recovery” (§4.18.1) directly with task q=π∘F. If F̄ exists, x and x′ with the same π pass through the same F̄ and give the same result, so π(F(x))=π(F(x′)). If this fiber condition holds, define F̄(y) as the common next-step representation; the proposition “Task Recovery” ensures unambiguity and uniqueness on the actual image. The static task q0=π is always recoverable by the identity decoder, but this does not guarantee recovery of the new task π∘F. [T-F2A; T-F1A]

The whole-domain condition supports finite-step induction. At t=0, π∘F⁰=Id_Y∘π. If π∘F^t=F̄^t∘π, then π∘F^(t+1)=(π∘F)∘F^t=(F̄∘π)∘F^t=F̄∘F̄^t∘π=F̄^(t+1)∘π. Since F maps X back into X, every step stays in the checked domain. Checking a few visited states or short trajectories cannot replace this whole-domain premise. [T-F2A]

With a permitted action set U, check equality of next-step representations within each fiber separately for every specific version F_u before composing any predetermined finite action sequence. If actions are implementable only in some merged source states, common implementability or an explicit domain restriction is also required. If one macro action name includes several micro implementations, the exact condition of this proposition requires identical macro responses across those implementations; calling them all ‘reset’ does not make them one F_u. Closeness within tolerance instead belongs to an approximation problem requiring separate errors, regions, and horizons and propagation under conditions such as those of “Error Propagation under Approximate Closure” (§4.18.5). Tolerance cannot establish the exact commutation or arbitrary finite-step equalities here. [T-F2A; T-F5A]

A finite stochastic system instead uses a transition kernel P and a given partition. For x and x′ in the same source block, every target block B must satisfy Σ_{z∈B}P(x,z)=Σ_{z∈B}P(x′,z). Define the common value as the macro kernel. Even if conditioning on the past changes the distribution within the source block, any weighted average remains this common value, so the macro next-step distribution is independent of hidden composition. If the same macro law must hold for all initial distributions, starting with point masses at x and x′ shows necessity as well. [T-F2A]

The preceding paragraph applies only to finite stochastic systems with a given partition; it does not generalize pointwise probabilities to continuous states. Equal next-step means do not imply equal distributions, and coincidence under one fixed initial mixture is not closure for all initial states. Natural dynamics, intervention dynamics, action feasibility, and normative adoptability each have their own conditions to meet; these mathematical conditions also do not directly award support to a real-world scale-closure test. [T-F2A; T-G4]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Replace the target of the proposition “Task Recovery” with π∘F to obtain necessary and sufficient conditions for a macro update to exist.

  2. 2

    Define the common next-step representation on each fiber to obtain F̄.

  3. 3

    Start at t=0 and use one-step commutation to prove every finite t by induction.

  4. 4

    Verify each specific F_u and common implementability, then compose a predetermined action sequence.

  5. 5

    For a finite stochastic partition, construct the macro kernel from target-block probability sums; point-mass distributions establish necessity for all initial states.

  6. 6

    Independently test empirical measurements, the permitted operation set, and the formal requirements of the scale-closure test.

Distinctions to keep clear

Sufficiency for the current query

Can recover q at this time.

≠

Dynamical closure

Can determine the next representation from the representation.

Closure of natural dynamics

A particular F commutes.

≠

Intervention closure

Every permitted F_u must also be tested separately.

Equal means

Preserves only one statistic.

≠

Distributional closure

Every target block has equal probability.

Actions sharing a name

Described by the same macro label.

≠

Equivalent implementations

Specific micro implementations also have identical macro responses.

Mathematical teaching construction: natural closure, intervention nonclosureTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe four states are the entire domain, the two deterministic functions are exact, and all listed actions are implementable within the model.

Partition states a,b,c,d into A={a,b} and B={c,d}. Natural F is a→c, b→d, c→a, d→b, so A always goes to B and B to A; the macro update swaps the blocks. Add action u: a→c, b→a, c→c, d→d. Both a and b initially represent A, but afterward they represent B and A respectively, so u is not closed. The natural-closure proof remains valid; the new action simply fails the same conditions.

BoundaryThis represents no actual system and does not imply failure of all interventions.

Mathematical teaching construction: equal means, different distributionsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsFive finite states, partition, and probabilities are given; c0/c1/c2 are each absorbing, completing the kernel.

A finite system has source states a,b and three absorbing states c0,c1,c2. a and b share block A; each c has its own target block with numerical label 0,1,2 respectively. a reaches the three target blocks with probabilities 1/2,0,1/2; b with probabilities 0,1,0. Both next-step label means are 1, yet probabilities of reaching, for example, the c1 block are 0 and 1, violating the blockwise probability-sum condition.

BoundaryThis only refutes substituting means for distributions and estimates no actual stochastic process.

What counterexamples change

Sourced counterexampleBoundary in the original text: static recovery does not automatically imply dynamical or intervention closure.

What it limitsStatic and dynamic tasks differ.

Sourced counterexampleBoundary in the original text: validity at a few visited states does not replace whole-domain conditions, and a fixed initial mixture does not replace a law for all initial states.

What it limitsWhole-domain and all-initial-state premises cannot be narrowed.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari, On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation

What it limitsChanging the operation changes closure qualification.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari, On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation

What it limitsMeans do not replace distributions.

Sourced counterexampleBoundary in the original text: common implementability and differing micro implementations require separate checks; mathematical closure creates no real-world authority.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    Why does the proposition “Closure under Dynamics and Admissible Interventions” follow from the proposition “Task Recovery”?

Why does the proposition “Closure under Dynamics and Admissible Interventions” follow from the proposition “Task Recovery”?

Set the recovery target to the next representation q=π∘F; the fiber-constancy condition of the proposition “Task Recovery” is exactly the closure condition.

Basis: Appendix C.8.

What is the macro rule for natural dynamics in the four-state example?

A and B swap, so any finite number of steps alternates by parity.

Basis: The given F and induction.

Why does the added action u fail?

a and b in block A go to B and A respectively; the single macrostate A cannot determine the next step.

Basis: The construction.

Can equal next-step means establish stochastic closure?

No. Check every target-block probability; the construction already conflicts at c1, with probabilities 0 and 1.

Basis: Finite stochastic kernel condition.

4.18.3Common Feasible Actions under Information Constraints (F3) ​

In briefIncomplete information does not always prevent action. The key is whether every state still possibly true now admits at least one common qualified action; each state having a solution differs from being able to choose the right solution now.

For a finite, single-round deterministic task, let the current materials be compatible with a nonempty set of states X_y, and let each state x have a set of eligible actions A_ok(x), already determined according to the target, protections, resources, and valid permissions. An action based only on the current representation y that qualifies in every compatible state exists if and only if ∩_{x∈X_y}A_ok(x) is nonempty. Identifying every state is therefore not a universal prerequisite for bounded action, while the availability of a solution in each state separately does not guarantee that the right choice can be made now. See Appendix C.12 for the proof; randomized strategies and sequential strategies must establish their own conditions.

4.18.3Note

Understanding this section

4.18.3 Common Feasible Actions under Information Constraints (F3)

Incomplete information does not always prevent action. The key is whether every state still possibly true now admits at least one common qualified action; each state having a solution differs from being able to choose the right solution now.

This proposition addresses only finite, single-round, deterministic tasks. Current representation y is compatible with a nonempty state set X_y, and each A_ok(x) has already been determined by task targets, protections, resources, and valid authority. It is neither a list of imaginable actions nor merely technically executable actions. Including real-world qualification in the set is a premise of applying the model; the theorem approves nothing for people. [T-F3; T-F3A]

The action may depend only on current y and therefore cannot vary with the still-undistinguished actual x. Qualification for every compatible state requires finding an a belonging simultaneously to every A_ok(x). This is a common-intersection problem, not a matter of finding each state’s optimal action separately and declaring execution possible now. [T-F3A]

Proof of necessity: if a depends only on y and is qualified for all x∈X_y, then a∈A_ok(x) for every x, so a belongs to the intersection and the intersection is nonempty. Proof of sufficiency: if the intersection is nonempty, choose an a from it; it belongs to every set and is therefore qualified for all states without knowing which x is actual. This proof concerns one choice at fixed y, not strategies involving future observation. [T-F3A]

This yields limits in both directions. Identifying all states is not a universal prerequisite for bounded action: a common qualified action suffices. Each state separately having a feasible action is also insufficient: {left} and {right} are both nonempty, yet their intersection is empty. Both statements are set-theoretic results, not policies of ‘always wait first’ or ‘always act immediately’. [T-F3A]

Waiting, additional observation, or preservation may change information and action sets, but these actions can themselves consume resources, alter risks, or require authority; they cannot be assumed safe and lawful. An independently verified preservation action satisfying the current bounded target, protections, resources, and authority may enter the common intersection. If it merely defers the original target without meeting the current task, establish a corresponding sequential or staged task separately rather than silently changing qualification. [T-F3A; T-C12]

The theorem covers only listed compatible states and does not guarantee that unknown states will never arise. Probabilistic choice with risk tolerance, randomized strategies, and action following multiple rounds of observation have different optimization targets and guarantees and require their own conditions. An empty intersection means only that the current representation admits no ‘single-round, deterministic action qualified for all listed states’; it does not prove that every probabilistic or sequential strategy is unsolvable. [T-F3A]

Terms used here

X_y: states compatible with the current material§4.18.3
Current material is compatible with a nonempty state set X_y; the proposition applies only to listed compatible states and cannot guarantee that unknown states never arise.
A_ok(x): qualified-action set§C.12
Each state x’s action set is already determined by targets, protections, resources, and valid authority; writing an action mathematically cannot replace these real-world conditions.
∩A_ok(x): common intersection§C.12
An action belonging to every compatible state’s qualified set belongs to the common intersection; each state’s set separately being nonempty is only necessary.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Specify a nonempty compatible-state set and A_ok already incorporating targets, protections, resources, and authority.

  2. 2

    If a common action exists, it belongs to every set, so the intersection is nonempty.

  3. 3

    If the intersection is nonempty, selecting an action from it qualifies for every compatible state.

  4. 4

    Check whether relevant possibilities are missing from the state set and whether waiting/observation carry separate costs or authority requirements.

  5. 5

    Do not generalize a single-round all-state guarantee into conclusions about randomized risk or sequential strategies.

Distinctions to keep clear

Every state has a solution

For every x, A_ok(x) is nonempty.

≠

A common solution is available now

∩_x A_ok(x) is nonempty; the quantifiers differ.

Identify the true state

Know the specific x.

≠

A common qualified action exists

The current bounded target can be met without knowing x.

The model set contains an action

Its qualification is artificially assumed.

≠

Actually authorized in reality

Requires actual material on targets, protections, resources, and authority.

Mathematical teaching construction: changed conditions turn an empty intersection nonemptyTeaching scenario

AssumptionsTwo finite states, one deterministic round, and given sets; H’s full qualification is an explicit mathematical premise of the second scenario.

In the first scenario, X_y={xA,xB}, A_ok(xA)={left}, and A_ok(xB)={right}; the intersection is empty. In another explicitly conditioned scenario, action H has been independently verified to meet the same current bounded target, protections, resources, and authority in both states. The sets are then {left,H} and {right,H}, whose intersection is {H}. The latter permits choosing H without knowing the actual state; it does not backfill qualification absent from the first scenario.

BoundaryNo actual preservation, waiting, or intervention is authorized; if H only defers the task without meeting its target, a different task must be constructed.

Mathematical teaching construction: another possible state shrinks the intersectionTeaching scenario

AssumptionsxC and its action set form another artificial extension scenario.

Continue the second scenario. If new material shows that state xC is also compatible and A_ok(xC)={right}, intersecting the original {H} with {right} makes the intersection empty. The original conclusion covered only the two originally listed states and cannot remain a guarantee for three states.

BoundaryThis does not claim that reality always contains omitted states; it only shows that guarantees change with the declared domain.

What counterexamples change

Sourced counterexampleCounterexample in the original text: {left} and {right} are each nonempty but have an empty intersection; separate solutions do not guarantee the right choice can be made now.

What it limitsStatewise existence is not common existence.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari, On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation

Sourced counterexampleBoundary in the original text: a common, already-qualified preservation action may exist without complete state identification, but the theorem cannot fabricate its qualification premises.

What it limitsComplete information is not a prerequisite for all bounded action.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari, On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation

Teaching counterexampleTeaching counterexample: if waiting misses a mandatory deadline in one state, it is absent from that state’s qualified set; ‘waiting is safest’ cannot insert it into the intersection.

What it limitsWaiting’s qualification requires a separate check.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari, On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation

Sourced counterexampleBoundary in the original text: unknown states, risk tolerance, randomization, and sequential strategies are not all handled by the current single-round theorem.

What it limitsA single-round guarantee cannot be generalized.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari, On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation

What does not follow

  • Counterexample in the original text: {left} and {right} are each nonempty but have an empty intersection; separate solutions do not guarantee the right choice can be made now.
  • Boundary in the original text: a common, already-qualified preservation action may exist without complete state identification, but the theorem cannot fabricate its qualification premises.
  • Teaching counterexample: if waiting misses a mandatory deadline in one state, it is absent from that state’s qualified set; ‘waiting is safest’ cannot insert it into the intersection.
  • Boundary in the original text: unknown states, risk tolerance, randomization, and sequential strategies are not all handled by the current single-round theorem.

Scope and open questions

This unit presents conditional propositions within explicitly specified mathematical objects, using complete public proofs and mathematical constructions. Real cases cannot certify premises in their place, so historical events are not forcibly matched to them, and no existing test of a real case is claimed.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    If every possible state has a qualified action, does that make action possible now?

  2. 2

    When can there still be a deterministic qualified action without knowing the true state?

  3. 3

    Can ‘wait’ always be placed in every qualified set?

  4. 4

    Does an empty intersection rule out all randomized strategies?

If every possible state has a qualified action, does that make action possible now?

Not necessarily; the sets’ common intersection may be empty.

Basis: Necessary and sufficient condition.

When can there still be a deterministic qualified action without knowing the true state?

When an action belongs to the qualified-action sets of all compatible states.

Basis: Proof of sufficiency.

Can ‘wait’ always be placed in every qualified set?

No. Waiting itself must satisfy targets, deadlines, resources, protections, and authority.

Basis: Appendix C.12 and the teaching boundary.

Does an empty intersection rule out all randomized strategies?

No. It only rules out the currently bounded single-round deterministic action qualified in every state; other targets need separate analysis.

Basis: Chinese source line 1056.

Proof of common action and the compatible-state boundary (Appendix C.12)Why formal feasibility still requires real-world grounds (§2.1.2)

4.18.4Task Preservation through Successive Conversions (F4) ​

In briefSuccessive transformations must address the same final question. The first step may preserve distinctions needed for the answer while the second merges them; each step ‘completing its task’ does not guarantee a correct final answer.

Let f:X→Z and h:Z→W, with the first stage satisfying q=g∘f. The composition h∘f can still recover the same final target q if and only if g is constant on every fiber of h restricted to the actual image f(X). The individual steps complete different local tasks; this cannot replace the condition at the shared endpoint. Preservation under a functional representation, causal effects connected in sequence, and joint implementation using shared resources need to be checked separately; a single mark reading “connected” cannot substitute for these different checks. See Appendix C.7 and C.12 for the proof and counterexamples.

4.18.4Note

Understanding this section

4.18.4 Task Preservation through Successive Conversions (F4)

Successive transformations must address the same final question. The first step may preserve distinctions needed for the answer while the second merges them; each step ‘completing its task’ does not guarantee a correct final answer.

Let f:X→Z and h:Z→W, with the first stage already satisfying q=g∘f. The final target remains the same q throughout. Whether the second stage is usable depends on whether intermediate states merged by h into the same w all share the same g value within the actually reachable intermediate set f(X), not whether each step independently accomplishes some local task. [T-F4；T-F4A]

Necessity: suppose a final decoder k satisfies q=k∘h∘f. Take any z,z′∈f(X) with h(z)=h(z′), and source states x,x′ with f(x)=z and f(x′)=z′. Then g(z)=q(x)=k(h(z))=k(h(z′))=q(x′)=g(z′). Thus g is constant on each fiber of h restricted to f(X). [T-F4A]

Sufficiency: if that constancy condition holds, define k(w), for every actual final representation w∈h(f(X)), as the fiber's common g value. This is unambiguous, so k(h(f(x)))=g(f(x))=q(x). The decoder need only be defined on the actual image. If a larger W is used, it may be extended arbitrarily at unused points into a nonempty target domain. Unreachable intermediate values must neither be mistaken for obstacles nor quietly added to the original state domain to change the question. [T-F4A]

In the original binary-position counterexample, the first step retains (x1,x2), the second retains only the sum, and the final question still concerns x1. Storage and counting each succeed, but their composition merges (0,1) with (1,0). Keeping the first bit's Boolean value repairs this task without restoring every detail. Changing the final target to the sum is a different successful task, not repair of the original question. [T-F4A]

Representational sufficiency must also be distinguished from correct execution of the actual rule. In the appendix's three-state example, f=(0,0,1), q=(0,1,1), and the actual rule outputs 0 for both representations 0 and 1. The first two states share a representation but require different answers, establishing insufficient information. The third state's representation 1 already determines the correct answer 1, yet the rule outputs 0, separately demonstrating an incorrect execution rule. Correcting the output at representation 1 to 1 repairs only the third state, not the conflict between the first two. The first state's correct result is not canceled by failures elsewhere. [T-F4A]

This is a proposition about preservation by functions, not proof that a causal chain or resource schedule connects. Causal chains require joint responses within the same case; average edge effects cannot simply be multiplied. With shared resources, separate feasibility does not imply joint feasibility. Even if a function can recover the answer, access before action, use of the correct implementation version, resources, and authority each require material. Unknown internal representations or contemporaneous rules do not justify forced unique attribution. [T-composition；T-formal；T-F4A]

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Fix the same final q and first check q=g∘f.

  2. 2

    Necessity: a final decoder gives the same answer for the same h value, implying constant g on actual intermediate fibers.

  3. 3

    Sufficiency: define k by each actual final fiber's common g value to obtain q=k∘h∘f.

  4. 4

    Constrain only reachable f(X); do not mix unreachable states into the condition.

  5. 5

    Separately check insufficient representation, incorrect actual rules, material timing, and causal/resource/authority responsibilities.

Distinctions to keep clear

Local task success

Each step completes its own assigned small objective.

≠

Preservation of a common final target

The composition can still recover the original q.

Actual image f(X)

Intermediate values genuinely producible by the original states.

≠

Entire intermediate space Z

May contain unreachable values and cannot indiscriminately be used to reject composition.

Insufficient representation

The same representation requires different answers.

≠

Incorrect rule

Sufficient distinctions exist, but the correct output rule is not used.

Functional connection

The same task answer can be recovered.

≠

Causal or resource connection

Has separate joint-response and implementation constraints.

Expanded mathematical counterexample from the original: local counting cannot replace the final position targetTeaching scenario

AssumptionsExactly four states, deterministic functions, and a final target fixed to the first bit.

X={0,1}², f preserves the state identically, g(x1,x2)=x1, and h(x1,x2)=x1+x2. Certainly q=g∘f holds. But z=(0,1) and z′=(1,0) both map under h to 1 while their g values are 0 and 1, violating this proposition's condition. If the second stage additionally stores x1, the final task becomes recoverable. Asking for the count instead changes the target rather than repairing the original query.

BoundaryA mathematical construction that does not erase counting's success at its own task.

Mathematical teaching construction: check only the actual imageTeaching scenario

Assumptionsw is explicitly unreachable from X, the target domain is nonempty, and all mappings are artificial assumptions.

Let X={a,b}, f(a)=u, f(b)=v, and let the intermediate space also contain unreachable w. Set g(u)=g(v)=7 and g(w)=99, while h maps u,v,w all to 0. The actual final target is 7 for both a and b, so k(0)=7 recovers it. Although g is not constant on the h fiber throughout Z, it is constant on actual f(X)={u,v}, satisfying the real condition.

BoundaryIf X is later expanded so that w becomes reachable, recheck the condition rather than ignoring it permanently.

Mathematical construction from the original: witnesses to two different failuresTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe original finite three-state model has known input representations and actual rules. It does not satisfy this proposition's initial exact-recovery premise; it separately illustrates diagnostic distinctions between representation and execution.

For states a,b,c, f is respectively 0,0,1 and q is 0,1,1. The actual rule g_actual(0)=g_actual(1)=0 produces outputs 0,0,0. a and b witness insufficient representation; c witnesses an incorrect rule despite sufficient information. Changing the rule to g_actual(0)=0 and g_actual(1)=1 yields 0,0,1, repairing c while b remains wrong and a remains correct throughout.

BoundaryIf internal representation or contemporaneous inputs are unknown in reality, retain the gap rather than mechanically applying failure labels.

Scope and open questions

This unit presents conditional propositions within explicitly specified mathematical objects, using complete public proofs and mathematical constructions. Real cases cannot certify premises in their place, so historical events are not forcibly matched to them, and no existing test of a real case is claimed.

Check your understanding

    If step one stores and step two counts correctly, what happens when the final question asks about the first bit?

  2. 2

If step one stores and step two counts correctly, what happens when the final question asks about the first bit?

It may fail: sum 1 merges states whose first bits are 0 and 1.

Basis: The public counterexample.

Why does the proposition “Task Preservation through Successive Conversions” not require g to be constant over the relevant fibers throughout Z?

Only actual f(X) is used; unreachable values do not affect recovery of the original task.

Basis: The necessity-and-sufficiency proof.

After correcting the rule at representation 1 in the three-state example, is everything recovered?

No. c is repaired and a remains correct, but b's conflict with a at shared representation 0 remains.

Basis: The three-state item-by-item results.

Does answer recovery through function composition establish sufficient resources for execution?

No. Functions, causality, and joint resource feasibility require separate checks.

Basis: Appendix C.12.

4.18.5Error Propagation under Approximate Closure (F5) ​

In briefIf every step is only slightly off, how large can the difference become over many steps? The answer depends on one-step discrepancy, whether the macro update amplifies or contracts existing error, and how long those conditions remain valid.

Let the target space have a metric d. Assume that the projection error is no greater than ε at every state reached at each step, and that the Lipschitz constant of the proposed macro-level update on the relevant region is no greater than L. Starting from the same initial representation, the error after t steps satisfies e_t≤ε∑_{j=0}^{t−1}L^j. This bound requires the error condition and the region condition to continue to hold at every step; mean fitting error cannot directly replace a state-by-state bound. When L<1, there is an upper bound ε/(1−L); when L=1, it is tε; when L>1, the upper bound may increase rapidly. See Appendix C.8 for the proof.

4.18.5Note

Understanding this section

4.18.5 Error propagation under approximate closure (F5)

If every step is only slightly off, how large can the difference become over many steps? The answer depends on one-step discrepancy, whether the macro update amplifies or contracts existing error, and how long those conditions remain valid.

Given a metric d, the actual model state advances by x_(t+1)=F(x_t), while the macro approximation advances by y_(t+1)=F̄(y_t). Assume every reached x at every step satisfies d(π(F(x)),F̄(π(x)))≤ε, and in the comparison region d(F̄(y),F̄(y′))≤L d(y,y′), with ε≥0 and L≥0. Initial states match: y0=π(x0), and e_t=d(π(x_t),y_t). This requires bounds state by state and step by step, not a training mean-squared error. [T-F5；T-F5A]

The triangle inequality splits next-step error into two terms: e_(t+1)=d(π(F(x_t)),F̄(y_t))≤d(π(F(x_t)),F̄(π(x_t)))+d(F̄(π(x_t)),F̄(y_t))≤ε+L e_t. The first term is this step's projected-model discrepancy; the second propagates existing representation error through the macro update. Both points and their relevant updates must remain inside the checked region. [T-F5A]

Recursing from e0=0 gives e1≤ε, e2≤ε+Lε, e3≤ε+Lε+L²ε. Inductively, if e_t≤εΣ_{j=0}^{t−1}L^j, substitution gives e_(t+1)≤ε+εΣ_{j=1}^{t}L^j=εΣ_{j=0}^{t}L^j. Thus the bound holds for every finite t over which the premises remain valid. For t=0, the empty sum gives bound 0. [T-F5A]

For 0≤L<1, the geometric sum is (1−L^t)/(1−L), so e_t≤ε/(1−L). For L=1, step discrepancies add to tε. For L>1, the bound is ε(L^t−1)/(L−1) and may grow rapidly. A growing bound does not mean actual error necessarily grows. If actual and macro updates agree exactly, for instance, actual error may remain 0 despite using a loose positive ε and large L as bounds. [T-F5A]

If initial error is nonzero, the same recursion adds L^t e0; the formula without that initial term no longer applies. If ε or L varies by step, recurse through e_(t+1)≤ε_t+L_t e_t instead of replacing fixed stepwise bounds with averages. Initial perturbations, measurement error, or external noise not included in the premises cannot be claimed covered by the original formula. [T-F5A；derivational extension]

Small average fitting error does not ensure small error at every step. Large discrepancies at rare states, or trajectories leaving the training region, may invalidate the original ε/L premises. Short-term bounds cannot be extrapolated indefinitely without conditions. A numerical formula also does not establish that actual-system measurements, operation sets, and applicability ranges were checked. This proposition supplies a conditional error budget, not evidential eligibility for a real-world scale-closure test. [T-F5；T-G4]

Terms used here

ε: upper bound on each step's projection error§C.8
Every reached x satisfies d(π(F(x)),F̄(π(x)))≤ε. Average fitting error cannot directly replace a statewise bound.
L: upper bound on the Lipschitz constant in the reached region§C.8
The macro update F̄ satisfies d(F̄(y),F̄(y′))≤L d(y,y′) within the reached region.
e_t: error at step t§C.8
Starting from the same initial representation y_0=π(x_0), e_t=d(π(x_t),y_t), with recursion e_{t+1}≤ε+Le_t.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Define actual and approximate trajectories, metric, and common initial state; specify statewise ε bounds and the L bound over the relevant region.

  2. 2

    Use the triangle inequality to separate current-step model discrepancy from propagation of existing error.

  3. 3

    Obtain e_(t+1)≤ε+Le_t.

  4. 4

    Induct from e0=0 to the geometric-sum bound, simplifying separately for L<1, L=1, and L>1.

  5. 5

    When initial error or time-varying parameters occur, retain the corresponding terms and recursion instead of mechanically applying the fixed formula.

  6. 6

    Check that each step remains within the region and original operation set. Average fit and real-world mapping carry separate evidential responsibilities.

Distinctions to keep clear

One-step statewise bound

Every reached state stays within ε.

≠

Average fitting error

A small average may still include states with large discrepancies.

Error upper bound

A guarantee not to be exceeded while the premises hold.

≠

Actual error

May be far smaller than the bound and need not grow with it.

L<1

A bounding condition under which existing error contracts.

≠

L>1

Allows amplification; the bound may grow rapidly.

Same initial state

e0=0。

≠

Different initial states

Also include L^t e0.

Mathematical teaching construction: a family of models attaining the error boundTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe entire real domain, exact equations, constant parameters, common zero initial state, and no additional noise or operation changes.

Use the real domain, identity π, absolute distance, F(x)=Lx+0.1, F̄(y)=Ly, x0=y0=0, and L≥0. The one-step discrepancy is always 0.1, and F̄ has Lipschitz constant L. y_t remains 0 and x_t=0.1Σ_{j=0}^{t−1}L^j, so actual error exactly attains the bound. For t=0 through 4: L=.5 gives 0,.1,.15,.175,.1875; L=1 gives 0,.1,.2,.3,.4; L=2 gives 0,.1,.3,.7,1.5.

BoundaryEntirely mathematical constructions. Attaining the bound shows it can be tight, not that every system attains it or grows in the same way.

Mathematical teaching construction: average error cannot guarantee the worst stepTeaching scenario

AssumptionsOnly a specified finite error table; no actual visitation probabilities or data-generation process are given.

Suppose an artificial table has 100 errors: 99 are 0 and one is 10. Mean absolute error is 10/100=0.1, while the maximum is 10. If the next step reaches the large-error state, substituting 0.1 for a uniform ε violates this proposition's premise. Accuracy on the other 99 items cannot compensate for this failure.

BoundaryDoes not estimate actual frequency or imply that average metrics are worthless. They answer a different loss question.

What does not follow

  • Mathematical counterexample: of 100 teaching errors, 99 are 0 and one is 10. Mean absolute error is 0.1 but the maximum is 10; the average cannot justify statewise ε=0.1.

Scope and open questions

This unit presents conditional propositions within explicitly specified mathematical objects, using complete public proofs and mathematical constructions. Real cases cannot certify premises in their place, so historical events are not forcibly matched to them, and no existing test of a real case is claimed.

With L=1, ε=.1, and a common initial state, what is the four-step bound?

0.4, the sum of four one-step bounds.

Basis: Geometric sum tε.

With L=.5 and ε=.1, what is the uniform bound?

0.1/(1−.5)=0.2; the tighter four-step bound is .1875.

Basis: Geometric sum and upper bound.

If the bound increases for L=2, must actual error increase?

Not necessarily. A bound is only a guarantee; model discrepancies may be zero or cancel.

Basis: Distinction between bound and actual quantity.

How must the formula change for initial error e0>0?

The recursion gives L^t e0+εΣL^j; the initial term cannot be omitted.

Basis: The same triangle recursion.

Can mean error .1 directly be recorded as ε=.1?

No. Statewise, stepwise bounds are required; the counterexample's maximum error is 10.

Basis: Premises of “Error Propagation under Approximate Closure” (§4.18.5).

4.19Task Families and Dynamic Refinement ​

In briefFiner state distinctions are not inherently better. Preserve distinctions the specified tasks and permitted actions actually discriminate. A complete finite model permits proof of the coarsest necessary partition; changed horizons, added actions, or allowed error require renewed checking.
Codes used in this section (1)
  • F1Task Recovery

Which distinctions a structural representation should retain depends on the tasks at issue and the operations allowed to act on the object. A finer representation can preserve more differences and also increases measurement, storage, explanation, and maintenance costs; not every detail is a necessary input to every task. In a fully specified finite deterministic model, it is possible to state precisely which states can be merged and compute the coarsest partition satisfying particular requirements.

Let X be a nonempty finite state set, Q a finite set of target functions q:X→V_q, and U a finite set of admissible actions. Each u∈U corresponds to a total deterministic update F_u:X→X; the actions are implementable in every state, and no external disturbance that has not been stated is introduced here. The empty action string denotes no update. For an action string w=u₁…u_k, write F_w=F_{u_k}∘…∘F_{u₁}. These conditions delimit the objects of the proposition below; they cannot be assumed satisfied merely because real-world operations share a name with it.

Proposition F6 The Coarsest Sufficient Partition for a Task Family. For a nonnegative integer H, define x∼_H x′ if and only if, for every q∈Q and every admissible action string w of length no greater than H, q(F_w(x))=q(F_w(x′)). This is an equivalence relation. The representation formed by its equivalence classes retains precisely the task answers within the given horizon. Any deterministic representation that answers these questions exactly may merge only states within the same equivalence class.

Proof: Reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity follow from the corresponding properties of equality of function values. The answer for every target and action string is constant within an equivalence class, so by proposition F1 it is uniquely determined by that class. If another representation merges two nonequivalent states, then by definition there must be a target and an admissible action string giving different answers; by proposition F1, that representation cannot recover both answers exactly. Thus, the partition induced by any sufficient representation is finer than or equal to this partition. This coarseness concerns a state partition relative to X, Q, U, and H; it does not establish the fewest parameters, the cheapest measurement, or the irreplaceability of a particular natural-language concept.

Sufficiency for a fixed finite horizon does not automatically produce dynamic closure for that same horizon. Take X={a,b,c,d}, with the sole target q(a)=q(b)=q(c)=0 and q(d)=1, and the sole action satisfying F(a)=c, F(b)=b, F(c)=d, and F(d)=d. States a and b both give 0 now and after one step, so a∼₁b. Their successors c and b, however, give different answers after one further step, so c and b do not belong to the same ∼₁ class. For H≥1, what is always guaranteed is that x∼_H x′ implies F_u(x)∼_{H−1}F_u(x′). When advancing, the remaining horizon should be reduced accordingly, or closure of the fixed partition under admissible actions must be required separately.

To preserve every target under admissible action strings of any finite length, define x∼_*x′ to hold when the answers agree for all such finite strings. This partition is closed under each F_u: prepending u to any subsequent string gives a string already compared in the definition. Conversely, any representation that recovers all targets in Q and is closed under all F_u can be advanced step by step and used to recover the targets after any finite string, so the partition it induces must be finer than or equal to ∼_*. Thus ∼_* is the unique coarsest state partition satisfying these conditions; uniqueness is determined by the equivalence classes, irrespective of their labels.

On a finite domain, this partition can be computed directly. Begin by grouping states by their values on all current targets to form P₀. Each round uses only the preceding partition P_h and splits its blocks synchronously by the signature ([x]_{P_h},([F_u(x)]_{P_h})_{u∈U}) to obtain P_{h+1}. Here [x]_{P_h} denotes the block containing x in the preceding partition. Each strict refinement adds at least one block, so at most |X|−1 strict refinements can occur. Once no block splits further, the blocks preserve the current targets and satisfy closure under each action. Level H of synchronous iteration corresponds exactly to target comparisons for strings of length at most H, so the stable partition equals ∼_*. With asynchronous refinement one block at a time, final stability can still be checked. Its operation count must not be used as the horizon H here. This procedure is computable on a complete finite table. It does not guarantee identification of true states from incomplete observations, much less tractability for large models within a given budget.

This result gives a conditional rule for simplification. Merge states that cannot be distinguished by the given targets and admissible operations. Retain a distinction only when a task or an operation actually distinguishes the states. Adding targets or admissible actions leaves the required partition unchanged or refines it. Shortening the horizon, narrowing the use, or restricting the operations can make a simpler representation sufficient. Adjusting the task can yield a legitimate new question, but the adjustment does not warrant declaring the original task complete.

Error tolerances require separate analysis. The condition “the two answers differ by no more than ε” is generally not transitive. The values 0 and ε are close, and ε and 2ε are close, but 0 and 2ε may differ by more than the tolerance. Approximate similarity therefore cannot directly replace the equivalence relation above or automatically yield a unique coarsest partition. One may use a bound on block diameter, worst-case recovery error, or a specified probabilistic loss. The optimal solution, stability, and computational cost for each require separate proof.

This section states a proposition about sets and dynamics in a finite model. Distinguishing states by input strings, forming equivalence classes, and refining them recursively have a direct mathematical connection to Moore’s work on sequential machines. The preservation of states and actions also connects to abstraction in controlled dynamics. The finite model stated in this section and its proof establish the conclusion without relying on additional optimality results for other classes of machines. 〔Moore, 1956, pp. 143 and 145–146; Ravindran and Barto, 2003〕 This section neither declares that nature has a single correct hierarchy nor reduces people’s legitimate claims to the current predictive targets. Which targets must be preserved, which actions may be implemented, and what error is acceptable still have to be determined separately on the basis of domain facts, normative reasons, and real-world permissions. When these givens are challenged, they are handled under §2.14.

4.19Note

Understanding this section

4.19 Task families and dynamic refinement

Finer state distinctions are not inherently better. Preserve distinctions the specified tasks and permitted actions actually discriminate. A complete finite model permits proof of the coarsest necessary partition; changed horizons, added actions, or allowed error require renewed checking.

Chinese source line 1068 first returns simplification to its use: finer representations may retain more distinctions while increasing measurement, storage, explanation, and maintenance costs. This section's proposition seeks the coarsest sufficient partition relative to given states, tasks, actions, and horizon, not nature's uniquely correct level or automatically the cheapest or lowest-parameter model. [T-419]

The premises must be complete: X is nonempty and finite; Q is a finite set of target functions, each q:X→V_q; U is a finite permitted-action set, each u corresponding to a total deterministic update F_u:X→X. Every action is feasible in every state, with no unstated external disturbance. Action string w=u1…uk applies u1 first, then u2, through uk, so F_w=F_uk∘…∘F_u1. The empty string makes no update and ensures current tasks are also compared. An identically named real operation does not automatically meet these conditions. [T-419]

For H≥0, define x∼_H x′ when every q∈Q and every permitted action string w of length ≤H satisfy q(F_w(x))=q(F_w(x′)). This compares an entire family of answers to “ask the task after operations.” H=0 compares only current Q. If Q is empty, the condition is an empty conjunction, so all states may form one class. That merely reflects that no tasks have been stated, not satisfaction of all actual needs. [T-419；direct inference from the definition]

The equivalence-relation proof follows item by item from equality: each answer equals itself, giving reflexivity; exchanging x and x′ preserves equality, giving symmetry; if x and x′, and x′ and x″, give equal answers for every (q,w), so do x and x″, giving transitivity. Represent by equivalence classes [x]_H. Each q∘F_w is constant within a class, so the proposition “Task Recovery” (§4.18.1) supplies the corresponding decoder. Any other deterministic representation merging two nonequivalent states has a witnessing (q,w) with different answers, violating the proposition “Task Recovery”; its partition can therefore only be finer or equal. This proves coarsest sufficiency. [T-419；T-F1]

“Coarsest” refers to refinement order among state partitions, not label names or code lengths. Representations merely renaming the same blocks count as the same partition. The minimum necessary state distinctions do not imply fewest parameters, cheapest measurement, simplest explanation, or irreplaceability of a natural-language concept. Costs require separate modeling and evaluation. [T-419；T-eval]

Finite-horizon sufficiency does not automatically give dynamic closure at that same horizon. In the original four-state example, q(a)=q(b)=q(c)=0, q(d)=1, F(a)=c, F(b)=b, F(c)=d, F(d)=d. a and b both give 0 now and after one step, so a∼1b; but their successors c and b give 1 and 0 after another step, so c is not ∼1-equivalent to b. Generally, for H≥1, x∼_H x′⇒F_u(x)∼_(H−1)F_u(x′): prefixing any successor string v of length ≤H−1 with u gives uv of length ≤H, so the original relation guarantees equal answers. Advancing consumes remaining horizon, unless closure of the fixed partition is separately checked. [T-419]

If all targets must remain recoverable after any finite action string, define ∼_*. Its classes are closed under every F_u: prefixing any successor string v with u still gives a finite string, so successors remain equivalent; the empty string ensures current Q is recoverable too. Conversely, a representation recovering Q and closed under every F_u can advance through any finite string and then recover q, so it cannot merge states nonequivalent under ∼_*. Therefore ∼_* is the unique coarsest partition satisfying Q recovery and closure under every action, with uniqueness by equivalence classes rather than names. [T-419；T-F2]

The algorithm initially partitions by the current target vector (q(x))_{q∈Q}, producing P0. At round h, retain the whole previous P_h and synchronously repartition using only sig_h(x)=([x]_{P_h},([F_u(x)]_{P_h})_{u∈U}), producing P_(h+1). Including the old block in the signature ensures splitting without merging. Read every successor block from the old partition; do not update one block and pass its new numbering off as old-layer information. [T-419]

Induction shows synchronous layer h equals ∼_h. P0 corresponds to empty-string targets. If P_h corresponds to answers for lengths ≤h, equal signatures mean the states retain their common old block and successors under every first action u give equal answers for all later strings of length ≤h, hence all strings of length ≤h+1 give equal answers. Conversely, agreement on all strings of length ≤h+1 includes old-layer questions and every u followed by a length-≤h string, so signatures match. Thus algorithmic layer count genuinely represents a horizon; the number of asynchronous blockwise operations has no such meaning. [T-419]

Let n=|X| and let P0 contain k0 nonempty blocks. Each strict refinement adds at least one block, up to at most n blocks, so the number of strict refinements is ≤n−k0≤n−1. When a complete round produces no split, current targets remain preserved and successor blocks for each action agree within each block, so closure holds. This stable partition recovers all finite strings by closure; moreover, no finite level separates ∼_* equivalent states, so it equals ∼_*. The round confirming stability may contain no strict split. This bound is not a guarantee of total computational steps, runtime, or budget. [T-419]

Adding targets, permitted actions, or a longer horizon adds same-answer conditions to satisfy simultaneously, so the partition can only remain unchanged or become finer. Restricting actions, shortening the horizon, or narrowing uses may make a coarser representation sufficient. Resetting the task may legitimately answer a different question, but success on that new task cannot establish completion of the original one. Whether actions are lawfully permitted and which targets cannot be omitted remain matters of domain requirements, norms, and permissions. [T-419; T-C12]

Closeness within a tolerance is not a ready-made equivalence relation. Take ε>0: 0 and ε are at distance ≤ε, as are ε and 2ε, but 0 and 2ε have distance 2ε>ε, so transitivity fails. Even requiring each block's diameter to be ≤ε may admit multiple valid coarse partitions that do not refine one another; unique coarseness cannot automatically be inherited. Optimal solutions, stability, and costs for worst-case recovery error, probabilistic loss, or dynamic approximation each require their own proofs. “Approximately equal” cannot simply replace the equality in this section's proposition. [T-419; T-F1; T-F5]

Chinese source line 1086 connects this section to Moore's input-string discrimination and recursive refinement, and to literature on controlled dynamical abstraction. This mathematical connection has specific objects and scope: Moore's cited minimal-machine discussion has its own machine-class conditions; Ravindran and Barto's SMDP model includes stochastic transitions, rewards, and state-dependent action recoding, unlike the finite deterministic model here with fixed U and actions feasible at every state. This section's conclusions rest on its own proof; it borrows no additional optimality or complexity results from other models. [P-Moore; P-RB; T-419]

Stopping points remain important in application. Computability from a complete finite table does not mean incomplete observations identify actual states, nor that a large table can be processed within the available time. If reality involves state-dependent action feasibility, unknown disturbances, continuous quantities, or measurement error, the model must be changed and its new premises tested. Mathematical indistinguishability also cannot reduce people's justified claims to existing prediction targets. Responsibility for selecting Q, U, and tolerances must remain public rather than being automatically decided by the refinement algorithm. [T-419; T-formal; T-C12]

The task family Q, permitted operations U, and horizon H determine what this formal proposition answers; the algorithm cannot decide on participants' behalf whether these conditions are appropriate. Through §2.14, v2 adds a reopening route: if Q omits a legitimate claim, record the challenge, retain the original refinement result, and reanalyze the new task. Formal sufficiency for the old task and insufficiency for the new one may both hold.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Fix in advance finite X, Q, U, total functions F_u, common feasibility, and the absence of additional disturbances.

  2. 2

    Define the finite-horizon same-answer relation across all targets and action strings, proving reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity individually.

  3. 3

    Use the proposition “Task Recovery” to prove the sufficiency of equivalence classes; use differing answers as witnesses excluding every coarser sufficient representation.

  4. 4

    Distinguish the countdown guarantee for finite H from closure of a fixed partition; prove closure and unique coarseness for the relation over all finite strings.

  5. 5

    Form P0 from current targets; in each round, synchronously refine using signatures from the old P_h only.

  6. 6

    Prove by induction that P_h equals ∼_h; use the block-count bound to prove finitely many strict refinements and explain why the stable partition equals ∼_*.

  7. 7

    Check monotonic refinement under target/action/horizon expansion item by item; prove approximate relations separately rather than directly substituting them for equivalence.

  8. 8

    Use the literature only as mathematical references with explicit scope; separately check real-world mappings, costs, norms, and authorization.

Distinctions to keep clear

Finite-horizon sufficiency

Answers all stated questions of length ≤H.

≠

Fixed dynamic closure

The same partition remains independently updatable after operations.

Coarsest state partition

It is itself sufficient, and every sufficient partition under the same conditions is finer than or equal to it.

≠

Minimum real-world cost

Measurement, parameter, explanation, and computational costs have separate objectives.

Synchronous level h

Each round uses the old partition and corresponds exactly to horizon h.

≠

Number of asynchronous operations

Does not directly correspond to an action-string horizon.

Number of strict refinements

Each increases the block count, permitting an n−1 bound.

≠

Actual runtime

Every round requires table reading and comparison, with further effects from scale and algorithmic cost.

Exact equivalence

All specified answers are equal; transitivity holds.

≠

Closeness within tolerance

Generally is not transitive and does not automatically yield a unique coarsest partition.

Task adjustment

Creates another question with an explicit scope.

≠

Original task completed

Cannot be retroactively established by success on a narrowed task.

Original mathematical construction expanded: finite horizons and synchronous refinementTeaching scenario

AssumptionsOne action, a complete deterministic four-state table, operations feasible at every state, and an exactly specified target.

Order the four states a,b,c,d, with q=(0,0,0,1) and F=(c,b,d,d). Current values give P0={a,b,c}|{d}. One-step answer pairs are a:(0,0), b:(0,0), c:(0,1), d:(1,1), so P1={a,b}|{c}|{d}. Two-step answer triples are a:(0,0,1), b:(0,0,0), c:(0,1,1), d:(1,1,1), so P2 has four singleton blocks. P3 remains the same as P2, confirming stability. There are two strict splits, exactly n−k0=4−2=2, plus another round to confirm stability.

BoundaryAn exact enumeration of the original model, not a measurement of a real system. Two splits do not mean an actual program requires only two operations.

Mathematical teaching construction: stability need not mean singleton blocksTeaching scenario

AssumptionsAnother complete four-state, single-action model, whose task contains only this binary q.

Alternatively, set q(a)=q(b)=0, q(c)=q(d)=1, F(a)=c, F(b)=d, F(c)=a, and F(d)=b. P0={a,b}|{c,d}. Every state in the same block enters the other block, so the first round produces no split and the partition is already stable. The two blocks' outputs alternate at every subsequent step, and states within a block always give the same answers. Since the two blocks have different current outputs, they cannot merge, so the coarsest partition has two blocks.

BoundaryRecovering a/b or c/d identities is not required; adding a target that distinguishes them requires renewed refinement.

Mathematical teaching construction: tolerance rules do not automatically ensure uniquenessTeaching scenario

AssumptionsA finite three-value static task; the diameter constraint is a separate approximate objective defined for this example, not the exact equivalence of this section's proposition.

Let static target values be 0, 1, 2, with tolerance 1 and each block required to have diameter ≤1. P={{0,1},{2}} is valid, as is R={{0},{1,2}}, and neither refines the other. Any partition coarser than both must put 0 and 1 together because of P, and 1 and 2 together because of R. Transitivity forces all three into one block, whose diameter 2 is invalid. Thus no unique coarsest valid partition exists.

BoundaryThis does not deny that valid approximation methods can be developed for other losses; it only rejects automatic inheritance of unique coarseness.

Moore's 1956 original text: the mathematical history of equivalence classes and recursive discriminationDocumented case

On printed page 143, Moore's original text constructs a reduced machine from equivalence classes of indistinguishable states; pages 145–146 recursively refine states by finite experiment length. Page 129 already explains that this is not a report of actual physical experimental results. It supports the mathematical connection stated in this section, but its minimal-machine theorem has its own conditions and cannot directly endorse this section's entire scope.

SourceEdward F. Moore，Gedanken-Experiments on Sequential MachinesAutomata Studies, 1956; printed pp. 129, 143, 145–146; PDF including cover, pp. 2, 16, 18–19.Reading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsFacts about the content of original mathematical literature are used here, not described as real machine experiments. This text's proposition “The Coarsest Sufficient Partition for a Task Family” rests on this text's conditions and proof; no additional optimality conclusions for Moore's class of strongly connected machines are borrowed.

Read the case and sources

SMDP homomorphisms in 2003: related but different abstraction conditionsDocumented case

In §3, Ravindran and Barto define SMDP homomorphisms with state mappings, state-dependent action recoding, and preservation conditions for transition probabilities and rewards. Their introduction also notes that reducing state counts need not reduce descriptive parameters. This provides a specialist reference for state/action abstraction; its stochastic and action-recoding model cannot simply be renamed this section's deterministic proposition with fixed actions, “The Coarsest Sufficient Partition for a Task Family”.

SourceRavindran and Barto, SMDP HomomorphismsIJCAI 2003, printed pp. 1011–1013/PDF 1–3; especially the §3 definition and explanation below it, printed 1012/PDF 2.Reading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsA mathematical reference, not evidence of this framework's real-world effectiveness. Its policy optimality, minimal state-action pair, and complexity conclusions are not transplanted.

What does not follow

  • Original-text boundary: coarseness is relative only to X/Q/U/H; it does not establish the fewest parameters, minimum cost, or a unique natural hierarchy.
  • Original-text boundary: asynchronous operation counts cannot be treated as synchronous horizon H; n−1 bounds only strict refinements.
  • Original mathematical counterexample: for ε>0, 0≈ε and ε≈2ε, but 0 is not ≈2ε; tolerance-based similarity is not transitive.
  • Mathematical teaching counterexample: with values 0, 1, 2 and block diameter ≤1, both {0,1}|{2} and {0}|{1,2} are allowed. Neither refines the other, and no valid partition is coarser than both.
  • Original-text boundary: actions sharing only a name, actions feasible in only some states, additional disturbances not stated, or an incomplete model table do not satisfy the premises of this section's proposition.

Scope and open questions

The real or historical material in this unit serves to locate the mathematical literature explicitly mentioned by the original text. It supports only authorship, dates, and original-paper content, not a test of this section's proposition as a real-world mechanism.

  • This lesson's constructions do not establish complete state tables, action feasibility, or error conditions for actual objects. If material is incomplete, mappings and identification remain unchecked.
  • Optimality, uniqueness, dynamic error, and budgets for approximate abstractions require proofs under separately specified objectives. This lesson provides only counterexamples, not a purported solution to the general approximation problem.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    Why must the proposition “The Coarsest Sufficient Partition for a Task Family” include the empty action string?

  2. 2

    In the original four-state example, why can a and b merge at H=1 but not continue under the same H after progression?

  3. 3

    What are synchronous P1 and P2 respectively?

  4. 4

    Does n−1 guarantee that the program executes at most n−1 operations?

  5. 5

    Can adding targets or permitted actions make the coarsest sufficient partition coarser?

  6. 6

    With tolerance 1, if 0 is close to 1 and 1 to 2, may all three directly be treated as one class?

  7. 7

    Does coarsest sufficiency prove it justified to merge all people into predictive equivalence classes?

Why must the proposition “The Coarsest Sufficient Partition for a Task Family” include the empty action string?

It ensures that current targets must also agree; comparing only futures could omit answers that need to be distinguished now.

Basis: Chinese source lines 1070–1072.

In the original four-state example, why can a and b merge at H=1 but not continue under the same H after progression?

Their current and one-step values are both 0; their successors c and b reach q=1 and 0 respectively one further step later. Only H−1 remains of the original guarantee.

Basis: Chinese source line 1076 and the enumeration.

What are synchronous P1 and P2 respectively?

P1={a,b}|{c}|{d}; P2 consists of four singleton blocks.

Basis: Target sequences and signatures from the old partition.

Does n−1 guarantee that the program executes at most n−1 operations?

No. It bounds only refinements that strictly increase block counts; reading tables, comparing entries, and confirming stability incur additional costs.

Basis: Chinese source line 1080.

Can adding targets or permitted actions make the coarsest sufficient partition coarser?

No. Additional same-answer conditions can only preserve or refine it; removing targets or restricting actions may make it coarser.

Basis: The conjunction in the definition.

With tolerance 1, if 0 is close to 1 and 1 to 2, may all three directly be treated as one class?

No. 0 and 2 exceed the tolerance, so the approximate relation is not transitive; two valid coarse partitions may also be incomparable.

Basis: Chinese source line 1084 and the three-value construction.

Does coarsest sufficiency prove it justified to merge all people into predictive equivalence classes?

No. Whether people's justified claims and protective targets must be preserved, and whether actions are permitted, requires normative and permission-based grounds; the algorithm does not decide.

Basis: Chinese source line 1086.
